The murderer became a deliverer.
The fugitive became a leader.
The shepherd became a prophet.
The failure became a testimony.
Not because Moses was extraordinary.
Because God is.
Maybe your burning bush moment has not happened yet.
Maybe you are still in Midian.
Still waiting.
Still wondering.
Still questioning.
Still carrying memories you wish you could erase.
Do not mistake silence for abandonment.
Do not mistake delay for rejection.
Do not mistake wilderness for disqualification.
The God who called Moses still calls people today.
The God who restored Moses still restores people today.
The God who rewrites stories still rewrites stories today.
And perhaps the greatest miracle was never the bush.
Never the staff.
Never the plagues.
Never even the Red Sea.
Perhaps the greatest miracle was that God looked at a broken man and said:
“I am not finished with you.”
Maybe that is what your soul needed to hear today.
Not that your past is small.
Not that your mistakes never happened.
Not that consequences disappear.
But that grace is greater.
Christ is greater.
The Gospel is greater.
And Jesus still specializes in turning wildernesses into callings, failures into testimonies, and scandals into stories of redemption.
If you desire to glorify God through Gospel-centered outreach, your support becomes part of that mission.
The bush burned, but it was not consumed—just like the calling God placed on your life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Disease That Killed Saul’s Peace
paragraphs:
The Disease That Killed Saul’s Peace
He Had the Crown, the Army, the Applause, and the Power—So Why Couldn’t He Sleep?
There is a disease more dangerous than cancer.
More destructive than famine.
More lethal than war.
It does not begin in the body.
It begins in the heart.
It slowly poisons joy, destroys gratitude, corrupts relationships, twists perception, and turns blessings into burdens.
It convinced a king to hunt an innocent man.
It transformed a worshipper into a murderer.
It turned a chosen leader into a tragic warning.
The disease that killed Saul’s peace was envy.
And if we are honest, many of us have felt its symptoms.
Not when we were losing.
But when someone else was winning.
The story begins with a king who should have been celebrating.
Israel had just witnessed a miracle.
A young shepherd named David had defeated Goliath.
The giant was dead.
The nation was safe.
God had delivered His people.
This should have been a moment of worship.
A moment of gratitude.
A moment of unity.
Instead, it became the birthplace of Saul’s destruction.
Scripture tells us:
“And the women sang one to another as they played, and said, Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.”
— 1 Samuel 18:7
One song.
One comparison.
One moment.
That was all it took.
The Hebrew text reveals something deeply painful.
Saul became intensely displeased.
The phrase used is וַיִּחַר לְשָׁאוּל מְאֹד (vayyichar l'Shaul me'od), literally meaning Saul burned greatly with anger.
His heart caught fire.
Not because David had harmed him.
Not because David had betrayed him.
Not because David had stolen from him.
David's success simply exposed what was already growing inside Saul.
Envy is rarely born in a moment.
It is usually revealed in a moment.
Many people think envy is merely wanting what someone else has.
Biblically, it is much deeper.
The Greek word often associated with envy is φθόνος (phthonos).
It means resentment at another person's blessing.
Not merely admiration.
Not inspiration.
Resentment.
The inability to rejoice when God blesses someone else.
And this disease spread through Saul's soul like poison in water.
The next verse says:
“And Saul eyed David from that day and forward.”
— 1 Samuel 18:9
The Hebrew word translated “eyed” comes from עָוָה (avah), carrying the idea of watching with hostile intent.
David became an obsession.
Saul could no longer enjoy what God had given him because he was consumed with what God was doing for someone else.
That is the terrifying power of envy.
It steals your ability to enjoy your own blessings.
Saul was still king.
He still had wealth.
He still had authority.
He still had servants.
He still had soldiers.
He still sat on the throne.
Yet none of it felt enough.
Envy has a way of making abundance feel like poverty.
Perhaps you know what that feels like.
You open social media.
Someone else gets married.
Someone else buys a home.
Someone else receives recognition.
Someone else launches a ministry.
Someone else grows a business.
Someone else appears happier.
And suddenly blessings you prayed for years ago feel invisible.
You stop thanking God for what He has done because your eyes are fixed on what He has done for somebody else.
That is the same disease.
Different century.
Same poison.
The tragedy of Saul is not that David rose.
The tragedy is that Saul forgot who gave him the throne in the first place.
Samuel had once told him:
“When thou wast little in thine own sight, wast thou not made the head of the tribes of Israel?”
— 1 Samuel 15:17
Saul began well.
His downfall started when his identity shifted from God’s approval to human comparison.
Comparison is one of Satan’s oldest weapons.
In the Garden of Eden, the serpent suggested that Eve lacked something.
In heaven, Lucifer became dissatisfied with the position God had assigned him.
Envy always whispers the same lie:
“God has been better to them than He has been to you.”
Yet Scripture repeatedly reveals a different truth.
God's blessings are not limited resources.
Someone else's promotion is not your rejection.
Someone else's breakthrough is not your abandonment.
Someone else's calling is not your disqualification.
The Kingdom of God is not a competition.
It is a family.
But Saul could no longer see that.
His envy eventually evolved into paranoia.
Then rage.
Then violence.
Then spiritual darkness.
One of the most chilling passages says:
“But the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the LORD troubled him.”
— 1 Samuel 16:14
Notice the sequence.
The loss of peace came before the loss of the throne.
Long before Saul physically lost his kingdom, he had already lost his rest.
And that is exactly what envy does.
It first steals peace.
Then perspective.
Then wisdom.
Then relationships.
Then joy.
Eventually, it steals the person you once were.
Saul spent years chasing David through caves, mountains, deserts, and wilderness regions.
Think about the insanity of it.
David was not chasing Saul.
Saul was chasing David.
The envied person often spends less time thinking about you than you spend thinking about them.
Envy traps people in prisons they build themselves.
Meanwhile David continued trusting God.
The shepherd understood something Saul never fully grasped.
God's promises do not require human manipulation.
If God opens a door, no man can close it.
If God closes a door, no man can force it open.
David refused to kill Saul even when opportunities presented themselves.
Why?
Because David trusted God's timing more than his own ambition.
The disease that destroyed Saul could not infect David because David's confidence rested in God's sovereignty.
This brings us to one of the most beautiful truths in the Gospel.
Every one of us has traces of Saul within us.
Every one of us has compared.
Every one of us has struggled with jealousy.
Every one of us has questioned God's timing.
Every one of us has looked sideways instead of upward.
The Bible does not merely expose this disease.
It reveals the cure.
The cure is found in Jesus Christ.
Where Saul grasped for glory, Jesus laid glory down.
Where Saul protected his throne, Jesus left His throne.
Where Saul sought praise, Jesus embraced a cross.
Paul describes Christ in Philippians 2 using the Greek phrase:
ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν (heauton ekenōsen)
“He emptied Himself.”
The King of Kings willingly humbled Himself.
The One who deserved everything surrendered everything.
The One who created the stars allowed Himself to be nailed to wood.
And because Jesus humbled Himself, believers no longer need to live enslaved to comparison.
The Gospel frees us from measuring our worth against other people.
Our value was settled at Calvary.
The cross declares that you are loved.
The resurrection declares that you are not forgotten.
The empty tomb declares that God is still writing your story.
Perhaps that is why Saul's story still grips hearts thousands of years later.
Not because it is about a king.
Because it is about us.
We know what it feels like to lose peace.
We know what it feels like to compare.
We know what it feels like to wonder why God seems to be blessing someone else.
But Saul's tragedy does not have to become our destiny.
Jesus offers something Saul never fully embraced.
A heart secure in God's love.
A soul at rest in God's sovereignty.
A life free from the exhausting burden of comparison.
Maybe today the Holy Spirit is exposing something hidden.
Not to shame you.
To heal you.
Maybe there is someone whose success secretly bothers you.
Maybe there is a wound you have covered with smiles.
Maybe there is resentment growing where gratitude should be.
Bring it to Christ.
Confess it.
Surrender it.
Let Him replace envy with worship.
Let Him replace comparison with contentment.
Let Him replace striving with trust.
Because peace does not come from having what everyone else has.
Peace comes from knowing the Shepherd who leads your life.
The same God who wrote David's story is writing yours.
The same God who opened doors for David can open doors for you.
The same God who raised Jesus from the dead is still working behind scenes you cannot see.
Your chapter is not late.
Your calling is not forgotten.
Your purpose is not canceled.
And your future is not determined by someone else's success.
It is determined by the faithfulness of God.
So before you leave, be honest.
Has envy been stealing your peace?
Your testimony may become the encouragement another believer desperately needs today.
There may come a day when comparison tries to return and you need this reminder again.
You never know which soul God intends to reach through a simple act of obedience.
One day you will realize the blessing you were begging God for was growing quietly while you were looking at somebody else's harvest.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Moment David Let His Guard Down
paragraphs:
The Moment David Let His Guard Down
One quiet decision. One lingering glance. One moment of spiritual drift. The king after God's own heart never planned to fall—but that is exactly how many falls begin.
There are moments in life that do not announce themselves as disasters.
They arrive quietly.
No thunder.
No warning sirens.
No visible collapse.
Just a small compromise.
A delayed obedience.
A neglected prayer.
A wandering thought.
A moment when a person who once stood strong slowly lowers their guard.
That is how one of the most heartbreaking chapters in Scripture begins.
Not with a battle.
Not with an enemy.
Not with a giant.
But with a king standing on a rooftop.
David.
The giant slayer.
The worshipper.
The songwriter.
The shepherd chosen by God.
The man whom Scripture describes as a man after God's own heart (Acts 13:22).
If someone had looked at David's life from a distance, they might have assumed he was untouchable.
Too anointed to fall.
Too experienced to fail.
Too blessed to stumble.
Yet Scripture tells a different story.
Because the Bible never hides the failures of its heroes.
It reveals them.
Not to shame them.
But to show us that every human being desperately needs grace.
The story begins in 2 Samuel 11:1:
"In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, David sent Joab..."
Those words may seem insignificant at first.
But they contain the first warning sign.
David was not where he was supposed to be.
The Hebrew text says:

לְעֵת צֵאת הַמְּלָאכִים
(le'et tset ha-melakhim)
"At the time when kings go out."
Kings.
Plural.
This was where kings belonged.
This was David's responsibility.
This was his assignment.
But David stayed behind.
Sometimes the greatest danger is not doing something obviously sinful.
Sometimes it is simply abandoning the place where God called you to be.
Many believers do not wake up one morning intending to destroy their lives.
They simply stop fighting.
They stop praying.
They stop pursuing God.
They become comfortable.
Spiritually passive.
Emotionally distracted.
And slowly, almost invisibly, vulnerability grows.
David remained in Jerusalem.
The army went to battle.
The king stayed home.
Then came the rooftop.
Scripture says:
"From the roof he saw a woman bathing; and the woman was very beautiful." (2 Samuel 11:2)
Notice something important.
Seeing Bathsheba was not David's sin.
Temptation itself is not sin.
Jesus Himself was tempted (Hebrews 4:15).
The problem was what David did next.
He kept looking.
He entertained what should have been rejected.
He pursued what should have been avoided.
He fed what should have been starved.
How many lives have been changed by a second look?
How many marriages have been damaged by a second look?
How many ministries have collapsed because someone convinced themselves they were strong enough to linger near temptation?
Sin rarely begins with action.
It usually begins with permission.
David gave temptation permission to stay.
Then desire gave birth to action.
James later described this exact process:
"Each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death." (James 1:14-15)
The Greek word for desire is:

ἐπιθυμία
(epithymia)
A craving.
A longing.
An appetite that demands satisfaction.
David knew God's commands.
He knew righteousness.
He knew covenant.
But in that moment he chose appetite over obedience.
And the consequences began immediately.
Bathsheba became pregnant.
David panicked.
Then came the cover-up.
Because sin never likes exposure.
David tried to manipulate circumstances.
He summoned Uriah.
He attempted deception.
He orchestrated lies.
When those efforts failed, he arranged something unimaginable.
The death of an innocent man.
Uriah.
A loyal soldier.
A faithful servant.
A man who possessed more integrity in that moment than the king himself.
The shepherd king who once risked his life protecting sheep now sacrificed a faithful sheep to protect himself.
That is what sin does.
It blinds.
It distorts.
It transforms things we never imagined we could become.
The tragedy was not merely David's adultery.
The tragedy was how many additional sins followed in an attempt to conceal the first one.
Yet perhaps the most chilling verse in the entire chapter is the final sentence:
"But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD." (2 Samuel 11:27)
Human beings can hide things from people.
We can manage appearances.
We can maintain reputations.
We can convince others we are fine.
But God sees everything.
The Hebrew word translated "displeased" carries the idea of something being evil in the eyes of God.
Not hidden.
Not overlooked.
Seen.
Every detail.
Every motive.
Every excuse.
Every rationalization.
Seen.
Perhaps that realization feels uncomfortable.
Maybe even frightening.
But there is another side to that truth.
The God who sees our sin is also the God who sees our pain.
The God who sees our rebellion is also the God who sees our wounds.
The God who sees our failures is also the God who provides redemption.
Because David's story does not end in scandal.
It moves through scandal into grace.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
That is why this story matters.
Nathan the prophet eventually confronted David.
Not with cruelty.
Not with humiliation.
But with truth.
David's defenses collapsed.
His excuses evaporated.
His pride shattered.
And then one of the most powerful confessions in Scripture emerged.
Psalm 51 preserves David's repentance.
He cried:

חָנֵּנִי אֱלֹהִים
(chaneni Elohim)
"Be gracious to me, O God."
Not because I deserve it.
Not because I earned it.
Not because I can fix myself.
Be gracious.
David understood something every believer must eventually learn.
The answer to sin is not self-improvement.
The answer is mercy.
David continues:
"Against You, You only, have I sinned and done what is evil in Your sight." (Psalm 51:4)
That statement does not deny he hurt Bathsheba.
Or Uriah.
Or Israel.
Rather, David recognized that every sin is ultimately an offense against God.
His heart had finally awakened.
His conscience had finally broken.
And in that brokenness, restoration began.
The Hebrew word often associated with repentance is:

שׁוּב
(shuv)
To turn back.
To return.
To come home.
That is what repentance truly is.
Not merely feeling bad.
Not merely experiencing guilt.
But turning back toward God.
Returning home.
And here is where David's story becomes everyone's story.
Because every reader has experienced moments of lowered defenses.
Moments of compromise.
Moments of hidden struggle.
Moments we wish we could erase.
Some carry secret addictions.
Some carry bitterness.
Some carry shame.
Some carry wounds nobody knows about.
Some have built entire identities around hiding what hurts.
Yet the Gospel declares that grace is greater.
The New Testament reveals what David could only glimpse from a distance.
The Messiah.
Jesus Christ.
The Son of David.
The true King.
The One who never let His guard down.
The One who never sinned.
The One who faced temptation and remained faithful.
The One who carried our failures to the cross.
When Jesus cried:

Τετέλεσται
(Tetelestai)
"It is finished." (John 19:30)
He declared that the debt of sin had been paid in full.
Not partially.
Not temporarily.
Completely.
David deserved judgment.
We deserve judgment.
Yet Jesus absorbed judgment so repentant sinners could receive mercy.
That is why the Gospel is not merely good advice.
It is good news.
Scandal does not have the final word.
Failure does not have the final word.
Shame does not have the final word.
Jesus does.
Maybe you came to this article carrying regret.
Maybe there is a chapter of your life you hope nobody discovers.
Maybe you know exactly what it feels like to stand on your own rooftop and make a decision you wish you could undo.
Hear this clearly.
David's greatest failure was not stronger than God's grace.
Neither is yours.
The enemy wants you to believe your story is over.
The cross declares otherwise.
The empty tomb declares otherwise.
The Gospel declares otherwise.
Jesus is still rewriting stories.
Jesus is still restoring broken people.
Jesus is still healing wounded hearts.
Jesus is still redeeming what seems beyond redemption.
And perhaps that is why David's story continues to resonate thousands of years later.
Not because he fell.
But because God lifted him.
Not because he failed.
But because God forgave him.
Not because scandal defined him.
But because grace did.
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
If your desire is to glorify God and help spread biblical truth in a world desperate for hope, your support becomes part of that mission.
Because someone else's restoration may begin with your share.
Because someone else's breakthrough may begin with your support.
Because someone else's encounter with Jesus may begin with your decision today.
And never forget this:
The same God who found David in his darkest chapter is still searching for hearts willing to come home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Book That Never Mentions God… Yet Reveals Him on Every Page
paragraphs:
The Book That Never Mentions God… Yet Reveals Him on Every Page
How the Silence of Esther Becomes One of the Loudest Testimonies of God's Sovereignty Ever Written—and Why Your Story May Feel Exactly the Same
There are seasons when heaven feels painfully silent.
You pray.
Nothing.
You cry.
Nothing.
You search for a sign.
Still nothing.

No miracle.
No burning bush.
No pillar of fire.
No audible voice.
Only silence.
Many believers quietly wonder what they are too afraid to ask aloud:
"God… where are You?"
That question has echoed through hospitals, empty bedrooms, broken marriages, financial collapse, gravesides, betrayal, depression, unanswered prayers, and sleepless nights.
If you've ever felt abandoned by God, then perhaps the most comforting book in the entire Bible is one where His name is never mentioned—not even once.
The Book of Esther.
At first glance, this almost seems impossible.
Every other historical book openly acknowledges God.
Yet Esther contains no explicit mention of God, YHWH (יהוה), Elohim (אֱלֹהִים), Adonai (אֲדֹנָי), prayer, worship, sacrifice, temple, covenant, or Jerusalem.
Not once.
Some critics throughout history even questioned whether Esther belonged in Scripture because of this astonishing omission.
But perhaps that silence is exactly the point.
Because sometimes the greatest evidence of God's presence is not hearing His voice.
It is discovering His fingerprints after everything is over.
That is the story of Esther.
And perhaps…
It is your story too.

The events unfold during the Persian Empire after many Jews remained scattered following the Babylonian exile. King Ahasuerus—identified by many scholars as Xerxes I—rules over 127 provinces stretching from India to Cush (Esther 1:1).
A royal banquet changes history.
Queen Vashti refuses the king's command.
She is removed.
A nationwide search begins for a new queen.
Among thousands of women stands a young Jewish orphan.
Her Hebrew name is הֲדַסָּה (Hadassah)—meaning "myrtle."
Her Persian name is אֶסְתֵּר (Estēr).

Some scholars connect Esther's Persian name with the Old Persian word related to "star," while others note similarities to the Babylonian goddess Ishtar. Whatever the linguistic history, Scripture identifies her faithfully as a Jewish woman living under foreign rule.
She is raised by her older cousin Mordecai after losing both parents.
Nothing about her circumstances looks extraordinary.
No prophet announces her future.
No angel appears.
No miraculous sign is recorded.
Yet the invisible hand of God quietly begins moving every ordinary event into place.
One beauty contest.
One orphan girl.
One promotion.
One sleepless night.
One overheard conversation.
One delayed execution.
One forgotten reward.
One royal banquet.
One seemingly insignificant decision after another.
Coincidence?
Or providence?
The Hebrew Bible often invites readers to notice what it does not explicitly explain.
The word "providence" itself never appears in Scripture, yet its reality fills its pages.
Behind every chapter of Esther stands an unseen King directing earthly kings.
The apostle Paul later writes,
"And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to His purpose." (Romans 8:28)
The Greek reads:

οἴδαμεν δὲ ὅτι τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν τὸν Θεὸν πάντα συνεργεῖ εἰς ἀγαθόν
(oidamen de hoti tois agapōsin ton Theon panta synergei eis agathon)
The verb συνεργεῖ (synergei) means "works together."
God is not merely watching events unfold.
He is orchestrating them.
That truth shines brilliantly through Esther without ever being directly stated.
Then darkness enters the story.
A powerful official named Haman rises within the kingdom.
His pride cannot tolerate one Jewish man refusing to bow.
Instead of punishing Mordecai alone, Haman determines to annihilate every Jew throughout the empire.
Genocide becomes law.
The decree is sealed.
Death appears inevitable.
The Hebrew word used for the Jews' destruction emphasizes complete extermination.
Everything appears finished.
The enemy believes he has already won.
How familiar that feels.
Cancer diagnoses.
Divorce papers.
Bankruptcy.
Addiction.
Loss.
Grief.
Sometimes life delivers decrees that seem irreversible.
Sometimes hell celebrates before heaven responds.
Then Mordecai sends Esther one of the most famous messages in Scripture.
"Who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (Esther 4:14)
The Hebrew reads:

וּמִי יוֹדֵעַ אִם־לְעֵת כָּזֹאת הִגַּעַתְּ לַמַּלְכוּת
(u-mi yodea im le'et kazot higa'at la-malkhut)
Literally:
"And who knows if for a time like this you have attained royalty?"
Notice what Mordecai does not say.
He never says,
"God told me."
He never claims divine revelation.
He simply trusts that God is working behind what everyone else sees.
Faith often lives inside uncertainty.
Faith is not pretending to know everything.
Faith is believing Someone else does.
Esther then speaks words that still inspire generations.
"If I perish, I perish."
In Hebrew:

וְכַאֲשֶׁר אָבַדְתִּי אָבָדְתִּי
(ve-ka'asher avadti avadti)
The repetition intensifies complete surrender.
"If I am destroyed—I am destroyed."
This is not reckless courage.
It is surrendered obedience.
She fasts.
Although prayer is never explicitly mentioned, fasting throughout Scripture consistently accompanies humble dependence upon God.
The omission once again invites careful readers to recognize what faithful Jews would naturally have understood.
She enters the king's presence.
Against all expectations...
She lives.
But notice something astonishing.
She does not immediately expose Haman.
She waits.
She prepares another banquet.
Why?
Because God's timing often matters as much as God's plan.
While Esther waits...
The king cannot sleep.
Such a tiny detail.
One restless night.
Yet that insomnia changes history.
Royal records are read.
Mordecai's forgotten act of loyalty is discovered.
The king realizes Mordecai was never rewarded.
The very next morning Haman arrives—planning Mordecai's execution.
Instead...
He is commanded to publicly honor the man he hates.
Can coincidence really become this precise?
Every chapter quietly whispers what it never explicitly says:
God is here.
The cross reveals this same pattern.
When Jesus hung upon Golgotha...
Rome believed it had won.
Religious leaders believed they had silenced Him.
Satan likely celebrated.
Even the disciples fled.
It appeared heaven had gone silent.
Then came Sunday.
The greatest apparent defeat became the greatest victory in history.
What looked like scandal became grace.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Joseph was sold.
David was hunted.
Daniel was exiled.
Esther was orphaned.
Paul was imprisoned.
Jesus was crucified.
Yet God rewrote every ending.
That is why the Gospel never minimizes suffering.
It transforms it.
The resurrection forever proves that God's silence is never His absence.
Sometimes He works most powerfully where He speaks least.
The early Church understood this.
The Greek New Testament repeatedly describes believers living by πίστις (pistis)—faith, trust, steadfast confidence—not by visible certainty.
As Paul writes,
"We walk by faith, not by sight." (2 Corinthians 5:7)
Greek:

διὰ πίστεως γὰρ περιπατοῦμεν, οὐ διὰ εἴδους
(dia pisteōs gar peripatoumen, ou dia eidous)
Faith continues walking while heaven appears quiet.
Esther ultimately reveals Haman's conspiracy.
The king's wrath turns.
The gallows built for Mordecai become Haman's own execution.
The decree of death cannot legally be revoked under Persian law, yet another decree grants the Jews authority to defend themselves.
The enemy's victory becomes his downfall.
The feast of Purim (פּוּרִים) is established to remember that deliverance.
The name comes from פּוּר (pur), meaning "lot," because Haman cast lots to determine the day of destruction.
Ironically, the very lottery intended to destroy God's people became the reminder of God's faithfulness.
Only God writes stories like that.
Perhaps you have wondered why God seems absent from your life.
Maybe your prayers feel unanswered.
Maybe your family is fractured.
Maybe your future seems uncertain.
Maybe you've mistaken silence for abandonment.
Esther gently reminds us that God's name may not always be obvious in the chapter you're living—but His hand is never missing from the story He is writing.
Long before Esther entered the palace, God was already arranging the throne.
Long before Haman plotted evil, God had prepared deliverance.
Long before the king lost sleep, heaven had already written the ending.
Your life is no different.
The Gospel declares that Jesus Christ entered humanity's greatest scandal—not merely to improve broken people but to redeem them completely.

The eternal Son of God took on flesh, lived the sinless life we could never live, bore our sins on the cross, died in our place, and rose bodily from the grave on the third day, conquering sin and death forever. Salvation is not earned by good works, religious effort, or personal merit, but received by grace alone through faith in Christ alone (Ephesians 2:8–9). Everyone who repents and believes in Him is forgiven, reconciled to God, adopted into His family, and given the sure hope of eternal life. This is the heart of the Gospel: God rescues sinners through Jesus, not because we deserve it, but because of His steadfast love and mercy.
Perhaps the greatest miracle in Esther is not that God is absent.
It is that He accomplishes everything without needing to announce Himself.
He never stopped being King simply because His name was not spoken.
And maybe that is exactly what you needed to hear today.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He Knew He Would Raise Lazarus… So Why Did Jesus Weep?
paragraphs:
He Knew He Would Raise Lazarus… So Why Did Jesus Weep?
The Tears That Changed Everything: Understanding the Deep Meaning of Jesus Weeping at Lazarus’ Tomb and What It Reveals About the Heart of God
If there is one verse in all of Scripture that seems simple on the surface but becomes infinitely deeper the longer you stare at it, it is found in John 11:35.
“Jesus wept.”
Two words.
Three in Greek.
Yet hidden inside those tears is one of the most breathtaking revelations of the heart of God ever recorded.
Because Jesus already knew what He was about to do.
He knew Lazarus would walk out of the tomb.
He knew death was about to lose.
He knew mourning would become celebration.
He knew the miracle before anyone else did.
And still...
He wept.
That reality should stop every believer in their tracks.
Why would the Son of God cry over a problem He was about to solve?
Why would the Creator of life stand before a temporary grave and shed tears?
Why would the Resurrection Himself mourn?
To understand this moment, we must walk slowly into Bethany.
Not as spectators.
As participants.
Because somewhere in this story, every one of us eventually finds ourselves.
A delayed prayer.
A closed door.
A funeral we never expected.
A loss we never prepared for.
A season where heaven feels silent.
The story begins in John 11 when Lazarus becomes gravely ill. Lazarus was not merely an acquaintance of Jesus. Scripture specifically tells us:
“Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.” (John 11:5)
This family was deeply loved.
Yet something shocking happens.
Jesus delays.
Instead of rushing to Bethany, He stays where He is for two more days.
Lazarus dies.
The sisters grieve.
The mourners gather.
Hope seems buried beneath a stone.
How many believers have lived inside that feeling?
You prayed.
You trusted.
You waited.
And Jesus seemed late.
But the Gospel repeatedly teaches that God's delays are not God's denials.
What feels like abandonment is often preparation.
What looks like silence is often divine orchestration.
When Jesus finally arrives, Martha meets Him with words that countless believers have whispered through tears:
“Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” (John 11:21)
Mary eventually says the exact same thing.
The pain is understandable.
The disappointment is real.
Faith and heartbreak are colliding in the same sentence.
Yet Jesus answers with one of the most powerful declarations ever spoken:
“I am the resurrection and the life.” (John 11:25)
Notice what He does not say.
He does not say, “I can perform a resurrection.”
He does not say, “I know about resurrection.”
He says, “I AM.”
The Greek reads:

Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή
(Egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē)
“I AM the resurrection and the life.”
The phrase Ἐγώ εἰμι (Egō eimi) deliberately echoes God's self-revelation.
In Exodus 3:14, God reveals Himself to Moses in Hebrew:

אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה
(Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh)
“I AM WHO I AM.”
Jesus is not merely offering comfort.
He is revealing identity.
The One standing before the tomb is the God who spoke existence into being.
The One crying is the same One who hung every star.
The One grieving is the Author of life itself.
Then comes the moment.
The shortest verse in English.
The deepest verse in human experience.
John 11:35.
In Greek:

ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς
(edakrysen ho Iēsous)
“Jesus wept.”
The Greek word used here is extraordinarily important.
John does not use the word describing loud public wailing.
He uses a word describing quiet tears.
Personal tears.
Deep tears.
The tears of someone whose heart has been pierced.
And this raises the question that has echoed through centuries.
Why?
Why did Jesus cry?
Some suggest He cried because He loved Lazarus.
That is certainly true.
The crowd itself observed:
“See how He loved him!” (John 11:36)
Love always grieves loss.
Even temporary loss.
Love mourns because love values.
Every funeral hurts because every life matters.
But there is something even deeper happening here.
When Jesus arrives, He sees Mary weeping.
He sees mourners weeping.
He sees devastation.
Brokenness.
Pain.
Death.
The consequences of sin's invasion into God's good creation.
John records that Jesus was “deeply moved.”
The phrase translated “deeply moved” comes from the Greek word:

ἐμβριμάομαι
(embrimaomai)
This word carries astonishing force.
It can describe indignation.
Strong emotional agitation.
Even righteous anger.
In other words, Jesus is not merely sad.
He is disturbed.
He is outraged.
Not at Martha.
Not at Mary.
Not at Lazarus.
He is confronting humanity's ancient enemy.
Death.
The tomb before Him represents everything sin brought into the world.
Every funeral.
Every cemetery.
Every goodbye.
Every hospital room.
Every tear shed over a loved one.
Every broken heart.
Every dream buried too soon.
Jesus stands before the devastation caused by sin and His soul is stirred with holy emotion.
His tears are not signs of weakness.
They are signs of divine compassion.
His tears reveal that God is not emotionally detached from human suffering.
Many people imagine God as distant.
Cold.
Unmoved.
Untouched by human pain.
John 11 destroys that misconception forever.
God enters the suffering.
God stands beside the grieving.
God feels the weight of human sorrow.
God weeps.
The prophet Isaiah foretold this centuries earlier:
“He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief.” (Isaiah 53:3)
The Hebrew phrase is:

אִישׁ מַכְאֹבוֹת
(Ish Mak'ovot)
“A man of sorrows.”
Jesus did not merely observe grief.
He carried it.
He entered it.
He experienced it.
This means something profoundly personal for every reader.
The tears Jesus shed at Lazarus' tomb reveal that God sees every tear you have ever cried.
Every hidden heartbreak.
Every private disappointment.
Every betrayal.
Every unanswered question.
Every lonely night.
Every prayer whispered through sobs.
Psalm 56:8 says:
“You have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in Your bottle.”
God does not ignore tears.
He collects them.
He remembers them.
He values them.
And Jesus proves that truth standing before Lazarus' tomb.
Yet there is another layer still.
Perhaps the most beautiful layer of all.
Jesus knew He would raise Lazarus.
The miracle was minutes away.
Yet He still entered the grief before ending it.
Why?
Because love does not rush past pain.
Love walks through it.
Jesus did not say, “Stop crying. Everything will be fine.”
He stood with them.
He mourned with them.
He shared their burden.
Before He changed their circumstances, He joined their suffering.
That is exactly what He still does today.
Many people want a God who immediately removes pain.
The Gospel offers something even greater.
A Savior who enters pain with us.
The cross itself would soon demonstrate this truth on an even grander scale.
At Calvary, Jesus would step into humanity's suffering completely.
He would carry sin.
Bear judgment.
Taste death.
Experience abandonment.
Not because He deserved it.
Because we did.
The tears at Lazarus' tomb point forward to the blood at Calvary.
Both reveal the same truth:
God loves sinners more than sinners understand.
And perhaps nowhere is that love more visible than in the theme that runs through all of Scripture.
Scandal to grace.
Because Lazarus' story is ultimately our story.
We were spiritually dead.
Buried in sin.
Hopeless.
Unable to save ourselves.
The Apostle Paul writes:
Dead people cannot resurrect themselves.
Yet Jesus stands before our spiritual tombs just as He stood before Lazarus'.
Then He speaks.
“Lazarus, come out.”
The dead man obeys.
Life enters where death once ruled.
Grace rewrites what seemed permanent.
That is the Gospel.
That is your testimony if you belong to Christ.
The scandal of sin became the story of redemption.
The grave became the birthplace of resurrection.
The ending changed because Jesus arrived.
Maybe you are reading this carrying your own tomb.
A buried dream.
A broken relationship.
A shattered future.
A secret sin.
A wound nobody knows about.
Remember Bethany.
Remember those tears.
Remember that the Savior who cried at Lazarus' tomb has not changed.
He still sees.
He still knows.
He still cares.
And He still calls dead things back to life.
The tears of Jesus were never the end of the story.
They were the beginning of a miracle.
And perhaps that is why this passage continues to grip hearts two thousand years later.
Because every believer lives somewhere between verse 35 and verse 44.
Between the tears and the resurrection.
Between the grief and the miracle.
Between the tomb and the breakthrough.
If this message stirred your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
What tomb are you trusting Jesus with right now?
Your testimony may become someone else's reason to keep believing.
Because sometimes the proof that God loves you is not that He stopped the tears... but that He cried beside you before He turned the page.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Advisor Whose Pride Destroyed a Kingdom
paragraphs:
The Advisor Whose Pride Destroyed a Kingdom
When the smartest voice in the room stopped listening to God, an entire nation paid the price.
There is a terrifying truth most people never realize until the damage is already done.
The greatest threat to your life is not always your enemy.
Sometimes it is your own wisdom.
Sometimes it is the voice inside your head that has been right so many times before that you slowly stop asking God if you're right this time.
Sometimes the kingdom falls not because of a sword, but because of pride wearing the mask of intelligence.
That is the tragedy of Ahithophel.
Most believers know the story of King David's failures. They know about Goliath. They know about Bathsheba. They know about Solomon's wisdom.
But very few stop long enough to stare into the dark and haunting story of the advisor whose pride helped ignite a rebellion and nearly destroyed God's chosen kingdom.
And if we're honest, many of us are much more like Ahithophel than we want to admit.
Because pride rarely announces itself.
It whispers.
It convinces us that we know better.
It tells us we are indispensable.
It tells us we deserve recognition.
It tells us we have earned the right to be offended.
And by the time we realize what it has done, entire kingdoms lie in ruins.
The Bible introduces Ahithophel as one of the most brilliant counselors in Israel.
Scripture says:
"Now in those days the counsel that Ahithophel gave was as if one consulted the word of God; so was all the counsel of Ahithophel esteemed." (2 Samuel 16:23)
That statement should make us pause.
This was not an ordinary advisor.
His counsel carried immense weight.
People listened when he spoke.
Kings trusted him.
Leaders followed him.
Nations moved because of his words.
In modern terms, he was the strategist behind the throne, the political genius, the trusted consultant, the voice everyone wanted in the room.
Yet brilliance without humility becomes a loaded weapon pointed at the soul.
The Hebrew word often associated with pride is גָּאוֹן (ga'on), meaning arrogance, exaltation, or self-glorification.
Pride always seeks elevation.
It wants the throne.
Even when it pretends to be serving someone else's kingdom.
Then came scandal.
David's sin with Bathsheba shook the nation.

Many scholars note that Ahithophel may have had a deeply personal connection to that tragedy. Bathsheba was the daughter of Eliam (2 Samuel 11:3), and Eliam appears connected to Ahithophel in David's list of mighty men (2 Samuel 23:34).
If this connection is correct, Bathsheba may have been Ahithophel's granddaughter.
Imagine the pain.
Imagine the humiliation.
Imagine watching the king abuse his authority and devastate your family.
The Bible does not explicitly tell us what was happening inside Ahithophel's heart.
But Scripture does show us where unresolved bitterness eventually led.
Years later, when David's son Absalom launched a rebellion against his father, Ahithophel joined the uprising.
The wounded advisor aligned himself against God's anointed king.
The offended counselor became a conspirator.
The wise man allowed pain to become poison.
Many people reading this know exactly what that feels like.
Someone betrayed you.
Someone disappointed you.
Someone wounded your trust.
Someone damaged your family.
And at first, your anger felt justified.
Maybe it was justified.
But the danger begins when pain becomes identity.
Because bitterness never stays contained.
It always spreads.
The New Testament uses the Greek word πικρία (pikria), meaning bitterness, resentment, or deep hostility.
Hebrews 12:15 warns:
"See to it that no root of bitterness springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled."
Notice the language.
A root.
Roots grow underground before anyone sees them.
That is how spiritual destruction works.
It begins in secret.
By the time everyone notices the fruit, the root has already been growing for years.
When Absalom sought to overthrow David, Ahithophel offered devastatingly effective advice.
His plan could have ended David's life quickly and secured the rebellion.
Humanly speaking, it was brilliant.
Militarily speaking, it was almost flawless.
But God intervened.
David prayed:
"O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness." (2 Samuel 15:31)
And God answered.
Another advisor named Hushai successfully undermined Ahithophel's strategy.
The rebellion slowed.
David escaped.
The kingdom survived.
And suddenly, the advisor who had built his identity on being right faced something he could not endure.
He was ignored.
The man whose counsel was treated almost like the voice of God could not tolerate being rejected.
Scripture records one of the saddest moments in the entire Bible:

"When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his donkey and went off home to his own city. He set his house in order and hanged himself. Then he died and was buried in the tomb of his father." (2 Samuel 17:23)
Read that again.
His kingdom was not destroyed first.
His reputation was not destroyed first.
His career was not destroyed first.
His pride was wounded first.
And that wound exposed what had been ruling his heart all along.
The tragedy of Ahithophel is not merely that he died.
The tragedy is that he stood so close to God's kingdom while remaining so far from God's heart.
He possessed wisdom but lacked surrender.
He possessed influence but lacked humility.
He possessed knowledge but lacked transformation.
And there are countless people sitting in churches today who face the same danger.
They know theology.
They know doctrine.
They know ministry.
They know Scripture.
Yet secretly they trust their own understanding more than the Lord.
The Hebrew text of Proverbs 3:5 says:
בְּטַח אֶל־יְהוָה בְּכָל־לִבֶּךָ וְאֶל־בִּינָתְךָ אַל־תִּשָּׁעֵן
Transliterated:
"B'tach el-YHWH b'khol libekha, v'el binatkha al tisha'en."
Translation:
"Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding."
That command is difficult because our understanding often feels trustworthy.
Especially when we have been right before.
Especially when others admire our intelligence.
Especially when success reinforces our confidence.
But Scripture repeatedly reminds us that wisdom detached from God eventually becomes foolishness.
And this is where the story shifts from scandal to grace.
Because there is another Counselor in Scripture.
Another Advisor.
Another Voice.
Unlike Ahithophel, this Counselor cannot be corrupted by pride.
The prophet Isaiah called Him:
"Wonderful Counselor" (Isaiah 9:6).
The Hebrew phrase is:
פֶּלֶא יוֹעֵץ
Transliterated:
Pele Yoetz.
Wonderful Counselor.
This is Jesus Christ.
Where Ahithophel's counsel led toward death, Christ's counsel leads toward life.
Where Ahithophel's pride destroyed, Christ's humility saves.
Where Ahithophel could not survive rejection, Jesus willingly endured rejection to rescue sinners.
The Greek text records the crowd shouting:
Σταύρωσον αὐτόν
Transliterated:
Staurōson auton.
Translation:
"Crucify Him."
The perfectly wise Counselor was rejected by the very people He came to save.
Yet unlike Ahithophel, He did not respond with self-destruction.
He responded with self-sacrifice.
He stretched out His hands upon the cross.
He absorbed wrath.
He carried shame.
He bore sin.
He conquered death.
He rose again.
And because of Him, every scandal can become grace.
Every failure can become redemption.
Every wound can become a testimony.
Every rebel can become a son or daughter of God.
Maybe you have been carrying bitterness.
Maybe pride has quietly taken root.
Maybe you have spent years proving how smart you are while neglecting the One who gave you your mind.
Maybe you have been building your own kingdom instead of serving Christ's.
Today is an invitation.
Not to become more impressive.
Not to become more influential.
Not to become more admired.
But to surrender.
Because the greatest victory is not winning an argument.
It is allowing Jesus Christ to reign over your heart.
And perhaps the most sobering question from Ahithophel's story is this:
What kingdom might my pride be destroying right now?
Your marriage?
Your family?
Your ministry?
Your friendships?
Your testimony?
Your relationship with God?
Do not wait until the damage becomes irreversible.
Bring your heart before Christ today.
Repent.
Confess.
Surrender.
Trust the Wonderful Counselor.
Because the same Jesus who forgave adulterers, restored failures, redeemed traitors, healed the broken, and transformed persecutors is still rewriting lives today.
If this message stirred something deep inside you, do not keep it to yourself.
"I choose surrender."
Or if you're struggling today:
"Pray for me."
Or if God exposed something hidden in your heart:
"Jesus forgive me."
Your testimony may be the encouragement another believer desperately needs.
Not because salvation can be purchased—it cannot.
Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone (Ephesians 2:8–9).
You will also gain access to deeper discipleship content and become part of a mission dedicated to helping people move from scandal to grace through the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Because sometimes the kingdom does not fall when the enemy attacks.
Sometimes it falls when pride convinces us we no longer need the King.
And the moment we finally kneel before Jesus is the moment He begins rewriting everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You’ve Been Told “Ask and You Shall Receive” Your Whole Life—But Almost Nobody Understands What Jesus Was Actually Saying
paragraphs:
You’ve Been Told “Ask and You Shall Receive” Your Whole Life—But Almost Nobody Understands What Jesus Was Actually Saying
The hidden meaning behind one of the most quoted promises in Scripture may completely transform how you pray, how you trust God, and how you understand His heart when the answer seems delayed, different, or silent.
There are few verses more loved, quoted, repeated, printed on coffee mugs, preached from pulpits, and whispered through tears than Jesus’ words:
“Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.” (Matthew 7:7)
For many believers, these words feel like a divine guarantee.
Ask for healing.
Ask for provision.
Ask for restoration.
Ask for a breakthrough.
Ask for the miracle.
Ask for the answer.
And receive.
Simple.
Yet if we are brutally honest, countless Christians carry a hidden wound because their experience does not always seem to match what they thought Jesus promised.
They asked.
The cancer remained.
They asked.
The marriage still broke.
They asked.
The prodigal child never returned.
They asked.
The door closed.
They asked.
And heaven felt silent.
That silent pain has caused many believers to wonder questions they are often afraid to say out loud.
Did I not have enough faith?
Did God ignore me?
Did Jesus make a promise that failed?
Or have I misunderstood what He was saying all along?
The answer may change everything.
The deeper meaning of “Ask and You Shall Receive” begins when we stop reading the verse in isolation and start listening to Jesus in His original context.
In Matthew 7:7, the Greek text records Jesus saying:
Αἰτεῖτε, καὶ δοθήσεται ὑμῖν· ζητεῖτε, καὶ εὑρήσετε· κρούετε, καὶ ἀνοιγήσεται ὑμῖν.
Transliterated:
Aiteite, kai dothēsetai hymin; zēteite, kai heurēsete; krouete, kai anoigēsetai hymin.
What most English readers never notice is that the verbs are written in a continuous present tense.
Jesus is not merely saying:
“Ask once.”
He is saying:
“Keep asking.”
“Keep seeking.”
“Keep knocking.”
The meaning is ongoing persistence.
A more literal understanding would sound like:
“Keep on asking, and it will be given to you. Keep on seeking, and you will find. Keep on knocking, and the door will be opened.”
Immediately, the passage becomes less like a vending machine and more like a relationship.
Jesus is not teaching a formula.
He is teaching dependence.
The entire Sermon on the Mount is centered on trusting the Father.
Not manipulating Him.
Not controlling Him.
Not forcing outcomes.
Trusting Him.
This becomes even clearer when Jesus continues:
“Or what man is there of you, whom if his son ask bread, will he give him a stone?” (Matthew 7:9)
Notice what Jesus emphasizes.
Not the son's ability to ask.
The father's goodness.
The foundation of the promise is not human faithfulness.
It is divine character.
The promise rests upon who God is.
This truth becomes even more powerful when we understand the Hebrew worldview behind Jesus' teaching.
Although Matthew records the words in Greek, Jesus likely taught them in Aramaic, the common language spoken by many Jews in first-century Judea.
The Aramaic concept behind asking was never merely requesting information or material blessings.
It carried the idea of coming near, depending, seeking relationship, and appealing to someone you trusted.
In Scripture, God's greatest gifts were never things.
They were Himself.
This is where many modern interpretations accidentally drift away from the heart of the Gospel.
Sometimes we approach prayer hoping to get God's hand.
Jesus is teaching us to pursue God's heart.
There is a profound difference.
Many people seek God because they want answers.
Jesus invites us to seek God until He becomes the answer.
This pattern appears throughout Scripture.
King David wrote:
“One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after...” (Psalm 27:4)
In Hebrew:
אַחַת שָׁאַלְתִּי מֵאֵת־יְהוָה
Achath sha'alti me'et Adonai.
“One thing I have asked of the LORD.”
David had enemies.
Battles.
Threats.
Needs.
Fears.
Yet his deepest request was not escape.
It was presence.
To dwell with God.
To behold His beauty.
To know Him.
This is why some prayers that seem unanswered are actually being answered in a deeper way than we expected.
We ask for immediate relief.
God offers Himself.
We ask for a changed circumstance.
God transforms our heart.
We ask for the removal of suffering.
God develops endurance, character, and deeper intimacy.
None of those answers feel easy in the moment.
But they reveal a Father who sees beyond today.
The Apostle Paul understood this painfully well.
Three times he pleaded for God to remove what he called a “thorn in the flesh.”
Three times.
He asked.
He sought.
He knocked.
And the answer was not removal.
The answer was:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9)
The request was denied.
Yet the deeper need was fulfilled.
Paul received something greater than what he originally asked for.
The presence of Christ sustaining him.
This is why “Ask and You Shall Receive” cannot mean that God grants every request exactly as desired.
Jesus Himself disproves that interpretation in Gethsemane.
The Son of God prayed:
“Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me...” (Luke 22:42)
Yet the cup remained.
The cross remained.
The suffering remained.
And through that apparent denial came the salvation of the world.
The greatest act of redemption in history emerged from a prayer that received a different answer than expected.
This is the scandal and beauty of grace.
God often sees a story we cannot yet see.
Joseph saw betrayal.
God saw preservation.
Ruth saw loss.
God saw redemption.
Peter saw failure.
God saw restoration.
The woman caught in adultery saw public shame.
Jesus saw a future.
The thief on the cross saw death.
Jesus saw paradise.
Again and again Scripture reveals the same theme.
People see endings.
Jesus sees rewrites.
That is why “Ask and You Shall Receive” is ultimately not about getting everything you want.
It is about discovering that God gives what is truly good.
Jesus says:
“How much more shall your Father which is in heaven give good things to them that ask him?” (Matthew 7:11)
Notice the phrase.
Good things.
Not all things.
Good things.
The Father filters every request through perfect wisdom, perfect love, perfect timing, and perfect knowledge.
A child may ask for something harmful.
A loving father says no.
A child may ask for something too early.
A loving father says wait.
A child may ask for something less than what the father intends to give.
A loving father gives something greater.
When we understand this, prayer stops being a transaction.
It becomes trust.
And trust becomes worship.
Perhaps the deepest fulfillment of Jesus' promise appears later in Scripture.
In Luke's parallel account, Jesus says:
“How much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?” (Luke 11:13)
The ultimate gift is not wealth.
Not success.
Not comfort.
Not even answered circumstances.
The ultimate gift is God Himself dwelling within His people.
The greatest answer to prayer is not receiving what we requested.
The greatest answer is receiving more of Christ.
Maybe that is why some of the strongest believers are not those who got everything they prayed for.
They are the ones who discovered Jesus was enough even when they did not.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying a prayer that still feels unanswered.
A prayer that has stretched your faith.
A prayer that has produced tears no one knows about.
A prayer you have whispered so many times that you are exhausted.
Hear the words of Christ again.
Not as a formula.
Not as a guarantee of immediate results.
But as an invitation from the heart of your Savior.
Keep asking.
Keep seeking.
Keep knocking.
Because every prayer offered through faith draws you closer to the Father who already knows what you need.
And even when the answer arrives differently than expected, His goodness never changes.
The cross settled that forever.
After all, the Gospel itself is the greatest proof that God knows how to answer deeper than we ask.
Humanity asked for rescue.
God gave His Son.
Humanity deserved judgment.
God offered grace.
Humanity wrote a story of rebellion.
Jesus rewrote it with redemption.
That is the heart of “Ask and You Shall Receive.”
Not that God becomes our servant.
But that through prayer we become more aware of His love, His wisdom, His presence, His timing, and His purposes.
The invitation was never merely to receive gifts.
The invitation was always to receive Him.
You never know how God may use a simple share to bring healing, conviction, hope, or restoration.
Have you ever prayed for something that God answered differently than you expected?
The prayer you think God ignored may be the very place where He is quietly rewriting your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Failure That Changed Judah Forever
paragraphs:
The Failure That Changed Judah Forever
The Night One Man’s Sin Nearly Erased a Nation—And the Scandal God Turned Into the Bloodline of Christ
Some failures leave scars.
Others leave graves.
But there is a kind of failure so devastating that it changes generations.
A failure that echoes through families, nations, and history itself.
A failure so shocking that many believers quietly skip over it when reading Scripture.
Yet God preserved every uncomfortable detail.
Not to embarrass Judah.
Not to humiliate Tamar.
Not to remind us how broken people can be.
But to reveal something far greater:
that Jesus Christ specializes in rewriting stories nobody else believes can be redeemed.
And perhaps that is exactly why you need this story today.
Because maybe your greatest regret is not the end of your story either.
The story begins in Genesis 38, one of the most scandalous chapters in all of Scripture.
At first glance it seems completely out of place.
Joseph has just been sold into slavery by his brothers.
The narrative suddenly pauses.
The spotlight shifts.
And Moses records an account that many would rather avoid.
Yet under the inspiration of God, every word remains.
Because hidden beneath the scandal is one of the greatest demonstrations of grace ever recorded.
Judah, whose name in Hebrew is יְהוּדָה (Yehudah), was one of the twelve sons of Jacob.
His name means “praise.”
Ironically, the man whose name meant praise would become known for one of the darkest moral failures in Genesis.
Years earlier, Judah had participated in the betrayal of Joseph.
Rather than stopping his brothers from selling Joseph, he suggested profiting from the crime.
Genesis 37:26–27 records Judah proposing that Joseph be sold instead of killed.
A brother betrayed.
A father deceived.
A family shattered.
And Judah walked away.
Sin rarely stays in one chapter.
It follows us.
It grows roots.
It waits.
Genesis 38 reveals the fruit of what had already begun growing in Judah’s heart.
He separated himself from his brothers and settled among the Canaanites.
There he married a Canaanite woman and had three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah.
When Er became old enough, Judah found him a wife named Tamar.
But Scripture says Er was wicked before the Lord.
God judged him, and he died.
According to ancient family responsibility, known later as levirate marriage, the next brother was expected to raise offspring in the deceased brother’s name.
Onan refused.
He wanted the benefits of the relationship without the responsibility.
His selfish rebellion resulted in judgment as well.
He died.
Two sons gone.
Judah was afraid.
Instead of trusting God, he blamed Tamar.
He sent her away with promises that were never fulfilled.
Years passed.
Tamar remained abandoned.
Forgotten.
Discarded.
Trapped between grief and injustice.
And this is where the story becomes almost unbelievable.
After Judah’s wife died, he traveled toward Timnah.
Tamar learned of his journey.
Desperate after years of being denied justice, she disguised herself and sat along the road.
Judah did not recognize her.
Believing she was a prostitute, he approached her.
The Hebrew text uses language that intentionally exposes the moral blindness of the moment.
A man who once judged others could no longer see his own darkness.
As payment, Judah promised a young goat.
Until payment arrived, Tamar requested collateral.
His seal.
His cord.
His staff.
The ancient equivalents of personal identification.
His signature.
His reputation.
His identity.
Judah agreed.
The encounter happened.
And afterward Tamar disappeared.
Months later, news reached Judah.
“Tamar your daughter-in-law has acted like a prostitute, and behold, she is pregnant.”
His response was immediate.
“Bring her out, and let her be burned.”
The hypocrisy is breathtaking.
The same man who had slept with the woman now demanded judgment upon her.
How often does sin make us experts at condemning in others what we excuse in ourselves?
Then came one of the most dramatic moments in all of Scripture.
As Tamar was brought forward, she sent Judah the seal, cord, and staff.
Along with a message.
Genesis 38:25:
“By the man to whom these belong, I am pregnant.”
Imagine the silence.
The shock.
The collapse of every excuse.
The exposure.
The humiliation.
The realization.
Judah knew instantly.
The evidence was undeniable.
His sin had found him.
His scandal was public.
His reputation shattered.
Everything hidden stood in the light.
And then something extraordinary happened.
Something that changed Judah forever.
Genesis 38:26 records his response:
צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי
“Tzadeqah mimmeni.”
“She is more righteous than I.”
These words may be among the most important words Judah ever spoke.
Not because they erased his sin.
Not because they removed consequences.
But because they revealed genuine repentance.
For the first time in Scripture, Judah stopped blaming others.
Stopped hiding.
Stopped deflecting.
Stopped pretending.
He owned his failure.
Completely.
The Hebrew expression carries the idea that Tamar had acted more justly than he had.
Judah publicly acknowledged his guilt.
No excuses.
No manipulation.
No self-defense.
Just truth.
Many people want forgiveness.
Far fewer want exposure.
Yet exposure often becomes the doorway to redemption.
Because grace cannot heal what pride refuses to reveal.
The story could have ended there.
A ruined reputation.
A cautionary tale.
A warning for future generations.
But God was writing something bigger.
Tamar gave birth to twins.
Perez and Zerah.
And here is where the story explodes into Gospel beauty.
Centuries later, the genealogy of Jesus Christ opens the New Testament.
Matthew intentionally includes names many ancient genealogies would hide.
Among them is Tamar.
Matthew 1:3:
“Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar.”
Read that again.
The scandal remained in the record.
God did not erase it.
He redeemed it.
The line leading to Jesus Christ passed directly through this broken story.
Not around it.
Not despite it.
Through it.
The Messiah entered history through a family tree filled with failures, sinners, outsiders, and redeemed people.
Because the Gospel is not the story of perfect people finding God.
It is the story of God finding broken people.
Judah's repentance transformed him.
Years later, when Benjamin's life was threatened in Egypt, Judah became a different man.
The selfish brother who once sold Joseph now offered himself as a substitute.
Genesis 44:33 records Judah pleading:
“Please let your servant remain instead of the boy.”
This is not the same Judah.
Grace had changed him.
Failure had humbled him.
Repentance had reshaped him.
The man who once sacrificed his brother now offered himself for his brother.
And from that transformed Judah would come King David.
And from David would come Jesus Christ.
The Lion of the Tribe of Judah.
Not the Lion of Joseph.
Not the Lion of Moses.
Not the Lion of Abraham.
The Lion of Judah.
The tribe connected forever to a man whose greatest failure became the backdrop for one of Scripture's greatest stories of redemption.
Maybe that is why this story refuses to let us look away.
Because we see ourselves in it.
Maybe your scandal is different.
Maybe yours is hidden.
Maybe yours happened years ago.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe you still replay the moment in your mind.
The words you wish you could take back.
The relationship you destroyed.
The compromise you justified.
The secret that became public.
The season you walked away from God.
The failure that still keeps you awake.
You wonder if your story can ever be redeemed.
Judah's story answers that question.
Not because his sin was small.
It was not.
Not because consequences disappeared.
They did not.
But because God's grace proved greater.
The New Testament word for grace is χάρις (charis).
A gift.
Unearned favor.
Undeserved kindness.
Not earned by performance.
Not purchased through religious effort.
Given freely through Jesus Christ.
The cross stands as the ultimate declaration that God specializes in rewriting impossible stories.
When Jesus cried, “Τετέλεσται” (Tetelestai)—“It is finished” (John 19:30)—He announced that the debt of sin had been fully paid.
Every repentant sinner who comes to Christ receives forgiveness.
Every shattered story can be rewritten.
Every failure surrendered to Him can become a testimony of grace.
Not because the past changes.
But because the Author changes the ending.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel Warrior mission.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If this article spoke to your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
More importantly, supporting Gospel Warrior is one practical way of helping spread biblical truth to people who may never walk into a church but will read a post shared by someone they trust.
Because one shared article can reach a struggling believer.
One saved article can become tomorrow's lifeline.
One comment can encourage someone to keep fighting.
And one surrendered failure can become the beginning of a redemption story only Jesus could write.
The devil wanted Judah remembered for his scandal.
God chose to remember him for his repentance.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Leah’s Eyes and the Pain Behind Them
paragraphs:
Leah’s Eyes and the Pain Behind Them
The Woman Nobody Chose, The God Who Saw Everything
There are wounds that never bleed where people can see them.
They hide behind forced smiles.
Behind accomplishments.
Behind serving everyone else.
Behind being the dependable one.
Behind the friend who is always available.
Behind the spouse who keeps giving.
Behind the believer who keeps showing up to church while carrying silent heartbreak.
Some wounds come from betrayal.
Others come from rejection.
But few wounds cut as deeply as the pain of not being chosen.
Maybe that is why Leah’s story still hurts thousands of years later.
Because if we are honest, many of us are Leah.
Not because we lived in ancient Mesopotamia.
Not because we were given in marriage through deception.
But because we know what it feels like to stand beside someone else and wonder why they received the love we desperately wanted.
We know what it feels like to be overlooked.
To be compared.
To be unwanted.
To feel invisible.
And hidden inside one of the most heartbreaking stories in Scripture is one of the greatest revelations of God’s grace ever recorded.
Because Leah’s story is not ultimately about rejection.
It is about redemption.
It is not about what people failed to give her.
It is about what God saw when nobody else did.
It is not about being forgotten.
It is about being found.
And by the time her story ends, the woman nobody wanted becomes part of the bloodline of Jesus Christ Himself.
Because from scandal to grace, Jesus rewrites everything.
The story begins in Genesis 29.
Jacob arrives in Haran and falls deeply in love with Rachel.
Scripture tells us:
"And Jacob loved Rachel." (Genesis 29:18)
The Hebrew word used for love here is אָהַב (ahav).
It speaks of affection, attachment, desire, and devotion.
Jacob wanted Rachel.
Everyone knew it.
Rachel knew it.
Leah knew it.
And that knowledge became the source of one of the deepest emotional wounds in the Bible.
Genesis 29:17 says:
"וְעֵינֵי לֵאָה רַכּוֹת"
"Ve'enei Leah rakkot."
Traditionally translated:
"Leah's eyes were delicate" or "Leah's eyes were weak."
The phrase has been debated for centuries.
The Hebrew word רַכּוֹת (rakkot) literally means soft, tender, delicate, weak, or gentle.
Many scholars believe the verse is intentionally contrasting Leah with Rachel's striking physical beauty.
Others suggest Leah's eyes reflected sorrow, tenderness, or emotional depth.
Whatever the exact meaning, the narrative immediately follows with:
"But Rachel was beautiful in form and appearance."
The comparison is painful.
Leah is introduced through contrast.
Rachel is desired.
Leah is measured against her.
Rachel is loved.
Leah is tolerated.
And many readers miss how devastating this would have been.
Imagine spending your entire life living in someone else's shadow.
Imagine every room reminding you that someone else is preferred.
Imagine every family gathering.
Every conversation.
Every glance.
Every comparison.
Imagine being known not for who you are but for who you are not.
Some people live there for years.
Some live there for decades.
Some still live there today.
Then comes the scandal.
Laban deceives Jacob.
Instead of Rachel, Leah is given in marriage.
Jacob wakes up and discovers the truth.
Genesis 29:25 records one of the most heartbreaking reactions in Scripture.
"When morning came, behold, it was Leah."
Behold.
The Hebrew word הִנֵּה (hinneh).
Look.
See.
Shock.
Surprise.
Disbelief.
Jacob's first recorded response to waking beside Leah is astonishment.
Not joy.
Not celebration.
Not gratitude.
Shock.
Can you imagine how that must have felt?
Leah enters marriage already knowing she was never the first choice.
She begins her life as a wife under the shadow of rejection.
Yet Scripture reveals something extraordinary.
Genesis 29:31 says:
"When the LORD saw that Leah was hated, He opened her womb."
The Hebrew says:
"וַיַּרְא יְהוָה כִּי שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה"
"Vayar YHWH ki senuah Leah."
The word שְׂנוּאָה (senuah) means hated, unloved, rejected, less loved.
Notice something critical.
Before God acts...
God sees.
The text does not say God heard first.
It does not say God intervened first.
It says God saw.
The God of Scripture is the God who sees.
El Roi.
אֵל רֳאִי
"The God Who Sees Me."
Genesis 16:13.
Long before Leah ever found acceptance, she was fully seen by God.
And maybe someone reading this needs that reminder today.
The world may overlook you.
People may misunderstand you.
The relationship may have ended.
The promotion may have gone to someone else.
The family may not appreciate you.
The church may not recognize your sacrifice.
But God sees every tear no one else notices.
Every prayer no one else hears.
Every disappointment no one else understands.
Nothing is hidden from Him.
Then Leah begins naming her children.
And every name becomes a window into her wounded heart.
Reuben.
רְאוּבֵן
"See, a son."
Because she says:
"The LORD has seen my affliction."
Genesis 29:32.
Then Simeon.
שִׁמְעוֹן
"Hearing."
Because:
"The LORD has heard that I am unloved."
Genesis 29:33.
Then Levi.
לֵוִי
"Attached."
Because:
"Now my husband will become attached to me."
Genesis 29:34.
Do you hear the pain?
She keeps hoping.
Maybe now.
Maybe this child.
Maybe this blessing.
Maybe this accomplishment.
Maybe this sacrifice.
Maybe now someone will finally love me.
And many people still live there.
Trying to earn love.
Trying to deserve acceptance.
Trying to prove their worth.
Trying to become enough.
Yet every human attempt leaves the same emptiness.
Because no human being can heal a wound that only God can touch.
Then everything changes.
Leah gives birth again.
And this time she says something radically different.
Genesis 29:35:
"הַפַּעַם אוֹדֶה אֶת־יְהוָה"
"Hapa'am odeh et-YHWH."
"This time I will praise the LORD."
The word used here is אוֹדֶה (odeh).
Praise.
Thank.
Celebrate.
Worship.
For the first time, Leah's focus shifts.
No mention of Jacob.
No mention of earning love.
No mention of being chosen.
No mention of comparison.
Only God.
And she names her son Judah.
יְהוּדָה
Yehudah.
"Praise."
This is where the story becomes astonishing.
Because centuries later, from the tribe of Judah comes King David.
And centuries after David comes Jesus Christ.
The Messiah.
The Lion of the Tribe of Judah.
Revelation 5:5.
Think about that.
Rachel was beautiful.
Rachel was desired.
Rachel was loved.
Yet God chose Leah's line for the Messiah.
Not because Leah was perfect.
Not because she was stronger.
Not because she deserved it.
But because grace has never operated according to human rankings.
The kingdom of God repeatedly chooses the overlooked.
The forgotten.
The weak.
The rejected.
The unlikely.
The scandalous.
And turns them into vessels of redemption.
That pattern reaches its climax in Jesus.
The prophet Isaiah says:
"He had no beauty or majesty to attract us to Him."
Isaiah 53:2.
The Messiah Himself would understand rejection.
He would be despised.
Mocked.
Abandoned.
Crucified.
The Greek text says:
ἐξουθενημένος
(exouthenēmenos)
Despised.
Rejected.
Treated as nothing.
Jesus entered the pain of Leah so He could redeem every Leah who would ever live.
Every person who feels unwanted.
Every person carrying shame.
Every person convinced they are less than someone else.
Every person exhausted from trying to earn love.
At the cross, Jesus absorbed humanity's rejection so we could receive God's acceptance.
The Gospel is not that you finally become lovable.
The Gospel is that Christ loved you while you were still broken.
Romans 5:8.
The Gospel is not that you finally become worthy.
The Gospel is that Jesus is worthy and gives His righteousness to all who trust Him.
The Gospel is not that you stop being Leah.
The Gospel is that Jesus meets Leah in her pain and transforms her story into something eternal.
Maybe that is why this story refuses to fade.
Because millions still stare into mirrors carrying Leah's wounds.
Still wondering if they matter.
Still wondering if they are enough.
Still wondering if God sees them.
The answer is yes.
He saw Leah.
He sees you.
And if He could take a rejected woman from an ancient scandal and weave her into the lineage of the Savior of the world, then He is more than capable of redeeming every broken chapter of your life.
Be honest.
Did Leah's story expose a hidden wound in your own heart?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
It helps expand Gospel-centered ministry, biblical teaching, discipleship resources, evangelistic outreach, and Christ-centered encouragement to more people around the world.
If you desire to glorify God through helping spread biblical truth, your support genuinely makes a difference.
Because sometimes the greatest evidence of worship is helping more people encounter Jesus.
The woman nobody wanted became part of the story that saved the world.
And maybe the chapter you are ashamed of today is the very chapter God intends to use for His glory tomorrow.
The rejection was real.
But it was never the final author of her story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Lesson I Learned From “Launch Out Into the Deep”
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From “Launch Out Into the Deep”
When Obedience Makes No Sense, When Failure Feels Final, and When Jesus Calls You Beyond the Shore
There are moments in life when God asks us to do something that feels completely unreasonable.
Not sinful.
Not impossible.
Just unreasonable.
Moments when everything we know, everything we have experienced, and everything our emotions are telling us says, “Stay where you are.”
Yet Jesus whispers, “Go deeper.”
That is the lesson I learned from one of the most powerful encounters in all of Scripture.
It begins on the shore of the Sea of Galilee with exhausted fishermen washing empty nets after a long night of failure.
Not a long night of inconvenience.
A long night of disappointment.
A long night of unanswered effort.
A long night where they did everything they knew how to do and still came home empty.
Many of us know exactly what that feels like.
You prayed.
Nothing happened.
You worked.
Nothing changed.
You gave.
Nothing returned.
You trusted.
You got hurt.
You stayed faithful.
The breakthrough never came.
The dream died.
The relationship collapsed.
The business struggled.
The ministry felt fruitless.
The depression stayed.
The temptation remained.
The tears continued.
And eventually, like Peter, you start cleaning up your nets and preparing yourself to accept disappointment as your new normal.
That is exactly where Jesus found Simon Peter.
Luke records the moment:
“Now when he had left speaking, he said unto Simon, Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught.” (Luke 5:4)
The Greek text uses the phrase:
«Ἐπανάγαγε εἰς τὸ βάθος»
(Epanagage eis to bathos)
Literally:
“Put out again into the deep.”
The word βάθος (bathos) means depth, deep water, profound places, places beyond the shoreline of comfort and visibility.
Jesus was not asking Peter to stay near safety.
Jesus was calling him away from it.
That alone should arrest our attention.
Because most believers want the blessing of deep waters while remaining anchored to shallow faith.
We want miracles without risk.
Growth without stretching.
Faith without uncertainty.
Victory without surrender.
Yet throughout Scripture, God repeatedly works in the deep.
Abraham left the familiar.
Moses stepped into impossible leadership.
Joshua crossed impossible waters.
David faced impossible giants.
Mary accepted an impossible pregnancy.
Paul endured impossible suffering.
And Peter was asked to launch into impossible waters.
The command becomes even more shocking when we remember who Peter was.
He was not a hobby fisherman.
He was a professional.
This was his trade.
His expertise.
His livelihood.
If anyone knew where fish were not located, it was Peter.
And he had just spent the entire night proving it.
Yet Jesus gave instructions that contradicted experience, logic, and professional expertise.
Peter's response reveals one of the most beautiful acts of faith in Scripture.
“Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net.” (Luke 5:5)
The phrase “Master” comes from the Greek word:
ἐπιστάτα (epistata)
Meaning commander, chief, one possessing authority.
Peter was essentially saying:
“Everything in me disagrees.
Everything I've experienced argues against this.
Everything I know says this won't work.
But because You said it, I will obey.”
That is faith.
Faith is not believing when evidence agrees.
Faith is obeying when evidence disagrees.
Peter's miracle began the moment his confidence shifted from his experience to Christ's authority.
Many of us are waiting for God to explain Himself before we obey.
But Jesus rarely reveals the entire plan before the first step.
The Kingdom has always operated on trust.
Noah built before rain.
Abraham walked before seeing.
Moses stretched out the rod before the sea opened.
The priests stepped into Jordan before the waters parted.
Peter launched into the deep before the fish appeared.
And perhaps God is asking you to do the same.
Maybe your deep water is forgiveness.
Maybe it is repentance.
Maybe it is surrender.
Maybe it is leaving behind secret sin.
Maybe it is sharing your faith.
Maybe it is starting again after failure.
Maybe it is trusting God after heartbreak.
Maybe it is answering a calling that terrifies you.
Whatever it is, the miracle is not on the shore.
The miracle is in the deep.
Then comes one of the most breathtaking moments in the Gospel narrative.
“And when they had this done, they inclosed a great multitude of fishes: and their net brake.” (Luke 5:6)
Not because Peter discovered something new.
