Rachel had grown up surrounded by these influences.
Though she belonged to the covenant family through marriage, old attachments still lingered.
Isn't that often how transformation works?
A person may genuinely begin following God while still carrying remnants of their old life.
Past fears.
Past wounds.
Past securities.
Past idols.
Many people imagine conversion as an instant removal of every struggle.
The Bible paints a far more realistic picture.
God saves people.
Then He spends a lifetime sanctifying them.
Rachel may have physically left her father's house long before she emotionally left it.
Many believers understand this tension.
Someone may leave destructive relationships but still carry the fear those relationships created.
Someone may leave addiction but still wrestle with the mindset it produced.
Someone may surrender to Christ yet still cling to old sources of comfort when life becomes uncertain.
Rachel was leaving everything familiar behind.
The future was unknown.
The journey was dangerous.
The promises of God required faith.
And faith often feels risky.
Idols feel safer.

Some scholars believe Rachel stole the teraphim because possession of them may have strengthened inheritance claims against Laban's estate. If true, Rachel may have been attempting to secure financially what she feared might otherwise be lost.
Others believe she may have wanted to prevent her father from using them in divination.
Still others suggest she remained emotionally attached to them because they represented familiarity and security.
Scripture does not explicitly tell us her motivation.
Perhaps that silence is intentional.
Because the deeper issue is not why Rachel stole them.
The deeper issue is why human beings continually create them.
An idol is anything we trust more than God.
Money can become an idol.
Success can become an idol.
Relationships can become an idol.
Reputation can become an idol.
Even ministry can become an idol.
Anything we run to for ultimate security instead of Christ becomes a modern teraphim.
What makes this story unforgettable is what happens next.
Laban discovers the idols are missing.
He pursues Jacob.
He searches everywhere.
Then we encounter one of the most dramatic scenes in Genesis.
Rachel hides the idols inside a camel saddle and sits on them.
Genesis 31:35 says:
"Rachel said to her father, 'Do not be angry, my lord, that I cannot stand up in your presence; I am having my period.' So he searched but could not find the household gods."
The irony is astonishing.
The objects that people believed possessed spiritual power were literally sitting beneath a woman pretending they were too insignificant to retrieve.
Moses seems to be making a profound theological statement.
These idols could not protect themselves.
They could not reveal themselves.
They could not save themselves.
They were powerless.
Psalm 115 later echoes the same truth:
"They have mouths, but cannot speak; eyes, but cannot see."
False gods always promise more than they deliver.
They demand devotion but cannot provide salvation.
They require sacrifice but offer no redemption.
They occupy the throne of the heart while being utterly powerless to rescue the soul.
Only Christ can do that.
The tragedy is that Rachel never appears to fully understand this lesson.
Years later, her life ends tragically while giving birth to Benjamin.
Genesis 35:18 records her final moments.
The woman who spent years longing for children dies bringing life into the world.
The woman who once grasped for security loses everything earthly she could hold.
The woman who stole idols eventually stands before the God those idols could never replace.
And that brings us to the Gospel.
Because Rachel's story is not ultimately about Rachel.
It is about us.
We all have our teraphim.
The hidden things we trust.
The secret securities we protect.
The fears we refuse to surrender.
The backup plans we cling to when God's promises seem uncertain.
But then Jesus enters the story.
The Greek New Testament repeatedly uses the word σῴζω (sōzō), meaning "to save," "to rescue," "to deliver."
Jesus did not come merely to improve people.
He came to rescue idolaters.
He came to save people who place their trust in the wrong things.
He came to redeem people who repeatedly choose substitutes over the Savior.
Paul writes:
The Gospel is not the story of perfect people finding God.
The Gospel is the story of God pursuing broken people who keep choosing lesser gods.
That is why the Bible is so honest.
It does not hide the failures of its heroes.
Abraham lied.
Moses doubted.
David fell.
Peter denied Christ.
Rachel stole idols.
Yet God continued writing.
God continued redeeming.
God continued transforming.
Because grace is greater than scandal.
This is the heartbeat of Scripture.
Not human perfection.
Divine redemption.
Not flawless saints.
A flawless Savior.
Not people who never failed.
A God who never stopped pursuing them.
Perhaps you are reading this while carrying your own household idols.
Not carved statues.
But hidden dependencies.
Fear.
Control.
Approval.
Money.
Comfort.
Status.
Success.
The invitation of Christ remains the same today.
Lay them down.
Trust Him fully.
The things you are sitting on cannot save you.
The things you are hiding cannot heal you.
The things you are protecting cannot redeem you.
Only Jesus can.
If this story exposed something hidden in your heart, be honest.
Your testimony may encourage someone else who is quietly fighting the same battle.
Sometimes one shared message becomes the moment God uses to change a life forever.
You never know who needs this reminder that Jesus is still calling people back to Himself.
Because the greatest tragedy is not that Rachel once stole idols.
The greatest tragedy would be hearing Christ call us to freedom while still refusing to let ours go.
And the most beautiful part of the story is that Jesus still welcomes people carrying idols, baggage, wounds, failures, and shame.
He welcomes them.
He forgives them.
He transforms them.
He rewrites them.
The God who pursued Rachel's family is still pursuing hearts today.
The God who redeemed scandal is still redeeming scandal.
The God who brought grace into broken stories is still bringing grace into ours.
One surrendered idol can become the beginning of an entirely new life.
And one encounter with Jesus can change a story forever.
The idols demanded loyalty but never loved you back. Jesus already proved His love at the cross.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Jesus Many People Miss in Revelation
paragraphs:
The Jesus Many People Miss in Revelation
The King Hidden Behind the Fear, the Lamb Hidden Behind the Judgment, the Savior Still Reaching for You
Most people are terrified of Revelation.
Not because they have read it.
Because they have heard about it.
They have heard about beasts.
Antichrists.
Trumpets.
Wars.
Judgments.
Plagues.
Fire.
The end of the world.
And somewhere along the way, countless people quietly concluded that Revelation is primarily a book about destruction.
A book about fear.
A book about wrath.
A book about everything that will happen to everyone else.
Yet what if the greatest tragedy is not misunderstanding the symbols?
What if the greatest tragedy is missing Jesus?
Because Revelation is not ultimately a book about the Antichrist.
It is not a book about beasts.
It is not a book about disasters.
It is not even a book about the end.
It is a book about Christ.
The very first verse announces this truth:
"The Revelation of Jesus Christ..." (Revelation 1:1)
Not the revelation of the beast.
Not the revelation of judgment.
Not the revelation of world events.
The Revelation of Jesus Christ.
The Greek text begins:

Ἀποκάλυψις Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
(Apokalypsis Iēsou Christou)
"Unveiling of Jesus Christ."
The word ἀποκάλυψις (apokalypsis) means unveiling, disclosure, uncovering.
Something hidden is being revealed.
Someone hidden is being revealed.
And that Someone is Jesus.
Many people open Revelation looking for monsters.
God wants them to see His Son.
That changes everything.
Because the Jesus revealed in Revelation is far bigger than the version many people carry in their minds.
Many know the baby in Bethlehem.
Many know the carpenter from Nazareth.
Many know the suffering Savior hanging on a Roman cross.
But Revelation pulls back the curtain and reveals the cosmic King who has always ruled heaven and earth.
John writes:
Then the description unfolds.
His eyes are like blazing fire.
His voice sounds like rushing waters.
His face shines like the sun.
A sharp sword proceeds from His mouth.
This is not a weaker Jesus.
This is not a defeated Jesus.
This is not a frustrated Jesus desperately trying to regain control of a world spinning out of His hands.
This is the risen King.
The exalted Christ.
The sovereign Lord.
John knew Jesus better than almost anyone.
He leaned against His chest during the Last Supper.
He watched Him heal.
He watched Him weep.
He watched Him bleed.
Yet when John saw Him in Revelation, Scripture says:
"When I saw Him, I fell at His feet as though dead." (Revelation 1:17)
The same disciple who once rested against Jesus now collapses before His glory.
Why?
Because there are dimensions of Christ's majesty that human language struggles to contain.
Yet the next words reveal the heart many people miss.
Jesus places His hand upon John.
And says:
"Fear not."
The Greek reads:

Μὴ φοβοῦ
(Mē phobou)
"Stop being afraid."
The terrifyingly glorious King still comforts trembling people.
The holy Judge still touches broken humanity.
The Almighty still speaks tenderness.
That is the Jesus many people miss in Revelation.
He is glorious beyond imagination.
Yet gentle beyond description.
The book repeatedly presents Him as both Lion and Lamb.
John hears about a Lion.
Revelation 5:5:
"Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah."
The Greek:
ὁ λέων ὁ ἐκ τῆς φυλῆς Ἰούδα
The victorious King.
The conquering ruler.
The promised Messiah.
But then John turns to see the Lion.
And what does he see?
A Lamb.
Revelation 5:6 says:
"A Lamb standing, as though it had been slain."
The Greek word is:

ἀρνίον
(arnion)
Little lamb.
The Lion conquers through sacrifice.
The King wins through crucifixion.
Power reveals itself through love.
Victory arrives through wounds.
And suddenly Revelation stops being merely a prophecy book.
It becomes a Gospel book.
Because at the center of heaven's throne room stands a Lamb who still bears evidence of sacrifice.
Even in glory.
Even after resurrection.
Even after ascension.
Jesus never forgets the cross.
The scars remain part of His eternal story.
Just as your scars remain part of yours.
Perhaps that is why so many people connect deeply with Him.
Because He understands pain from the inside.
He understands betrayal.
Rejection.
False accusations.
Loneliness.
Suffering.
Abandonment.
Grief.
Death.
And because He entered those places Himself, He can meet us there.
Maybe that is where you are right now.
Smiling publicly.
Breaking privately.
Posting photographs while carrying wounds nobody sees.
Serving others while secretly wondering if anyone notices your own pain.
You are not invisible to Christ.
The Jesus of Revelation walks among the lampstands.
He sees His churches.
He sees His people.
He sees you.
Nothing escapes His eyes of fire.
Not because He is looking for reasons to condemn.
Because He knows every place healing must still reach.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly describe God as the One who sees.
In Genesis 16:13, Hagar calls Him:

אֵל רֳאִי
(El Roi)
"The God who sees me."
That truth does not disappear in Revelation.
It becomes even more beautiful.
The King of Glory sees you.
Fully.
Completely.
Without illusion.
Without deception.
Without misunderstanding.
And He still loves you.
That may be the most shocking revelation of all.
Not that judgment is coming.
But that mercy has lasted this long.
Not that wrath exists.
But that grace keeps reaching.
Not that humanity deserves punishment.
But that Christ keeps offering salvation.
Peter reminds us:
"The Lord is not slow concerning His promise... but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish." (2 Peter 3:9)
The Jesus of Revelation is not eager to destroy people.
He is eager to save them.
The warnings exist because love warns.
The judgments exist because evil cannot reign forever.
The justice exists because victims deserve vindication.
The final victory exists because darkness does not get the last word.
Jesus does.
And when Revelation reaches its climax, the story becomes breathtakingly personal.
John sees a new heaven and a new earth.
He hears these words:
"Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man."
Then comes one of the most beautiful promises in all Scripture:
"He will wipe away every tear from their eyes." (Revelation 21:4)
Think about that.
Not an angel.
Not a representative.
God Himself.
The Creator of galaxies personally wiping tears.
Every tear.
The ones caused by betrayal.
The ones caused by regret.
The ones caused by addiction.
The ones caused by shame.
The ones caused by loss.
The ones caused by your own failures.
The ones nobody else ever saw.
And suddenly Revelation is no longer a horror story.
It becomes a restoration story.
A redemption story.
A homecoming story.
A story where Jesus makes all things new.
The final chapter of Scripture echoes the heartbeat of the entire Bible.
Not "Run from Me."
Not "Figure it out yourself."
Not "Earn your way back."
Instead Revelation 22:17 declares:
"The Spirit and the Bride say, 'Come.'"
The Greek:

Ἔρχου
(Erchou)
"Come."
One word.
An invitation.
The same Savior who stretched out His arms on a cross still stretches them toward humanity.
Come.
The same Jesus who forgave Peter.
Come.
The same Jesus who restored failures.
Come.
The same Jesus who welcomed sinners.
Come.
The same Jesus who died and rose again.
Come.
The same Jesus revealed in Revelation.
Come.
Maybe you expected Revelation to end with fear.
Instead it ends with invitation.
Because the heart of Jesus has never changed.
And maybe that is the revelation you needed most.
Not merely that He is returning.
But that He is still calling.
Still pursuing.
Still saving.
Still transforming.
Still rewriting stories.
Including yours.
Maybe your life feels like a scandal right now.
A chapter filled with mistakes.
Failures.
Compromise.
Addiction.
Broken relationships.
Hidden sins.
Lingering shame.
But Revelation reminds us that Jesus specializes in impossible endings.
The Lamb who was slain became the King who reigns.
The crucified Savior became the victorious Lord.
The rejected Messiah became the center of heaven's worship.
And if Jesus can rewrite that story, He can rewrite yours.
If this article stirred your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
Let your testimony encourage someone silently scrolling in despair.
Someone's eternity may be closer to hope than you realize.
The Lamb still bears scars because love never forgets who it died to save.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Lust Is Never Satisfied
paragraphs:
Why Lust Is Never Satisfied
The Appetite That Promises Everything, Takes Everything, and Leaves the Soul Starving
There is a hunger inside the human heart that never seems to say, “Enough.”
It whispers in the dark when everyone else is asleep.
It follows people into marriages, relationships, careers, ministries, and even church pews.
It survives broken promises.
It survives guilt.
It survives tears.
It survives consequences.
And every time it is fed, it somehow becomes hungrier.
The Bible calls this reality lust.

Not merely sexual desire, because God created desire and called His creation good (Genesis 1:31). Lust is something deeper and darker. Lust is desire that has escaped God's design and enthroned itself as a master.
That is why people often discover something terrifying.
The fantasy they thought would satisfy them becomes the prison they cannot escape.
The secret they thought would fulfill them becomes the shame they cannot carry.
The pleasure they thought would free them becomes the chain that drags behind them.
Many people spend years believing they have a lust problem when, in reality, they have a worship problem.
Because lust is not primarily about the body.
It is about the heart.
Jesus shocked His listeners when He exposed the true battlefield.
In Matthew 5:28, He said:
“But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
The Greek text uses the phrase:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν (pros to epithymēsai autēn)

The verb ἐπιθυμέω (epithymeō) means more than noticing beauty. It refers to setting one's desire upon something in order to possess it. It is the heart reaching beyond God's boundaries and saying, “I want this for myself regardless of God's will.”
That is why Jesus moves the discussion away from behavior and into worship.
Because before sin is committed with the hands, it has usually been embraced by the heart.
The frightening truth is that lust always disguises itself as a promise.
It promises intimacy.
It delivers isolation.
It promises excitement.
It delivers emptiness.
It promises freedom.
It delivers slavery.
It promises life.
It delivers death.
This pattern is as old as humanity itself.
In Genesis 3, Eve saw the forbidden fruit.
The text says it was “pleasant to the eyes.”
The Hebrew reveals a progression:
תַאֲוָה (ta'avah) — desire, craving, longing.
What began as seeing became wanting.
What became wanting became taking.
What became taking became ruin.
That pattern still exists today.
Lust always starts by convincing us that God is withholding something good.
It is the ancient lie repackaged for every generation.
“God doesn't really want what's best for you.”
“You deserve this.”
“You need this.”
“You cannot be happy without this.”
“Just one look.”
“Just one conversation.”
“Just one secret.”
“Just one compromise.”
But lust never stops at one.
Because lust is fundamentally different from love.
Love gives.
Lust takes.
Love sacrifices.
Lust consumes.
Love seeks another person's good.
Lust seeks personal gratification.
Love becomes fuller when it gives itself away.
Lust becomes emptier the more it receives.
This is why Scripture repeatedly describes sinful desire as something that grows when fed.
Ecclesiastes 1:8 says:
“The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.”
Human desire detached from God possesses no natural stopping point.
It is like pouring water into a bucket with no bottom.
No amount is enough.
No image is enough.
No relationship is enough.
No fantasy is enough.
No success is enough.
No experience is enough.
The problem is not the size of the appetite.
The problem is that the appetite is searching in the wrong place.
Saint Augustine famously wrote:
“Our hearts are restless until they rest in You.”
Thousands of years before modern psychology, Scripture already revealed humanity's deepest crisis.
We were created for God.
Anything else becomes too small.
That is why lust can never satisfy.
The human soul was not designed to be completed by pleasure.
It was designed to be completed by communion with its Creator.
This is exactly what James describes.
James 1:14–15 says:
“But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.”
The Greek word translated “lust” is:
ἐπιθυμία (epithymia)
A powerful craving.
An over-desire.
A desire that has become a ruler.
Notice the progression.
Desire.
Sin.
Death.
The world advertises desire.
Scripture reveals the destination.
And yet there is something even more heartbreaking.
Many believers secretly believe they are beyond restoration.
They carry hidden shame.
Private addictions.
Silent failures.
Memories they cannot erase.
Screens they wish they had never opened.
Conversations they wish they had never started.
Relationships they wish they had never entered.
They assume God is tired of them.
Disappointed in them.
Finished with them.
But the Gospel begins exactly where human hope ends.
The Bible is not a collection of stories about good people impressing God.
It is a collection of stories about sinners being rescued by grace.
Abraham lied.
Jacob deceived.
David committed adultery.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Yet Jesus rewrote their stories.
Because grace is greater than scandal.
This is why our theme matters.
The Gospel does not minimize lust.
It crucifies it.
The Gospel does not excuse sin.
It pays for it.
The Gospel does not merely improve people.
It resurrects them.
When Jesus died on the cross, He was not dying only for respectable sins.
He was dying for hidden sins.
Secret sins.
Embarrassing sins.
Recurring sins.
The sins nobody else knows.
The sins that keep people awake at night.
The sins that whisper, “You will never change.”
And then came the empty tomb.
Because the resurrection announces something extraordinary.
Sin is powerful.
But Christ is greater.
Shame is heavy.
But Christ is stronger.
Addiction is real.
But Christ still delivers.
This is why Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 5:17:
The Greek phrase:
καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis)
means a new creation.
Not repaired.
Not patched.
Not slightly improved.
Made new.
That is the hope of every believer battling lust.
Victory is not found in stronger willpower.
Victory is found in a stronger Savior.
The answer is not merely trying harder.
The answer is surrendering deeper.
The answer is not loving sin less.
The answer is loving Christ more.
Because what captures the heart ultimately controls the life.
And no counterfeit pleasure can compete with the beauty of Jesus Christ.
The more clearly we see Him, the less attractive our idols become.
The more deeply we know Him, the less persuasive temptation sounds.
The more fully we treasure Him, the less power lust possesses.
Maybe you started reading this article because you were curious.
Maybe because you are struggling.
Maybe because you know someone who is.
Maybe because behind the smiles, church attendance, social media posts, and routines, there is a battle nobody sees.
If so, hear this clearly.
You are not hopeless.
You are not beyond redemption.
You are not the exception to God's grace.
The same Jesus who forgave David still forgives.
The same Jesus who restored Peter still restores.
The same Jesus who transformed Paul still transforms.
And the same Jesus who walked out of the grave still breaks chains today.
Perhaps the reason this article feels personal is because the Holy Spirit is gently exposing what has been hidden.
Not to condemn you.
But to free you.
Not to shame you.
But to heal you.
Not to destroy you.
But to rewrite your story.
If this message exposed something you've been carrying, be honest.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
Not to embarrass them, but because truth shared at the right moment can become the beginning of freedom.
You may need this reminder on a difficult day.
Because one day every secret temptation, every hidden battle, every tear of repentance, and every victory of grace will be fully revealed before the throne of God.
And on that day, nobody will celebrate how powerful their self-control was.
They will celebrate how powerful their Savior was.
The greatest miracle is not that Jesus can satisfy a hungry soul.
The greatest miracle is that He still wants hungry souls to come to Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Saul Didn't Begin as a Villain
paragraphs:
Saul Didn't Begin as a Villain
The Most Feared Enemy of the Church Wasn't Born Evil—He Was Convinced He Was Serving God. That Should Terrify Every One of Us.
There is something deeply unsettling about Saul of Tarsus.
Not because he persecuted Christians.
Not because he approved of Stephen's execution.
Not because he dragged believers from their homes, separating families and filling prisons.
Those things are horrifying enough.
But the most terrifying truth about Saul is this:
He believed he was right.
That is what makes his story so unforgettable.

History remembers villains who knowingly embrace evil. Scripture gives us something far more sobering—a man who loved God, studied Scripture, prayed, fasted, defended truth, and yet found himself fighting against the very Messiah he claimed to be waiting for.
That should humble every Christian.
Because if it happened to Saul, we should never assume we are beyond self-deception.
Saul was not introduced in Scripture as a monster.
He was introduced as a brilliant young Pharisee.
Educated.
Disciplined.
Respected.
Passionate.
Absolutely convinced that he was protecting the holiness of Israel.
When Stephen preached that Jesus of Nazareth was the promised Messiah, Saul did not hear hope.
He heard blasphemy.
Acts tells us that those who stoned Stephen laid their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul (Acts 7:58), and immediately afterward Scripture records something chilling:
"And Saul approved of his execution." (Acts 8:1)
Those few words reveal a heart completely persuaded that violence against Christians honored God.
Imagine that.
He wasn't chasing pleasure.
He wasn't driven by greed.
He wasn't building an empire.
He sincerely believed he was defending the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
That is exactly why Jesus later asked him one of the most penetrating questions ever spoken.
Not...
"Why are you persecuting Christians?"
Not...
"Why are you hurting innocent people?"
Instead He said,
"Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?" (Acts 9:4)
Because Jesus is so united with His people that every wound inflicted upon His Church is felt personally by Christ Himself.
That truth alone should change how we treat one another.
Saul's confidence came from years of religious excellence.
He later described himself this way:
"Circumcised the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee... as to righteousness under the law, blameless." (Philippians 3:5–6)
Notice something remarkable.
He never claimed to have been lazy.
He wasn't spiritually indifferent.
He wasn't morally reckless.
He was extraordinarily devoted.
Yet devotion without Christ still leaves a person spiritually blind.
That is one of the central messages of the Gospel.
Religion alone cannot save.
Only Jesus can.

Saul's very name reflects his Jewish identity. In Hebrew it is שָׁאוּל (Sha'ul), meaning "asked for" or "requested," the same name as Israel's first king. His Roman name, Paul (Paulos in Greek, Παῦλος), simply means "small" or "humble." Scripture never says Jesus renamed him. Rather, Acts gradually begins using his Roman name as his ministry increasingly focused on the Gentile world (Acts 13:9). This detail reminds us that the transformation was not in his name but in his heart.
His story reached its turning point on the road to Damascus.
He traveled there carrying official authority to arrest followers of Jesus.
His destination was destruction.
But heaven had another plan.
Luke records:
"Suddenly a light from heaven shone around him." (Acts 9:3)

The Greek word translated "light" is φῶς (phōs), meaning light, radiance, or divine illumination. Throughout the New Testament, phōs often symbolizes God's self-revelation, exposing darkness and revealing truth (John 1:4–9). Saul was not merely startled by brightness; he was confronted by the glory of the risen Christ.
Then came the voice.
"Σαούλ, Σαούλ, τί με διώκεις;" (Saoul, Saoul, ti me diōkeis?)
Translated literally:
"Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?"
The Greek verb διώκω (diōkō) means to pursue, chase down, persecute, or relentlessly hunt. Saul thought he was pursuing heretics. In reality, he was pursuing the Lord Himself.
The response is heartbreaking.
"Who are You, Lord?"
Not because Saul lacked intelligence.
Because everything he thought he knew suddenly collapsed.
Then came the answer that changed history forever.
"I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting."
One sentence.
One revelation.
One encounter.
Everything changed.
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not begin with condemnation.
He did not immediately recite every sin Saul had committed.
He first revealed Himself.
Because true repentance begins when we see Christ as He truly is.
The Hebrew Scriptures had long anticipated this reality. In Isaiah 53:5 we read:
וְהוּא מְחֹלָל מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ (Vehu mecholal mippesha'einu)
"He was pierced because of our transgressions."

The Servant whom Israel awaited had indeed come—not as a political conqueror, but as the suffering Messiah who bore humanity's sin. Saul knew Isaiah. Yet until he encountered Jesus, he had not understood that the prophecy pointed to Him.
Grace often arrives where judgment seems most deserved.
Saul deserved justice.
Instead, he received mercy.
The man who hunted Christians became one.
The man who imprisoned believers wrote letters that now strengthen believers around the world.
The man who tried to silence the Gospel became its greatest missionary.
Only Jesus writes stories like that.
Some people wonder whether Saul's conversion was too dramatic to be believable.
Yet that is precisely the point.
The Gospel is not merely about improving people.
It is about making them new.
As Paul later wrote:
"Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come." (2 Corinthians 5:17)
The Greek phrase καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis) means "a new creation"—not merely repaired or upgraded, but something qualitatively new. The Gospel does not simply polish a life; it recreates it.
Perhaps the most beautiful irony in Saul's story is found in the meaning of the Gospel itself.
The Greek word εὐαγγέλιον (euangelion) means "good news."
Not good advice.
Not self-improvement.
Not religious achievement.
Good news.
News announces what has already been accomplished.
Jesus accomplished what sinners never could.
That is why salvation is by grace through faith (Ephesians 2:8–9), not by works, lest anyone should boast.

Saul spent years believing righteousness could be attained through strict observance of the Law. After meeting Christ, he understood that the Law reveals sin but cannot justify the sinner (Romans 3:20). Justification comes through faith in Jesus Christ, who fulfilled the Law perfectly and bore its curse on our behalf (Galatians 3:13).
Perhaps this is where Saul's story intersects with yours.
Maybe you have never arrested Christians.
Maybe you have never breathed threats against the Church.
But have you ever mistaken religious activity for a relationship with Christ?
Have you ever defended traditions while neglecting love?
Have you ever assumed that because you know about God, you truly know Him?
Saul reminds us that sincerity is not enough.
Truth matters.
And truth is ultimately found in a Person.
Jesus said,
"I am the way, and the truth, and the life." (John 14:6)
Notice He did not merely teach truth.
He is Truth.

If you have wandered, the same Savior who met Saul on the Damascus road still calls sinners to Himself today. His grace is not reserved for those with spotless records. It is extended to all who repent and believe the Gospel. No past is beyond His redemption, and no heart is too hardened for His transforming power.
If this story has exposed something hidden in your own heart, don't keep it there. Be honest before God. Your words may encourage another person who is quietly wrestling with the same questions.

Your support helps us create Christ-centered articles, devotionals, discipleship resources, and Gospel content that reaches more people with the hope of Jesus. More importantly, your partnership is an act of stewardship that helps advance Gospel-centered ministry.
Because in the end, Saul's story was never really about Saul.
It has always been about Jesus.
The Savior who turns persecutors into preachers.
The Redeemer who transforms enemies into family.
The King who replaces shame with purpose.
The Shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to pursue the one.
The Author who still takes lives that seem ruined beyond repair and writes endings no human could ever imagine.
Scandal is never the final chapter when Christ holds the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Did Moses Struggle with Pride?
paragraphs:
Did Moses Struggle with Pride?
The Hidden Battle That Nearly Cost the Humblest Man on Earth Everything
What if one of the greatest men in Scripture wrestled with the very thing most believers refuse to admit still lives inside them?
Not lust.
Not greed.
Not unbelief.
Pride.
The uncomfortable kind.
The subtle kind.
The kind that hides behind good intentions, spiritual success, leadership experience, ministry accomplishments, and years of walking with God.
The kind that can quietly grow in the heart while everyone around you assumes you're holy.
Because if pride could find its way into the life of Moses, it can find its way into ours.
And that realization should stop every one of us in our tracks.
Most Christians know Moses as the great deliverer of Israel.
The man who stood before Pharaoh.
The man through whom God split the Red Sea.
The man who received the Torah on Mount Sinai.
The man who spoke with God "face to face" as a friend speaks with a friend.
Yet Scripture records one shocking moment that still echoes through history.
One moment.
One outburst.
One decision.
And Moses lost the privilege of entering the Promised Land.
That should make every believer lean in.
Because God is not trying to embarrass Moses.
God is warning us.
The story unfolds in Numbers 20.
Israel is once again complaining about water.
After decades of witnessing miracles, the people are still grumbling.
Still accusing.
Still doubting.
Still acting as if God has abandoned them.
Moses and Aaron fall before the Lord.
God gives a clear instruction.
Speak to the rock.
Not strike it.
Speak to it.
The Hebrew text is remarkably direct.

"וְדִבַּרְתֶּם אֶל־הַסֶּלַע"
(ve-dibbartem el-ha-sela)
"Speak to the rock."
Yet Moses does something different.
Standing before the rebellious congregation, he says:

"שִׁמְעוּ־נָא הַמֹּרִים"
(shim'u-na ha-morim)
"Hear now, you rebels."
Then comes the statement that should make every reader pause.

"הֲמִן־הַסֶּלַע הַזֶּה נוֹצִיא לָכֶם מָיִם"
(ha-min ha-sela hazeh notzi lakhem mayim)
"Shall we bring water for you out of this rock?"
Notice the word.
"We."
Not God.
"We."
Then Moses strikes the rock twice.
Water pours out.
The people drink.
The miracle still happens.
But God is not pleased.
In fact, He is angry.
Many readers have wondered why the punishment seems so severe.
After all, Moses was under pressure.
The people were exhausting.
The miracle succeeded.
Water came out.
What was the real issue?
God Himself explains.

"Because you did not trust in Me to uphold Me as holy in the eyes of the people of Israel..."
(Numbers 20:12)
The problem was not merely striking the rock.
The deeper issue was that Moses misrepresented God.
For a brief but devastating moment, Moses placed himself at the center of what belonged entirely to the Lord.
Was this pride?
Scripture never explicitly says, "Moses became proud."
But the evidence forces us to ask the question.
The Bible describes Moses as:

"Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all people who were on the face of the earth."
(Numbers 12:3)
The Hebrew word is:

"עָנָו"
(anav)
It describes someone who is lowly before God, dependent upon Him, surrendered to Him.
Yet humility is not something you achieve once and keep forever.
Humility is something you continually choose.
Even the humblest man on earth can stumble if he stops depending on God.
That should both humble and encourage us.
Because many believers assume that maturity removes temptation.
It does not.
Spiritual maturity often changes the form temptation takes.
Young believers may struggle with obvious sins.
Older believers may struggle with invisible ones.
Recognition.
Influence.
Control.
Self-importance.
The need to be right.
The desire for credit.
The temptation to believe God needs them.
And that is where pride becomes most dangerous.
Not when it shouts.
When it whispers.
Moses had spent decades carrying an impossible burden.
Leading difficult people.
Enduring constant criticism.
Interceding for rebels.
Sacrificing comfort.
Bearing responsibility.
Could years of pressure have produced frustration?
Certainly.
Could frustration have opened the door for pride?
Possibly.
Could pride and anger have become intertwined?
Scripture strongly suggests they did.
Because pride often reveals itself when our authority is challenged.
When people do not appreciate us.
When our sacrifices go unnoticed.
When we feel justified in our anger.
The truth is that pride rarely announces itself.
It disguises itself as righteousness.
That is why so many believers fail to recognize it.
The Pharisees were proud and thought they were defending truth.
The older brother in Jesus' parable was proud and thought he was being faithful.
Peter was proud and thought he was being loyal.
Even after walking on water, Peter eventually declared:
"Even if all fall away, I never will."
A few hours later he denied Christ three times.
Pride always overestimates itself.
Humility always depends on God.
The Greek word often associated with humility in the New Testament is:

"ταπεινοφροσύνη"
(tapeinophrosynē)
It literally means lowliness of mind.
Not self-hatred.
Not insecurity.
Not weakness.
It is seeing yourself accurately before God.
Nothing more.
Nothing less.
And that is where Moses' story becomes deeply personal.
Because most of us are not worried about becoming Pharaoh.
We are worried about surviving another week.
Paying bills.
Raising children.
Healing from betrayal.
Fighting temptation.
Leading ministries.
Serving families.
Navigating disappointment.
Yet pride sneaks into ordinary lives every day.
When we refuse correction.
When we need recognition.
When we compare ourselves to others.
When we secretly believe we deserve better.
When we make God's work about our reputation.
When our identity becomes tied to our achievements rather than Christ.
The scandal is not that Moses struggled.
The scandal is that any of us think we are incapable of the same thing.
Yet this is where the Gospel changes everything.
Because Moses' story does not end in failure.
It ends in grace.
Years after his death, another mountain appears.
Another glorious moment.
Another revelation.
This time it is not Sinai.
It is the Mount of Transfiguration.
And standing beside Jesus is Moses.
The man who failed.
The man who struck the rock.
The man who never entered the earthly Promised Land.
Now standing in glory with the Messiah Himself.
What a picture of redemption.
What a picture of grace.
What a picture of the Gospel.
Failure did not get the final word.
Jesus did.
This is why Christianity is unlike every false religion in the world.
The Bible never hides the failures of its heroes.
Noah got drunk.
Abraham lied.
Jacob deceived.
David committed adultery.
Peter denied Christ.
Moses failed.
Yet God keeps writing.
Keeps redeeming.
Keeps restoring.
Keeps transforming.
Because our hope is not found in flawless people.
Our hope is found in a flawless Savior.
Even Moses ultimately points beyond himself.
In 1 Corinthians 10, Paul explains that the rock in the wilderness pointed to Christ.
The rock was never the hero.
Moses was never the hero.
Israel was never the hero.
Jesus was always the hero.
The One who would be struck for our sins.
The One who would provide living water.
The One who would satisfy thirsty souls forever.
The One who takes proud rebels and turns them into redeemed children.
Maybe that is why this story still grips us thousands of years later.
Because we recognize ourselves in it.
We know what it feels like to be frustrated.
We know what it feels like to fail.
We know what it feels like to let God down.
We know what it feels like to discover ugly things hiding in our hearts.
But we also know what it feels like to be pursued by grace.
The same grace that restored Peter.
The same grace that transformed Paul.
The same grace that welcomed Moses into glory.
The same grace that still calls your name today.
Maybe pride has been hiding beneath your success.
Maybe beneath your ministry.
Maybe beneath your pain.
Maybe beneath your accomplishments.
Maybe beneath your wounds.
Ask God to reveal it.
Not to condemn you.
To heal you.
Because humility is not thinking less of yourself.
Humility is thinking of Christ more.
And when Christ becomes greater, pride begins to lose its grip.
Be honest.
This probably hit harder than you expected.
The same hand that wrote grace over Moses' failure is still writing over your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He Didn't Mean What You Think He Meant
paragraphs:
He Didn't Mean What You Think He Meant
The Shocking Deeper Meaning of “Turn the Other Cheek” That Changes Everything
Most people think Jesus was teaching weakness.
That is why so many Christians struggle with His words.
They read them. They quote them. They even admire them.
But deep inside, something feels wrong.

Because when life punches you in the mouth, betrays your trust, humiliates your name, abuses your kindness, destroys your reputation, or wounds your heart, “turn the other cheek” sounds less like wisdom and more like surrender.
It sounds like becoming a doormat.
It sounds like allowing evil to win.
It sounds like letting injustice continue unchecked.
And because of that misunderstanding, countless people either reject Christ's teaching altogether or spend their lives trying to obey words they never truly understood.
But what if Jesus was saying something far more revolutionary?
What if “turn the other cheek” is not a command to become weaker?
What if it is actually a declaration of spiritual strength so powerful that it exposes evil without becoming evil?
What if these words reveal one of the greatest examples of divine courage ever spoken?

And what if understanding them correctly could transform your marriage, your family, your enemies, your wounds, your bitterness, your social media arguments, your workplace conflicts, and even your relationship with God?
Let's go deeper.
The words appear in Matthew 5:39:
"But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also."
At first glance, many assume Jesus is prohibiting all forms of resistance.
Yet the original language immediately reveals something deeper.
The Greek text reads:
"ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν μὴ ἀντιστῆναι τῷ πονηρῷ"
Egō de legō hymin mē antistēnai tō ponērō.
The key word is "ἀντιστῆναι" (antistēnai).
This word does not simply mean resisting in a general sense.
It often carries the idea of violent retaliation, armed opposition, revenge-driven resistance, or responding to evil with evil.
Jesus is not commanding passivity.
He is forbidding revenge.
There is a massive difference.
Scripture consistently affirms justice.
Scripture consistently condemns oppression.
Scripture consistently protects the vulnerable.
Jesus Himself confronted hypocrisy.
He overturned tables in the Temple.
He rebuked corrupt religious leaders.
He exposed evil publicly.
He was never passive toward sin.
So what exactly is happening here?
The answer is hidden in one small detail most readers overlook.
Jesus specifically mentions the RIGHT cheek.
"Whoever slaps you on your right cheek..."
Think about that.
Most people are right-handed.
For a right-handed person to strike another person's RIGHT cheek, the most natural action would be a backhanded slap.
Not a punch.
Not an assault intended to kill.
A backhand.
In the ancient world, a backhanded slap was an insult.
It was a gesture of humiliation.
A statement of superiority.
A master to a servant.
A Roman soldier to a conquered people.
A wealthy person to someone considered beneath them.
The issue is not primarily physical injury.
The issue is public degradation.
Shame.
Dishonor.
Scandal.
Jesus is speaking into a culture built upon status, pride, power, and public humiliation.
Now everything changes.
When Jesus says:
"Turn to him the other also,"
He is not saying:
"Keep abusing me."
He is not saying:
"I have no value."
He is not saying:
"Evil has won."
He is not saying:
"Justice doesn't matter."
Instead, He is teaching a form of courageous nonviolent resistance.
Imagine the scene.
A powerful man backhands a servant.
The servant then turns the other cheek.
Suddenly the aggressor faces a dilemma.
The other cheek cannot easily be struck with another backhand.
To strike it, the aggressor would have to use a different form of blow.
The servant has silently refused humiliation.
Without striking back.
Without surrendering dignity.
Without becoming violent.
Without becoming hateful.
Without becoming what wounded them.
The victim stands before the aggressor as an equal human being bearing the image of God.
The act exposes the evil.
It unmasks the heart.
It forces a choice.
And that is exactly how Jesus confronted darkness throughout His ministry.
Not by mirroring evil.
But by revealing it.
This pattern appears throughout Scripture.
When Jesus stood before those who falsely accused Him, He did not retaliate.
When soldiers mocked Him, He did not curse them.
When they nailed Him to a cross, He did not call down legions of angels.
Instead He prayed:
"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." (Luke 23:34)
This was not weakness.
This was power under perfect control.
The world sees power as domination.
Jesus reveals power as self-mastery.
The world sees victory as crushing enemies.
Jesus reveals victory as overcoming evil with good.
The world sees strength as revenge.
Jesus reveals strength as refusing to surrender your soul to hatred.
And perhaps nowhere is this clearer than in the cross itself.
The cross looked like defeat.
It looked like humiliation.
It looked like scandal.
The Messiah stripped naked.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Abandoned.
Crucified.
Yet what appeared to be the greatest scandal in history became the greatest display of grace the world has ever known.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
This is why our message has always been:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
The betrayal becomes redemption.
The wound becomes testimony.
The ashes become beauty.
The sinner becomes a saint.
The outcast becomes a child of God.
The cross becomes salvation.
And perhaps some of us need to hear that today.
Because someone humiliated you.
Someone lied about you.
Someone abandoned you.
Someone shattered your trust.
Someone wounded you in ways words can barely describe.
You replay the conversation.
You rehearse the revenge.
You imagine the perfect comeback.
You carry the bitterness.
You carry the anger.
You carry the burden.
And slowly, the wound begins shaping your identity.
But Jesus offers another way.
Not because justice doesn't matter.
Not because pain isn't real.
But because your soul matters more than your revenge.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending evil never happened.
Forgiveness means refusing to allow evil to become your master.
Turning the other cheek is not surrendering your dignity.
It is reclaiming it through Christ.
It is declaring:
"You may wound me, but you will not define me."
"You may insult me, but you will not own my heart."
"You may betray me, but you will not turn me into a person who hates."
That kind of freedom terrifies darkness.
Because darkness knows how to handle violence.
Darkness knows how to handle rage.
Darkness knows how to handle revenge.
Darkness does not know what to do with a soul transformed by Jesus Christ.
The earliest believers understood this.
Many suffered persecution.
Many lost homes.
Many lost livelihoods.
Many lost their lives.
Yet the Gospel spread across the Roman Empire because Christians refused to become what persecuted them.
The blood of the martyrs became the seed of the Church.
The world expected retaliation.
Instead it witnessed grace.
The world expected hatred.
Instead it encountered forgiveness.
The world expected scandal.
Instead it found redemption.
And two thousand years later, the same Savior still transforms lives.
Maybe your story feels like a scandal right now.
Maybe you carry regret nobody knows.
Maybe your failures haunt your nights.
Maybe shame follows you into every room.
Maybe you have spent years trying to outrun your past.
But Jesus specializes in rewriting stories.
The woman caught in adultery thought her story was over.
The thief on the cross thought his story was over.
Peter thought his story was over after denying Christ.
Paul thought his story was over while persecuting believers.
Yet grace rewrote every chapter.
Because that is what Jesus does.
The Gospel is not the story of perfect people finding God.
It is the story of a perfect Savior finding broken people.
And if He can rewrite their stories, He can rewrite yours.
If this message stirred your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
Have you ever struggled to forgive someone who deeply hurt you?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
Because every share spreads the Gospel.
Every comment builds community.
Every save preserves truth.
And every transformed life brings glory to Jesus Christ.
One day you will realize the greatest victory was never getting even—it was becoming more like Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Revelation Begins With Jesus, Not the Antichrist
paragraphs:
Revelation Begins With Jesus, Not the Antichrist
The Most Misunderstood Book in the Bible Was Never Meant to Make You Fear the Future—It Was Written to Make You Fall in Love With Christ
Most people open Revelation looking for the Antichrist.
God opens Revelation by showing us Jesus.
That single mistake has caused millions of believers to read the final book of Scripture through fear instead of worship.
They search for hidden codes.
They search for world leaders.
They search for economic systems.
They search for signs.
Meanwhile, the One standing at the center of the entire book waits to be seen.
The tragedy is that many Christians can spend years studying Revelation and still miss the very Person Revelation was written to reveal.
The book does not begin with the Antichrist.
It does not begin with the Beast.
It does not begin with the Mark.
It does not begin with judgment.
It does not begin with Armageddon.
It begins with Jesus Christ.
The very first words of Revelation are impossible to ignore:
"The Revelation of Jesus Christ..." (Revelation 1:1)
In Greek, the phrase is:

Ἀποκάλυψις Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
(Apokalypsis Iēsou Christou)
The word Apokalypsis does not mean catastrophe.
It does not mean destruction.
It does not mean apocalypse in the modern Hollywood sense.
It means unveiling, disclosure, revealing, uncovering something previously hidden.
The final book of Scripture is literally called:
"The Unveiling of Jesus Christ."
Not the unveiling of the Antichrist.
Not the unveiling of the Beast.
Not the unveiling of global chaos.
The unveiling of Jesus.
That changes everything.
Because if Revelation is primarily about Jesus, then every chapter must be read through Him.
Every judgment reveals His holiness.
Every promise reveals His faithfulness.
Every warning reveals His mercy.
Every victory reveals His sovereignty.
Every page reveals His glory.
For many believers, Revelation became a source of anxiety because someone taught them to start with the wrong character.
Imagine watching a movie and focusing only on the villain while ignoring the hero.
Imagine reading a love story while obsessing over the antagonist.
Imagine standing before a masterpiece while staring only at the frame.
That is what happens when Revelation becomes more about the Antichrist than Christ.
The enemy loves that confusion.
Because fear-filled Christians rarely become effective witnesses.
But believers captivated by Jesus become impossible to silence.
When the Apostle John received this revelation, he was not sitting in comfort.
He was exiled on Patmos.
Alone.
Isolated.
Rejected by the world.
Yet in the middle of suffering, heaven did not show him the power of Rome.
Heaven showed him Jesus.
John writes:
Then suddenly he hears a voice.
Not merely loud.
Not merely commanding.
But overwhelming.
The voice of the risen Christ.
When John turns, he sees something that changes him forever.
His eyes are like fire.
His voice is like many waters.
His face shines like the sun.
His authority shakes creation.
His holiness overwhelms the human soul.
The same disciple who once leaned against Jesus at the Last Supper now collapses at His feet.
John writes:
This is not because Jesus became less loving.
It is because John now sees what was hidden behind the veil of flesh.
The carpenter from Nazareth is also the King of Kings.
The Lamb is also the Lion.
The Savior is also the Judge.
The One crucified is also glorified.
And then comes one of the most beautiful moments in all Scripture.
Jesus places His hand on John.
The glorified Christ touches a trembling man.
And He says:
"Fear not."
In Greek:

Μὴ φοβοῦ
(Mē phobou)
Do not fear.
The same Jesus whose glory causes men to collapse is the same Jesus who comforts the broken.
This is the heartbeat of Revelation.
Majesty and mercy.
Power and compassion.
Holiness and grace.
Justice and love.
The world often tries to separate these truths.
Jesus never does.
The Hebrew Scriptures anticipated this moment centuries earlier.
Isaiah saw a glimpse of God's glory and cried:

הוֹי־לִי כִּי־נִדְמֵיתִי
(Hoy-li ki nidmeiti)
"Woe is me, for I am ruined." (Isaiah 6:5)
Whenever sinful humanity encounters divine holiness, the response is the same.
Not pride.
Not self-confidence.
Not self-esteem.
Repentance.
Yet every genuine encounter with God's holiness is followed by grace.
Isaiah receives cleansing.
John receives comfort.
Peter receives restoration.
And sinners receive a Savior.
This pattern runs through the entire Bible.
From Genesis to Revelation.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
That is why Revelation should not terrify believers.
It should transform believers.
The central message is not that darkness becomes stronger.
The central message is that Jesus remains sovereign.
Empires rise and fall.
Kings come and go.
Economies collapse.
Cultures change.
False prophets appear.
Persecution increases.
But Christ remains enthroned.
Nothing in Revelation suggests that evil is winning.
In fact, the opposite is true.
Every chapter moves history toward the complete victory of Jesus Christ.
The Lamb never loses control.
The throne never becomes vacant.
The King never panics.
The Father never abandons His plan.
The Holy Spirit never stops working.
The Church never stops belonging to Christ.
The cross never loses its power.
And grace never stops reaching sinners.
Perhaps that is why so many people avoid Revelation.
Not because it is confusing.
But because it confronts us.
Revelation reminds us that Jesus is not merely a life coach.
Not merely a moral teacher.
Not merely an inspirational figure.
He is Lord.
The Greek word repeatedly used is:

Κύριος
(Kyrios)
Lord.
Master.
Supreme authority.
Owner.
King.
And every human heart must answer the same question.
Who sits on the throne?
Jesus?
Or something else?
For some, it is money.
For others, relationships.
Success.
Pleasure.
Politics.
Reputation.
Comfort.
Control.
But Revelation relentlessly pulls our eyes back to the throne.
Because whoever occupies the throne of your heart determines the direction of your life.
Maybe that is why this message feels personal.
Because deep down, every one of us knows what it feels like to chase lesser kings.
We know what it feels like to build identities around things that eventually fail us.
We know what it feels like to search for meaning in places that leave us empty.
We know what it feels like to smile publicly while quietly carrying fear.
But Revelation points us toward the One who cannot fail.
The One who conquered death.
The One who defeated sin.
The One who promises:
"I am the Alpha and the Omega."
In Greek:

Ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Ἄλφα καὶ τὸ Ὦ
(Egō eimi to Alpha kai to Ō)
The beginning and the end.
The first and the last.
The author and finisher of history.
The One who writes the first sentence and the final chapter.
And if He holds history in His hands, He can hold your life too.
The greatest scandal in human history was not political corruption.
It was humanity's rebellion against God.
The greatest grace in human history was not self-improvement.
It was Jesus stepping into that rebellion and carrying our punishment to the cross.
The same Christ revealed in Revelation is the same Christ crucified at Calvary.
The scars remain.
The victory remains.
The invitation remains.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Him.
Trust Him.
Worship Him.
Because Revelation was never written merely to satisfy curiosity about the future.
It was written to create devotion to Jesus in the present.
And perhaps today, that is exactly what your heart needs.
Not another prediction.
Not another theory.
Not another headline.
Not another fear-driven message.
You need Jesus.
The One Revelation unveils.
The One who still says, "Fear not."
The One who still saves.
The One who still restores.
The One who still rewrites broken stories.
The One who still turns scandal into grace.
If this article helped you see Jesus more clearly, don't keep it to yourself.
What part of Revelation has impacted your walk with Jesus the most?
Your testimony may encourage someone else today.
Every article, devotional, teaching resource, and discipleship tool exists to point people toward Jesus Christ and the transforming power of the Gospel.
Most importantly, your support helps expand Gospel-centered outreach and allows more people to encounter the life-changing message of Jesus Christ.
One day every headline will be forgotten, every empire will be dust, every prophecy fulfilled, and every eye fixed on the One Revelation was revealing all along.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Sanballat Never Attacks Before You Move
paragraphs:
Sanballat Never Attacks Before You Move
The Hidden Lesson From Nehemiah That Explains Why Critics Always Arrive When God Begins Building Something Through You
There is a painful moment almost every believer experiences but rarely understands.
You finally decide to obey God.
You finally leave the old life behind.
You finally forgive.
You finally start reading Scripture consistently.
You finally begin serving.
You finally step into the calling God has been whispering into your heart for years.
And suddenly...
The criticism begins.
The accusations multiply.
People misunderstand your motives.
Old friends become distant.
Unexpected opposition rises.
You wonder...
"Did I miss God's will?"
Maybe the better question is this:
Why did the opposition wait until you started building?
That is exactly where Sanballat enters the story.
Many Christians know Nehemiah for rebuilding Jerusalem's walls.
Fewer remember the names of the men determined to stop him.
Yet one of them has become one of Scripture's greatest lessons about spiritual resistance.
His name was Sanballat.
And chances are...
You've already met him.
Not the historical man.
But the spirit behind the criticism.
The pattern.
The strategy.
The opposition that always seems to appear whenever God's people begin moving forward.
Nehemiah begins with heartbreak.

Jerusalem—the city where God chose to place His Name—lay in ruins. Its walls were broken down, and its gates had been burned with fire (Nehemiah 1:3). For ancient Israel, walls represented protection, stability, dignity, and covenant identity. Their destruction was more than military defeat; it symbolized deep national shame.
Nehemiah did not respond with anger first.
He responded with tears.
He fasted.
He prayed.
He confessed not only Israel's sins but identified himself with them.
Only after prayer did he move into action.
That order matters.
Prayer before planning.
Dependence before strategy.
God before accomplishment.
When King Artaxerxes granted Nehemiah permission to rebuild Jerusalem (Nehemiah 2), everything appeared to be falling perfectly into place.
Until one verse quietly changes the atmosphere.

"But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant and Geshem the Arab heard of it, they were greatly displeased that someone had come to seek the welfare of the people of Israel." (Nehemiah 2:10, ESV)
Notice something remarkable.
Sanballat was angry...
before a single wall had been rebuilt.
Progress had barely started.
Yet opposition had already arrived.
Why?
Because darkness often recognizes God's work before God's people fully understand what He is doing.
Sanballat's problem was never bricks.
His problem was restoration.

The Hebrew word translated "wall" throughout Nehemiah is חוֹמָה (ḥōmāh). It refers not merely to stone architecture but to a fortified boundary that protects a people and establishes security. Rebuilding the ḥōmāh symbolized the restoration of covenant life under God's care.
Sanballat understood something many believers forget.
If Jerusalem stood again...
Israel's hope would stand again.
If the walls rose...
Worship would rise.
If worship returned...
God's people would regain their identity.
The enemy has always feared restored people more than broken people.
This pattern continues throughout Scripture.
When Moses rose, Pharaoh opposed him.
When David was anointed, Saul hunted him.
When Elijah confronted idolatry, Jezebel pursued him.
When Jesus began proclaiming the Kingdom, religious leaders plotted against Him.
When the apostles preached Christ crucified and risen, persecution spread.
Opposition often follows obedience—not because obedience failed, but because it matters.
Jesus Himself warned His disciples:
"If the world hates you, know that it has hated Me before it hated you." (John 15:18)

The Greek verb translated "hates" is μισεῖ (misei) from μισέω (miseō), meaning to reject, detest, or oppose with settled hostility. Jesus never promised universal approval. He promised faithful presence.
Sanballat first chose ridicule.
Nehemiah 4 records him mocking the builders:
"What are these feeble Jews doing?"
He attacked their strength.
Their intelligence.
Their project.
Their future.
Mockery is one of Satan's oldest weapons because ridicule attempts to make obedience look foolish.
If mockery fails...
Fear comes next.
Sanballat later planned violence.
Then intimidation.
Then distraction.
Then false accusations.
Then character assassination.
The tactics changed.
The goal never did.
Stop the work.
One of the enemy's favorite strategies appears in Nehemiah 6.
Sanballat repeatedly invited Nehemiah to meet with him.
It sounded reasonable.
Peaceful.
Diplomatic.
Nehemiah saw through it.
He answered:
"I am doing a great work and cannot come down." (Nehemiah 6:3)
The Hebrew phrase מְלָאכָה גְדוֹלָה (melākhāh gedōlāh) literally means "a great work."
Notice what Nehemiah refused to do.
He would not come down.
Sometimes the greatest victory is refusing unnecessary battles.
Not every accusation deserves an answer.
Not every critic deserves your attention.
Not every invitation deserves your time.
Sometimes spiritual maturity sounds like:
"I cannot come down."
Jesus modeled this perfectly.
False witnesses accused Him.
Crowds misunderstood Him.
Religious leaders slandered Him.
Pilate questioned Him.
Yet Isaiah had already prophesied:
"Like a sheep before its shearers is silent, so He opened not His mouth." (Isaiah 53:7)
Silence is not always weakness.
Sometimes silence is confidence that God is the final Judge.
One of the most overlooked details in Nehemiah is that the builders worked with one hand while holding a weapon in the other (Nehemiah 4:17).
Building and battling happened simultaneously.
Many believers expect one season for growth...
and another for spiritual warfare.
Scripture rarely separates them.
The moment you build your marriage...
opposition appears.
The moment you restore your family...
opposition appears.
The moment you commit to purity...
opposition appears.
The moment you forgive...
opposition appears.
The moment you begin sharing Christ...
opposition appears.
Not because God abandoned you.
But because kingdom work always threatens the kingdom of darkness.
The apostle Paul wrote:
"For a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries." (1 Corinthians 16:9)
Notice that Paul did not say the adversaries proved the door was closed.
The adversaries confirmed the opportunity mattered.
Many people assume criticism means they should stop.
Nehemiah teaches the opposite.
Sometimes criticism is evidence that the wall is actually rising.
Yet Scripture also gives an important caution.
Not every critic is a Sanballat.

The book of Proverbs repeatedly teaches that wise correction is a gift (Proverbs 9:8–9; 12:1). Faithful rebuke from godly brothers and sisters can expose sin, refine character, and lead us toward greater holiness. We must never dismiss biblical correction simply because it is uncomfortable.
How do we tell the difference?
Godly correction seeks repentance and restoration.
Sanballat sought discouragement and destruction.
One points you toward Christ.
The other tries to pull you away from obedience.
Discernment requires humility.
The greatest scandal in history was not Sanballat's opposition.
It was Calvary.
The perfectly holy Son of God was mocked, beaten, falsely accused, condemned, crucified, and displayed publicly in shame.
Isaiah had foretold it centuries earlier:
"He was pierced for our transgressions; He was crushed for our iniquities." (Isaiah 53:5)
The New Testament reveals why.
Paul writes:

The Greek phrase ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν (hyper hēmōn) means "on our behalf" or "for our sake." Christ stood in the place of guilty sinners. At the cross, He bore the judgment we deserved so that all who repent and trust in Him might receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and the gift of eternal life—not by works, but by grace through faith (Ephesians 2:8–9).
The resurrection declared that sin, death, and Satan had been defeated. Because Christ lives, His people can endure opposition with hope, knowing that no criticism can overturn God's saving purpose.
That is the heartbeat of our theme:
Perhaps today your Sanballat is not a person.
Perhaps it is fear.
Shame.
Failure.
A painful memory.
A voice telling you that rebuilding is pointless.
But the God who strengthened Nehemiah still strengthens His people. The Lord Jesus Christ is still building His Church (Matthew 16:18), and He is still restoring broken lives through His gospel.

If you have never turned to Christ, today is the day. Repent of your sin. Trust wholly in His finished work on the cross and His victorious resurrection. He does not merely repair lives—He makes all things new.
And if you are already His disciple, keep building.
Do not come down.
Do not surrender your calling because someone laughed.
Do not abandon obedience because someone misunderstood you.
The wall God has called you to build is too important.
One faithful stone laid in obedience may outlast a lifetime of criticism.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Sin That Wears Your Face
paragraphs:
The Sin That Wears Your Face
Why Pride Is So Difficult to Detect—and How Jesus Still Rewrites the Story You Thought Was Beyond Redemption
You probably came here expecting an article about arrogant people.
The loud ones.
The boastful ones.
The people who always think they're right.
The people who never apologize.
The people who always need to be noticed.
But what if the greatest danger isn't the pride everyone can see?
What if the deadliest pride is the one that quietly learns how to look like humility?
What if the person pride has deceived the most...
...is you?
That possibility should make every follower of Christ pause.
Because Scripture never presents pride merely as an attitude.
It presents pride as a spiritual blindness.
And blind people rarely know they're blind.
That is why pride is one of the most terrifying sins in all of Scripture.
It hides behind intelligence.
It disguises itself as conviction.
It dresses itself as discernment.
It even enters church wearing the language of holiness.
Long before Satan tempted Eve...
Long before Cain murdered Abel...
Long before Babel reached toward heaven...
Pride had already begun its rebellion.
Isaiah records the heart of Lucifer's fall.
"I will ascend."
"I will exalt my throne."
"I will make myself like the Most High."
The Hebrew repeatedly uses the first-person determination "אֶעֱלֶה" ('e'eleh — "I will ascend"), exposing the essence of pride: self-exaltation before God (Isaiah 14:13–14).
Pride is not simply thinking highly of yourself.
Pride is placing yourself where only God belongs.
That is why pride is cosmic treason.
It attempts to relocate the throne.
Not outwardly first...
but inwardly.
Every sin ultimately asks one question.
"Will God rule...
or will I?"
This explains why Proverbs 16:18 declares,
"Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall."
The Hebrew word translated "pride" is גָּאוֹן (ga'on).
It literally speaks of exaltation...
being lifted up...
rising beyond proper boundaries.
Pride always elevates something.
Usually ourselves.
Sometimes our opinions.
Sometimes our accomplishments.
Sometimes even our suffering.
It is possible to become proud of success.
It is equally possible to become proud of sacrifice.
Some become proud because they have much.
Others become proud because they believe they have endured more than everyone else.
Pride is remarkably adaptable.
It survives almost anywhere.
That is why it is so difficult to detect.
It never introduces itself honestly.
It whispers.
"You deserve better."
"They should recognize you."
"You're spiritually stronger."
"You understand Scripture better."
"You're more faithful."
"You would never do what they did."
The frightening part is that every one of those thoughts can feel completely reasonable.
Which is exactly why pride survives.
Jesus confronted this hidden disease constantly.
Perhaps nowhere more clearly than in Luke 18.
Two men entered the Temple.
One Pharisee.
One tax collector.
One prayed eloquently.
The other barely looked toward heaven.
Jesus records the Pharisee saying,
"God, I thank You that I am not like other men."
Notice something astonishing.
His prayer mentions God...
but revolves around himself.
That is pride's favourite disguise.
Religious language.
The tax collector simply cried,
"God, be merciful to me, a sinner."
The Greek reads,

Ὁ Θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ
(Ho Theos, hilastheti moi tō hamartōlō.)
The verb ἱλάσθητί (hilastheti) is far richer than "be merciful."
It carries the idea,
"Provide atonement."
"Cover my guilt."
"Be my propitiation."
He was not bargaining.
He was pleading for undeserved grace.
Jesus shocked His audience.
The religious expert left unjustified.
The broken sinner went home justified.
Because heaven measures hearts differently.
Pride compares.
Grace confesses.
Pride performs.
Grace surrenders.
Pride demands recognition.
Grace kneels.
The tragedy is that pride often grows strongest inside sincere believers.
The longer we walk with Christ...
the easier it becomes to compare ourselves with those walking behind us.
Soon we stop marvelling that Christ saved us...
and start wondering why others haven't become more like us.
That is not spiritual maturity.
That is pride learning Christian vocabulary.
James writes,
"God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble."
The Greek is unforgettable.

Ὁ Θεὸς ὑπερηφάνοις ἀντιτάσσεται
(Ho Theos hyperēphanois antitassetai.)
The word ἀντιτάσσεται (antitassetai) is a military expression.
It means...
to arrange battle lines against.
Imagine that.
The Creator of the universe personally resists pride.
Not because He enjoys punishment...
but because pride destroys the very relationship He desires with us.
Grace cannot fill a heart already convinced it needs nothing.
This explains why Jesus consistently welcomed sinners...
yet confronted the self-righteous.
The prostitutes listened.
The tax collectors repented.
The thieves believed.
The Pharisees plotted murder.
The difference was not the size of their sins.
It was the posture of their hearts.
Pride makes repentance unnecessary.
Humility makes grace irresistible.
Perhaps this is why Jesus began the Beatitudes with,
"Blessed are the poor in spirit."
The Greek phrase,
πτωχοὶ τῷ πνεύματι (ptōchoi tō pneumati)
does not describe moderate need.
It describes absolute spiritual bankruptcy.
A beggar.
Someone with nothing.
Someone who cannot rescue themselves.
The Kingdom begins there.
Not with confidence in ourselves...
but complete dependence upon Christ.
The Apostle Peter understood this painfully.
Hours before denying Jesus three times, Peter confidently declared he would never fall.
The others might.
He never would.
That confidence collapsed before sunrise.
Sometimes God lovingly allows our confidence in ourselves to break...
so that our confidence in Christ may finally begin.
Failure became Peter's classroom.
Grace became Peter's teacher.
Humility became Peter's strength.
How many of us secretly pray like the Pharisee?
Not aloud.
But inside.
We silently compare.
Silently rank.
Silently evaluate.
Silently judge.
Social media has only amplified this temptation.
We compare ministries.
Followers.
Views.
Platforms.
Influence.
Knowledge.
Appearance.
Success.
Even spiritual content can become another mirror reflecting ourselves instead of Christ.
We start asking,
"Did people notice me?"
instead of,
"Was Jesus glorified?"
That question exposes far more than we realize.
Pride also explains why correction feels unbearable.
When someone lovingly confronts us...
our first instinct is often defence.
Excuses.
Explanation.
Counter-accusation.
Yet Proverbs says,
"Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge."
Humility sees correction as grace.
Pride experiences it as attack.
One grows.
The other hardens.
The Gospel completely overturns pride.
At the cross, no one earns anything.
No one arrives superior.
No one purchases forgiveness.
Every believer stands on identical ground.
Mercy.
Paul writes in Ephesians,
"For by grace you have been saved through faith... not by works."
The Greek phrase,
οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων (ouk ex ergōn)
means exactly what it says.
Not from works.
Not because of merit.
Not because of performance.
Not because we deserved another chance.
Everything points back to Christ.
That is why Christianity leaves no room for boasting.
Our salvation is not our achievement.
It is Christ's accomplishment.
And this changes everything.
Because the Gospel is not a story about impressive people finding God.
It is a story about a holy God pursuing broken people.
It is not about our strength.
It is about His mercy.
It is not about our record.
It is about His righteousness.
It is not about our perfection.
It is about His sacrifice.
This is why our ministry exists under one simple declaration:
Every testimony begins with scandal.
Every redemption ends in grace.
Every believer has chapters they wish nobody could read.
Yet Jesus writes new endings.
Not by ignoring sin...
but by paying for it.
Not by lowering God's holiness...
but by satisfying it through His own blood.
The cross exposes pride because it tells us something uncomfortable.
Our sin was so serious...
the Son of God had to die.
Yet it also destroys despair.
Because His love was so great...
He willingly chose to die.
That is the Gospel.
Truth without compromise.
Grace without limit.
If this article unsettled you...
good.
The Holy Spirit often begins healing where comfort ends.
Be honest before God today.
Ask Him to reveal hidden pride.
Not so He can shame you...
but so He can free you.
You do not have to pretend.
You do not have to defend yourself.
You do not have to perform.
Jesus already knows every hidden corner of your heart.
And He still stretches out nail-scarred hands.
Perhaps the greatest evidence of God's grace is not that He found perfect people...
but that He never stopped pursuing proud ones until they learned to kneel.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Lesson I Learned From the Good Samaritan
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From the Good Samaritan
The Day I Realized I Wasn't the Hero in the Story
There are some stories in Scripture that comfort us.
There are others that confront us.
And then there are stories that quietly dismantle the version of ourselves we have spent years trying to protect.
For most of my life, I read the parable of the Good Samaritan believing I knew exactly who I was in the story.
I was the Samaritan.
Or at least I wanted to be.
I wanted to think I was the compassionate one.
The helpful one.
The one who would stop.
The one who would care.
The one who would do what was right when everyone else walked away.
But the older I became, the more honest God forced me to be.
And honesty can be painful when it collides with pride.
Because one day I realized something that shook me deeply:
I was not the hero in the story.
I was the man bleeding on the side of the road.
And so are you.
Jesus tells this unforgettable parable in Luke 10:25-37 after a lawyer asks Him a question intended to test Him:
“Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?”
The conversation eventually leads to another question:
“And who is my neighbor?”
What follows is one of the most powerful stories ever spoken.
Jesus says a man was traveling from Jerusalem to Jericho when robbers attacked him, stripped him, beat him, and left him half dead.
A priest came by.
He passed.
A Levite came by.
He passed.
Then a Samaritan arrived.
And everything changed.
The original Greek text says the Samaritan was moved with compassion.
The word used is σπλαγχνίζομαι (splagchnizomai).
This is not casual sympathy.
This is gut-level mercy.
A deep internal stirring.
A compassion so powerful it moves someone to action.
The Samaritan did not merely feel sorry.
He stopped.
He touched.
He bandaged.
He carried.
He paid.
He stayed.
He sacrificed.
He loved.
And suddenly the story becomes much bigger than helping strangers.
Because throughout the Gospels, that same word—splagchnizomai—is repeatedly used to describe Jesus Himself.
Jesus sees crowds and is moved with compassion.
Jesus sees the suffering and is moved with compassion.
Jesus sees the broken and is moved with compassion.
The Samaritan is not merely an example of kindness.
He is a shadow pointing toward Christ.
And that changes everything.
Because if we are honest, we are not naturally the Samaritan.
We are the wounded traveler.
Beaten by sin.
Broken by failure.
Exhausted by regret.
Lying helpless on a road we never expected to travel.
The prophet Isaiah described our condition perfectly:
“All we like sheep have gone astray” (Isaiah 53:6).
The Hebrew word translated "gone astray" is תָּעָה (ta'ah), meaning to wander, stagger, lose direction, or become lost.
That is humanity.
Not merely making mistakes.
Lost.
Spiritually wounded.
Unable to rescue ourselves.
And then Jesus came.
Not when we deserved rescue.
Not when we earned rescue.
Not when we cleaned ourselves up.
Romans 5:8 tells us:
“But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Not after.
While.
The Good Samaritan crossed barriers to save a wounded stranger.
Jesus crossed Heaven itself to save His enemies.
The Samaritan spent his own money.
Jesus spent His own blood.
The Samaritan risked inconvenience.
Jesus embraced the Cross.
The Samaritan carried a wounded man to safety.
Jesus carried our sins to Calvary.
The deeper I studied this parable, the more I realized that it is not primarily about becoming a better person.
It is about recognizing our need for a Savior.
The road from Jerusalem to Jericho is every human life.
The robbers are the destructive power of sin.
The wounded traveler is humanity.
