Death into resurrection.
Sinners into saints.
Enemies into children.
Scandal into grace.
Because Jesus Christ changes the ending.
Perhaps Eliezer never sat in Abraham's place.
But his faithful service became part of the story that ultimately brought the promised Seed into history.
Every believer who quietly serves Christ should find hope in that.
Your obedience matters.
Your unseen faithfulness matters.
Your prayers matter.
Your sacrifices matter.
Even when your name is forgotten on earth, heaven never overlooks those who faithfully serve the King.
Jesus Himself said,
"Well done, good and faithful servant."
Notice what He celebrates.
Not fame.
Not influence.
Not inheritance.
Faithfulness.
Maybe that is exactly what someone reading this needed to hear today.
You thought the closed door meant God had forgotten you.
Maybe He is writing a better chapter.
You thought another person's blessing meant your story was over.
Maybe heaven is preparing you for a greater purpose you cannot yet see.
You thought your disappointment was the conclusion.
Perhaps it is only the turning point.
Because our God specializes in rewriting endings.
That is the heartbeat of the gospel.
That is the beauty of grace.
That is why Jesus came.

He entered humanity's greatest scandal—our sin—and carried it to the cross so that everyone who trusts in Him might receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life through His death and resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith in Christ, not earned by our works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
Sometimes we need to be reminded that God is still writing the next chapter even when we cannot yet read it.
One faithful servant almost inherited a household, but through God's greater plan the world inherited a Savior.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Disappearance of the Bronze Serpent
paragraphs:
The Disappearance of the Bronze Serpent
The Day Israel Destroyed a Miracle—and Why Millions Are Still Worshiping the Wrong Thing Today
There are moments in Scripture so shocking that they almost feel out of place.
Moments that force us to ask whether we have truly understood God at all.
The disappearance of the Bronze Serpent is one of those moments.
It was not stolen.
It was not lost.
It was not buried by invading armies.
It was smashed.
Destroyed.
Reduced to pieces by God's own people.
And what makes this story even more startling is that the object being destroyed was once personally commanded by God Himself.
That fact alone should stop us in our tracks.
Because sometimes the greatest threat to our relationship with God is not rebellion.
Sometimes it is turning yesterday's blessing into today's idol.
The story begins in the wilderness.
Israel was tired.
Frustrated.
Impatient.
Angry.
Again and again God had delivered them, fed them, protected them, and guided them, yet they continued to complain.
Numbers 21 records one of their darkest moments.
The people spoke against God and against Moses.
As judgment, venomous serpents entered the camp.
People began dying.
The Hebrew text calls them הַנְּחָשִׁים הַשְּׂרָפִים (ha-nechashim ha-seraphim), literally "fiery serpents."
The pain was severe.
Death spread rapidly.
Suddenly the people realized the seriousness of their sin.
They cried out for mercy.
And God responded with a solution unlike anything anyone expected.
Numbers 21:8 says:
"Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live."
The Hebrew reads:
עֲשֵׂה לְךָ שָׂרָף וְשִׂים אֹתוֹ עַל־נֵס
"Asseh lecha saraph, vesim oto al nes."
"Make for yourself a fiery serpent and place it upon a standard."
Moses obeyed.
He crafted a bronze serpent.
In Hebrew:
נְחַשׁ נְחֹשֶׁת
Nechash Nechoshet.
The phrase itself is almost poetic.
A serpent of bronze.
Those who looked upon it in faith lived.
Those who refused died.
Notice carefully.
The bronze serpent possessed no power.
The metal did not heal.
The shape did not save.
The miracle was never in the object.
The miracle was in trusting the word of God.
Faith brought healing.
Not bronze.
This becomes even more profound when Jesus Himself explains the event.
In John 3:14–15 Jesus says:
"And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up: That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life."
The Greek text says:
Καὶ καθὼς Μωϋσῆς ὕψωσε τὸν ὄφιν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ
"Kai kathos Mōysēs hypsōse ton ophin en tē erēmō."
"And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness..."
Jesus was revealing something astonishing.
The bronze serpent was never the destination.
It was a shadow.
A prophetic sign.
A living illustration pointing toward Christ.
The serpent was lifted up.
Jesus would be lifted up.
The people looked in faith and lived.
Sinners would look to Christ and be saved.
The bronze serpent was never about a snake.
It was always about Jesus.
Yet human hearts have a tragic tendency.
We often fall in love with the sign and forget what it was pointing toward.
Generations passed.
Israel entered the Promised Land.
Kings rose and fell.
Empires shifted.
Centuries rolled by.
The bronze serpent survived.
The very object God had once commanded remained among the people.
At first it may have been preserved as a reminder.
A testimony.
A historical artifact.
A sacred memory.
But something happened.
Slowly.
Gradually.
Almost imperceptibly.
The people began treating the symbol as though it possessed power.
What was meant to point toward God began replacing God.
What was meant to strengthen faith became an object of misplaced faith.
The object that once represented healing became an idol.
Then came King Hezekiah.
One of the most faithful kings in Judah's history.
A reformer.
A man who loved the Lord.
A king unwilling to tolerate counterfeit worship.
And then Scripture records one of the most shocking acts of spiritual courage in all the Bible.
2 Kings 18:4 says:

"He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan."
The Hebrew word is fascinating:
נְחֻשְׁתָּן
Nehushtan.
Most scholars understand it as something like:
"Just a piece of bronze."
Imagine that.
For centuries people revered this object.
They honored it.
Protected it.
Burned incense to it.
Perhaps some even believed it carried divine power.
Then Hezekiah looked at it and essentially said:
"It is only bronze."
And he smashed it.
Can you imagine the outrage?
The criticism?
The accusations?
How many people must have protested?
How many likely said:
"But God used this!"
"This has history!"
"This is sacred!"
"This has been with us for generations!"
Yet Hezekiah understood something many believers still struggle to grasp.
Anything that takes the place of God must go.
Even if God originally used it.
That truth cuts deeply.
Because bronze serpents still exist.
Not literally.
Spiritually.
Sometimes it is a ministry.
Sometimes a tradition.
Sometimes a church building.
Sometimes a denomination.
Sometimes a preacher.
Sometimes a platform.
Sometimes a memory.
Sometimes even a past spiritual experience.
Things God genuinely used.
Things that once pointed us toward Christ.
Things that blessed us.
Helped us.
Strengthened us.
Yet over time we begin trusting them more than we trust Jesus.
We defend them more passionately than we defend the Gospel.
We cling to them even when God is calling us forward.
The danger is subtle.
Because idols rarely announce themselves.
They often arrive disguised as blessings.
The bronze serpent teaches us a painful but necessary lesson.
God is not interested in preserving our idols.
Even religious ones.
He is interested in preserving our hearts.
And sometimes the most loving thing God can do is allow the destruction of something we have elevated above Him.
Perhaps that is where you find yourself today.
Maybe something has disappeared from your life.
A relationship.
A position.
A ministry.
A dream.
A season.
A source of comfort.
And you have been asking why.
Could it be that God is removing what you were tempted to worship so you can rediscover the One who deserves worship?
Because God has never shared His glory with idols.
Not ancient ones.
Not modern ones.
Not even Christian-looking ones.
The bronze serpent vanished because its purpose had been fulfilled.
Its mission was complete.
Its role had always been temporary.
Jesus is different.
The serpent pointed toward salvation.
Jesus is salvation.
The serpent was lifted up.
Jesus was crucified and resurrected.
The serpent healed physical bodies.
Jesus heals eternal souls.
The serpent disappeared.
Jesus remains forever.
Hebrews 13:8 declares:
"Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and today, and forever."
The Greek reads:
Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς χθὲς καὶ σήμερον ὁ αὐτός καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας
"Iēsous Christos chthes kai sēmeron ho autos kai eis tous aiōnas."
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.
That is why the Gospel remains the greatest story ever told.
Because every human being carries a scandal.
A past.
A failure.
A wound.
A regret.
A secret.
Something that whispers they are too far gone.
Yet the cross announces a different verdict.
Jesus specializes in rewriting stories.
He takes what sin destroyed and transforms it through grace.
He takes shame and gives forgiveness.
He takes rebellion and offers reconciliation.
He takes brokenness and creates beauty.
He takes scandal and writes redemption.
That is exactly what the bronze serpent was pointing toward all along.
Not an object.
Not a relic.
Not a tradition.
Not a monument.
A Savior.
And His name is Jesus Christ.
Maybe today is the day you stop looking at the bronze serpent.
Maybe today is the day you stop trusting symbols and start trusting the Savior.
Maybe today is the day you surrender fully to Christ.
If this message stirred something inside your heart, do not keep scrolling.
Be honest.
This may have touched something deeper than you expected.
The most dangerous idol is often the one that once reminded you of God.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Lesson I Learned From Peter’s Tears The Night a Broken Disciple Discovered That Failure Is Not the End of Your Story
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From Peter’s Tears
The Night a Broken Disciple Discovered That Failure Is Not the End of Your Story
There are moments in life that haunt us long after everyone else has forgotten them.
A sentence we wish we never said.
A promise we swore we would keep.
A temptation we thought we had defeated.
A secret compromise nobody knows about except us and God.
Most people know what it feels like to fail.
But not everyone knows what it feels like to look Jesus in the eyes immediately after failing Him.
Peter did.
And that is why his tears still speak across two thousand years.
Because somewhere between his confidence and his collapse, between his devotion and his denial, between his scandal and his restoration, Peter became a mirror for all of us.
His story is not just about a fisherman from Galilee.
It is about every believer who has ever loved Christ deeply and still found themselves falling.
It is about every person carrying regret.
Every exhausted soul trying to pretend everything is fine.
Every Christian wondering if God can still use someone who knows better yet failed anyway.
Peter's tears answer that question.
And the answer is more beautiful than most people realize.
On the night Jesus was betrayed, Peter was overflowing with confidence.
When Jesus warned the disciples that they would scatter, Peter immediately separated himself from everyone else.
Matthew records his words:
"Though they all fall away because of You, I will never fall away." (Matthew 26:33)
Peter genuinely believed it.
He was not lying.
He was not pretending.
He meant every word.
That is what makes his fall so tragic.
The greatest spiritual dangers often arrive wearing the mask of sincerity.
Peter loved Jesus.
Yet Peter trusted Peter more than he trusted Jesus.
That was the real problem.
Jesus knew what was coming.
In Luke 22:34, He told Peter:
"Before the rooster crows today, you will deny three times that you know Me."
Peter could not imagine such a thing.
How could the man who walked on water deny Christ?
How could the disciple who confessed Jesus as the Messiah suddenly abandon Him?
How could someone so passionate fail so completely?
Yet this is exactly what happened.
Because love alone is not enough when pride is still alive.
The Gospel of Luke records one of the most heartbreaking moments in Scripture.
After Jesus was arrested, Peter followed from a distance.
That phrase alone preaches an entire sermon.
He followed.
But from a distance.
Close enough to watch.
Too far away to stand with Him.
Many believers live there.
Not completely gone.
Not completely surrendered.
Still watching Jesus.
Still interested in Jesus.
Still believing in Jesus.
But following from a distance.
The distance always becomes dangerous.
Then came the questions.
A servant girl recognized him.
"You also were with Him."
Peter denied it.
Another person noticed.
Again he denied it.
A third accusation came.
This time Peter denied Jesus with even greater force.
Three opportunities.
Three denials.
Exactly as Jesus predicted.
Then Luke records something so devastating that it almost hurts to read.
"The Lord turned and looked at Peter." (Luke 22:61)
No sermon.
No rebuke.
No condemnation.
No public humiliation.
Just a look.
The Greek text says:
"καὶ στραφεὶς ὁ Κύριος ἐνέβλεψεν τῷ Πέτρῳ"
(kai strapheis ho Kyrios eneblepsen tō Petrō)
"The Lord turned and looked intently at Peter."
Imagine that moment.
The sound of Peter's own words still hanging in the air.
The rooster crowing.
The realization crashing over him.
Then the eyes of Jesus meeting his.
The eyes of the Savior he loved.
The eyes of the One he swore he would never abandon.
The eyes of the One he had just denied.
Luke tells us:
"And he went out and wept bitterly." (Luke 22:62)
The phrase "wept bitterly" comes from the Greek:
"ἔκλαυσεν πικρῶς"
(eklausen pikrōs)
It describes deep anguish.
Uncontrollable grief.
Soul-level sorrow.
These were not polite tears.
These were tears that came from the wreckage of a shattered heart.
Peter's tears were not merely tears of embarrassment.
They were tears of revelation.
For the first time, Peter saw himself clearly.
Not the version of himself he imagined.
Not the version he presented to others.
The real Peter.
The weak Peter.
The fearful Peter.
The broken Peter.
And strangely, this became the beginning of his transformation.
Many people assume spiritual growth begins with strength.
Scripture often shows the opposite.
Spiritual growth frequently begins where self-confidence dies.
The Old Testament contains a powerful Hebrew word:
"לֵב נִשְׁבָּר"
(lev nishbar)
A broken heart.
Psalm 51:17 says:
"The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, You will not despise."
God does not despise broken hearts.
He rebuilds them.
Peter's tears were not evidence that God was finished with him.
They were evidence that God was beginning a deeper work.
Judas also regretted what he had done.
Both men failed.
Both men felt sorrow.
Both men faced their sin.
Yet their stories ended differently.
Why?
Because one ran from Jesus.
The other eventually ran back to Him.
Repentance is not merely feeling bad.
Repentance is turning toward the Savior.
Peter's tears drove him toward grace.
And grace was waiting.
That is the lesson that changed my life.
For years I assumed my greatest failures would become permanent labels.
I thought my worst moments would define me.
I thought my mistakes would always have the final word.
But Peter's tears tell a different story.
Failure is not the final chapter.
Jesus is.
The same disciple who denied Christ became the disciple who boldly proclaimed Christ.
The same man who trembled before a servant girl would later stand before crowds and preach with fearless conviction.
The same Peter who once hid in shame would eventually write Scripture under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.
The same Peter who failed publicly became a pillar of the early church.
How?
Because Jesus rewrites stories.
After the resurrection, Jesus deliberately sought Peter.
Not to destroy him.
Not to embarrass him.
Not to remind him of his failure.
To restore him.
In John 21, Jesus asked Peter three times:
"Do you love Me?"
Three questions.
One for every denial.
Not because Jesus needed the answer.
Peter needed the healing.
Grace was not ignoring the wound.
Grace was restoring what had been broken.
The conversation culminated with Jesus saying:
Not "prove yourself."
Not "earn another chance."
Not "make up for your failure."
The Gospel has always been scandalous because it gives hope to people who cannot save themselves.
It restores people who deserve judgment.
It welcomes people carrying shame.
It transforms people who thought they were beyond repair.
That is why Peter's tears matter.
Because they remind us that our worst moment does not have authority over God's grace.
Perhaps you know what it feels like to sit in the ashes of regret.
Perhaps there are memories you wish you could erase.
Perhaps there are sins nobody knows about.
Perhaps there are failures that still whisper accusations into your mind.
Peter's story speaks directly into that darkness.
The same Jesus who looked at Peter still looks at us today.
Not with indifference.
Not with approval of sin.
But with a love strong enough to tell the truth and powerful enough to redeem.
The cross proves that God's answer to human failure is not abandonment.
It is redemption.
At Calvary, Jesus carried every denial.
Every betrayal.
Every hidden shame.
Every scandal.
Every sin.
The Aramaic words Jesus cried from the cross were:
"ܐܝܠ ܐܝܠ ܠܡܢܐ ܫܒܩܬܢܝ"
(Eli, Eli, lama shbaqtani)
"My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?"
He entered the deepest darkness so sinners could be brought into the light.
He bore judgment so grace could be offered freely.
He took our place so our story could be rewritten.
That is why Peter's tears still matter.
Because they reveal a Savior who specializes in restoration.
A Savior who sees beyond failure.
A Savior who writes redemption where others write condemnation.
A Savior who transforms scandal into grace.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
One look from Jesus broke Peter's heart, but that same look rebuilt his future.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The One Verse Hidden in Genesis That Reveals God's Heart Forever
paragraphs:
The One Verse Hidden in Genesis That Reveals God's Heart Forever
Long before the Cross... before Israel... before Moses... before the Law... God whispered one sentence that exposed His heart for every broken soul—including yours.
There are verses we memorize.
There are verses we quote.
And then there are verses that quietly change everything we thought we knew about God.

Genesis is often remembered for creation, Adam and Eve, Noah, Abraham, Joseph, and the beginning of history. Yet buried within its earliest pages is a single verse that many people read without realizing they have just encountered one of the greatest revelations of God's character in the entire Bible.
It is not found during creation.
It is not spoken from heaven with thunder.
It is spoken after humanity has done the unthinkable.
After rebellion.
After shame.
After hiding.
After sin entered the world.
The verse is Genesis 3:21.
"The LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife and clothed them." (ESV)
At first glance it sounds almost ordinary.
Almost insignificant.
Almost like a passing detail.
But nothing in Scripture is accidental.
This quiet verse reveals the heartbeat of God from Genesis all the way to Revelation.
It is the first picture of grace.
It is the first picture of substitution.
It is the first picture of atonement.
It is the first whisper of the Gospel.
And once you see it, you will never read the Bible the same way again.
Before this moment, Adam and Eve had everything.
Perfect fellowship.
Perfect peace.
Perfect innocence.
The Hebrew word used for "naked" in Genesis 2:25 is עֲרוּמִּים ('ărummîm), describing complete innocence without shame. They had nothing to hide because sin had not yet distorted their hearts.
Then came the serpent.
The temptation.
The choice.
The rebellion.
Sin did not merely break a rule.
It fractured the relationship between humanity and its Creator.
Immediately, Genesis 3:7 says,
"Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked."
For the very first time...
Shame entered creation.
Fear entered humanity.
Hiding became natural.
Sound familiar?
How many people still live exactly like Adam and Eve?
We hide behind success.
Behind careers.
Behind church attendance.
Behind social media.
Behind carefully edited smiles.
Behind achievements.
Behind religion.
Behind busyness.
Because deep inside, we are afraid someone will discover what we really are.
Adam and Eve's first response was not repentance.
It was self-salvation.
Genesis 3:7 tells us,
"They sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths."
Humanity's first religion was sewing fig leaves.
Trying to fix ourselves.
Trying to earn acceptance.
Trying to cover guilt with our own effort.
Nothing has changed.
Today our fig leaves simply look different.
Money.
Status.
Relationships.
Popularity.
Good deeds.
Moral performance.
Religious rituals.
But fig leaves have always shared one fatal weakness.
They cannot remove guilt.
They only hide it.
When God came into the garden, He asked,
"Where are you?" (Genesis 3:9)
The Hebrew reads:
אַיֶּכָּה ('ayyekkāh)
This was never because God lacked information.
The all-knowing God was inviting sinners to come out of hiding.
Not because He needed to find them.
Because He wanted them to find Him.
That question still echoes across every generation.
Where are you?
Not geographically.
Spiritually.
Emotionally.
Are you hiding?
Pretending?
Performing?
Running?
Trying to sew another layer of fig leaves over wounds only Christ can heal?
Then comes the verse that changes everything.
Genesis 3:21.
"The LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife and clothed them."
The Hebrew is breathtaking.
וַיַּעַשׂ יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים לְאָדָם וּלְאִשְׁתּוֹ כָּתְנוֹת עוֹר וַיַּלְבִּשֵׁם
Vayya'as YHWH Elohim le'adam u-le'ishto kotnot 'or vayyalbishem.
Notice the final word.
וַיַּלְבִּשֵׁם (vayyalbishem)
"He clothed them."
God Himself clothed them.
Not angels.
Not Adam.
Not Eve.
God.
The Creator personally covered the shame of sinners.
But garments of skin require something.
Death.
For the first time in history, innocent life was taken because guilty people sinned.

The text never explicitly names the animal, and Scripture wisely remains silent where God remains silent. We should not speculate beyond what is written. What we do know is that an animal died so Adam and Eve could be covered.
This is the first biblical portrait pointing toward substitutionary sacrifice.
An innocent life covering the guilty.

Centuries later, this pattern would continue through the sacrificial system described in Leviticus—not because animal blood could permanently remove sin, but because it pointed forward to Someone greater.
Hebrews explains:
"For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins." (Hebrews 10:4)
Those sacrifices anticipated the perfect sacrifice.
John the Baptist would finally identify Him:
"Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!" (John 1:29)
The Greek is unforgettable.
Ἴδε ὁ ἀμνὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ (Ide ho amnos tou Theou)
"Look!
The Lamb of God."
Not merely another sacrifice.
The sacrifice.
Genesis whispers.
John announces.
Calvary fulfills.
When Jesus hung upon the cross, He became what every sacrifice had anticipated.
Paul writes,
"For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God." (2 Corinthians 5:21)
Jesus wore our shame so we could wear His righteousness.
Adam wore garments of skin.
Believers are clothed with Christ.
Paul says in Galatians 3:27,
"For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ."
The Greek phrase is:
Χριστὸν ἐνεδύσασθε (Christon enedysasthe)
"You have clothed yourselves with Christ."
The Bible begins with God clothing sinners.
It ends with redeemed people clothed in white robes before His throne (Revelation 7:9–14).
The story has always been about grace.
Notice something else that is easy to miss.
God clothed Adam and Eve before they had done anything to deserve restoration.
They had not proven themselves.
They had not earned forgiveness.
They had not accumulated enough good works.
Grace always moves first.
As the Apostle John later wrote,
"We love because he first loved us." (1 John 4:19)
From Genesis to Revelation, salvation is God's initiative.
Not man's achievement.
Religion says, "Cover yourself."
The Gospel says, "God has covered you in Christ."
Religion says, "Work harder."
Grace says, "It is finished."
Religion says, "Become worthy."
Jesus says,
"Come to me..." (Matthew 11:28)
Maybe you have spent years stitching together spiritual fig leaves.
Trying harder.
Doing better.
Pretending longer.
Looking stronger.
But underneath, your soul still whispers the same words Adam spoke:
"I was afraid."
Fear has always been one of sin's loudest echoes.
Yet Genesis 3:21 declares that God's answer to shame was never abandonment.
It was covering.
His answer to guilt was not indifference.
It was sacrifice.
His answer to sinners was not destruction.
It was redemption unfolding across history until it reached the cross.
That is why Genesis is not merely the beginning of the Bible.
It is the beginning of the Gospel.
Long before Bethlehem...
Long before Golgotha...
Long before the empty tomb...
God was already revealing His heart.
A heart that pursues.
A heart that provides.
A heart that covers.
A heart that redeems.

If you've ever believed your past disqualifies you from God's love, remember the very first sinners did not receive God's final word in the garden. They received His promise (Genesis 3:15) and His gracious covering (Genesis 3:21). Judgment against sin was real, yet mercy shone through it. That pattern reaches its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, where God's justice and mercy meet perfectly at the cross (Romans 3:25–26).
Perhaps today you feel like Adam, hiding.
Perhaps you feel like Eve, carrying regret that refuses to loosen its grip.
Perhaps you've spent years trying to sew together another set of fig leaves that never truly cover the ache inside.
Hear the quiet voice that has echoed since Eden:
"Where are you?"
It is not the voice of a God eager to shame you.
It is the voice of a Father calling you out of hiding and toward the only covering that can truly remove your guilt—the finished work of Jesus Christ.
If this message has stirred your heart, don't let it end here. Your testimony may become the encouragement another reader needs today.
One quiet verse in Eden still echoes louder than every accusation your past can make.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Truth About Sex Most Christians Are Afraid to Talk About
paragraphs:
The Truth About Sex Most Christians Are Afraid to Talk About
The desire you keep hiding may not be your greatest shame—it may be the battlefield where Jesus wants to reveal His greatest victory.
There are sins Christians confess publicly.
Then there are sins Christians whisper about.
And then there are the struggles so deeply buried that many believers spend years pretending they do not exist at all.
Sex often lives there.
Not because God made it dirty.
Not because desire itself is evil.

But because somewhere between God's original design and humanity's rebellion, something beautiful became tangled with shame, secrecy, confusion, addiction, exploitation, loneliness, fear, and wounds many people never learned how to heal.
For countless believers, the topic of sex creates immediate tension.
Some feel guilt.
Some feel anger.
Some feel embarrassment.
Some feel exhausted from fighting temptations they thought would disappear years ago.
Others carry memories they wish they could erase.
And many are quietly wondering something they have never dared say out loud:
"If God created sex, why does it feel like such a source of pain?"
That question deserves an honest answer.
Because the truth about sex is not found in culture.
It is not found in pornography.
It is not found in celebrity opinions.
It is not found in political debates.
The truth about sex begins in Genesis before sin ever entered the world.
The first pages of Scripture reveal something astonishing.
God creates humanity and then declares:
"Male and female He created them." (Genesis 1:27)
Then God blesses them.
Not tolerates them.
Not merely permits them.
Blesses them.
The Hebrew word used repeatedly throughout Genesis for God's blessing is "בָּרַךְ" (barakh), carrying the idea of divine favor, flourishing, and life-giving abundance.
Sex was never created as a curse.
It was created within God's blessing.
Before lust existed.
Before abuse existed.
Before pornography existed.
Before exploitation existed.
Before shame existed.
There was God's design.
A husband.
A wife.
Complete trust.
Complete safety.
Complete intimacy.
Genesis 2:25 says:
"And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed."
The Hebrew phrase is profound:
"וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ" (velo yitboshashu)
"And they felt no shame."
Imagine that.
No insecurity.
No comparison.
No performance anxiety.
No manipulation.
No hidden guilt.
No fear of rejection.
No pretending.
No masks.
That was God's original intention.
Sex was designed to be a covenant expression of love, unity, trust, vulnerability, and self-giving commitment.
Then everything changed.
Genesis 3 records humanity's rebellion against God.
Sin entered the world.
And almost immediately shame entered human sexuality.
The same people who once stood before each other without shame suddenly hid.
The same intimacy that once reflected God's goodness became fractured by fear.
This is where every modern sexual struggle begins.
Not merely with behavior.
But with separation from God.
The deeper issue is not sex itself.
The deeper issue is sin.
This is why the world keeps offering solutions that never fully heal.
We are told that unlimited sexual freedom will satisfy us.
Yet loneliness is increasing.
We are told that pornography is harmless.
Yet countless lives and marriages are being devastated.
We are told that desire should become identity.
Yet confusion continues growing.
We are told to follow our hearts.
Yet Scripture repeatedly warns that the human heart itself is fallen.
Jeremiah 17:9 says:
"The heart is deceitful above all things."
The Bible's diagnosis is uncomfortable.
But it is accurate.
Humanity's problem is not a lack of sexual freedom.
Humanity's problem is sin.
And that includes every one of us.
The Greek word used throughout the New Testament for sin is "ἁμαρτία" (hamartia).
It literally means "missing the mark."
Not merely breaking rules.
Missing God's design.
Missing God's purpose.
Missing what we were created for.
That changes everything.
Because suddenly the conversation is not about whether someone has struggled sexually.
The conversation becomes whether anyone has perfectly lived according to God's standard.
And Scripture's answer is clear.
"No, not one." (Romans 3:10)
The church often speaks as if sexual sinners belong in one category and everyone else belongs in another.
Jesus never taught that.
At the foot of the cross, all of us arrive the same way.
Broken.
Guilty.
Needing mercy.
Needing grace.
This is why one of the most powerful stories in Scripture involves a woman caught in sexual sin.
Religious leaders dragged her into public humiliation.
They wanted judgment.
They wanted condemnation.
They wanted stones.
What they did not expect was Jesus.
One by one, her accusers disappeared.
Then Christ looked at her and said:
"Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more." (John 8:11)
Notice what Jesus did not do.
He did not excuse the sin.
He did not redefine the sin.
He did not celebrate the sin.
But He also did not destroy the sinner.
Grace and truth met perfectly in Christ.
The Greek word translated "grace" is "χάρις" (charis).
It carries the idea of unearned favor.
Undeserved kindness.
A gift that cannot be earned.
This is the heart of the Gospel.
Many people think Christianity teaches that good people go to heaven.
The Bible never says that.
Christianity teaches that guilty people can be forgiven because Jesus paid the price they could never pay themselves.
That includes sexual sinners.
That includes porn addicts.
That includes adulterers.
That includes those carrying secret shame.
That includes those who have had abortions.
That includes those who have been sexually abused and still carry wounds.
That includes people who believe they have gone too far.
The cross declares otherwise.
The Apostle Paul wrote to believers who once lived in sexual immorality, idolatry, adultery, and countless other sins.
Then he made one of the most hopeful statements in all Scripture:
"And such were some of you." (1 Corinthians 6:11)
Were.
Past tense.
Not because they fixed themselves.
Not because they became morally superior.
But because Jesus transformed them.
The verse continues:
"But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ."
The Gospel is not behavior modification.
It is transformation.
The enemy wants people trapped in one of two lies.
Either:
"My sin is not serious."
Or:
"My sin is too serious."
Both are false.
Your sin is serious enough that Jesus had to die.
Your sin is not too serious because Jesus did die.
That is the scandal of grace.
That is why the Gospel still shocks people.
God takes rebels and calls them sons.
God takes prostitutes and gives them dignity.
God takes addicts and gives them freedom.
God takes the ashamed and gives them a new name.
God takes the broken and gives them hope.
God takes scandals and turns them into testimonies.
The truth about sex most Christians are afraid to talk about is that sexual sin is real, destructive, and deadly.
But another truth is even more powerful.
Jesus is greater.
Greater than pornography.
Greater than adultery.
Greater than lust.
Greater than shame.
Greater than addiction.
Greater than regret.
Greater than your past.
Greater than every label people have placed on you.
The Gospel never minimizes sin.
It simply magnifies the Savior.
Perhaps that is why this message feels personal.
Because maybe you are not merely reading an article.
Maybe you are seeing yourself.
Maybe nobody knows what you struggle with.
Maybe your browser history knows.
Maybe your memories know.
Maybe your conscience knows.
And maybe for the first time in a long time, the Holy Spirit is reminding you that hiding is not healing.
Jesus never asked people to clean themselves before coming to Him.
He simply said:
"Come to me." (Matthew 11:28)
The invitation remains open today.
Not to condemnation.
Not to religious performance.
Not to pretending.
But to repentance, forgiveness, restoration, and transformation through Jesus Christ.
Your honesty may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
Supporting this mission is one practical way to help spread God's truth to more people around the world.
Because someone else's breakthrough may begin with the truth you choose to share today.
And because the chapter you're ashamed of may become the testimony God uses to save someone else tomorrow.
The same hands that were pierced for your sin are still reaching for you today.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: What Happens When You Refuse to Forgive?
paragraphs:
What Happens When You Refuse to Forgive?
The Prison Nobody Sees, The Wound That Never Stops Bleeding, And The Grace That Can Rewrite Everything
Some people think unforgiveness is strength.
They think holding onto the pain proves what happened mattered.
They think releasing someone means excusing what they did.
But what if the person you're refusing to forgive is no longer trapped by the offense?
What if the prison door is locked from the inside?
What if the person suffering most from your unforgiveness is you?
Some wounds do not begin with strangers.
They begin with fathers.
Mothers.
Spouses.
Friends.
Pastors.
Church members.
People who promised they would never hurt you.
The deepest betrayals are often delivered by the hands you trusted most.
And because the pain is real, forgiveness can feel impossible.
Not difficult.
Impossible.
Maybe you still remember the exact words.
The betrayal.
The abandonment.
The lie.
The humiliation.
The moment your heart shattered.
Years may have passed, but the memory still feels fresh.
You smile in public but replay the scene in private.
You move forward physically while remaining emotionally chained to yesterday.
Many people don't realize that unforgiveness quietly becomes part of their identity.
The offense becomes the lens through which they view every relationship.
Every conversation.
Every opportunity.
Every future blessing.
The wound stops being something that happened to them and becomes something that defines them.
That is exactly why Jesus spoke so strongly about forgiveness.
Because He knew what unforgiveness would eventually do to the human soul.
In Matthew 6:14-15, Jesus said:
"For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses."
These words are not comfortable.
They are not easy.
But they are Christ's words.
And Christ never spoke casually.
The Greek word used for forgive is "ἀφίημι" (aphiēmi).
It literally means "to send away," "to release," "to let go," or "to dismiss."
Biblical forgiveness is not pretending evil never happened.
It is releasing your right to personally carry the debt.
It is placing justice into God's hands.
Many believers mistakenly think forgiveness means saying what happened was acceptable.
It does not.
God never calls evil good.
He never minimizes abuse.
He never celebrates betrayal.
He never ignores sin.
The cross itself proves how seriously God takes sin.
Forgiveness does not deny justice.
Forgiveness entrusts justice to the Judge of all the earth.
In Romans 12:19, Paul writes:
Notice what God is saying.
He is not asking you to pretend.
He is asking you to surrender.
Because the burden of vengeance was never designed for human shoulders.
Every day you carry it, it crushes you a little more.
Some people have spent decades replaying offenses that happened years ago.
The person who hurt them moved on.
The offender forgot.
The world continued turning.
Yet the injured soul remained trapped in a moment that no longer exists.
That is one of Satan's favorite victories.
Not merely getting someone hurt.
Getting them stuck.
Because a believer trapped in bitterness struggles to experience the fullness of God's peace.
Hebrews 12:15 warns:
"Looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled."
The original Greek word for bitterness is "πικρία" (pikria).
It describes sharpness.
Poison.
A piercing condition of the soul.
Bitterness never remains isolated.
It spreads.
It infects marriages.
Families.
Churches.
Friendships.
Entire generations.
One unforgiven wound can become a family legacy if left surrendered to resentment instead of Christ.
Maybe that is why some of us still react to old pain as if it happened yesterday.
Because we never truly released it.
We preserved it.
Protected it.
Fed it.
Rehearsed it.
And every rehearsal reopened the wound.
Then Jesus tells a story that should shake every believer.
In Matthew 18, He speaks about a servant forgiven an impossible debt.
The debt was so large that repayment was humanly impossible.
Yet after receiving mercy, that servant refused to forgive someone who owed him far less.
The result was devastating.
Why?
Because forgiven people are meant to become forgiving people.
Not because the offense was small.
But because the cross was greater.
The Gospel itself is built upon forgiveness.
The entire Christian faith stands on a scandalous truth.
God forgave people who did not deserve it.
That includes every one of us.
Scripture declares:
"For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." (Romans 3:23)
The Hebrew concept behind sin is often connected to the idea of missing the mark.
Falling short.
Failing God's perfect standard.
Every believer stands before God as someone who needed mercy.
Every believer stands before God as someone who could never save themselves.
Every believer approaches the cross empty-handed.
That reality changes everything.
Because when we realize how much we've been forgiven, our perspective begins to shift.
Not instantly.
Not magically.
But genuinely.
The cross forces us to confront two uncomfortable truths at the same time.
What they did was wrong.
And yet Christ still forgave me.
What they did wounded me.
And yet Christ still died for sinners.
What they did was unfair.
And yet the cross was the greatest injustice in human history.
The innocent Son of God suffered for the guilty.
Isaiah prophesied centuries before Christ:
"He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities."
The Hebrew word for wounded here is "מְחֹלָל" (mecholal), carrying the idea of being pierced through.
Jesus was pierced because of sins He never committed.
He absorbed wrath He did not deserve.
He carried shame that belonged to others.
And while hanging on the cross, bleeding and mocked, Jesus prayed:
"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do."
Think about that.
The very people driving the nails.
The very people mocking Him.
The very people rejecting Him.
And still He spoke forgiveness.
That is not weakness.
That is divine strength.
That is not surrender to evil.
That is victory over it.

The Aramaic language spoken by Jesus carried a depth difficult to fully capture in English. The cry of forgiveness flowing from the cross reflects a heart that chose mercy while suffering unimaginable injustice.
And this is where many readers feel resistance.
Because forgiveness sounds beautiful until the wound is personal.
Until it has your story attached to it.
Your betrayal.
Your abandonment.
Your scars.
Yet Jesus never asked us to do something He was unwilling to do Himself.
He walked the road first.
Every painful step.
Every tear.
Every rejection.
Every wound.
Which means when Christ commands forgiveness, He is not speaking from distance.
He is speaking from experience.
Maybe someone reading this has spent years carrying anger.
Maybe the offense still burns.
Maybe you feel justified.
Maybe you are justified.
But being justified in your hurt and being healed from your hurt are not always the same thing.
Jesus desires more than your validation.
He desires your freedom.
The enemy wants you chained to the memory.
Jesus wants you released from it.
The enemy wants the wound to become your identity.
Jesus wants grace to become your testimony.
The enemy wants your pain to write the final chapter.
Jesus rewrites stories.
That is what He has always done.
Rahab the prostitute became part of the Messianic line.
David the adulterer became a man after God's own heart through repentance.
Peter the denier became a bold preacher of the Gospel.
Paul the persecutor became a missionary.
The Bible is filled with people whose stories should have ended in scandal.
Yet grace intervened.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that includes the story you're carrying right now.
Maybe the next chapter begins the moment you finally surrender the offense.
Not because the offender deserves it.
But because Christ deserves your trust.
If this article exposed something hidden inside your heart, be honest before God today.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
Because one day you may discover the person forgiveness finally set free was not the one who hurt you.
It was you.
The chains you refuse to release today may be the chains keeping you from tomorrow's healing.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: What Happens When You Make Marriage an Idol?
paragraphs:
What Happens When You Make Marriage an Idol?
The Silent Betrayal Happening in Christian Hearts Every Day—and Why Only Jesus Can Carry the Weight You Keep Putting on Another Human Being
There is a kind of heartbreak that nobody warns you about.
Not the heartbreak of divorce.
Not the heartbreak of betrayal.
Not the heartbreak of abandonment.
But the heartbreak of finally getting everything you prayed for... and discovering it still cannot save you.

Many believers spend years asking God for a husband. Asking God for a wife. Asking God for companionship. Asking God for someone who will understand them, complete them, heal their loneliness, and finally make life feel whole.
The prayers are sincere.
The desire is understandable.
Marriage itself is God's idea.
Yet somewhere along the journey, something dangerous can quietly happen.
A good gift slowly becomes an ultimate thing.
A blessing slowly becomes a savior.
A spouse slowly takes a place that belongs only to Jesus Christ.
And when that happens, marriage stops being worship.
It becomes idolatry.
Most idols in Scripture were carved from wood, stone, gold, or silver.
Modern idols are often made from dreams.
The human heart has always been remarkably creative in manufacturing replacements for God.
The prophet Ezekiel recorded God's words concerning people who had "taken their idols into their hearts" (Ezekiel 14:3).
Notice that God did not say the idols were merely on shelves.
They were inside.
Hidden.
Protected.
Loved.
Worshiped.
That is where the most dangerous idols live.
Not in temples.
In hearts.
Marriage becomes an idol whenever we expect it to provide what only Christ can provide.
Security.
Identity.
Purpose.
Healing.
Fulfillment.
Worth.
Salvation.
The Bible never teaches that marriage is our ultimate relationship.
In fact, Scripture reveals something shocking.
Marriage itself is temporary.
Jesus said in Matthew 22:30:
"At the resurrection people will neither marry nor be given in marriage."
Marriage is a sacred earthly covenant.
Christ is the eternal Bridegroom.
The entire purpose of marriage is ultimately to point beyond itself.
Paul reveals this mystery in Ephesians 5:31-32:
"For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh."
Then Paul adds:
"This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church."
The Greek word translated "mystery" is μυστήριον (mystērion).
A divine truth once hidden but now revealed.
Marriage was never the destination.
Marriage was always the signpost.
The sign was never meant to replace the reality.
Yet millions unknowingly stare at the sign and miss Christ.
Some enter marriage believing:
"When I finally get married, I will be happy."
"When I finally get married, I will feel complete."
"When I finally get married, the loneliness will disappear."
"When I finally get married, life will make sense."
Those expectations sound harmless.
But they place god-sized burdens on human shoulders.
No husband can carry that weight.
No wife can carry that weight.
Only Jesus can.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly describe God as the ultimate source of satisfaction.
Psalm 16:11 declares:
"In Your presence there is fullness of joy; at Your right hand are pleasures forevermore."
Notice what David did not say.
He did not say fullness of joy is found in romance.
He did not say fullness of joy is found in marriage.
He did not say fullness of joy is found in another person.
He said fullness of joy is found in God's presence.
The Hebrew phrase שֹׂבַע שְׂמָחוֹת (sova semachot) literally conveys abundance and completeness of joy.
A joy overflowing beyond human capacity.
The kind of joy no spouse was ever designed to provide.
This is why idolized marriages often become painful marriages.
The spouse cannot satisfy expectations they were never created to fulfill.
One person becomes disappointed.
The other becomes exhausted.
Resentment grows.
Bitterness develops.
Conflict increases.
The marriage begins collapsing under the crushing weight of misplaced worship.
What looked like a marriage problem is often a worship problem.
The issue is not that the spouse failed.
The issue is that they were expected to be God.
Many marriages suffer because one partner unconsciously says:
"You are responsible for my happiness."
"You are responsible for my identity."
"You are responsible for my peace."
"You are responsible for making me feel valuable."
Those are impossible assignments.
Even the strongest marriages eventually crack beneath them.
Only Christ can carry what belongs to Christ.
The first commandment remains as relevant today as it was thousands of years ago:
"You shall have no other gods before Me." (Exodus 20:3)
In Hebrew:
לֹא יִהְיֶה־לְךָ אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים עַל־פָּנָיַ
Lo yihyeh-lecha elohim acherim al-panai.
No other gods before My face.
No rivals.
No substitutes.
No replacements.
Not even good gifts.
Especially not good gifts.
Because the greatest idols are often not evil things.
They are good things elevated above God.
Marriage is beautiful.
Marriage is holy.
Marriage is sacred.
But marriage makes a terrible god.
When Jacob first saw Rachel, he fell deeply in love.
Genesis tells us he worked seven years for her.
Yet Scripture says those years seemed only a few days because of his love for her.
It sounds romantic.
And in many ways it was.
But Jacob's story eventually reveals something deeper.
The man who thought Rachel would complete him still struggled.
Still suffered.
Still wrestled.
Still needed God.
Because Rachel was never his savior.
And neither is your spouse.
Many readers know exactly what this feels like.
You gave someone a place in your heart that belonged to Jesus.
You made them your emotional oxygen.
Your daily validation.
Your sense of purpose.
Your source of peace.
And when they disappointed you, it felt like your entire world collapsed.
That collapse was painful.
But it may also have been merciful.
Because God loves His children too much to let idols satisfy them.
He often allows idols to fail so we can rediscover the One who never will.
Perhaps that is why some of your greatest disappointments became turning points.
The relationship ended.
The engagement dissolved.
The marriage struggled.
The dream shattered.
And in the ruins you found Jesus waiting.
Not condemning.
Not mocking.
Not saying "I told you so."
But gently reminding you:
"I was always what you were actually searching for."
The Gospel is ultimately the story of misplaced worship being restored.
Humanity exchanged God for substitutes.
Christ came to bring us back.
The Apostle Paul writes in Romans 1 that people exchanged the truth of God for created things.
That exchange still happens today.
Sometimes the created thing is money.
Sometimes success.
Sometimes approval.
Sometimes marriage.
Yet the solution remains the same.
Jesus Christ.
The One who never leaves.
Never betrays.
Never abandons.
Never changes.
Never disappoints in His character.
Never fails His promises.
The Bridegroom who gave His own life for His bride.
When Jesus cried from the cross, "It is finished," the Greek word was τετέλεσται (tetelestai).
Paid in full.
Completed.
Accomplished.
Nothing lacking.
Nothing missing.
Nothing unfinished.
Your spouse cannot complete you.
Jesus already did what no human being ever could.
This truth changes everything.
It transforms singleness.
It transforms marriage.
It transforms expectations.
It transforms relationships.
When Christ becomes your ultimate satisfaction, marriage becomes healthier because it is no longer carrying responsibilities God never assigned to it.
The husband becomes a gift.
The wife becomes a gift.
Not a god.
Not a savior.
Not an idol.
A gift.
And gifts are enjoyed best when they are received with gratitude rather than worshiped with desperation.
Perhaps as you read this, the Holy Spirit is exposing something hidden.
Maybe you realize you have been asking your spouse to carry burdens only Christ can bear.
Maybe you realize your deepest disappointment was actually revealing your deepest idol.
Maybe you realize Jesus is calling you back to first love.
Back to worship.
Back to surrender.
Back to Himself.
If this spoke directly into your heart, be honest.
Your testimony may become the encouragement another believer desperately needs today.
One practical way to glorify God through this ministry is by helping expand the reach of Gospel-centered truth.
Because sometimes the thing you thought would save you was only meant to lead you to the One who actually can.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Should Parents Approve Who You Marry?
paragraphs:
Should Parents Approve Who You Marry?
The Question That Has Broken Hearts, Divided Families, and Tested Faith—What Does God Actually Say?
There is a moment in almost every serious relationship when love collides with another voice.
Sometimes it is the quiet hesitation of a father.
Sometimes it is the tears of a mother.
Sometimes it is an entire family saying, "We don't approve."
And suddenly the question no longer feels theoretical.
Should parents approve who you marry?
Many have walked away from true love because of family pressure.
Others ignored every warning, married anyway, and discovered too late that wisdom had been speaking through people they refused to hear.
Some parents have become controlling.
Others have become prayer warriors.
Some children have honored their parents.
Others have confused honor with lifelong slavery.
So where does Scripture stand?
Not culture.
Not tradition.
Not modern romance.
Not personal opinion.
What does God actually say?
The answer may surprise you.
Because this is not merely a family issue.
It is a discipleship issue.
It is a question of authority.
It is a question of wisdom.
It is a question of whether Jesus truly rewrites every relationship—including the ones that hurt the most.
The Bible begins by establishing one of the greatest commandments ever given.
In Exodus 20:12 God commands:
"Honor your father and your mother..."
The Hebrew reads:

כַּבֵּד אֶת־אָבִיךָ וְאֶת־אִמֶּךָ
(Kabbed et-avikha ve'et immekha.)

The verb כַּבֵּד (kabbed) comes from כָּבֵד (kāḇēḏ), meaning "to make weighty," "to regard as significant," "to treat with great honor." Honor is not shallow politeness. It is recognizing the God-given value and role of one's parents.
The command is repeated in the New Testament.
Ephesians 6:2 says:
"Honor your father and mother."
The Greek reads:

Τίμα τὸν πατέρα σου καὶ τὴν μητέρα.
(Tíma ton patera sou kai tēn mētera.)
The verb τίμα (tíma) means to esteem, value, respect, and give proper honor.
Notice something important.
Scripture commands honor.
It never commands lifelong parental control over every decision of an adult child.
Honor is mandatory.
Absolute parental authority over a married adult is not.
Then comes Genesis.
One verse changes everything.
Genesis 2:24 says:
"Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh."
The Hebrew reads:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ
(Al ken ya'azov ish et aviv ve'et immo vedavaq be'ishto.)
The word יַעֲזָב (ya'azov) means "leave," not in the sense of abandoning or dishonoring, but of establishing a new primary covenant relationship. Marriage creates a new household under God.
Then comes וְדָבַק (vedavaq).
It means "cling," "cleave," "hold firmly," "be permanently joined."
Marriage is not merely romance.
It is covenant.
The priority shifts.
Parents remain honored.
The spouse becomes the closest earthly relationship.
Jesus Himself quoted this exact passage in Matthew 19:5, affirming that marriage creates a new covenant ordained by God.
This means something profound.
Parents are incredibly important.
But they are not the final authority over whom a mature believer marries.
God is.
However...
That truth has also been abused.
Some people say, "God told me to marry this person," while ignoring every warning from wise parents, pastors, mature believers, and Scripture itself.
That is not faith.
That is often pride wearing spiritual language.
Proverbs 15:22 reminds us:
"Without counsel plans fail, but with many advisers they succeed."
God frequently speaks through wise counsel.
Many parents see dangers that love refuses to notice.
Manipulation.
Addiction.
Abuse.
Financial irresponsibility.
Spiritual compromise.
Character flaws hidden behind attraction.
Parents have lived longer.
Many have already survived mistakes their children have yet to experience.
Ignoring godly wisdom simply because it feels inconvenient is never biblical.
But neither is allowing fear to replace obedience.
Sometimes parents oppose a marriage for reasons God never does.
Different social status.
Different ethnicity.
Different income.
Different church traditions.
Different expectations.
Human preferences must never override God's revealed truth.
The Pharisees were experts at elevating tradition above God's commands.
Jesus confronted them repeatedly.
The same danger still exists today.
The central biblical question is not:
"Do my parents like this person?"
Nor is it:
"Am I in love?"
The real question is:
Does this relationship glorify Christ?
Is this person surrendered to Jesus?
Are they producing the fruit of the Spirit?
Are they walking in repentance?
Do they display humility?
Can they lead—or help build—a Christ-centered home?
Will this marriage make both of you look more like Jesus?
Those questions matter infinitely more than chemistry alone.
Scripture repeatedly warns believers not to enter spiritually divided marriages.
Second Corinthians 6:14 says:
"Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers."
The Greek phrase is:

Μὴ γίνεσθε ἑτεροζυγοῦντες
(Mē ginesthe heterozygountes.)

The word ἑτεροζυγοῦντες (heterozygountes) describes animals yoked together that do not fit properly, making the work difficult and unstable. Paul's primary point concerns spiritual partnership and shared devotion to Christ. While the passage is broader than marriage, the principle has long been recognized as especially relevant to the closest covenant relationship.
Marriage was never designed merely to survive.
It was designed to reflect Christ.
Ephesians 5 tells us marriage points toward the relationship between Christ and His Church.
Every Christian marriage is meant to preach the Gospel without words.
That changes everything.
The question is no longer merely:
"Who makes me happy?"
Instead it becomes:
"Who helps me worship Jesus more faithfully?"
That question has saved countless marriages before they ever began.
The Bible gives us beautiful examples of parental involvement without portraying parents as infallible.

Abraham's servant sought a wife for Isaac under Abraham's guidance (Genesis 24), but the narrative also highlights God's providence and Rebekah's willingness. When Rebekah was asked whether she would go, she answered, "I will go" (Genesis 24:58). Her consent mattered.
Likewise, Scripture also records painful family failures.
Samson pursued relationships against wise counsel and against God's revealed purposes, with devastating consequences (Judges 14–16).
Yet there are also moments when faithful people followed God's calling despite misunderstanding from family.
The Bible never presents a simplistic formula.
Instead, it calls believers to wisdom, prayer, discernment, humility, and obedience to God.
If your parents love Jesus deeply, treasure their counsel.
Listen longer than your emotions want to.
Ask questions.
Invite correction.
Pray together.
If they raise concerns rooted in Scripture, take them seriously.
But if their objections are based solely on pride, prejudice, manipulation, or personal control, remember that your highest allegiance belongs to Christ.
Even Jesus taught that loyalty to Him surpasses every earthly relationship (Matthew 10:37). That does not cancel the command to honor parents; it establishes the proper order of every allegiance.
For parents reading this, remember that your children do not ultimately belong to you.
They belong to God.
Your role is not to control every decision.
It is to disciple, pray, counsel, bless, and entrust them to the Lord.
The strongest Christian families are not built on domination.
They are built on truth wrapped in grace.
And for those who have already made painful mistakes...
Perhaps you married against wise counsel.
Perhaps you ignored warning signs.
Perhaps your parents rejected someone they never should have rejected.
Perhaps your family relationships still ache today.
Hear this clearly.
The Gospel is not merely for perfect decisions.
The Gospel is for broken people.
Peter denied Christ.
David committed grievous sins.
The Samaritan woman carried the weight of shattered relationships.
Yet Jesus met each of them with truth and mercy, calling them to repentance and restoration.
That is why our message has always been:
He rewrites prodigals.
He rewrites broken marriages.
He rewrites stubborn hearts.
He rewrites controlling families.
He rewrites bitterness.
He rewrites regret.
He rewrites every surrendered life.

If you are still single, seek God's kingdom first. Pray for discernment. Invite wise, biblically grounded counsel. Honor your parents without making them your savior. Trust Christ above your emotions without despising the wisdom He often provides through mature believers.
If you are a parent, remember that the greatest gift you can give your children is not merely your approval but your example of faithful discipleship.
If this message challenged you, be honest before God.
If this article helped you understand God's Word more deeply, don't keep it to yourself.
One act of obedience today can echo through generations tomorrow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Goliath Didn’t Expect a Shepherd Boy
paragraphs:
Goliath Didn’t Expect a Shepherd Boy
The Day God Proved That Your Pasture Is Not a Prison—It Is Preparation for Purpose
No one wakes up expecting the biggest battle of their life.
Most of us are simply trying to survive another ordinary day.

Another shift.
Another prayer.
Another disappointment.
Another season where it feels like everyone else is moving ahead while we remain forgotten.
David knew that feeling.
Long before he was remembered as Israel's greatest king, he was simply the youngest son no one expected much from.
While his brothers marched into battle wearing armor, David was left behind with sheep.
While everyone celebrated warriors, David cleaned up after lambs.
While others chased recognition, David learned obedience where nobody was watching.
The world saw insignificance.
God saw preparation.
Perhaps that is where you are today.
Not abandoned.
Not overlooked.
Prepared.
That changes everything.
The story begins in 1 Samuel 17, where an entire nation trembled before one giant.
The Philistine champion was named Goliath.
The Hebrew text calls him גָּלְיָת (Golyāṯ).
His name has uncertain origins, but throughout Scripture he becomes the living picture of impossible opposition.

He stood "six cubits and a span" tall (1 Samuel 17:4). Depending on textual tradition, this is roughly nine feet nine inches (Masoretic Text), while some ancient witnesses, including a Dead Sea Scroll and the Septuagint, describe him as about six feet nine inches. Regardless of the precise height, the biblical point remains unchanged: Goliath was an overwhelming and terrifying champion whose military strength dwarfed that of ordinary soldiers.
His armor weighed more than many people could comfortably carry.
His spear looked like a weaver's beam.
His voice echoed across the valley with one challenge.
"Choose a man for yourselves..."
Every day.
Morning.
Evening.
Forty days.
The Hebrew emphasizes the relentless nature of the intimidation.
Fear became routine.
Eventually, fear feels normal.
Maybe you've lived there.
The doctor's report.
The broken marriage.
The addiction nobody knows.
The anxiety that smiles in public.
The financial pressure that steals your sleep.
The guilt from sins you thought God could never forgive.
Giants rarely begin by attacking your body.
They attack your courage.
The enemy has always understood that frightened people stop trusting God.
King Saul certainly did.
The tallest man in Israel hid among the fearful.
The army followed their king's example.
Leadership without faith spreads fear.
Then a shepherd arrived carrying lunch.
Imagine the scene.
No polished armor.
No decorated sword.
No military reputation.
Just bread.
Cheese.
And simple obedience to his father.
That was David.
The Hebrew text repeatedly calls him דָּוִד (Dāwīḏ).
His name is commonly understood to mean "beloved."
Before David became Israel's beloved king, he already belonged to the God who loved him.
That matters.
Your identity before God always comes before your assignment from God.
David heard the same insults everyone else heard.
But he listened differently.
Where others heard an unbeatable warrior...
David heard someone insulting the living God.
That changed the entire battle.
His famous question still echoes today:
"Who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?" (1 Samuel 17:26)
Notice what David did not ask.
He did not ask:
"How big is he?"
"How experienced is he?"
"What are my chances?"
Faith asks different questions.
Faith asks:
"How great is God?"
Too many believers spend their lives measuring giants instead of measuring God's faithfulness.
David remembered something the soldiers forgot.
God had already been faithful.
While nobody applauded him...
God had been there.
David later testified:
"The LORD who delivered me from the paw of the lion and from the paw of the bear will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine." (1 Samuel 17:37)
This is one of the most beautiful patterns in Scripture.
Private victories prepare us for public battles.
The lion was not random.
The bear was not random.
The lonely fields were not random.
Every hidden trial became training.
Every unseen prayer became preparation.
Every quiet act of faithfulness became spiritual strength.
Nothing God wastes.
The New Testament echoes this truth in Romans 8:28, not as a promise that every circumstance is good, but that God works in all things for the good of those who love Him according to His purpose.
When Saul offered David his armor, something remarkable happened.
David refused it.
Why?
Because borrowed confidence cannot replace genuine faith.
The armor had never been tested by David.
The Hebrew word often translated "tested" carries the idea of proven by experience.
David would rather enter battle with what God had already trained him to use than pretend to be someone else.
How many believers lose spiritual battles because they spend their lives trying to wear someone else's calling?
God never asked you to become another Moses.
Another Paul.
Another Peter.
Another pastor.
Another influencer.
Another celebrity Christian.
He called you.
Comparison has quietly become one of the greatest thieves inside the modern Church.
Yet the kingdom of God has never advanced through imitation.
It advances through faithful obedience.
David walked toward the brook.
Five smooth stones.
One sling.
One God.
People often wonder why David chose five stones.

Scripture never explicitly says why, so we should not claim certainty where God has not spoken. Some suggest practical preparation in case more were needed. Others note that Goliath had relatives later mentioned in Scripture. These are possibilities, not biblical certainties.
One stone was enough.
Not because David was extraordinary.
Because the Lord was.
David declared one of the greatest confessions of faith recorded in the Old Testament:
"You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts..." (1 Samuel 17:45)
The phrase "LORD of hosts" translates יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת (YHWH Ṣəḇāʾôṯ).
It means the LORD of heavenly armies.
David saw more on the battlefield than anyone else.
The visible battle included one giant.
The invisible battle included the armies of heaven.
Faith sees what fear cannot.
Then came the moment that changed history.
The stone flew.
The giant fell.
Israel advanced.
Victory belonged to God.
The Hebrew narrative is strikingly understated. David did not win because of superior weaponry or human strength. The theological point is stated plainly:
"The battle is the LORD's." (1 Samuel 17:47)
Centuries later another seemingly impossible battle unfolded.
Not in a valley.
But on a hill called Golgotha.
The Greek word Γολγοθᾶ (Golgotha) comes from an Aramaic term meaning "Place of a Skull."
There, another unlikely victory occurred.
Jesus Christ did not defeat sin by military power.
He conquered through the cross.

The prophet Isaiah had already foretold this Servant who would bear our sins (Isaiah 53), and the New Testament proclaims its fulfillment in Christ. The resurrection became the decisive declaration that sin, death, and Satan had been defeated.
The Apostle Paul writes:
David defeated one giant.
Jesus defeated the greatest enemies humanity has ever faced.
Sin.
Death.
Condemnation.
Hopelessness.
The Greek word for grace is χάρις (charis).
It means God's freely given favor—undeserved, unearned, and overflowing in Christ.
That is why our story is always From Scandal to Grace.
David himself was not a flawless hero. His later sins remind us that even the greatest king needed mercy.
Jesus alone is the perfect King.
David points beyond himself to Christ.
Every page of Scripture ultimately leads us there.
Perhaps your giant today is not nine feet tall.
Perhaps it is shame.
Regret.
Divorce.
Depression.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Fear.
Loneliness.
Secret sin.
A lifetime of believing you are too damaged for God to use.
Hear the Gospel clearly.
Jesus did not come for people who had already conquered every giant.
He came for sinners.
He came for the broken.
He came for the weary.
He came for people exactly like us.
The cross forever declares that your deepest scandal is not stronger than God's grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Sometimes the simplest act of sharing God's Word becomes the very means He uses to reach a weary soul.
You will also gain access to a growing community committed to knowing God's Word more deeply.
One faithful step toward Christ today may become the testimony that changes someone else's eternity tomorrow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Are Jesus’ Genealogies Different?
paragraphs:
Why Are Jesus’ Genealogies Different?
The Apparent Contradiction That Becomes One of the Most Beautiful Proofs That Jesus Really Is the Messiah
Most people never notice it.
Others notice it and immediately become troubled.
Skeptics point to it as evidence that the Bible contradicts itself.
Believers sometimes read past it without asking questions.
Yet hidden inside two long lists of unfamiliar names is one of the most astonishing testimonies to the identity of Jesus Christ.
Open the Gospel of Matthew.
Read the genealogy of Jesus.
Then open the Gospel of Luke.
Read his genealogy there.
At first, everything seems fine.
But then the names begin to diverge.
Matthew says one thing.
Luke says another.
The lists are not identical.
The fathers are different.
The sequence is different.
Even the direction of the genealogy is different.
And suddenly a question emerges:
If both genealogies belong to Jesus, why are they different?
For some people, this question becomes a stumbling block.
For others, it becomes a doorway.
Because when we examine the evidence carefully, what first appears to be a scandal becomes a masterpiece of divine design.
And that is exactly how Jesus works.
Again and again.
What looks like a contradiction becomes confirmation.
What looks like a failure becomes redemption.
What looks like a scandal becomes grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Matthew begins with these words:
“Βίβλος γενέσεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ” (Biblos geneseōs Iēsou Christou)
Literally:
“Book of the origin/genealogy of Jesus Christ.”
(Matthew 1:1)
Immediately Matthew signals his purpose.
He is writing primarily to a Jewish audience.
His concern is proving that Jesus is the promised King.
The Messiah.
The Son of David.
The rightful heir to Israel’s throne.
That is why Matthew starts with Abraham and moves forward through history until he reaches Jesus.
His genealogy is royal.
Legal.
Kingly.
Matthew carefully traces the line through David’s son Solomon.
“David was the father of Solomon...” (Matthew 1:6)
This matters tremendously.
God had promised David:
“Your house and your kingdom shall endure before Me forever; your throne shall be established forever.”
(2 Samuel 7:16)
Every faithful Jew knew the Messiah must come from David’s royal line.
Matthew demonstrates exactly that.
Jesus legally inherits the throne through Joseph, His earthly legal father.
But then we arrive at Luke.
And suddenly everything changes.
Luke traces the genealogy backward.
Instead of beginning with Abraham, he goes all the way back to Adam.
Not merely to Israel.
Not merely to David.
Not merely to Abraham.
All the way to humanity itself.
Luke’s concern is different.
Matthew presents Jesus as King.
Luke presents Jesus as Savior of all mankind.
Luke ultimately reaches:
“τοῦ Ἀδὰμ, τοῦ Θεοῦ”
“of Adam, of God.”
(Luke 3:38)
Luke emphasizes Jesus as the Second Adam, the Redeemer for the entire human race.
Yet the biggest surprise comes before that.
When Luke reaches David, he does not follow Solomon.
He follows another son.
Nathan.
Luke writes:
(Luke 3:31)
Now many readers stop and ask:
How can Jesus descend from David through Solomon in Matthew and through Nathan in Luke?
Did somebody make a mistake?
The answer is no.
What appears to be a contradiction is actually two different genealogies serving two different purposes.
Matthew records Joseph’s legal royal lineage.
Luke appears to record Mary’s biological lineage.
Notice something fascinating.
Matthew explicitly says:
“Jacob was the father of Joseph, the husband of Mary, by whom Jesus was born.”
(Matthew 1:16)
Matthew is focused on Joseph.
Luke, however, uses language that strongly suggests a different emphasis.
“Jesus... being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph, the son of Heli.”
(Luke 3:23)
Joseph cannot have two biological fathers.
Matthew says Jacob.
Luke says Heli.
The earliest Christian understanding recognized that Luke is tracing Jesus through Mary’s family while using Joseph’s name because genealogies were typically recorded through males.
In this understanding, Heli would be Mary’s father, making Joseph his son-in-law.
This elegantly explains the difference.
Matthew gives Jesus’ legal right to David’s throne through Joseph.
Luke gives Jesus’ blood descent from David through Mary.
Together they establish something extraordinary.
Jesus possesses both the legal claim and the biological claim to Davidic ancestry.
But the story gets even deeper.
A shadow hangs over Matthew’s genealogy.
A curse.
A scandal.
A problem so severe that it appears capable of destroying the Messianic claim entirely.
In Matthew 1, the genealogy passes through King Jeconiah.
Also known as Coniah.
God declared judgment upon him:
“Write this man childless... for none of his descendants shall prosper sitting on the throne of David and ruling again in Judah.”
(Jeremiah 22:30)
At first glance this seems devastating.
If Jesus comes through Jeconiah’s line, how can He inherit David’s throne?
The answer reveals breathtaking divine wisdom.
Jesus inherits the legal royal right through Joseph’s line.
Yet He is not Joseph’s biological son.
He was conceived by the Holy Spirit.
The curse passes through biological descent.
The royal rights pass through legal inheritance.
Jesus receives the throne without inheriting the curse.
Only God could write a story like this.
Centuries before Bethlehem.
Centuries before the cross.
Centuries before the empty tomb.
God was already arranging every detail.
What looked like a dead end became a pathway.
What looked like a curse became evidence.
What looked like a scandal became grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And maybe that is where this stops being merely a theological discussion.
Maybe this is where it becomes personal.
Because many of us know what it feels like to carry a family story we wish did not belong to us.
Generational failures.
Broken homes.
Addictions.
Abandonment.
Betrayal.
Abuse.
Shame.
Secrets.
We know what it feels like to look at our family tree and see wounds.
We know what it feels like to wonder if our past has already written our future.
Yet when God chose to send His Son into the world, He did not hide the scars.
Matthew’s genealogy contains adulterers.
Murderers.
Liars.
Outcasts.
Foreigners.
Scandals.
Broken people.
Tamar.
Rahab.
Bathsheba.
Judah.
David.
Names carrying stories many churches would be uncomfortable discussing.
Yet God left every one of them in the record.
Why?
Because the genealogy of Jesus is not merely a list of names.
It is a testimony.
A declaration.
A Gospel before the Gospel.
It announces that God specializes in redemption.
That grace is greater than shame.
That mercy is greater than failure.
That your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
The genealogy itself preaches Christ.
The genealogy itself whispers hope.
The genealogy itself shouts that God has never needed perfect people to accomplish perfect purposes.
And perhaps that is exactly why the genealogies are different.
Not because God made a mistake.
But because God wanted us to see a fuller picture of His Son.
Matthew shows us the King.
Luke shows us the Savior.
Matthew shows us the throne.
Luke shows us humanity.
Matthew shows us covenant.
Luke shows us creation.
Matthew connects Jesus to Abraham.
Luke connects Jesus to Adam.
Together they reveal the complete Christ.
Fully qualified.
Fully human.
Legally rightful.
Biologically descended.
The promised Son of David.
The promised Son of Abraham.
The Son of Man.
The Son of God.
The Messiah.
The Savior.
The King.
And perhaps today somebody reading this needs the same truth these genealogies proclaim.
Your past is not stronger than God's purpose.
Your failures are not stronger than God's grace.
Your family history is not stronger than Christ's redemption.
The same God who turned apparent contradictions into confirmation can turn your broken story into a testimony.
The same God who transformed scandal into salvation can transform your deepest wounds into evidence of His glory.
The same Jesus who fulfilled every promise of Scripture can fulfill His promise to make all things new.
They may need this reminder that God's truth withstands careful examination.
Be honest. Your testimony could become somebody else's hope.
Your support helps us proclaim Jesus Christ, defend biblical truth, and reach more people with the Gospel.
And if this article blessed you, sharing it is one of the simplest ways to glorify God by helping biblical truth reach someone who desperately needs it.
The genealogy was never just about where Jesus came from—it was always about where Jesus can take you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Last Words of Moses: The Farewell That Still Calls Your Name
paragraphs:
The Last Words of Moses: The Farewell That Still Calls Your Name
