Maybe that is where you are today.
In a hidden season.
A confusing season.
A painful season.
A season where it feels like heaven is silent.
A season where nobody sees your faithfulness.
Nobody sees your struggle.
Nobody sees your tears.
Take heart.
The God who was working during Moses' hidden months is still working now.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly reveal a God who prepares before He reveals.
Who develops before He deploys.
Who conceals before He commissions.
What feels like delay may actually be divine preparation.
What feels like abandonment may actually be protection.
What feels like obscurity may actually be God's workshop.
Do not despise hidden seasons.
Some of God's greatest miracles begin there.
And if this message found you at the right moment, do not keep it to yourself.
What season are you in right now?
Your testimony may become encouragement for someone reading beside you.
Because every share helps spread the Gospel.
Every comment helps reach another soul.
And every act of faithfulness becomes another thread in the story God is writing.
The same God who protected Moses in the reeds is still protecting purposes that have not yet been revealed.
The chapter that feels hidden may become the testimony that changes everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Before You Say “I Do,” There Is One Conversation That Could Save Your Marriage
paragraphs:
Before You Say “I Do,” There Is One Conversation That Could Save Your Marriage
The Question Most Engaged Couples Avoid—Yet Scripture Shows It May Be the Difference Between Lifelong Covenant and Lifelong Regret
Two people can spend years planning a wedding and only a few hours preparing for a marriage.

They can compare venues, flowers, photographers, invitations, honeymoon destinations, and color palettes... while quietly avoiding the conversations that will eventually determine whether they flourish together—or slowly drift apart.
Many couples assume love will solve everything.
Scripture never says that.
The Bible teaches something deeper.
Love is not sustained by emotion alone.
Love is sustained by truth, sacrifice, forgiveness, repentance, humility, and complete surrender to Jesus Christ.
That is why every engaged couple needs to discuss one question before saying, "I do."
Not where you'll live.
Not how many children you'll have.
Not who manages the finances.
Not even your career goals.
Those conversations matter.
But there is something even more foundational.
The question is this:
Will Christ truly be the Lord of our marriage—or only a guest invited to our wedding?
That question changes everything.
Because marriage was never created merely to make two people happy.
Marriage exists to glorify God.
The first pages of Scripture reveal this beautiful design.
Genesis declares:
"Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh." (Genesis 2:24)
The Hebrew expression for "hold fast" is דָּבַק (dāḇaq).
It means far more than simply staying together.
It carries the idea of clinging, adhering, pursuing with unwavering loyalty, being permanently joined together.
It describes covenant.
Not convenience.
Not temporary affection.
Not conditional commitment.
A covenant.
That is why Jesus later quoted this passage in Matthew 19.
He added these unforgettable words:
"What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate."
Marriage begins with God before it ever begins with us.
If Christ is removed from the center, the covenant begins carrying a weight it was never designed to bear.
Many relationships collapse because each person quietly expects the other to become what only Jesus can be.
The perfect comfort.
The perfect provider.
The perfect healer.
The perfect source of identity.
The perfect forgiver.
The perfect satisfaction.
No human being can carry that burden.
Only Christ can.
The Greek New Testament repeatedly describes Jesus as Κύριος (Kyrios)—"Lord."
Not merely teacher.
Not merely Savior.
Lord.
Master.
Supreme Authority.
Every engaged couple should ask one another:
"Will Jesus truly be our Kyrios?"
Because eventually one spouse will disappoint the other.
One will fail.
One will sin.
One will say something careless.
One will struggle.
One may battle fear.
One may experience seasons of doubt.
One may lose a job.
One may become sick.
One may grow spiritually dry.
If Christ is not Lord, those moments often become breaking points.
If Christ is Lord, they become opportunities for grace.
The Apostle Paul paints perhaps the greatest picture of Christian marriage in Ephesians 5.
He doesn't begin with romance.
He begins with surrender.
"Submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ." (Ephesians 5:21)
The word translated "submit" comes from the Greek ὑποτάσσω (hypotassō).
It was never intended to describe domination.
It means willingly placing oneself under God's designed order out of love and devotion.
The passage never portrays marriage as a competition.
It portrays it as mutual sacrifice under the authority of Christ.
Paul then compares marriage to the relationship between Christ and His Church.
That comparison should humble every husband.
It should comfort every wife.
Jesus never ruled His Bride through selfishness.
He loved sacrificially.
He washed feet.
He forgave sinners.
He carried a cross.
He laid down His own life.
That is biblical leadership.
Not power.
Not control.
Sacrificial love.
Likewise, the Church responds to Christ not because He manipulates, but because His love transforms.
This is why every engaged couple should discuss forgiveness before discussing furniture.
Because eventually forgiveness will be needed.
Not once.
Thousands of times.
The Greek word χάρις (charis) means grace.
Grace is God's undeserved favor.
Grace says:
"I know you failed.
I know you hurt me.
I know you aren't perfect.
But because Christ has shown mercy to me, I will choose forgiveness instead of revenge."
Without grace, marriages keep score.
With grace, marriages keep growing.
Then there is repentance.
The New Testament repeatedly calls believers to μετάνοια (metanoia).
Many think repentance simply means feeling guilty.
It does not.
The Greek word literally describes a change of mind that produces a changed life.
Repentance is transformation.
Healthy marriages are not built by perfect people.
They are built by people who repent quickly.
Who apologize sincerely.
Who seek reconciliation humbly.
Who refuse to let pride become a permanent resident inside the home.
One of the greatest dangers for engaged couples is assuming conflict means incompatibility.
Scripture teaches something different.
Conflict often reveals where Christ still wants to transform us.
James writes:
Imagine if every disagreement began with listening instead of defending.
Imagine if every argument ended with prayer instead of silence.
Imagine if every failure ended with repentance instead of resentment.
Imagine a marriage where both spouses compete—not to win arguments—but to outdo one another in showing Christlike love.
That kind of marriage becomes a testimony.
Not because it never struggles.
Because Jesus keeps rewriting it.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
We all entered God's story through scandal.
Sin.
Failure.
Brokenness.
Rebellion.
Yet the cross declares something astonishing.
Jesus specializes in rewriting stories that seemed beyond redemption.
Peter denied Christ.
David committed adultery and murder.
Rahab was known for prostitution.
The Samaritan woman carried the shame of multiple broken relationships.
Paul persecuted Christians.
None of those stories ended with scandal.
They ended with grace.
That is why our theme remains eternally true:
Perhaps you are engaged while carrying hidden fears.
Perhaps one of you has a painful past.
Perhaps there are family wounds.
Financial uncertainty.
Trust issues.
Regret.
Pornography.
Anxiety.
Addiction.
Shame.
Past abortions.
Broken homes.
None of those should be hidden behind smiling engagement photos.
Bring them into the light.
Not because they define your future.
Because Jesus redeems what is surrendered to Him.
John writes:

The Greek word ὁμολογέω (homologeō) means "to confess," literally "to say the same thing." True confession agrees with God about our sin instead of minimizing or excusing it. Forgiveness is never earned by confession; it is granted because of Christ's finished work on the cross, received by faith. That is why confession is an act of hope, not despair.
The strongest marriages are not those with the least brokenness.
They are those where brokenness continually meets the grace of Christ.
If you are preparing for marriage, don't simply ask whether you love one another.
Ask whether both of you are willing to become more like Jesus.
Ask whether Scripture—not feelings—will become your highest authority.
Ask whether prayer will be your first response instead of your last resort.
Ask whether repentance will be practiced regularly.
Ask whether forgiveness will remain open.
Ask whether Christ will always occupy the center.
Because if Jesus is truly Lord of your marriage, every season—even suffering—can become another chapter of redemption.
Someone reading this right now needed this reminder.
Not because your relationship is perfect.
Not because it is falling apart.
But because God is inviting you to build on the only foundation that cannot be shaken.

Share one word that describes what you want God to build in your future or current marriage—"Faithfulness," "Grace," "Trust," "Purity," "Healing," or simply, "Jesus." Your testimony may become the encouragement another couple desperately needs today.
Sometimes God uses an ordinary share to begin an extraordinary conversation that changes a family's future for generations.
God's Word remains true long after emotions change.
Because the wedding lasts a day.
The covenant shapes eternity.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Prophet’s Servant Who Sold His Integrity
paragraphs:
The Prophet’s Servant Who Sold His Integrity
He Thought No One Saw Him. But Heaven Recorded Every Step.
Some scandals begin with a crowd.
Others begin with a whisper.
A hidden desire.
A private compromise.
A moment when nobody is watching.
Or at least that's what we tell ourselves.
The most dangerous sins rarely start with rebellion. They start with justification.
Just this once.
Just a little.
Nobody will know.
I deserve this.
God understands.
That is exactly how one of the most heartbreaking stories in Scripture unfolds.
Not through an idol-worshiping king.
Not through a pagan nation.
Not through a notorious criminal.
But through a servant standing beside one of God's greatest prophets.
His name was Gehazi.
And he sold his integrity for things that could never satisfy his soul.
The tragedy is not merely that Gehazi fell.
The tragedy is that he stood closer to God's power than most people who have ever lived.
He witnessed miracles.
He heard prophetic wisdom.
He walked alongside Elisha, the prophet through whom God displayed extraordinary power.
Yet proximity to God is not the same as surrender to God.
Many people sit in churches every week.
Many know Bible verses.
Many listen to sermons.
Many post Christian content.
Many wear crosses around their necks.
Yet their hearts quietly chase something else.
Gehazi's story is not ancient history.
It is a mirror.
And if we are honest, it reflects more of us than we would like to admit.
The story is found in 2 Kings 5.
A powerful military commander named Naaman suffered from leprosy.
Despite his position, wealth, and influence, he carried a disease that no amount of money could heal.
In many ways, Naaman represents every human being.
Successful perhaps.
Respected perhaps.
But spiritually diseased by sin.
Scripture declares:
"The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick" (Jeremiah 17:9).
Sin creates a condition no human effort can cure.
But God, in His mercy, offered healing.
Naaman eventually obeyed God's command through Elisha and was miraculously cleansed.
After experiencing God's grace, Naaman attempted to reward Elisha with gifts.
Yet Elisha refused.
Why?
Because God's grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation cannot be bought.
Forgiveness cannot be earned.
The Gospel has always pointed toward this truth.
The Hebrew concept of grace often appears through the word חֵן (chen), meaning favor freely given.
The Greek New Testament uses χάρις (charis), meaning grace, undeserved favor, a gift flowing from God's goodness rather than human merit.
Grace is not a transaction.
Grace is God's gift.
Ephesians 2:8-9 says:
"For by grace (χάριτι, chariti) you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast."
Elisha understood something Gehazi did not.
The miracle was never for sale.
But after Naaman left, Gehazi's heart began negotiating with temptation.
The text reveals a chilling sentence:

"But Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the man of God, said, 'See, my master has spared this Naaman the Syrian, in not accepting from his hand what he brought. As the LORD lives, I will run after him and get something from him.'" (2 Kings 5:20)
Notice where the fall began.
Not in his hands.
In his heart.
Not with theft.
With desire.
Not with action.
With rationalization.
Gehazi convinced himself that what God had freely given should become an opportunity for personal gain.
He chased what grace had refused.
How many people are doing the same today?
Using ministry for personal recognition.
Using truth for popularity.
Using service for applause.
Using faith for financial gain.
Using God as a means to obtain something other than God Himself.
The human heart has not changed.
Gehazi ran after Naaman.
He lied.
He invented a story.
He manipulated a miracle.
He received silver and garments under false pretenses.
Then he hid them.
Sin always promises profit.
Then demands secrecy.
That pattern has never changed.
The enemy rarely advertises the consequences.
He advertises the reward.
A little compromise.
A little pleasure.
A little dishonesty.
A little hidden sin.
But hidden things never stay hidden before God.
David wrote:
"Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence?" (Psalm 139:7)
When Gehazi returned, Elisha asked a question that must have frozen his soul.
"Where have you been, Gehazi?"
Again, Gehazi lied.
The scandal deepened.
Because unrepented sin never remains isolated.
One lie requires another.
One compromise requires another.
One secret demands more secrets.
Then came the devastating revelation.
Elisha already knew.
God had seen everything.
Every step.
Every conversation.
Every motive.
Every hidden intention.
Every deception.
Then judgment came.
The leprosy that had left Naaman fell upon Gehazi.
The servant who wanted Naaman's wealth received Naaman's former disease.
The story ends in heartbreaking silence.
A man who had witnessed miracles lost everything because he loved temporary gain more than eternal truth.
Yet even in this tragedy, the Gospel shines brighter.
Because Gehazi's story exposes something deeper than greed.
It exposes the disease all humanity shares.
Sin.
The Hebrew word often used for sin is חַטָּאת (chatta'th), carrying the idea of missing the mark.
The Greek word ἁμαρτία (hamartia) carries the same meaning.
Humanity was created for God's glory.
Yet we have all missed the mark.
Romans 3:23 declares:
"For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God."
Every one of us has a little Gehazi inside.
The temptation to manipulate.
The temptation to hide.
The temptation to pretend.
The temptation to chase what God never intended us to pursue.
The temptation to sell integrity for temporary gain.
That is why we need more than moral improvement.
We need redemption.
We need a Savior.
We need Jesus Christ.
Where Gehazi failed, Christ succeeded.
Where Gehazi lied, Christ is truth.
Where Gehazi pursued selfish gain, Christ emptied Himself.
Where Gehazi sought silver, Jesus shed His blood.
Where Gehazi took what was not his, Jesus gave what was infinitely His.
The Gospel reaches its breathtaking climax at the cross.
There Jesus carried not merely a disease of the skin but the disease of sin itself.
Isaiah prophesied:
"Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows."
The Hebrew phrase נָשָׂא (nasa') means to carry, bear, lift away.
Christ bore what we could never remove ourselves.
On the cross, grace triumphed over scandal.
Mercy triumphed over guilt.
Forgiveness triumphed over condemnation.
And three days later, the empty tomb announced that Jesus rewrites stories no one else can repair.
That is the heartbeat of our mission.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Perhaps your scandal is not greed.
Perhaps it is addiction.
Perhaps it is bitterness.
Perhaps it is pornography.
Perhaps it is deception.
Perhaps it is pride.
Perhaps it is a secret nobody knows.
Perhaps you have become exhausted carrying what Christ already died to remove.
The Gospel is not an invitation to hide better.
The Gospel is an invitation to come home.
The Aramaic word Jesus likely spoke when calling people to follow Him carried the simplicity of invitation and surrender.
Come.
Trust.
Follow.
The same invitation still stands today.
No sin is stronger than His grace.
No failure is greater than His mercy.
No scandal is beyond His power to redeem.
Jesus is still rewriting stories.
Maybe this article found you for a reason.
Maybe the Holy Spirit is exposing something hidden.
Not to destroy you.
To rescue you.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
Supporting this mission is more than supporting content—it is helping spread the message of Jesus Christ to people around the world.
One compromise almost destroyed Gehazi.
One act of surrender can transform your eternity.
And the beautiful truth is this:
Jesus is still writing chapters that human failure said should never exist.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Did Hannah Never Fight Peninnah?
paragraphs:
Why Did Hannah Never Fight Peninnah?
The Silent Battle That Changed History, the Pain Nobody Saw, and the Grace That Still Speaks to Every Wounded Heart
Some battles are fought with swords.
Some are fought with words.
And some are fought in silence.
That is what makes Hannah's story so unforgettable.
Because if we are honest, most of us would have fought back.
Most of us would have defended ourselves.
Most of us would have answered every insult with another insult.
Most of us would have demanded justice long before God brought it.
Yet Hannah did something that feels almost impossible in today's world.
She refused to become what hurt her.
She refused to let her pain rewrite her character.
She refused to let bitterness become her identity.
And because of that, her story became one of the greatest examples of God's power to transform scandal into grace.
The story begins in 1 Samuel 1.
Elkanah had two wives. Hannah and Peninnah.

The arrangement itself already reflected human brokenness. God's design from the beginning was one man and one woman becoming one flesh (Genesis 2:24), yet throughout Israel's history many people lived outside that ideal and suffered the consequences.
Peninnah had children.
Hannah did not.

In the ancient world, barrenness carried enormous emotional weight. A woman was often valued according to her ability to bear children. Infertility was not merely a private sorrow. It was public pain.
Scripture tells us:
"And her rival also provoked her severely, to make her miserable, because the LORD had closed her womb." (1 Samuel 1:6)
The Hebrew word translated "provoked" is כַּעַס (ka'as), carrying the sense of provoking, vexing, irritating, or stirring deep grief.
This was not occasional teasing.
This was intentional cruelty.
Repeated humiliation.
Targeted emotional abuse.
Year after year.
The Bible says:
"So it was, year by year." (1 Samuel 1:7)
Year after year.
Not days.
Not weeks.
Years.
Imagine living with the person who constantly reminds you of your deepest wound.
Imagine eating at the same table.
Seeing the same face.
Hearing the same comments.
Feeling the same ache.
Year after year.
Yet something astonishing happens.
Scripture never records Hannah attacking Peninnah.
Not once.
No insults.
No revenge.
No retaliation.
No schemes.
No attempts to destroy her rival.
No public humiliation.
Nothing.
The silence of Hannah becomes one of the loudest lessons in the entire Bible.
Why?
Because Hannah understood something many believers still struggle to learn.
Not every battle is won by fighting people.
Some battles are won by surrendering them to God.
When Peninnah spoke, Hannah prayed.
When Peninnah mocked, Hannah wept before the Lord.
When Peninnah attacked, Hannah carried her pain into God's presence.
The text says:
"She was deeply distressed and prayed to the LORD and wept bitterly." (1 Samuel 1:10)
The Hebrew expression וּבָכֹה תִבְכֶּה (uvakho tivkeh) intensifies the action.
It literally carries the sense of "weeping she wept."
Deep sobbing.
Uncontrollable grief.
The kind of crying that leaves no words.
The kind of pain heaven hears.
Many people assume strength means showing no weakness.
Hannah teaches the opposite.
Biblical strength is not pretending you are okay.
Biblical strength is bringing your brokenness honestly before God.
The world says hide your tears.
God says bring them to Me.
The world says get even.
God says trust Me.
The world says destroy your enemies.
God says let Me handle what you cannot.
Perhaps that is why Hannah's prayer changed history.
Because she stopped trying to control what only God could fix.
Standing before the tabernacle, she poured out her soul.
The phrase she uses in 1 Samuel 1:15 is remarkable.
"אֶשְׁפֹּךְ אֶת־נַפְשִׁי לִפְנֵי יְהוָה"
(Eshpokh et nafshi lifnei Adonai)
"I have poured out my soul before the LORD."
This is not religious performance.
This is complete surrender.
Nothing hidden.
Nothing polished.
Nothing filtered.
Just a shattered heart placed before a holy God.
And heaven responded.
Not immediately.
Not according to Hannah's timeline.
But faithfully.
Because God is never indifferent to suffering.
Sometimes He is preparing something greater than we can see.
Eventually Hannah conceived and gave birth to Samuel.
His name comes from the Hebrew:
שְׁמוּאֵל
(Shemu'el)
Often understood as "heard by God."
Every time Hannah called her son, she remembered God's faithfulness.
Every time she said his name, she remembered that heaven had listened.
And what happened next changes everything.
Samuel would become prophet.
Judge.
King-maker.
Spiritual leader.
A pivotal figure in Israel's history.
The woman mocked for having no child became the mother of one of the most influential men in Scripture.
The woman others viewed as forgotten became central to God's redemptive story.
The woman who suffered silently became remembered forever.
Peninnah fades into history.
Hannah becomes a testimony.
That is one reason she never had to fight.
Because God was writing a larger story.
And this points us directly to Jesus Christ.
Hannah's story is ultimately not about Hannah.
It is about the God who sees.
The God who hears.
The God who redeems.
The God who turns wounds into testimonies.
The God who transforms shame into glory.
When we reach the New Testament, we see the perfect fulfillment of that truth in Jesus.
Christ Himself was mocked.
Rejected.
Humiliated.
Falsely accused.
Yet the Apostle Peter writes:
The Greek text says:
λοιδορούμενος οὐκ ἀντελοιδόρει
(loidoroumenos ouk anteloidorei)
"Being insulted, He did not insult back."
Jesus did what Hannah foreshadowed.
He entrusted Himself to the Father.
He absorbed injustice without becoming injustice.
He suffered without surrendering to bitterness.
He carried the cross instead of seeking revenge.
And because He did, salvation became available to sinners like us.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Every one of us has been Peninnah.
Every one of us has wounded others.
Failed God.
Chosen pride.
Chosen selfishness.
Chosen sin.
Yet Jesus stepped into our scandal.
Took our guilt.
Carried our shame.
Paid our debt.
And offered grace we could never earn.
That is why our theme remains true:
Maybe you are carrying a Peninnah in your life right now.
Someone who wounded you.
Betrayed you.
Humiliated you.
Lied about you.
Abandoned you.
Maybe every instinct tells you to fight back.
Maybe you spend sleepless nights replaying conversations and planning responses.
Maybe the hurt feels fresh even after years.
Hannah's story does not teach passivity toward evil.
It teaches trust in God's justice.
It teaches surrender instead of bitterness.
It teaches that your deepest wounds do not have to define your future.
The same God who heard Hannah still hears His children today.
The same God who saw her tears still sees yours.
The same God who rewrote her story still rewrites stories through Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is why this account continues to grip hearts thousands of years later.
Because every person knows what it feels like to suffer.
Every person knows what it feels like to be misunderstood.
Every person knows what it feels like to carry a wound nobody else sees.
Yet Hannah reminds us that God often does His greatest work in the places where we feel most broken.
If this story spoke to your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
You never know who is carrying a hidden burden and desperately needs this reminder today.
What battle are you trusting God with instead of fighting yourself?
Your testimony may encourage someone who feels completely alone.
One meaningful way to glorify God is by supporting Gospel-centered ministry that faithfully spreads His Word.
Because sometimes the greatest victory is not proving your enemy wrong.
It is allowing God to prove Himself faithful.
And years from now, the thing that broke your heart may become the very testimony that brings someone else to Jesus.
The tears Hannah cried in secret still echo across generations.
And the God who heard her still listens today.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: TAKE NO THOUGHT FOR TOMORROW
paragraphs:
TAKE NO THOUGHT FOR TOMORROW
The Verse Almost Everyone Quotes Wrong—and the Life-Changing Freedom Jesus Was Actually Offering
There are people reading this right now who look completely fine on the outside.
They smiled today.
They answered messages.
They went to work.
They paid bills.
They posted photos.
They even told others they were doing okay.
But beneath the surface, they are carrying conversations that have not happened yet.
Arguments that have not happened yet.
Disasters that have not happened yet.
Losses that have not happened yet.
Failures that have not happened yet.
Tomorrow has become a prison cell built from imagination.
And what makes it even more painful is that many believers live there too.
We quote Scripture.
We pray.
We worship.
Yet our minds constantly race ahead of God.
That is why one of the most quoted—and most misunderstood—statements of Jesus is so important.
In Matthew 6:34, Jesus said:
"Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof."
Many people hear that verse and assume Jesus was telling believers not to plan.
Not to prepare.
Not to think about the future.
But that interpretation falls apart when compared with the rest of Scripture.
The Bible praises wisdom, preparation, stewardship, and diligence.
Joseph prepared for famine.
Nehemiah planned a rebuilding project.
Paul organized ministry journeys.
The Proverbs repeatedly praise foresight and preparation.
So what was Jesus really saying?
The answer becomes clearer when we look at the original Greek language.
Matthew 6:34 uses the word:
"μεριμνήσητε" (merimnēsēte)
from the root word:
"μεριμνάω" (merimnaō)
This word does not simply mean "to think."
It means to be anxious.
To be troubled.
To be pulled apart internally.
To be consumed with worry.
The word itself carries the idea of being divided.
A person whose heart is being dragged in multiple directions.
Jesus was not forbidding planning.
He was forbidding anxiety.
He was confronting a deeper spiritual problem.
The illusion that worrying gives us control.
The context makes this undeniable.
Just moments earlier Jesus points to birds.
Birds do not own barns.
They do not store investments.
They do not know what tomorrow holds.
Yet the Father feeds them.
Then Jesus points to flowers.
Flowers do not obsess over appearance.
Yet God clothes them with beauty greater than Solomon's glory.
Jesus asks:
"If God so clothe the grass of the field... shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?" (Matthew 6:30)
Notice what Jesus exposes.
The issue is not tomorrow.
The issue is trust.
The issue is whether we believe God is as faithful to us as He claims to be.
And that question reaches much deeper than finances.
It reaches relationships.
Health.
Family.
Ministry.
Dreams.
Calling.
Purpose.
The future.
Every fear ultimately asks the same question:
"Can God really be trusted?"
That question is as old as Eden.
In Genesis 3, the serpent's first attack was not against God's power.
It was against God's character.
The enemy planted suspicion.
Can God really be trusted?
Thousands of years later, humanity is still wrestling with the same lie.
We worry because somewhere deep inside us, we fear God may not come through.
We fear He may forget.
We fear He may abandon us.
We fear He may not provide.
Yet Scripture repeatedly reveals the opposite.
The Hebrew Scriptures describe God as:
"יְהוָה יִרְאֶה" (YHWH Yireh)
"The LORD Will Provide"
Genesis 22:14.
Abraham discovered this truth on a mountain of impossible obedience.
When everything appeared lost.
When the promise seemed threatened.
When the future looked terrifying.
God provided.
Not early.
Not late.
Exactly on time.
The same God has not changed.
Many people think anxiety is produced by uncertainty.
But uncertainty is not the true source.
The true source is believing we must carry what God never asked us to carry.
That is why 1 Peter 5:7 says:
"Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you."
The word "care" comes from the Greek:
"μέριμνα" (merimna)
The same family of words connected to anxiety.
Peter is essentially saying:
"Throw your worries onto God because He is already carrying concern for you."
What an astonishing picture.
God never intended your shoulders to hold the weight of tomorrow.
Those shoulders were never designed for it.
No wonder so many people feel exhausted.
No wonder so many people feel overwhelmed.
No wonder so many people cannot sleep.
They are attempting to carry a burden that belongs to God.
Jesus was not offering motivational advice.
He was offering divine liberation.
Yet this message becomes even more powerful when viewed through the lens of the Gospel.
Because the greatest source of human anxiety is not finances.
It is not politics.
It is not health.
It is not uncertainty.
It is sin.
Every human heart carries a deeper fear.
What happens when I stand before a holy God?
What happens with my failures?
My secrets?
My rebellion?
My shame?
My guilt?
My scandal?
The Gospel answers those questions in a way no self-help philosophy ever could.
At the cross, Jesus carried the ultimate tomorrow.
He entered the judgment humanity deserved.
He absorbed the wrath against sin.
He bore the punishment we could never survive.
Isaiah 53:5 declares:
"But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities."
The Hebrew word for wounded is:
"מְחֹלָל" (mecholal)
Pierced.
Profaned.
Wounded deeply.
Christ took upon Himself what should have fallen upon us.
The greatest future threat humanity faced was eternal separation from God.
Jesus conquered it.
That changes everything.
Because if God solved our greatest problem through the cross, why should we believe He will abandon us in our smaller ones?
Romans 8:32 asks:
"He that spared not his own Son... how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?"
The cross becomes God's eternal proof of commitment.
Every nail.
Every wound.
Every drop of blood declares:
"You can trust Me."
That is why "take no thought for tomorrow" is not a command rooted in positive thinking.
It is a command rooted in the character of God revealed through Jesus Christ.
The believer does not deny tomorrow exists.
The believer simply refuses to worship it.
The believer does not pretend problems are absent.
The believer remembers God is present.
And perhaps someone reading this desperately needed that reminder.
You have been fighting battles that have not happened.
Losing sleep over situations that may never occur.
Creating worst-case scenarios in your mind.
Living in a future God has not asked you to enter yet.
Meanwhile, today's grace remains untouched.
Today's strength remains available.
Today's mercy remains sufficient.
Jesus never promised grace for imaginary tomorrows.
He promised grace for today.
That is why He said:
"Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof."
In other words:
Today has enough challenges.
Do not import tomorrow's burdens into today's battlefield.
Trust God when tomorrow arrives.
Just as He has always been faithful before.
Maybe that is why some of the most powerful testimonies in Scripture begin with impossible situations.
Abraham.
Moses.
David.
Ruth.
Peter.
Paul.
Mary Magdalene.
Each story seemed headed toward disaster.
Yet God rewrote every chapter.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
The world sees scandal.
Jesus sees redemption.
The world sees failure.
Jesus sees restoration.
The world sees brokenness.
Jesus sees transformation.
The world sees endings.
Jesus writes new beginnings.
And perhaps your story is not falling apart.
Perhaps God is writing a chapter you cannot understand yet.
If this message spoke directly to your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
"I trust Jesus with tomorrow."
There is power in bringing hidden burdens into the light.
And never forget this:
The same hands that hold your eternal future are holding tomorrow too.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Lesson I Learned From the Lost Coin
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From the Lost Coin
She Wasn't Lost Because She Was Worthless. She Was Lost Because She Was Valuable Enough To Search For.
There is a kind of pain that few people talk about.
The pain of feeling forgotten.
Not abandoned.
Not hated.
Just... overlooked.
You can sit in a room full of people and still feel invisible.
You can smile in family photos and still feel broken inside.
You can serve at church, help everyone around you, carry everyone's burdens, and secretly wonder if anyone would notice if you disappeared tomorrow.
Maybe that's why Jesus told a story about a coin.
Because He knew many of us would spend our lives feeling exactly like one.
In Luke 15:8-10, Jesus said:

"Or what woman having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, 'Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.' Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents."
At first glance, it feels like a simple story.
A woman loses a coin.
She searches.
She finds it.
Everyone celebrates.
But beneath that simplicity is one of the most emotionally powerful revelations in all of Scripture.
The Greek word translated "lost" is ἀπολέσασα (apolesasa), from apollymi, meaning to ruin, destroy, lose, or cause something to perish.
The coin was not removed from her ownership.
It still belonged to her.
Its condition had not changed.
Its value had not changed.
Its identity had not changed.
Only its location had changed.
And that changes everything.
Because many people believe that when they wander away from God, they lose their worth.
The enemy whispers:
"You've failed too much."
"You've sinned too deeply."
"You've gone too far."
"You've ruined God's plan for your life."
But Jesus tells a different story.
The coin never stopped being valuable.
The woman did not search because the coin was worthless.
She searched because it was precious.
Let that sink in.
God does not pursue you because you are useful.
He pursues you because you are His.
Long before you ever searched for Him, He was searching for you.
This truth echoes throughout Scripture.
In Genesis, after Adam and Eve sinned, God came into the garden asking:
"אֵיכָּה" (Ayekah?)
"Where are you?" (Genesis 3:9)
Not because God lacked information.
Because God was revealing His heart.
Humanity ran.
God pursued.
Humanity hid.
God searched.
Humanity covered itself with shame.
God moved toward them anyway.
The entire Bible is the story of a God who refuses to stop searching.
A God who enters scandals.
A God who walks into messes.
A God who steps into broken family trees, failed marriages, addictions, betrayals, and rebellion.
A God who specializes in rewriting endings.
That is why our theme is not merely a slogan.
It is the Gospel itself.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Many people reading this are carrying invisible shame.
You know what you did.
You know where you've been.
You know the nights nobody knows about.
The secret sins.
The compromises.
The bitterness.
The addiction.
The affair.
The lies.
The resentment.
The pride.
The wounds.
The regrets.
The failures.
And somewhere along the journey you began believing that God loves everyone except people like you.
But the lost coin destroys that lie.
The coin was not found because it found its way home.
It was found because someone loved it enough to search relentlessly.
Notice the language Jesus uses.
The woman "seek diligently."
The Greek phrase implies careful, persistent, intentional searching.
This was not casual.
This was passionate.
She lit a lamp.
She swept the house.
She searched until she found it.
Not until she got tired.
Not until it became inconvenient.
Not until she felt discouraged.
Until she found it.
That is the picture Jesus wants us to see.
God's pursuit is not half-hearted.
He is not reluctantly tolerating you.
He is not rolling His eyes at your failures.
He is not waiting for you to become perfect before approaching you.
He searches.
He calls.
He convicts.
He pursues.
He knocks.
He reaches.
He rescues.
And He does not stop.
The prophet Isaiah captured this beautifully:
"We all like sheep have gone astray." (Isaiah 53:6)
The Hebrew word for "gone astray" is תָּעִינוּ (ta'inu), meaning to wander, stagger, or drift away.
That sounds familiar, doesn't it?
Most people do not wake up one morning planning to destroy their lives.
They drift.
A compromise here.
A secret there.
One neglected prayer.
One ignored conviction.
One unchecked temptation.
One little step at a time.
Until they find themselves somewhere they never intended to be.
Lost.
Yet Jesus enters that darkness carrying a lamp.
In John 8:12 He declares:
"ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ φῶς τοῦ κόσμου"
(Ego eimi to phōs tou kosmou)
"I am the light of the world."
The woman in the parable lit a lamp to find the coin.
Jesus became the Lamp to find us.
He stepped into our darkness.
He entered our brokenness.
He walked into our scandal.
He carried our sin.
He bore our shame.
He endured the Cross.
The Cross was not an accident.
It was a rescue mission.
The lost coin was valuable enough to search for.
You were valuable enough to die for.
Think about that.
The Son of God left Heaven.
Entered history.
Took on flesh.
Was mocked.
Rejected.
Beaten.
Spit upon.
Crucified.
And rose again.
For sinners.
For failures.
For wanderers.
For lost coins.
For people exactly like us.
And then Jesus reveals something astonishing.
Heaven celebrates when one sinner repents.
Not merely tolerates.
Celebrates.
The Greek word for rejoice is χαρά (chara), meaning joy, delight, gladness, overwhelming celebration.
Can you imagine that?
The angels of Heaven rejoicing over your return.
Not because you became impressive.
Not because you became famous.
Not because you became successful.
Because you came home.
Somebody reading this needs to hear this today.
Your story is not over.
Your failures are not your final chapter.
Your worst mistake is not your identity.
Your scandal is not your destiny.
Jesus still rewrites everything.
That relationship.
That addiction.
That broken marriage.
That depression.
That shame.
That regret.
That hidden struggle.
That wandering heart.
He still rewrites everything.
Maybe that's why this parable continues to grip hearts after two thousand years.
Because every one of us knows what it feels like to be lost.
And every one of us longs to be found.
So let me ask you something.
What if the conviction you're feeling right now is not condemnation?
What if it is the sound of Heaven's search party drawing near?
What if God has been pursuing you all along?
What if this article is one more sweep of the broom?
One more flash of the lamp?
One more reminder that you are still loved?
One more invitation to come home?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
It helps spread the Gospel, create Christ-centered biblical content, equip believers, reach the lost, and continue producing resources that point people to Jesus Christ.
Because someone you know may feel exactly like that lost coin right now.
And they need to discover what Jesus has been saying all along.
They were never worthless.
They were always worth searching for.
The God who searched for you is still searching for them.
And He has never once lost track of where grace can reach.
Even now, Heaven still celebrates every soul that comes home.
And maybe today, that soul is you.
The same God who found you in the dust can still turn your deepest scandal into His greatest testimony of grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Person Who Weaponized Religion
paragraphs:
The Person Who Weaponized Religion
He knew every rule, defended every tradition, and believed he was serving God... until he discovered he was fighting against the very Messiah he claimed to honor.
There is something terrifying about being sincerely wrong.
Not because you intended evil.
Not because you hated God.
But because you loved your version of God so much that you stopped recognizing Him when He stood directly in front of you.
That was the scandal of Saul of Tarsus.

Long before he became the Apostle Paul, before churches were planted, before letters were written, before miracles were performed, Saul was a religious celebrity in the making. He was educated, respected, disciplined, zealous, and completely convinced he was on God's side.
If Saul lived today, many believers would probably admire him.
He knew Scripture.
He defended truth.
He opposed what he believed was heresy.
He was passionate.
Committed.
Fearless.
And completely blind.
That is what makes his story so frighteningly relatable.
Because the greatest danger to the soul is not always rebellion.
Sometimes it is religion without Christ.
Sometimes it is truth without love.
Sometimes it is defending God while resisting the work of God.
Saul first appears in Scripture during the murder of Stephen.
Acts 8:1 records:
"And Saul approved of his execution."
The Greek text says:
"Σαῦλος δὲ ἦν συνευδοκῶν τῇ ἀναιρέσει αὐτοῦ"
(Saulos de ēn syneudokōn tē anairesei autou)
Literally:
"Saul was giving approval to his destruction."
He was not merely present.
He was pleased.
He believed righteousness was being defended.
He believed he was protecting God's honor.
He believed violence was justified if it preserved religious purity.
History has seen this tragedy repeated countless times.
People have burned others in the name of God.
Condemned others in the name of God.
Excluded others in the name of God.
Destroyed others in the name of God.
All while believing they were serving God.
Jesus warned this would happen.
In John 16:2, He said:
"They will put you out of the synagogues. Indeed, the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God."
The Greek phrase is:
"λατρείαν προσφέρειν τῷ Θεῷ"
(latreian prospherein tō Theō)
Meaning:
"to present worship or sacred service to God."
Imagine that.
Thinking you are worshiping God while opposing what God is doing.
That was Saul.
Religion had become a weapon.
Scripture had become ammunition.
Conviction had become cruelty.
The law had become a shield protecting his pride.
Yet beneath all his certainty was a desperate problem.
He knew about God.
But he did not know Christ.
And without Christ, even religion can become dangerous.
Then came the road to Damascus.
One moment Saul was hunting Christians.
The next moment heaven interrupted him.
Acts 9:3-4 says:
"Suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. And falling to the ground he heard a voice saying to him, 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?'"
Notice what Jesus did not ask.
He did not say:
"Why are you persecuting My followers?"
He said:
"Why are you persecuting Me?"
Because Christ is so united with His people that what is done to them is done to Him.
Saul thought he was attacking Christians.
Jesus revealed he was attacking Christ Himself.
Everything changed with one question.
A question powerful enough to shatter decades of religious certainty.
A question many of us still need to hear.
Could it be possible that some of the things we defend most passionately are actually keeping us from seeing Jesus clearly?
Could it be possible that our traditions, preferences, pride, political loyalties, denominational identities, or religious habits sometimes become more important than Christ Himself?
Saul discovered that being convinced is not the same as being correct.
The Hebrew Scriptures had always pointed to Jesus.
Isaiah pointed to Him.
The Psalms pointed to Him.
The sacrifices pointed to Him.
The prophets pointed to Him.
Everything pointed to Him.
Yet Saul missed Him.
How?
Because knowledge without surrender produces blindness.
The Hebrew word often translated "know" is יָדַע (yada).
It means far more than intellectual awareness.
It means intimate relationship.
Experiential knowledge.
Personal encounter.
Saul had information.
What he lacked was transformation.
Many people today are exactly where Saul once stood.
They know verses.
They know sermons.
They know theology.
But they do not truly know Jesus.
And the distance between knowing about Christ and knowing Christ is the distance between death and life.
Then comes one of the most beautiful moments in all of Scripture.
Jesus could have destroyed Saul.
He could have judged him instantly.
He could have condemned him for every Christian imprisoned, beaten, or killed.
Instead, Jesus pursued him.
Grace found the man who least deserved it.
That is the Gospel.
Not that good people find God.
But that God finds sinners.
Paul would later write:
(1 Timothy 1:15)
Notice he did not say he was formerly the foremost.
Even years later, Paul never forgot the scandal of his past.
He never stopped marveling at grace.
Because those who understand how much they have been forgiven rarely become proud.
They become grateful.
The story of Saul becoming Paul is not merely a conversion story.
It is a resurrection story.
A story proving nobody is beyond redemption.
Not the addict.
Not the adulterer.
Not the skeptic.
Not the hypocrite.
Not the religious legalist.
Not the church critic.
Not the person carrying decades of shame.
Not even the person who once fought against Jesus.
Because the Gospel specializes in impossible transformations.
That is why our ministry exists.
Because we believe there are countless modern-day Sauls scrolling right now.
People exhausted from pretending.
People hiding behind religion.
People carrying guilt.
People who think their failures have permanently defined them.
People who believe their story is over.
But Jesus still rewrites stories.
That is what He does.
From blindness to sight.
From condemnation to forgiveness.
From death to life.
Maybe that is why this article found you today.
Not by accident.
Not by coincidence.
But because God is still asking the same question He asked Saul.
Are you willing to surrender everything you think you know and truly follow Jesus?
You may need it again during a season when pride tries to disguise itself as righteousness.

Someone in your family, a friend, a struggling believer, a prodigal son or daughter, or even someone who has been wounded by religion may desperately need this reminder that Jesus still transforms lives.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else needs today.

More importantly, your support helps place Gospel-centered content in front of people who may never walk into a church but may encounter Jesus through a shared post, an article, a testimony, or a message of hope.

If God has used this ministry to bless you, supporting and sharing its work is one meaningful way to help spread the Gospel and steward the resources He has entrusted to us. Not because salvation can be purchased, earned, or supported financially—it cannot. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone (Ephesians 2:8-9). Rather, supporting Gospel ministry is one way believers participate in advancing the message of Christ to others.
Because one shared article can reach a wandering soul.
One testimony can break someone's silence.
One act of obedience can become part of another person's rescue story.
And one encounter with Jesus can rewrite everything.
The same Savior who stopped Saul on a dusty road is still stopping people in the middle of their rebellion, pride, confusion, religion, shame, and brokenness today.
The greatest miracle was never that Saul became Paul.
The greatest miracle was that Jesus loved Saul before Saul ever loved Jesus.
And He still does the same for us.
The grace you have been running from may be the very thing running after you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Real Reason Sex Was Meant Only for Marriage
paragraphs:
The Real Reason Sex Was Meant Only for Marriage
The Truth Modern Culture Hid From You: Why God Created Sexual Intimacy as a Covenant, Not a Casual Experience
There is a question that almost nobody asks anymore.
Not because it is unimportant.
But because the world has become terrified of the answer.
Why did God create sex?
Not why people want it.
Not why culture celebrates it.
Not why entertainment markets it.
Why did God create it?
Because until we understand the Creator's purpose, we will continue using His gift in ways that wound the very hearts it was designed to heal.
Most people have been told that God's boundaries around sex are restrictive. Outdated. Unrealistic. Oppressive.
But what if the exact opposite is true?
What if God's design for sexual intimacy inside marriage is not about limiting joy but protecting it?

What if the deepest heartbreaks, betrayals, regrets, addictions, insecurities, broken families, and emotional scars surrounding sexuality today exist because humanity abandoned the blueprint given by the One who invented it?
The Bible begins not with prohibition but with purpose.
In Genesis 2:24, Scripture says:
"Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh."
The Hebrew phrase for "one flesh" is בָּשָׂר אֶחָד (basar echad).
This is not merely physical union.
It describes a profound joining together of lives, identities, futures, responsibilities, and covenant commitment.
God never designed sex as a recreational activity detached from relationship.
He designed it as the physical expression of a spiritual covenant.
A covenant is not a contract.
Contracts are maintained as long as both parties benefit.
Covenants remain even when sacrifice becomes necessary.
That is why marriage matters.
Marriage provides the covenant container strong enough to hold the power of sexual intimacy.
Without covenant, intimacy becomes vulnerable to abandonment.
Without commitment, vulnerability becomes dangerous.
Without lifelong devotion, the deepest parts of the human heart remain exposed.
This is why Scripture consistently places sexual intimacy inside marriage.
Not because God hates pleasure.
Because He understands the human soul better than we do.
The world often says sex is merely physical.
The Bible never says that.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:16:
The Greek phrase is:
οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν (hoi duo eis sarka mian)
Again, the language points beyond physical activity.
Something deeper occurs.
God created human beings as integrated creatures.
Body.
Mind.
Heart.
Soul.
What affects one affects all.
That is why sexual experiences often leave emotional memories long after physical contact has ended.
People may try to separate the body from the heart.
But the Creator never designed them to operate independently.
Many people know exactly what this feels like.
You thought it was just a relationship.
Just dating.
Just a moment.
Just an experience.
Yet years later, memories remain.
Wounds remain.
Comparisons remain.
Regrets remain.
Because something deeper was involved.
God was not trying to keep you from pleasure.
He was trying to protect you from pain.
Modern culture teaches that freedom means removing boundaries.
Scripture teaches that freedom comes from living within God's design.
A fish is not free outside water.
A train is not free off the tracks.
A human being is not free while violating the Creator's design.
The enemy's oldest strategy has always been the same:
Convince people that God's boundaries are actually barriers to happiness.
That lie began in Eden.
And it has never stopped working.
Today entire industries profit from convincing people that sexual fulfillment can be found apart from God's design.
Yet despite unprecedented sexual freedom, loneliness is increasing.
Anxiety is increasing.
Relationship instability is increasing.
Broken homes are increasing.
People have more access to intimacy than ever before and often feel more disconnected than ever before.
Because physical closeness without covenant cannot satisfy what God created to be fulfilled through covenant.
At its deepest level, sex was never merely about sex.
It was always pointing beyond itself.
Marriage itself is a living picture of something greater.
Ephesians 5:31-32 says:
"For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh."
Then Paul says:
"This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church."
The Greek word translated "mystery" is:
μυστήριον (mystērion)
Meaning a divine truth once hidden but now revealed.
Marriage was always designed to reflect the Gospel.
Think about that.
A faithful husband.
A faithful bride.
Sacrificial love.
Permanent commitment.
Covenant loyalty.
Forgiveness.
Grace.
Restoration.
These are not random marriage principles.
They mirror Jesus Christ.
The Gospel is the ultimate love story.
Christ pursued a broken people.
A sinful people.
A rebellious people.
A people who repeatedly failed Him.
Yet He remained faithful.
At the cross, Jesus demonstrated covenant love unlike anything the world has ever seen.
He did not leave when we failed.
He stayed.
He suffered.
He bled.
He died.
He redeemed.
Marriage reflects that covenant.
Sex becomes the physical celebration of that covenant.
Remove the covenant and the symbol loses its intended meaning.
This is why Scripture consistently reserves sexual intimacy for marriage.
Not because God is anti-sex.
The Bible celebrates marital intimacy.
The book of Song of Songs is evidence of that.
God created desire.
God created attraction.
God created passion.
God created intimacy.
What He opposes is not sex.
He opposes the destruction that occurs when His gifts are separated from His design.
Maybe as you read this, conviction is rising.
Not condemnation.
Conviction.
There is a difference.
Condemnation says there is no hope.
Conviction says there is still a way home.
Some readers have sexual regrets.
Some carry shame.
Some have wounds from relationships that promised forever but disappeared overnight.
Some have experienced betrayal.
Some are fighting private addictions.
Some feel disqualified from God's love.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel was never written for perfect people.
It was written for broken people.
The woman caught in adultery expected stones.
She encountered grace.
The Samaritan woman had five failed relationships.
She encountered grace.
David committed sexual sin and shattered lives.
He encountered grace after repentance.
Peter denied Christ.
He encountered grace.
The Bible is filled with scandal.
Because the Bible is ultimately about redemption.
That is our story too.
The message of Christianity is not that good people earn God's love.
The message of Christianity is that sinners can be transformed by God's grace through Jesus Christ.
The cross stands as eternal proof.
No failure is stronger than His mercy.
No shame is deeper than His forgiveness.
No past is greater than His power to redeem.
If sexual sin is part of your story, it does not have to be the end of your story.
Jesus still rewrites lives.
Jesus still restores purity.
Jesus still heals wounds.
Jesus still breaks chains.
Jesus still makes all things new.
And maybe that is why this message matters so much.
Because this is not ultimately about rules.
It is about relationship.
It is about trusting the God who loves you enough to tell you the truth.
It is about believing that His design is better than our alternatives.
It is about discovering that holiness is not the enemy of joy.
It is the pathway to it.
If this article challenged you, encouraged you, convicted you, or reminded you of God's grace, do not keep it to yourself.
Let that be your declaration of faith.
Let it be your reminder that your past does not define your future.
Because every share becomes a witness.
Every comment becomes a testimony.
Every follow becomes a step toward truth.
And every life surrendered to Christ becomes evidence that grace still changes everything.
The greatest tragedy is not that you have fallen.
It is believing you cannot be raised again.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Taste and See: The Day Psalm 34:8 Stopped Being a Verse and Became a Lifeline
paragraphs:
Taste and See: The Day Psalm 34:8 Stopped Being a Verse and Became a Lifeline
Most people have read Psalm 34:8. Very few have truly tasted it. And that changes everything.
Some Scriptures are read.
Some are studied.
Some are memorized.
And then there are the verses that find you when life has stripped away every illusion you were using to survive.
Psalm 34:8 is one of those verses.
Not because it is complicated.
But because it is devastatingly personal.
Not because it is difficult to understand.
But because it demands something far more uncomfortable than understanding.
It demands experience.
The verse says:
“Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good; blessed is the man who trusts in Him.” (Psalm 34:8, NKJV)
At first glance, it sounds beautiful.
Comforting.
Almost poetic.
But hidden beneath these familiar words is a depth that most people never stop long enough to explore.

And if you truly understand what David was saying, this verse may change the way you see your failures, your wounds, your unanswered prayers, your salvation, and even your relationship with Jesus Christ.
Because Psalm 34 was not written from a palace.
It was written from a scandal.
David wrote these words after one of the lowest moments of his life.
The future king of Israel was running for his life.
Hunted.
Terrified.
Broken.
Desperate.
He fled to Gath, the hometown of Goliath—the giant he had killed years earlier.
When the Philistines recognized him, fear consumed him.
Scripture tells us that David pretended to be insane.
He scratched on doors.
Let saliva run down his beard.
Acted like a madman.
Humiliated himself just to survive.
This is the backdrop of Psalm 34.
Not victory.
Not applause.
Not success.
Shame.
Fear.
Embarrassment.
Failure.
And yet it is from this place that David writes:
That should stop us in our tracks.
Because most people wait until life is perfect before declaring God's goodness.
David declared God's goodness while standing in the wreckage of his own weakness.
The Hebrew text makes this even more powerful.
The word translated "taste" is the Hebrew word טָעַם (ta'am).
It means far more than taking a sample.
It means to experience personally.
To perceive by direct encounter.
To know firsthand.
David is not saying:
"Read about God's goodness."
He is not saying:
"Study God's goodness."
He is not saying:
"Listen to someone else's testimony about God's goodness."
He is saying:
"Experience Him yourself."
Because secondhand faith will never sustain you in seasons where your heart is breaking.
At some point every believer must move beyond inherited faith and encounter God personally.
The tragedy of modern Christianity is that many people know facts about God but have never truly tasted Him.
They know church.
They know sermons.
They know Christian culture.
But they do not know Him.
And there is a difference.
The next word is equally powerful.
"See."
The Hebrew word is רָאָה (ra'ah).
To perceive.
To behold.
To understand through direct observation.
The order matters.
David does not say:
"See and then taste."
He says:
"Taste and see."
Experience comes first.
Understanding follows.
Many people spend their lives waiting until they understand everything before they trust God.
But God often works in reverse.
Trust first.
See later.
Walk first.
Understand later.
Obey first.
See the wisdom later.
That pattern echoes throughout Scripture.
When Abraham was called, he walked before he knew where he was going.
When Peter stepped out of the boat, he stepped before he understood how water could hold him.
When the blind man obeyed Jesus and washed in the pool, his healing came afterward.
Faith has always involved tasting before seeing.
And nowhere is this more beautifully fulfilled than in Jesus Christ.
The Gospel itself is an invitation to taste and see.
Not merely to admire Christ.
Not merely to agree with facts about Christ.
But to encounter Him.
The Apostle John writes:
God did not send information.
He sent Himself.
The eternal Son entered human history.
The One who created galaxies stepped into our scandal.
Our brokenness.
Our rebellion.
Our shame.
And this is where Psalm 34 becomes deeply personal.
Because every human being carries a story.
A secret.
A regret.
A wound.
A chapter they wish could be removed.
Many people spend years trying to hide what Jesus came to heal.
They wear smiles over heartbreak.
Strength over exhaustion.
Confidence over insecurity.
Religion over repentance.
But Jesus has never been intimidated by human failure.
The Gospel is built on scandal transformed by grace.
Think about it.
Rahab was a prostitute.
Moses was a murderer.
Jacob was a deceiver.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted believers.
Yet God rewrote every one of their stories.
The cross itself looked like the greatest scandal in history.
An innocent Savior publicly executed.
Mocked.
Rejected.
Abandoned.
Bleeding.
Dying.
But what appeared to be defeat became redemption.
What looked like the end became the beginning.
What looked like condemnation became salvation.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
This is why we say:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Even now.
Even your story.
The goodness David tasted ultimately pointed forward to Christ.
The New Testament uses similar language.
In 1 Peter 2:3 we read:
“If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is gracious.”
The Greek word is γεύομαι (geuomai).
To taste.
To experience personally.
To partake.
Again, Scripture points beyond intellectual agreement.
The invitation is relational.
Personal.
Transformational.
Christianity is not merely accepting truths about Jesus.
It is knowing Jesus.
Walking with Jesus.
Trusting Jesus.
Being transformed by Jesus.
And those who truly encounter Him discover something shocking.
God's goodness is often most visible in the places we least expected to find it.
Sometimes His goodness appears in healing.
Sometimes it appears in waiting.
Sometimes it appears in provision.
Sometimes it appears in pruning.
Sometimes it appears in rescue.
Sometimes it appears in the strength to endure.
The cross teaches us that God's goodness cannot always be measured by present circumstances.
It must be measured through the character of God revealed in Jesus Christ.
The cross forever answers the question:
"Is God good?"
Because a God who willingly bears our sin, our guilt, our judgment, and our shame is a God whose goodness reaches deeper than human understanding.
That is why Psalm 34:8 remains one of the most powerful invitations ever written.
It does not say:
"Taste and see that life is easy."
It does not say:
"Taste and see that every prayer will be answered exactly as you wish."
It does not say:
"Taste and see that suffering disappears."
It says:
"Taste and see that the LORD is good."
His goodness remains even when circumstances change.
His goodness remains when prayers seem delayed.
His goodness remains when tears fall.
His goodness remains when answers are hidden.
His goodness remains because He remains.
Maybe that is why this verse continues speaking to generation after generation.
Because every human heart is searching for something.
Success cannot satisfy it.
Money cannot satisfy it.
Pleasure cannot satisfy it.
Achievement cannot satisfy it.
Only Christ can.
The invitation remains open today.
Taste.
See.
Trust.
Come to the One who turns failures into testimonies.
Shame into redemption.
Wounds into worship.
Scandal into grace.
The same Savior who transformed David, Peter, Paul, Rahab, and countless others is still rewriting stories today.
Perhaps yours is next.
And if this message stirred something in your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
What part of your story are you trusting Jesus to rewrite?
It is partnering in the spread of the Gospel and helping others move from darkness to light, from bondage to freedom, and from scandal to grace through Jesus Christ.
One day you will realize the chapter that almost destroyed you became the chapter Jesus used to introduce His grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE THOUGHT GOD WAS DONE WITH HIM
paragraphs:
HE THOUGHT GOD WAS DONE WITH HIM
The Shocking Depth of 1 Chronicles 16:34 and Why God's Love Still Reaches the People Who Feel Beyond Redemption
There are verses so familiar that we stop hearing them.
We quote them.
We memorize them.
We place them on coffee mugs, wall art, journals, and social media graphics.
Then one day God opens our eyes and we realize we have spent years standing beside a treasure chest without ever opening it.
That is exactly what happens with 1 Chronicles 16:34.
"Give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever." (KJV)
Simple.
Beautiful.
Comforting.

Yet beneath those few words lies a truth so powerful that it has carried broken people through wars, failures, betrayals, funerals, addictions, scandals, prodigal seasons, and moments when they believed God could never love them again.
This verse was not written by people who had perfect lives.
It was sung by people who knew what it felt like to fail.
People who knew what it felt like to disappoint God.
People who knew what it felt like to watch entire generations suffer because of sin.
And somehow, after all of that, they still declared:
"Give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever."
That should make us pause.
Because most people can thank God when life is going well.
But what about after the divorce?
After the addiction?
After the affair?
After the abortion?
After the years wasted?
After the secret nobody knows?
After the scandal?
After the shame?
After the moment you look in the mirror and no longer recognize who you have become?
Can a person still say God is good then?
That is the question hidden inside this verse.
The Hebrew text reads:
הוֹדוּ לַיהוָה כִּי־טוֹב כִּי לְעוֹלָם חַסְדּוֹ
"Hodu l'Adonai ki tov, ki le'olam chasdo."
The phrase "הוֹדוּ" (hodu) means more than casual gratitude.
It carries the sense of confessing, acknowledging, proclaiming publicly.
This is not private appreciation.
This is public testimony.
This is the language of someone who cannot stay silent about what God has done.
Then comes:
"כִּי־טוֹב" (ki tov)
"For He is good."
Not because circumstances are good.
Not because life is easy.
Not because suffering has disappeared.
God is good because goodness is His nature.
His character does not fluctuate with our circumstances.
The economy changes.
Governments change.
Relationships change.
Health changes.
Emotions change.
Human promises fail.
But God's goodness remains untouched.
Then we arrive at the heart of the verse.
The word that changes everything.
"חַסְדּוֹ" (chasdo).
Usually translated as "mercy."
Yet no single English word fully captures its meaning.
The Hebrew word "chesed" is one of the richest words in all Scripture.
It refers to covenant love.
Faithful love.
Loyal love.
Steadfast love.
Mercy that refuses to quit.
Grace that keeps pursuing.
Love that remains even when it has every reason to leave.
This is not ordinary affection.
This is covenant commitment.
It is the kind of love God shows people who repeatedly fail Him.
The kind of love that pursued Abraham after mistakes.
Jacob after deception.
Moses after fear.
David after adultery and murder.
Peter after denial.
Thomas after doubt.
You and me after everything.
The verse says His "chesed" endures forever.
"לְעוֹלָם" (le'olam)
Forever.
Eternally.
Without expiration.
Without cancellation.
Without depletion.
Without end.
That means God's mercy lasts longer than your worst mistake.
Longer than your darkest season.
Longer than your rebellion.
Longer than your shame.
Longer than your regret.
Longer than your scandal.
The greatest lie Satan whispers is this:
"You've finally crossed the line."
But Scripture tells another story.
A story repeated from Genesis to Revelation.
A story that reaches its climax at the cross.
Because 1 Chronicles 16:34 is not merely about David's generation.
It points forward to Jesus Christ.
The entire Bible is moving toward Him.
The mercy celebrated in Chronicles becomes visible in Christ.
John 1:14 says:
"And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us."
The Greek says:
Καὶ ὁ Λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
"Kai ho Logos sarx egeneto."
The eternal God stepped into human history.
The mercy of God put on flesh.
The steadfast love of God walked among sinners.
The covenant faithfulness of God sat beside tax collectors.
Touched lepers.
Restored prostitutes.
Forgave criminals.
Welcomed outcasts.
And then carried a cross.
When Jesus hung on Calvary, every ounce of human scandal met divine grace.
Every failure.
Every sin.
Every secret.
Every act of rebellion.
Every stain.
The justice of God and the mercy of God met at the cross.
There we discover the deepest meaning of 1 Chronicles 16:34.
God's mercy is not cheap.
It is costly.
It was purchased through the blood of His Son.
The Greek word often translated as grace is:
χάρις (charis)
Unmerited favor.
A gift that cannot be earned.
A gift that cannot be bought.
A gift that can only be received.
That is why Christianity is unlike every man-made religion.
Religion says:
Clean yourself up and then come.
Jesus says:
Come and I will clean you up.
Religion says:
Earn acceptance.
Jesus says:
Acceptance is found in Me.
Religion says:
Try harder.
Jesus says:
Trust Me.
The Gospel is the story of God pursuing people who cannot save themselves.
Maybe that is why this verse continues to grip hearts thousands of years later.
Because deep down, every person knows they need mercy.
The successful businessman needs mercy.
The exhausted mother needs mercy.
The addicted son needs mercy.
The grieving widow needs mercy.
The wandering believer needs mercy.
The church leader hiding secret struggles needs mercy.
The atheist who thinks he has no need for God needs mercy.
Every human heart eventually arrives at the same conclusion:
Without God's mercy, we are hopeless.
With God's mercy, no story is beyond redemption.
That is why our theme remains:
Not because scandals are glorious.
But because grace is greater.
David understood this.
His life contained some of Scripture's most devastating failures.
Yet God was not finished with him.
Peter denied Christ three times.
Yet Jesus restored him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Yet God made him an apostle.
The woman caught in adultery expected condemnation.
Instead she encountered mercy.
The thief on the cross expected death.
Instead he received paradise.
Again and again, Scripture reveals the same truth.
Jesus rewrites stories.
The enemy writes shame.
Jesus writes redemption.
The enemy writes guilt.
Jesus writes forgiveness.
The enemy writes endings.
Jesus writes new beginnings.
Maybe that is why you are reading this right now.
Not by accident.
Not by coincidence.
Perhaps because God wants you to know that your story is not over.
The chapter that embarrasses you is not the final chapter.
The season you regret is not the conclusion.
The failure that still haunts your memory is not the end of your testimony.
The cross has the final word.
And the empty tomb proves that God specializes in impossible restorations.
So today, give thanks unto the Lord.
Not because everything is perfect.
Not because life is easy.
Not because pain is absent.
But because He is good.
Because His chesed still pursues sinners.
Because His mercy still reaches prodigals.
Because His grace still transforms lives.
Because Jesus Christ is still saving, healing, restoring, and rewriting stories.
And if this message awakened something inside your spirit, do not keep it to yourself.
Or if you are still fighting through a difficult season:
"I'm still fighting."
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
One share can reach a stranger.
One comment can encourage a wounded believer.
One testimony can point a soul toward Jesus.
One act of obedience can echo into eternity.
And remember this:
The cross was never God's response to perfect people—it was His rescue plan for broken ones.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Before You Get Married… Read This Before You Promise Forever
paragraphs:
Before You Get Married… Read This Before You Promise Forever
The Wedding Lasts a Day. The Covenant Shapes Eternity. Don't Prepare for a Ceremony While Neglecting Your Soul.
You've imagined the wedding.
The music.
The dress.
The suit.
The flowers.
The photographs.
The laughter.
The first kiss.
The first dance.
The happily-ever-after.
But almost nobody tells you to prepare for the marriage itself.
We spend months planning one beautiful day while neglecting the lifelong covenant that begins after the guests go home.
That may be one of the greatest tragedies of our generation.
Many people are searching for "the one."
Scripture tells us to become someone who belongs completely to the One who never leaves.
Marriage was never designed to complete you.
Jesus Christ is.
That truth alone has the power to save countless hearts from unnecessary heartbreak.
If your identity depends on another imperfect sinner, your foundation will eventually crack.
But if your identity rests in Christ, your marriage stands upon a Rock that storms cannot destroy.
Jesus said:
"Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock." (Matthew 7:24)
Notice something remarkable.
He did not promise there would be no storms.
He promised the foundation would survive them.
That principle applies to marriage just as much as it applies to every other part of life.
The first wedding in history did not begin with romance.
It began with God's design.
Genesis tells us:
"Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh." (Genesis 2:24)
The Hebrew expression דָּבַק (dāḇaq) means "to cling," "to hold fast," "to stick firmly."
This is not casual attachment.
It describes covenant loyalty.
Permanent commitment.
Faithful perseverance.
Marriage was never intended to be disposable.
It is covenant before convenience.
Commitment before comfort.
Faithfulness before feelings.
Feelings rise.
Feelings fall.
Covenants remain.
Modern culture often asks,
"Does this person make me happy?"
God first asks,
"Will you both help one another become holy?"
Those are very different questions.
The Apostle Paul reveals one of marriage's deepest mysteries:
"This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church." (Ephesians 5:32)
Marriage is not merely about two people.
It is a living picture of the Gospel.
Every act of forgiveness reflects Christ.
Every sacrifice reflects Christ.
Every moment of undeserved grace reflects Christ.
Every restoration points back to the Cross.
Marriage was always meant to preach Jesus without saying a word.
That changes everything.
Before asking whether someone is attractive...
Ask whether they are teachable.
Before asking whether they are successful...
Ask whether they are submitted to Christ.
Before asking whether they make your heart race...
Ask whether they help your soul grow.
Beauty fades.
Money comes and goes.
Careers change.
Health changes.
Bodies age.
But a heart surrendered to Christ grows more beautiful with every passing year.
The Hebrew word חֶסֶד (ḥesed) is often translated "steadfast love," "covenant love," or "lovingkindness."
There is no perfect English equivalent because it carries the idea of loyal, faithful, covenant mercy that refuses to abandon.
That is how God loves His people.
Marriage becomes strongest when husbands and wives learn to love with that same covenant faithfulness.
Not because the other deserves it every day.
Because Christ loved us when we deserved judgment.
Romans reminds us:
"God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us." (Romans 5:8)
Notice the order.
Grace came before we deserved it.
That is the Gospel.
And healthy marriages breathe that same air every day.
Not perfect people.
Forgiven people.
The Greek word Paul uses for love in 1 Corinthians 13 is ἀγάπη (agápē).
It is not primarily emotional attraction.
It is self-giving love.
Love that chooses.
Love that sacrifices.
Love that remains.
Love that serves.
Love that reflects God Himself.
This is why Scripture says:
"Love is patient and kind... it does not insist on its own way... it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never ends." (1 Corinthians 13:4–8)
Imagine how different marriages would become if couples memorized this passage before memorizing wedding vows.
Many couples ask,
"How do I know if this is God's will?"
Perhaps a better question is,
"Are we becoming more like Christ together?"
Because two people can share chemistry and still destroy one another spiritually.
Spiritual compatibility is not merely attending church together.
It is pursuing Christ together.
Praying together.
Repenting together.
Growing together.
Serving together.
Forgiving quickly.
Confessing honestly.
Encouraging consistently.
Keeping Christ at the center when emotions fail.
Amos asks:
"Can two walk together, unless they have agreed to meet?" (Amos 3:3)
The principle remains timeless.
Shared direction matters.
Shared worship matters.
Shared surrender matters.
Before marriage, ask difficult questions.
Can we resolve conflict biblically?
Can we forgive?
Can we admit when we're wrong?
Can we pray even after arguments?
Can we submit our opinions to Scripture?
Can we choose humility over pride?
Marriage does not create character.
It reveals it.
Pressure exposes what comfort often hides.
Many people enter marriage believing love will erase selfishness.
Instead, marriage often reveals how much selfishness still remains.
That is not failure.
It is an invitation for sanctification.
