Mercy is beautiful.
But biblical mercy never asks us to hide from truth.
The same Jesus who forgives also transforms.
The same Savior who welcomes sinners also calls them to follow Him.
The same King who extends grace also changes lives.
Maybe this article exposed something buried deeper than you expected.
Your testimony may be the encouragement another believer desperately needs today.
Because one day every scandal, every failure, every regret, every tear, and every broken chapter will stand before the Author of Redemption.
And He is still writing.
The grave could not stop Him, and your story is not stronger than His grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Day Nehemiah Wept Over a City
paragraphs:
The Day Nehemiah Wept Over a City
He Was Safe. Comfortable. Successful. Then One Report Broke His Heart and Changed History Forever.
Some people cry because life becomes difficult.
Nehemiah cried because God showed him what everyone else had learned to ignore.
That is what makes this story so dangerous.
Because the moment you truly see what breaks the heart of God, comfort stops feeling comfortable.
And suddenly this ancient story stops being about a ruined city thousands of years ago.
It becomes about us.

It becomes about the places in our lives where the walls have fallen, where compromise has entered, where faith has weakened, where wounds remain open, and where entire generations are drifting further from God while many believers continue scrolling as if nothing is happening.
The Book of Nehemiah opens with a man who seemingly had everything.

Nehemiah was serving as cupbearer to King Artaxerxes of Persia (Nehemiah 1:11). This was not a lowly servant position. A cupbearer was trusted, influential, protected, respected, and close to the king himself.
His future was secure.
His career was stable.
His life was comfortable.
Yet God was about to interrupt all of it.
When Nehemiah's brother Hanani arrived from Judah, Nehemiah asked about the Jewish remnant who had survived the exile and about Jerusalem.
The answer shattered him.

"They said to me, 'The remnant there in the province who survived the exile are in great trouble and disgrace. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates have been burned with fire.'" (Nehemiah 1:3)
The Hebrew word translated as "disgrace" is חֶרְפָּה (cherpah).
It means shame.
Reproach.
Humiliation.
Public disgrace.
Jerusalem was not merely damaged.
God's covenant people were living under shame.
The city that represented God's presence among His people had become a visible testimony of ruin.
And when Nehemiah heard this report, Scripture says:
"When I heard these words, I sat down and wept and mourned for days, and I continued fasting and praying before the God of heaven." (Nehemiah 1:4)
Notice something remarkable.
Nehemiah had never even seen Jerusalem.
He was born in exile.
Yet he wept over a city he had never personally known.
Why?
Because his heart was aligned with God's heart.
Many people today only cry over personal losses.
Nehemiah cried over God's glory.
That is spiritual maturity.
When God's reputation matters more than our comfort.
When souls matter more than entertainment.
When truth matters more than popularity.
When eternity matters more than temporary pleasure.
The deeper you walk with God, the more you begin grieving what grieves Him.
This is why Nehemiah's tears were not weakness.
They were worship.
His weeping was not emotional instability.
It was spiritual sensitivity.
And perhaps that is one of the greatest tragedies of our generation.
Not that people are too emotional.
But that many believers have become emotionally numb to the things that matter most.
We see broken families.
We see addiction.
We see depression.
We see churches compromising truth.
We see biblical illiteracy spreading.
We see people walking away from Christ.
And often we move on with our day.
Nehemiah could not.
Something holy broke inside him.
Yet what happened next is even more powerful.
He did not simply cry.
He prayed.
Many people complain.
Nehemiah prayed.
Many people criticize.
Nehemiah prayed.
Many people blame others.
Nehemiah prayed.
His prayer contains one of the most profound confessions in all Scripture.
"O Lord God of heaven, the great and awesome God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments..." (Nehemiah 1:5)
The phrase "steadfast love" comes from the Hebrew word חֶסֶד (chesed).
One of the richest words in Scripture.
It describes God's covenant love.
His loyal mercy.
His faithful kindness.
His unwavering commitment to His people.
Nehemiah knew Jerusalem's walls had failed.
But God's covenant had not.
Everything looked broken.
Yet God's promises remained intact.
Perhaps someone reading this needs that reminder today.
Your marriage may feel broken.
Your family may feel broken.
Your finances may feel broken.
Your future may feel broken.
Your heart may feel broken.
But God's covenant faithfulness is not broken.
Never confuse ruined circumstances with a ruined Savior.
Then Nehemiah does something most people avoid.
He confesses sin.
Not only the nation's sin.
His own.
"I confess the sins we Israelites, including myself and my father's family, have committed against you." (Nehemiah 1:6)
Did you catch that?
Nehemiah was not personally responsible for Jerusalem's destruction.
Yet he identified with the people.
He carried the burden.
He stood in the gap.
That sounds familiar.
Because centuries later another Man would come.
A Man without sin.
A Man who would carry burdens that were not His.
A Man who would stand in the gap between God and humanity.
His name is Jesus Christ.
The Gospel echoes throughout Nehemiah's story.
Because every broken wall points to humanity's greater problem.
Sin.
Every burned gate points to our separation from God.
Every ruined city points to our fallen condition.
And every restoration points forward to Christ.
The Greek New Testament uses the word χάρις (charis) for grace.
Grace is not merely kindness.
It is unearned favor.
Undeserved mercy.
Divine rescue for people who cannot save themselves.
That is the story of Scripture.
That is the story of Jerusalem.
That is the story of Nehemiah.
And that is your story if you belong to Christ.
Because God specializes in rebuilding ruins.
The enemy writes scandal.
Jesus writes redemption.
The enemy writes failure.
Jesus writes restoration.
The enemy writes shame.
Jesus writes grace.
The enemy writes endings.
Jesus writes resurrection.
That is why our theme is not simply a slogan.
It is biblical reality.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
The story continues as God opens impossible doors.
A pagan king grants permission.
Resources are provided.
Protection is given.
Walls begin rising.
Opposition comes.
Mockers appear.
Enemies threaten.
But God remains faithful.
The city that once symbolized disgrace eventually becomes a testimony of restoration.
And that is exactly what God still does today.
He rebuilds people.
He restores marriages.
He heals hearts.
He redeems stories.
He transforms prodigals.
He raises spiritual ruins back to life.
Maybe your own life feels like Jerusalem today.
Walls down.
Gates burned.
Dreams shattered.
Faith exhausted.
Hope fading.
Listen carefully.
The same God who rebuilt Jerusalem has not changed.
The same Savior who conquered death still reigns.
The same grace that transformed sinners in Scripture is available right now.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about good people becoming better.
It is about dead people being made alive through Jesus Christ.
That is why the cross remains the greatest scandal-to-grace story in history.
Humanity gave Christ rejection.
Christ gave humanity redemption.
Humanity gave Him nails.
He gave us salvation.
Humanity gave Him a cross.
He gave us eternal life.
And perhaps the most important question is not whether Nehemiah wept over Jerusalem.
The question is whether we still weep over the things that matter to God.
Do we grieve for lost souls?
Do we pray for revival?
Do we care about truth?
Do we hunger for holiness?
Do we love Christ enough to be interrupted by His burdens?
Because the day Nehemiah wept was the day restoration began.
Revival often starts with tears before it starts with celebration.
Be honest.
Did this expose something hidden in your heart?
Your testimony may encourage someone who feels alone today.
One day every earthly wall will fall, every kingdom will fade, and every accomplishment will disappear—but the souls reached for Jesus Christ will remain forever.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Day Jonathan Climbed the Cliff
paragraphs:
The Day Jonathan Climbed the Cliff
When Everyone Else Saw an Impossible Wall, One Man Saw a Way for God to Rewrite the Story
Some battles are not fought in valleys.
Some battles are fought on cliffs.
Not the cliffs made of stone and earth.
The cliffs made of fear.
The cliffs made of disappointment.
The cliffs made of unanswered prayers.
The cliffs made of shame.
The cliffs that stand between where you are and where God is calling you to go.
Most people never climb those cliffs.
That is why the story of Jonathan is so unforgettable.
Because on one ordinary day, while an entire nation sat paralyzed by fear, one young man decided he would rather trust God on a cliff than live comfortably in defeat.
The account is recorded in 1 Samuel 14.
Israel was facing the Philistines.
The situation looked hopeless.
King Saul sat beneath a pomegranate tree with hundreds of soldiers around him. They had weapons. They had numbers. They had position.
Yet they had no movement.
No courage.
No victory.
The army of God was frozen.
Meanwhile, the enemy stood confidently on the other side.
That scene feels strangely familiar.
Many believers know what it feels like to sit beneath their own pomegranate tree.
Waiting.
Analyzing.
Delaying.
Praying without moving.
Believing without obeying.
Watching opportunities pass by while fear disguises itself as wisdom.
Then Jonathan did something extraordinary.
Scripture says:
"One day Jonathan son of Saul said to his young armor-bearer, 'Come, let's go over to the Philistine outpost on the other side.'" (1 Samuel 14:1)
He told nobody.
Not even his father.
Not because he was rebellious.
Because faith often begins before anyone else understands what God is doing.
Between Jonathan and the enemy stood two massive rocky cliffs.
Scripture even names them.
Bozez and Seneh.
One cliff on one side.
One cliff on the other.
A narrow path between them.
A place where retreat would be difficult and victory would seem impossible.
The Hebrew text paints the picture vividly.
The name "Bozez" likely carries the idea of something shining or slippery.
"Seneh" is connected to thorny ground.
A slippery cliff.
A thorn-covered cliff.
The pathway to victory looked dangerous from every angle.
Yet Jonathan kept moving.
Then he spoke one of the most faith-filled statements in the entire Old Testament.
"Perhaps the LORD will act in our behalf. Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few." (1 Samuel 14:6)
The Hebrew reads:
"אֵין לַיהוָה מַעְצוֹר לְהוֹשִׁיעַ בְּרַב אוֹ בִמְעָט"
Ein la'YHWH ma'atzor lehoshia berav o bime'at.
"There is no restraint for Yahweh to save by many or by few."
Jonathan did not have certainty about the outcome.
He had certainty about God.
That is the difference.
Modern culture teaches people to trust outcomes.
Biblical faith teaches people to trust God.
Jonathan never said, "I know we will win."
He said, "Nothing limits God."
That single truth changed everything.
Many believers spend years waiting until they feel completely certain.
Jonathan moved while trusting the character of God.
The greatest obstacle was never the Philistines.
The greatest obstacle was fear.
And fear is still one of Satan's favorite weapons.
Fear tells you the cliff is too high.
Fear tells you the addiction will never break.
Fear tells you the marriage will never heal.
Fear tells you the depression will never lift.
Fear tells you the calling is too big.
Fear tells you your past disqualifies you.
Fear tells you the scandal defines you.
But the Gospel tells a different story.
The Bible is filled with people who looked disqualified.
Abraham was old.
Moses was insecure.
Rahab was a prostitute.
David was overlooked.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted believers.
Yet Jesus rewrote every one of their stories.
That is why our mission is called From Scandal to Grace.
Because the entire Bible is a testimony that God specializes in rewriting what humans believe is beyond repair.
Jonathan and his armor-bearer climbed.
Hand over hand.
Rock after rock.
Step after painful step.
The Philistines looked down and laughed.
The enemy always laughs before God moves.
The world laughed at Noah.
The world laughed at Sarah.
The world laughed at Jesus hanging on a cross.
Yet every time heaven had the final word.
When Jonathan reached the top, God intervened.
Scripture records that panic spread throughout the Philistine camp.
An earthquake shook the ground.
Confusion erupted.
The enemy began collapsing from within.
What started with two faithful men became a national victory.
One act of faith became a catalyst for thousands.
Think about that.
An entire nation was changed because one man climbed.
Many people underestimate the power of personal obedience.
They assume their faith only affects themselves.
But biblical faith is never isolated.
One father following Jesus can change generations.
One mother praying faithfully can alter family history.
One believer sharing the Gospel can impact eternity.
One act of courage can create a ripple effect far beyond what human eyes can see.
This truth reaches its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Jonathan climbed a cliff to save Israel from temporary oppression.
Jesus climbed a hill called Golgotha to save humanity from eternal separation from God.
Jonathan risked his life.
Jesus gave His life.
Jonathan trusted God for victory.
Jesus became the victory.
The Greek text of John 19:30 records Christ's final declaration:
"Τετέλεσται"
Tetelestai.
"It is finished."
Not "I am finished."
"It is finished."
The debt of sin.
Finished.
The power of condemnation.
Finished.
The separation between God and humanity.
Finished.
The victory over death.
Finished.
The rescue plan of redemption.
Finished.
The greatest cliff humanity could never climb was climbed by Jesus Himself.
That is the Gospel.
Not that we reached God.
But that God came for us.
Not that we earned grace.
But that grace found us.
Not that we rewrote our story.
But that Jesus rewrote it.
Maybe today you feel trapped between your own Bozez and Seneh.
A slippery cliff on one side.
A thorn-covered cliff on the other.
Perhaps nobody sees your struggle.
Perhaps everyone around you has stopped moving.
Perhaps fear has convinced you to settle beneath the pomegranate tree.
But Jonathan's story still whispers across the centuries.
Nothing can hinder the Lord from saving.
Nothing.
Not your past.
Not your failures.
Not your addiction.
Not your shame.
Not your wounds.
Not your doubts.
Not your scandal.
Not your fears.
The same God who empowered Jonathan still reigns.
The same Christ who conquered death still saves.
The same Holy Spirit still transforms lives today.
And maybe this article found you at exactly the right moment.
Not by accident.
But by providence.
If this message stirred your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
You never know who is standing at the bottom of their own cliff waiting for a reminder that God has not abandoned them.
What cliff are you facing right now?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
If you truly desire to glorify God through this ministry, one practical way is to help sustain and expand the work so more souls can encounter the Gospel.
Because sometimes the greatest miracle is not that God removes the cliff.
It is that He teaches you to climb it with Him.
And one day you look back and realize the cliff that terrified you became the very place where you discovered who God truly is.
The enemy saw a cliff.
Jonathan saw an opportunity.
Jesus saw a cross.
And through that cross, He rewrote everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Thing People Missed in Lot’s Story
paragraphs:
The Thing People Missed in Lot’s Story
The man everyone remembers for Sodom may actually be one of the Bible’s most uncomfortable mirrors.
Most people think Lot’s story is about judgment.
They think it is about fire falling from heaven.
About sexual immorality.
About a wicked city finally receiving what it deserved.
But that is not the deepest tragedy in Lot’s story.
The deepest tragedy is that Lot did not wake up one morning and decide to live close to destruction.
It happened slowly.
Quietly.
Reasonably.
One compromise at a time.
And if we are honest, that is why his story is so terrifying.
Because most people do not destroy their lives through one massive decision.
They drift there.
The first time Lot appears as an adult, he is walking with Abraham.
He has a godly mentor.
A godly example.
A godly family.
The blessing of God surrounds him.
Yet when conflict arises between their herdsmen, Abraham gives Lot first choice of the land.
Genesis 13:10 says:
"Lot lifted up his eyes and saw all the plain of the Jordan."
The Hebrew phrase is:

"וַיִּשָּׂא־לוֹט אֶת־עֵינָיו"
(Va-yissa Lot et einav)
"Lot lifted his eyes."
At first glance that sounds harmless.
But throughout Scripture, what we choose to fix our eyes upon often reveals the direction of our hearts.
Lot saw wealth.
Opportunity.
Comfort.
Success.
The land looked prosperous.
Beautiful.
Promising.
Genesis 13:12 tells us:
"Lot settled among the cities of the valley and moved his tent as far as Sodom."
Notice the wording.
He did not move into Sodom immediately.
He pitched his tent toward Sodom.
Toward it.
Not in it.
Yet.
That single word may explain thousands of spiritual shipwrecks throughout history.
People rarely fall into darkness overnight.
They simply keep facing it.
They orient their lives toward it.
They justify proximity.
They normalize compromise.
They tell themselves they are strong enough.
Wise enough.
Spiritual enough.
Until one day they wake up where they never intended to be.
Later we find Lot no longer near Sodom.
He is living inside it.
Then eventually sitting at its gate.
Genesis 19:1 reveals that Lot was seated at the gate of Sodom.
In ancient cities, the gate was where leaders, judges, and influential men gathered.
Lot had not merely moved into Sodom.
Sodom had moved into Lot.
What began as a direction became an identity.
What began as proximity became participation.
What began as observation became assimilation.
And that should make every believer stop and think.
Because culture does not usually conquer us through open warfare.
It conquers us through gradual acceptance.
The enemy rarely says, "Reject God today."
Instead he whispers:
"Just move a little closer."
"Just compromise a little."
"Just make this one exception."
"Just blend in."
The Greek New Testament later describes Lot in a shocking way.
2 Peter 2:7 calls him:

"δίκαιον Λώτ"
(dikaion Lot)
"Righteous Lot."
That surprises many people.
Righteous?
After everything that happened?
Yet Scripture says he was distressed by the lawless deeds around him.
His soul was tormented.
He still belonged to God.
But belonging to God and walking closely with God are not always the same thing.
Lot is proof.
A believer can be saved and still suffer devastating consequences from compromise.
Many Christians today know exactly what that feels like.
You still love Jesus.
But your soul feels exhausted.
You feel distant.
Dry.
Compromised.
Pulled in two directions.
You are not living in outright rebellion.
Yet you know your tent has been facing Sodom for a long time.
And perhaps that is why this story hurts.
Because it is easier to identify with Abraham than with Lot.
Yet most of us have had Lot moments.
Moments when career mattered more than calling.
Moments when comfort mattered more than obedience.
Moments when fitting in mattered more than faithfulness.
Moments when we justified what God warned us about.
Then comes the part everyone remembers.
The angels arrive.
Judgment approaches.
Fire is coming.
But even here we discover something astonishing about God.
Genesis 19:16 says:
"But he lingered."
Lot hesitated.
Delayed.
Stalled.
Even with destruction approaching.
Even after being warned.
Even after mercy arrived at his doorstep.
He lingered.
The Hebrew word carries the idea of hesitation and reluctance.
He knew the truth.
Yet struggled to leave.
And perhaps this is the verse many believers understand better than they want to admit.
Because sometimes we linger too.
We linger in bitterness.
We linger in sin.
We linger in unhealthy relationships.
We linger in habits God is trying to free us from.
We linger even while God is calling us out.
But then one of the most beautiful pictures of grace appears.
The verse continues:
"Because the LORD was merciful to him."
The angels literally take Lot by the hand.
They pull him toward safety.
Not because he earned it.
Not because he deserved it.
Not because he had everything together.
Because God was merciful.
The Hebrew word behind mercy here reflects God's compassionate covenant love.
The same mercy that runs throughout the entire Bible.
The same mercy that pursued Adam after Eden.
The same mercy that restored David after failure.
The same mercy that welcomed Peter after denial.
The same mercy that carried Lot out of Sodom.
And the same mercy that still reaches for us today.
This is the part people miss.
Lot's story is not primarily about fire.
It is about mercy.
Not primarily about judgment.
But rescue.
Not primarily about human failure.
But divine compassion.
The Bible never hides the scandals of its people.
Because the Bible is not ultimately a story about human heroes.
It is a story about a holy God who keeps pursuing broken people.
That story reaches its highest expression in Jesus Christ.
When humanity was lingering in sin, Christ came.
When humanity could not save itself, Christ came.
When humanity deserved judgment, Christ came.
The Greek word used repeatedly throughout the New Testament for grace is:

"χάρις"
(charis)
Grace.
Unearned favor.
Undeserved kindness.
God moving toward sinners with redemption.
At the cross, justice and mercy met.
Jesus absorbed the judgment we deserved so we could receive the mercy we could never earn.
That is why the Gospel remains the greatest story ever told.
Because Jesus does not merely improve people.
He rewrites them.
He rewrites failures.
He rewrites scandals.
He rewrites regrets.
He rewrites prodigals.
He rewrites broken marriages.
He rewrites addictions.
He rewrites shame.
He rewrites stories that seem impossible to redeem.
And maybe that is where you find yourself today.
Perhaps you know what it means to linger.
To compromise.
To drift.
To look back and wonder how you ended up where you are.
If so, Lot's story is not merely a warning.
It is an invitation.
The God who reached into Sodom can still reach into your situation.
The God who took Lot by the hand can still take yours.
The God who rescued him can rescue you.
No one is too far gone for grace.
No scandal is bigger than the cross.
No failure is beyond redemption.
No chapter is final when Jesus is the Author.
Be honest. This hit harder than many expected.
Your support helps us create more biblical content, discipleship resources, evangelistic outreach, and faith-building materials that point people to Jesus Christ.
You will also gain deeper access to discipleship content while helping us expand the reach of the Gospel to people who desperately need hope.
The mercy that pulled Lot from Sodom is the same mercy still reaching for you right now.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Moment Saul Became Jealous
paragraphs:
The Moment Saul Became Jealous
The Day One Song Turned a Hero into a Threat, a King into a Prisoner, and a Heart Away from God
There are moments in life that seem small on the surface but become the dividing line between who we were and who we become.
A conversation.
A compliment given to someone else.
A promotion.
A relationship.
A social media post.
A celebration that wasn't ours.
A song.
For King Saul, it was a song.
Not a battle.
Not a rebellion.
Not an assassination attempt.
A song.
And that song exposed a wound that had been growing quietly inside him for years.
The tragedy is not that David became great.
The tragedy is that Saul could not rejoice when God blessed someone else.
Many people think jealousy begins when another person succeeds.
Scripture reveals something deeper.
Jealousy begins when our identity is no longer anchored in God.

The story unfolds in 1 Samuel 18 after one of the greatest victories in Israel's history. David, the shepherd boy from Bethlehem, had defeated Goliath. The giant who terrified an entire nation fell before a teenager who trusted the Lord.
Israel celebrated.
Families rejoiced.
Children sang.
The nation finally had hope.
As Saul and David returned from battle, the women of Israel came out dancing and singing.
The Hebrew text records their words:
"שָׁאוּל הִכָּה בַאֲלָפָיו וְדָוִד בְּרִבְבֹתָיו"
Sha'ul hikah ba'alafav, veDavid berivvotav.
"Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands."
(1 Samuel 18:7)
To most people, it sounded like celebration.
To Saul, it sounded like replacement.
The next verse reveals the fracture inside his soul.
"Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him."
(1 Samuel 18:8)
The Hebrew is even stronger.
"וַיִּחַר לְשָׁאוּל מְאֹד"
Vayichar leSha'ul me'od.
Literally:
"It burned greatly within Saul."
Something ignited.
Something dark.
Something destructive.
Not because David attacked him.
Not because David dishonored him.
Not because David sought the throne.
Saul became jealous because David was loved.
Because David was celebrated.
Because David was succeeding.
The frightening reality is that David did absolutely nothing wrong.
Sometimes the people who resent you the most are not angry because you harmed them.
They are angry because your blessing exposes what they have lost.
Saul's battle was never with David.
Saul's battle was with Saul.
Years earlier, God had chosen him.
God had elevated him.
God had anointed him.
God had blessed him.
Yet Saul continually chose his own way over God's commands.
The prophet Samuel warned him.
The Lord corrected him.
But Saul's heart drifted.
Eventually Samuel declared:
"The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you."
(1 Samuel 15:28)
Notice something important.
God removed Saul because of disobedience long before David ever appeared.
David did not steal Saul's crown.
Saul surrendered it through rebellion.
Jealousy often convinces us that someone else is responsible for what our own choices created.
That is why jealousy is so dangerous.
It blinds us.
It rewrites reality.
It creates villains where there are none.
It turns brothers into competitors.
Friends into enemies.
Blessings into threats.
The Greek word often associated with jealousy in the New Testament is φθόνος (phthonos).
It means envy, resentment, ill will toward the success of another.
Paul lists it among the works of the flesh.
Not because God wants to remove joy from our lives.
Because envy destroys joy.
The jealous person suffers twice.
First from what they lost.
Then from what someone else gained.
Saul could no longer enjoy victories because David was winning them too.
He could no longer celebrate Israel's success because David received applause.
His identity became imprisoned by comparison.
And comparison is a prison with no release date.
How many people are living there today?
Scrolling endlessly.
Watching everyone else's milestones.
Everyone else's weddings.
Everyone else's ministries.
Everyone else's businesses.
Everyone else's blessings.
Everyone else's opportunities.
Secretly wondering:
"Why not me?"
"What about my season?"
"When will God notice me?"
If that question remains unresolved, jealousy will begin whispering lies.
The enemy rarely starts with hatred.
He starts with comparison.
Then comparison becomes insecurity.
Insecurity becomes resentment.
Resentment becomes obsession.
Obsession becomes destruction.
Saul eventually reached the point where he hurled a spear at David.
Twice.
Imagine that.
A young man risked his life for Israel.
Defeated their greatest enemy.
Served the king faithfully.
Played music to soothe Saul's torment.
And Saul tried to kill him.
Jealousy always attacks the people it should appreciate.
Yet the story is not merely about Saul.
It is about every human heart.
Because every one of us has felt that sting.
The promotion someone else received.
The recognition we wanted.
The ministry that grew faster.
The prayer that seemed answered for everyone except us.
The marriage we hoped for.
The breakthrough we desperately needed.
The temptation is to stare at David.
God invites us to look at Jesus.
Because Jesus never operated from jealousy.
Though He was equal with God, He humbled Himself.
Though He deserved glory, He embraced a cross.
Though He was rejected, He chose forgiveness.
Though He was betrayed, He loved anyway.
The Greek text of Philippians 2 reminds us:
"ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν"
Heauton ekenōsen.
"He emptied Himself."
(Philippians 2:7)
Christ did not cling to status.
He surrendered Himself for others.
That is the cure for jealousy.
Not self-improvement.
Not positive thinking.
A transformed heart centered on Christ.
When Jesus becomes enough, another person's blessing no longer threatens us.
When Jesus becomes our identity, another person's success no longer diminishes us.
When Jesus becomes our treasure, comparison loses its power.
Saul spent years chasing David.
David spent those same years chasing God.
One lost a kingdom.
The other inherited one.
The difference was not talent.
Not opportunity.
Not popularity.
It was the condition of the heart.
And perhaps that is why this story still grips us thousands of years later.
Because somewhere deep inside we recognize ourselves.
We know what it feels like to be overlooked.
To be forgotten.
To wonder whether God has another plan.
To battle emotions we never wanted.
To smile publicly while struggling privately.
But the Gospel offers hope even here.
Jesus specializes in rewriting stories.
The same God who forgave Peter after denial.
Who restored John Mark after failure.
Who transformed persecuting Saul of Tarsus into the Apostle Paul.
Is still changing hearts today.
No matter how long jealousy has lived inside us.
No matter how deeply comparison has wounded us.
No matter how many relationships have been damaged.
Grace remains available.
Repentance remains possible.
Transformation remains real.
Because the Gospel is not about pretending darkness never existed.
It is about Jesus bringing light into the darkest places of the human heart.
And maybe the greatest question this story asks is not whether David was blessed.
It is whether we can celebrate when God blesses someone else.
Because the kingdom of God is not diminished when another believer succeeds.
It expands.
The victory of one child of God is not a threat to another.
It is evidence that the Father is still working.
If this article exposed something hidden in your heart, be honest.
Because sometimes the battle that destroys us is not the giant standing in front of us.
It is the comparison quietly growing within us.
From Scandal to Grace, the journey begins the moment we stop chasing someone else's crown and start surrendering our hearts to the King who already gave us His.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Untold Story of Abishag and the Struggle for a Kingdom
paragraphs:
The Untold Story of Abishag and the Struggle for a Kingdom
She Never Wore a Crown. She Never Sat on a Throne. Yet a Nation Nearly Went to War Because of Her.
Most people read her name and keep going.
One verse. A brief appearance. A forgotten woman standing quietly in the shadows of kings.
But sometimes the people history barely notices are standing at the center of battles that change everything.
Abishag was one of them.
And if you've ever felt used, overlooked, caught in someone else's conflict, or trapped inside a story you never asked to enter, her story might hit closer to home than you expect.
Because Abishag's story is not ultimately about politics.
It's about power.
It's about ambition.
It's about the hunger of the human heart.
And it's about how Jesus Christ transforms even the darkest scandals into testimonies of grace.
The story begins in the final days of King David.
The mighty giant-slayer was old.
The warrior who defeated Goliath could no longer keep himself warm.
Scripture says:
"Now King David was old and advanced in years. Although they covered him with clothes, he could not get warm." (1 Kings 1:1)
His servants searched throughout Israel and found a young woman named Abishag from Shunem.
The Hebrew text calls her:

אֲבִישַׁג הַשּׁוּנַמִּית
(Avishag HaShunammit)
"Abishag the Shunammite."
She was brought into the palace to care for David.
The Bible carefully records:
"The young woman was very beautiful, and she was of service to the king and attended to him, but the king knew her not." (1 Kings 1:4)
The phrase "knew her not" is significant.
The Hebrew uses language indicating David did not have sexual relations with her.
Why does Scripture emphasize this?
Because God wanted future generations to understand the truth.
Abishag was not David's lover.
She was not his wife.
She was not part of some hidden scandal.
She was a caretaker serving an aging king.
Yet after David's death, everything changed.
Whenever a throne is empty, ambitious men begin dreaming.
David's son Adonijah believed the kingdom should belong to him.
He was handsome.
Powerful.
Popular.
Confident.
The kind of man people naturally follow.
And before David died, Adonijah attempted a coup.
He gathered supporters.
He organized celebrations.
He essentially declared himself king.
But God had already chosen Solomon.
David confirmed Solomon as king.
Adonijah's dream collapsed.
At least outwardly.
But ambition rarely dies quietly.
It usually waits.
It hides.
It watches.
It looks for another door.
Then comes one of the most misunderstood moments in Scripture.
Adonijah approaches Bathsheba, Solomon's mother.
His request sounds harmless.
Almost romantic.
Almost innocent.
He asks for Abishag.
Just one woman.
Nothing more.
But Solomon immediately understands what is happening.
Modern readers often miss the political significance.
Ancient kingdoms did not view royal women the way modern cultures do.
Possessing a king's harem or household women was often viewed as a claim to royal authority.
This is why Absalom publicly took David's concubines during his rebellion.
It was not merely sexual.
It was political.
It was symbolic.
It was a declaration.
It was saying:
"I am the king now."
When Solomon hears Adonijah's request, he responds:
"And why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask for him the kingdom also." (1 Kings 2:22)
Solomon sees the deeper agenda immediately.
This was never truly about love.
It was about power.
The kingdom was at stake.
A nation stood on the edge of instability.
And somehow Abishag found herself caught in the middle.
Again.
Imagine that.
She never sought influence.
Never sought political leverage.
Never asked to become a symbol.
Yet powerful men kept trying to use her for their own purposes.
Many people know exactly what that feels like.
Being valued for what you represent rather than who you are.
Being treated as a means to an end.
Being pulled into battles you never started.
Being wounded by the ambitions of others.
Being reduced to a tool.
A possession.
An opportunity.
A stepping stone.
Abishag's story reveals something uncomfortable about humanity.
Sin does not merely corrupt actions.
It corrupts desires.
The Greek New Testament later describes sinful ambition using the word:
ἐριθεία (eritheia)
Selfish ambition.
Political maneuvering.
Self-serving pursuit of power.
The kind of ambition that elevates self while ignoring God's will.
James warns:
"Where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice." (James 3:16)
That perfectly describes the atmosphere surrounding Abishag.
Everyone wanted the throne.
Everyone wanted influence.
Everyone wanted power.
And in the middle stood a young woman whose voice is never recorded.
Yet perhaps that silence speaks louder than words.
Because Scripture is not ultimately about Abishag.
Nor David.
Nor Solomon.
Nor Adonijah.
The Bible is ultimately about Jesus.
Every kingdom struggle points forward to the true King.
Every failed ruler points forward to the perfect King.
Every scandal points forward to the Savior who redeems scandals.
Human kingdoms rise through manipulation.
Christ's kingdom comes through sacrifice.
Human rulers grasp power.
Jesus surrendered power.
Human kings protect their thrones.
Jesus carried a cross.
Human kingdoms are built on ambition.
Christ's kingdom is built on grace.
The prophet Isaiah foretold Him centuries earlier:
"The government shall be upon His shoulder." (Isaiah 9:6)
Not seized.
Not stolen.
Not manipulated into existence.
Given by God.
The Greek New Testament repeatedly calls Jesus:
Χριστός (Christos)
"The Anointed One."
The true King every earthly king failed to be.
The One who never exploits people for power.
The One who never uses people as stepping stones.
The One who sees every forgotten Abishag.
Every overlooked soul.
Every wounded heart.
Every person trapped inside someone else's selfishness.
And perhaps that is why this ancient story still matters.
Because our world has not changed.
People still chase power.
Still chase status.
Still chase recognition.
Still build little kingdoms.
Still sacrifice relationships on the altar of ambition.
Still try to sit on thrones that belong to God.
But Jesus offers another way.
The way of surrender.
The way of humility.
The way of grace.
The way of redemption.
The way where broken stories become testimonies.
The way where scandals become sermons.
The way where wounds become worship.
The way where failures become foundations for future faithfulness.
The Hebrew word often translated as grace is:
חֵן (Chen)
Favor.
Beauty.
Undeserved kindness.
The New Testament expands this through the Greek word:
χάρις (Charis)
Grace freely given.
Grace freely received.
Grace that cannot be earned.
Grace that rewrites everything.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Because every one of us has moments we wish could be erased.
Mistakes.
Regrets.
Failures.
Embarrassments.
Scandals.
Secrets.
Yet Jesus specializes in rewriting stories people think are beyond repair.
Peter denied Him.
Paul persecuted believers.
The Samaritan woman carried shame.
Zacchaeus carried greed.
Mary Magdalene carried brokenness.
Yet Jesus transformed every one of them.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that's why you're still reading.
Maybe deep down you're carrying something you think God cannot redeem.
A chapter you wish nobody knew.
A wound that still hurts.
A failure that still haunts you.
A secret battle you're tired of fighting.
Hear this clearly:
Jesus Christ is still in the business of rewriting stories.
Your story included.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
If this ministry has strengthened your walk with God, one meaningful way to glorify Him is by helping us continue spreading biblical truth to more people.
Because someone else's breakthrough may be waiting on the article you almost didn't share.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Lesson I Learned From Moses’ Excuses
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From Moses’ Excuses
The Day God Called Him Changed Everything—But Not Before Moses Tried to Talk His Way Out of Destiny
There is a moment in almost every believer’s life when God places something in front of them that feels impossibly bigger than they are.
A calling.
A responsibility.
A mission.
A step of obedience.
And in that moment, many of us respond exactly the same way.
We make excuses.
Not because we hate God.
Not because we lack faith entirely.
But because deep down we are painfully aware of our weaknesses.
That is why the story of Moses feels so personal.
Because Moses was not standing on a mountain when God called him.
He was hiding in a desert.
Not reigning in victory.
Not leading nations.
Not performing miracles.
Not writing Scripture.
Just tending sheep.
Forty years earlier, Moses had been a prince of Egypt. Then came the scandal.
The failure.
The impulsive act.
The murder.
The shame.
The exile.
Everything he thought his life would become disappeared.
If Moses had social media, people would have called him disqualified.
Cancelled.
Finished.
A wasted potential.
But God specializes in finding people in the ashes of their own mistakes.
That is why our theme has always been true:
When Moses encountered the burning bush, God revealed Himself with words that still shake history.
In Exodus 3:14, God declared:

Hebrew:
"אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה"

Transliteration:
Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh

Literal meaning:
"I Am Who I Am" or "I Will Be What I Will Be."
The God who exists independently of all creation was speaking directly to a broken shepherd.
The God who created galaxies was calling a man who barely believed in himself.
And what happened next may be one of the most relatable conversations in all of Scripture.
Moses began making excuses.
The first excuse was identity.
"Who am I?"
Exodus 3:11 says:
"Who am I that I should go unto Pharaoh, and that I should bring forth the children of Israel out of Egypt?"
Notice what Moses focused on.
Himself.
His limitations.
His inadequacies.
His past.
His failures.
But God never answered Moses by boosting his self-esteem.
God answered by redirecting his attention.
"Certainly I will be with thee."
The solution was never Moses.
The solution was God.
Many believers spend years waiting until they feel qualified enough to obey.
But Scripture repeatedly shows that God calls people before they feel ready.
Abraham was old.
David was young.
Gideon was afraid.
Jeremiah felt inexperienced.
Peter was impulsive.
Paul carried a painful past.
Moses had excuses.
Yet God used them all.
The second excuse was uncertainty.
"What if they ask who sent me?"
Moses wanted guarantees.
Proof.
A detailed explanation.
A complete roadmap.
But God gave him Himself.
The Christian life has never been built on having all the answers.
It has always been built on trusting the One who does.
Sometimes we delay obedience because we want clarity.
Yet God often provides clarity through obedience.
The third excuse reveals something even deeper.
Moses said:
"They will not believe me."
Fear of rejection is one of humanity's oldest struggles.
We fear being misunderstood.
Ignored.
Mocked.
Criticized.
Rejected.
Moses imagined failure before he ever took a step.
How many dreams die the same way?
How many ministries never begin?
How many testimonies stay hidden?
How many believers remain silent because they already decided people will not listen?
Yet God responded by giving signs that demonstrated His power.
Because the mission was never supposed to depend upon Moses' ability to convince people.
It depended upon God's authority.
The fourth excuse cuts even closer to home.
Exodus 4:10 says:
"O my Lord, I am not eloquent."
The Hebrew expression suggests difficulty with speech.
Whether Moses had a speech impediment, lacked confidence, or simply felt inadequate, the point remains the same.
He believed his weakness disqualified him.
Many Christians still believe that lie.
They think:
"I'm not educated enough."
"I'm not talented enough."
"I'm not experienced enough."
"I'm not gifted enough."
"I'm not spiritual enough."
But God replied:
"Who hath made man's mouth?"
In other words:
"I know exactly what you lack. I created you anyway."
God is not surprised by our weaknesses.
He already accounted for them before He called us.
The final excuse exposed the real issue.
Exodus 4:13:
"O my Lord, send, I pray thee, by the hand of him whom thou wilt send."
In plain language:
"Please send someone else."
This is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because Moses had moved beyond insecurity.
He was resisting obedience.
And if we are honest, we have all been there.
We say we need more time.
More preparation.
More resources.
More confirmation.
More certainty.
Yet sometimes what we really mean is:
"Lord, please choose someone else."
Still, the grace of God appears.
God did not abandon Moses.
He corrected him.
Strengthened him.
Provided Aaron to assist him.
And then sent him anyway.
That detail matters.
Because God's grace does not merely forgive us.
God's grace transforms us.
The New Testament uses the Greek word χάρις (charis) for grace.
It means favor freely given.
A gift undeserved.
Yet biblical grace is never passive.
Grace changes people.
Grace empowers obedience.
Grace turns fugitives into leaders.
Grace turns failures into testimonies.
Grace turns broken stories into redemptive ones.
Moses arrived at the burning bush as a shepherd hiding from his past.
He left carrying God's mission.
The man making excuses became the man confronting Pharaoh.
The man doubting his voice became the man delivering God's Word.
The man afraid of failure became the man through whom God parted the sea.
That is what God does.
And that is why Moses' story points beyond Moses.
It points to Jesus Christ.
Because every excuse Moses made ultimately finds its answer in Christ.
"Who am I?"
You are someone for whom Christ died.
"What if I fail?"
Christ remains faithful.
"What if people reject me?"
They rejected Him first.
"I am not enough."
He is.
"Send someone else."
He sent His Son so you could be part of His mission.
Jesus did not come for people who had everything together.
He came for sinners.
Failures.
Outcasts.
The ashamed.
The weary.
The broken.
The scandalized.
The disqualified.
The people everyone else had given up on.
The Gospel is not the story of impressive people earning God's favor.
The Gospel is the story of a holy God extending mercy through Jesus Christ.
That is why no excuse is stronger than His grace.
No past is stronger than His redemption.
No failure is stronger than His forgiveness.
No weakness is stronger than His power.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying your own excuses.
You feel too broken.
Too late.
Too wounded.
Too sinful.
Too ordinary.
Too forgotten.
Moses once felt the same way.
Yet God looked beyond every excuse and saw the leader Moses would become.
Today, through Christ, God still rewrites stories.
He still restores.
He still redeems.
He still calls.
He still transforms.
And perhaps the greatest lesson Moses ever taught us is this:
God is not looking for perfect people.
God is looking for willing people.
The question is not whether you have excuses.
The question is whether you will surrender them.
Because the moment Moses stopped arguing and started obeying, history changed.
And perhaps your story is waiting for the same moment.
Be honest. This hit harder than some expected.
The excuse that almost kept Moses from his calling became the testimony that proved God's power.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Cast It Where It Belongs: The Deeper Meaning of 1 Peter 5:7 and the Scandal of a God Who Wants Your Burdens
paragraphs:
Cast It Where It Belongs: The Deeper Meaning of 1 Peter 5:7 and the Scandal of a God Who Wants Your Burdens
Why the Weight You're Carrying May Be the Very Thing Jesus Is Asking You to Release
There are burdens so heavy that no one sees them.
The smile still appears in public.
The church attendance remains consistent.
The social media posts look normal.
The conversations sound fine.
But somewhere beneath the surface, anxiety has become a silent roommate.
Fear sleeps beside you.
Regret follows you.
Questions haunt you.
And the exhaustion isn't from physical labor.
It's from carrying things God never asked you to carry.
Perhaps that is why one of the most beloved verses in Scripture remains one of the most misunderstood:
"Casting all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you." (1 Peter 5:7)
Simple.
Beautiful.
Comforting.
Yet beneath those few words lies a depth that can completely transform the way we understand God, suffering, trust, and the Gospel itself.
The apostle Peter did not write these words from a place of theory.
He wrote them as a man who knew failure.
A man who publicly denied Jesus three times.
A man who wept bitterly after his greatest spiritual collapse.
A man whose story became proof that grace is greater than scandal.
And perhaps that is why Peter understood something many of us still struggle to believe:
God is not merely willing to save your soul.
He wants your burdens too.
The Greek text reads:
"ἐπιρίψαντες πᾶσαν τὴν μέριμναν ὑμῶν ἐπ' αὐτόν, ὅτι αὐτῷ μέλει περὶ ὑμῶν"
(epiripsantes pasan tēn merimnan hymōn ep' auton, hoti autō melei peri hymōn)
The word translated as "casting" is epiripsantes.
This is not a gentle suggestion.
It literally means to throw upon.
To hurl.
To place the full weight of something onto another object.
The same word appears when garments were thrown onto the colt before Jesus entered Jerusalem (Luke 19:35).
Peter is not telling believers to politely hand God a portion of their concerns.
He is commanding them to throw every burden onto Christ.
Everything.
Not some things.
Not only spiritual concerns.
Not only respectable concerns.
Not only church-approved concerns.
Everything.
The fear.
The addiction.
The shame.
The secret.
The diagnosis.
The uncertainty.
The grief.
The future.
The past.
The entire weight.
The next word is equally powerful.
"Merimna" — anxiety.
In Greek thought, the root idea refers to something that divides the mind.
Something that pulls a person in multiple directions.
Anxiety fragments.
It separates.
It scatters focus.
It drains peace.
It fractures trust.
How many people reading this know exactly what that feels like?
You are physically present in one room.
Mentally trapped in another.
Trying to enjoy today while worrying about tomorrow.
Trying to pray while simultaneously planning every possible disaster.
Trying to trust God while secretly acting as if everything depends entirely on you.
Peter says that divided mind can be cast onto Christ.
Why?
Because of one astonishing phrase:
"ὅτι αὐτῷ μέλει περὶ ὑμῶν"
"Because it matters to Him concerning you."
Most English translations simply say:
"Because He cares for you."
That translation is accurate.
But the original language reveals something even more intimate.
The Greek word melei means to be concerned with, to care deeply about, to have personal interest in something.
This is not distant concern.
This is not detached awareness.
This is personal investment.
God is not observing your pain from heaven.
He is personally concerned with it.
The Creator of galaxies is emotionally invested in His children.
Let that settle into your heart.
The God who spoke stars into existence cares about the tears you never told anyone about.
The God who numbers every star also numbers every hair on your head.
The God who governs the universe is not too busy for your broken heart.
That truth becomes even more breathtaking when viewed through the lens of the entire Bible.
In Hebrew thought, God's covenant love is often expressed through the word:
"חֶסֶד" (chesed)
A word so rich that no single English term can fully capture it.
It means steadfast love.
Faithful love.
Loyal covenant mercy.
Relentless kindness.
Unfailing devotion.
God's love is not based on your performance.
His care is not dependent on your success.
His concern is not determined by your worthiness.
He loves because He is love.
This is where the Gospel changes everything.
Because many people secretly believe God cares for the righteous version of themselves.
The cleaned-up version.
The victorious version.
The disciplined version.
The spiritual version.
But Scripture reveals something scandalous.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners (Romans 5:8).
Not after we fixed ourselves.
Not after we became worthy.
Not after we stopped failing.
Before.
The Gospel begins where human merit ends.
Peter understood this personally.
The man who wrote "cast your anxiety on Him" was once crushed beneath the weight of his own failure.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine hearing the rooster crow.
Imagine making eye contact with Jesus after denying Him.
Imagine believing your story was over.
Yet Jesus rewrote Peter's story.
Not with condemnation.
Not with rejection.
Not with humiliation.
But with restoration.
That is the heartbeat of our theme:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
The same Lord who restored Peter still restores people today.
The same Savior who carried Peter's shame still carries ours.
The same Christ who bore the cross still bears burdens.
Isaiah foresaw this centuries before Calvary:
"Surely He has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows." (Isaiah 53:4)
The Hebrew word for "borne" is:
"נָשָׂא" (nasa)
To lift.
To carry.
To bear away.
The burden you are carrying is not merely something Jesus understands.
It is something He willingly carried.
Ultimately, every burden finds its answer at the cross.
There, Christ carried humanity's greatest anxiety.
Separation from God.
Sin.
Judgment.
Death.
Condemnation.
And when He cried out:
"Τετέλεσται" (Tetelestai)
"It is finished."
The debt was paid.
The burden was carried.
The victory was secured.
This is why 1 Peter 5:7 is not merely a self-help verse.
It is a Gospel verse.
It points directly to the character of Jesus.
A Savior who does not merely sympathize.
A Savior who saves.
A Savior who carries.
A Savior who restores.
A Savior who rewrites stories.
Maybe you came to this article carrying something you have hidden for years.
A private battle.
A secret fear.
A wound no one knows exists.
A disappointment you never recovered from.
A prayer that still seems unanswered.
Hear the invitation of Christ.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you become stronger.
Not when you become more spiritual.
Now.
Cast it on Him.
Throw it on Him.
Release it to Him.
Because the One who carried a cross can certainly carry your burden.
And perhaps that is why this message needs to be shared.
Someone you know is silently carrying what Jesus died to bear.
Someone scrolling tonight is exhausted.
Someone feels forgotten.
Someone is one step away from giving up.
Not for popularity.
Not for algorithms.
But because eternity matters.
Because people matter.
Because souls matter.
And because the Gospel is too good to keep to ourselves.
Be honest.
What burden do you need to place in Christ's hands today?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
Because one shared article can reach a struggling heart.
One testimony can inspire faith.
One act of obedience can impact eternity.
And one surrendered burden can become the beginning of an entirely rewritten story.
The burden was never yours to carry forever.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Satan Loves Busy Christians
paragraphs:
Why Satan Loves Busy Christians
The Most Dangerous Trap in the Church Isn't Sin That Shocks You—It's Distraction That Silences You
The enemy does not always arrive wearing darkness.
Sometimes he arrives wearing productivity.
Sometimes he arrives carrying ministry calendars, endless notifications, packed schedules, noble responsibilities, church commitments, family obligations, business goals, and good intentions.
Because Satan understands something many Christians still do not.
If he cannot make you abandon Jesus, he will try to keep you too busy to sit with Him.
That is why some believers are exhausted but not transformed.
Active but not intimate.
Serving but not listening.
Running but not abiding.
And perhaps the most terrifying reality is this:
Many Christians mistake spiritual activity for spiritual health.
The devil is perfectly comfortable with believers filling every hour of their day—as long as Jesus gets the leftovers.
Think about that.
The greatest commandment was never "Stay busy."
It was never "Stay productive."
It was never "Stay occupied."
Jesus said:
"You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind."
(Matthew 22:37)
The Greek word used for love here is agapēseis (ἀγαπήσεις), speaking of wholehearted, sacrificial devotion.
Not divided affection.
Not leftover attention.
Not fragmented loyalty.
Wholehearted surrender.
Yet modern Christianity often rewards busyness more than intimacy.
We celebrate packed calendars.
We applaud endless activity.
We admire visible accomplishments.
Meanwhile many believers quietly lose the very relationship that gave those activities meaning.
Satan understands the principle hidden behind every healthy relationship.
Relationships die when communication dies.
And prayer is communication.
Worship is communication.
Meditation on Scripture is communication.
Stillness before God is communication.
The enemy knows that if he can interrupt those things long enough, spiritual drift becomes inevitable.
Not overnight.
Not dramatically.
Slowly.
Almost invisibly.
One distracted day becomes one distracted week.
One distracted week becomes one distracted month.
One distracted month becomes one distracted year.
Then one day a believer suddenly realizes they know about God more than they know God.
This strategy is not new.
It appeared in one of the most relatable moments in Scripture.
In Luke 10:38-42, Jesus enters a home occupied by two sisters.
One is Martha.
The other is Mary.
Martha is working.
Mary is listening.
Martha is moving.
Mary is receiving.
Martha becomes frustrated and asks Jesus to correct her sister.
But Jesus responds with words that still pierce hearts two thousand years later.
The Greek text records:
"Μάρθα Μάρθα μεριμνᾷς καὶ θορυβάζῃ περὶ πολλά."
"Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things."
The word merimnas (μεριμνᾷς) means distracted by cares, pulled apart internally.
Jesus was not condemning service.
He was exposing misplaced priorities.
Then He says:
"One thing is necessary."
One thing.
Not fifty.
Not ten.
One.
Mary chose the better portion because she chose Jesus before everything else.
How many believers today would have looked more like Martha than Mary?
How many of us wake up reaching for our phones before reaching for Scripture?
How many spend hours consuming content and minutes consuming God's Word?
How many know every breaking headline but cannot remember the last verse that broke their heart open before the Lord?
This is not condemnation.
This is invitation.
Because Jesus never exposed wounds merely to shame people.
He exposed wounds to heal them.
That has always been His way.
The Bible's greatest stories are not stories about perfect people.
They are stories about distracted, broken, scandal-ridden people being pursued by relentless grace.
David was an adulterer.
Peter denied Christ.
The Samaritan woman carried a history she wanted hidden.
Paul persecuted believers.
Yet Jesus rewrote every one of their stories.
That is why our mission remains:
Because Jesus truly rewrites everything.
Even distracted Christians.
Even exhausted Christians.
Even believers who feel spiritually numb.
Even those who have spent years running on empty.
The enemy wants Christians overwhelmed because overwhelmed believers rarely hear whispers.
And God often speaks through whispers.
When Elijah stood on the mountain, Scripture says God was not in the wind.
Not in the earthquake.
Not in the fire.
Then came what the Hebrew text describes as:
"קוֹל דְּמָמָה דַקָּה"
Qol demamah daqqah.
A gentle whisper.
A thin silence.
A quiet voice.
The problem is not that God stopped speaking.
The problem is that many believers have surrounded themselves with so much noise that they cannot hear Him anymore.
And Satan loves that.
Because distracted Christians are easier to discourage.
Easier to deceive.
Easier to isolate.
Easier to exhaust.
Easier to tempt.
The enemy understands that what captures your attention eventually shapes your affection.
What shapes your affection eventually directs your worship.
And what directs your worship ultimately determines your life.
This is why Jesus repeatedly withdrew from crowds.
Repeatedly escaped noise.
Repeatedly sought solitude.
Repeatedly prioritized communion with His Father.
If the sinless Son of God needed regular time alone with the Father, how much more do we?
Perhaps that is why so many believers secretly feel empty.
Not because they do not love Jesus.
But because they have been surviving on spiritual crumbs while trying to fight spiritual battles.
No soldier wins a war starving.
No disciple flourishes disconnected from Christ.
Jesus Himself said in John 15:5:
"I am the vine; you are the branches."
The Greek word for abide is menō (μένω).
Remain.
Stay.
Continue.
Dwell.
Not visit occasionally.
Remain.
A branch disconnected from the vine may look alive temporarily.
But death has already begun.
And perhaps some readers feel that truth deeply right now.
Maybe your prayer life has become mechanical.
Maybe your Bible sits unopened.
Maybe worship feels distant.
Maybe your heart feels tired.
Maybe you've been carrying responsibilities that slowly pushed Jesus to the margins.
If that's you, hear this clearly.
Jesus is not standing with folded arms waiting to reject you.
He is standing with scarred hands inviting you back.
The Gospel has always been about restoration.
The Cross has always been about reconciliation.
Grace has always been greater than failure.
And Christ has always specialized in rewriting stories that seemed beyond repair.
The same Savior who restored Peter after denial can restore distracted believers today.
The same Savior who welcomed prodigals still welcomes them.
The same Savior who raised the dead still revives weary souls.
You are not too far gone.
You are not too distracted.
You are not too exhausted.
You are not beyond grace.
And perhaps today is the day you stop running long enough to hear the voice that has been calling your name all along.
Someone reading may be carrying the exact burden you understand.
Do not suffer alone.
The Body of Christ was never designed for isolation.
Sometimes sharing is more than posting content.
Sometimes sharing is ministry.

Not because the Gospel is for sale—it never will be—but because supporting this mission helps spread biblical truth, discipleship, encouragement, evangelism, and Christ-centered content to more people who desperately need hope.
The world is growing louder.
Truth is growing rarer.
But Jesus is still calling people to Himself.
One day many believers will discover that the greatest thief in their spiritual life was not persecution.
It was distraction.
And by then, they will wish they had guarded their time with Jesus more fiercely.
Do not wait for that day.
Choose the better portion now.
Because eternity belongs to those who never stopped making room for Christ.
The devil does not fear Christians who are merely busy.
He fears Christians who are close enough to Jesus to hear His whisper.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Day David Heard About Saul’s Death
paragraphs:
The Day David Heard About Saul’s Death
When the Man Who Hunted You Dies, What Does Grace Do Next?
There are moments in life that reveal who we truly are.
Not when everything is going well.
Not when people applaud us.
Not when prayers are answered exactly the way we hoped.
The deepest revelations of the human heart often emerge when an enemy falls.
What happens when the person who wounded you finally loses?
What happens when the one who lied about you, betrayed you, humiliated you, opposed you, or spent years trying to destroy your life suddenly collapses under the weight of their own choices?
Most people think they know how they would respond.
Until the moment actually arrives.
David discovered the answer on one of the darkest days in Israel's history.
And what happened next is one of the most shocking displays of grace ever recorded in Scripture.
The story begins in 2 Samuel 1.
The Hebrew text opens with these words:
וַיְהִי אַחֲרֵי מוֹת שָׁאוּל
Vayehi acharei mot Sha'ul
"After the death of Saul..."
Simple words.
Yet behind them stands a lifetime of pain.
Saul had not merely disliked David.
He hunted him.
Pursued him.
Slandered him.
Drove him into caves.
Separated him from family.
Forced him into exile.
Turned soldiers against him.
Obsessed over destroying him.
For years David lived as a fugitive because of Saul's jealousy.
The man who should have mentored him tried repeatedly to murder him.
Imagine carrying that burden.
Imagine living every day knowing someone powerful wants you gone.
Imagine years of injustice.
Years of misunderstanding.
Years of running.
Years of waiting.
Then one day a messenger arrives.
Covered in dust.
Breathing heavily.
Carrying news that would change everything.
Saul is dead.
Jonathan is dead.
Israel has been defeated.
The king is gone.
The throne is now open.
Everything David had been promised is finally within reach.
This is the moment readers expect celebration.
This is where Hollywood writes the victory scene.
This is where revenge stories climax.
This is where enemies finally get what they deserve.
But David belongs to a different Kingdom.
The messenger assumes David will be thrilled.
To increase his chances of reward, he claims he personally finished Saul off.
He thinks David will celebrate.
He thinks David will thank him.
He thinks David will honor him.
Instead, David tears his clothes.
Every expectation shatters.
Scripture says:
"וַיַּחֲזֵק דָּוִד בִּבְגָדָיו וַיִּקְרָעֵם"
Vayachazek David bivgadav vayikra'em
"Then David took hold of his clothes and tore them."
(2 Samuel 1:11)
He weeps.
His men weep.
They mourn.
They fast.
The Hebrew word used repeatedly is:
בָּכָה
Bakah
To weep.
To cry deeply.
To lament from the heart.
The man who spent years running from Saul now cries over Saul's death.
Pause for a moment.
Let that sink in.
David mourned someone who had tried to kill him.
Not because Saul deserved it.
Because David's heart had been transformed by God.
The world teaches us to celebrate when enemies fall.
The Kingdom teaches us to grieve what sin destroys.
David understood something many people still miss today.
A fallen enemy is still a person made in the image of God.
A broken life is still a tragedy.
A soul lost to rebellion is not a victory worth celebrating.
Proverbs 24:17 says:
"Do not rejoice when your enemy falls."
David lived those words long before many people even knew them.
Then comes one of the most emotionally devastating songs in Scripture.
David composes a lament.
A funeral song.
A national cry.
His grief becomes poetry.
His heartbreak becomes worship.
Repeatedly he declares:
"אֵיךְ נָפְלוּ גִבּוֹרִים"
Eikh naflu gibborim
"How the mighty have fallen!"
(2 Samuel 1:19)
Three times the phrase echoes through the chapter.
How the mighty have fallen.
Not mockery.
Not sarcasm.
Not triumph.
Heartbreak.
The mighty king has fallen.
The beloved Jonathan has fallen.
The nation has fallen.
Sin has done what sin always does.
It destroys.
It takes.
It kills.
It leaves ruins behind.
The tragedy of Saul's life was never merely that he lost a kingdom.
The tragedy was that he repeatedly resisted the God who wanted to save him.
Saul's story is one of the Bible's greatest warnings.
A man can be anointed and still drift.
Gifted and still fall.
Powerful and still become spiritually empty.
Close to God's blessings while becoming distant from God's heart.
David understood this.
That is why his response was not self-righteousness.
It was humility.
Because every believer is capable of becoming Saul apart from God's grace.
And this is where the story suddenly becomes personal.
Most readers are not David.
Most readers are not Saul.
Most readers are both.
There are places where we have been wounded like David.
And there are places where we have wounded others like Saul.
There are scars we carry.
And scars we caused.
Failures we regret.
Words we wish we could take back.
Relationships we damaged.
Opportunities we squandered.
Moments we chose pride over obedience.
Fear over faith.
Control over surrender.
Every one of us has chapters we wish were removed from our story.
Scandal.
Failure.
Shame.
Regret.
Hidden battles.
Private sins.
Broken dreams.
Yet this is exactly why the Gospel is such astonishing news.
Jesus specializes in rewriting stories.
The New Testament reveals this through the Greek word:
χάρις
Charis
Grace.
Not earned.
Not deserved.
Not purchased.
Given.
Freely.
Lavishly.
Completely.
Through Christ.
The same grace that restored Peter after denial.
The same grace that transformed Paul from persecutor to apostle.
The same grace that welcomed the thief on the cross.
The same grace still reaches people today.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of good people succeeding.
It is the story of sinners being rescued.
The Gospel declares that no scandal is stronger than the cross.
No failure is bigger than the empty tomb.
No shame is greater than the mercy of God.
This is why our mission remains simple.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you are carrying Saul-like regrets.
Maybe you are carrying David-like wounds.
Maybe both.
The invitation of Christ remains the same.
Come.
Repent.
Surrender.
Receive mercy.
Be transformed.
The cross still stands.
The tomb is still empty.
The Savior still saves.
The grace of God is still changing lives.
And perhaps that is why David's tears still speak across thousands of years.
Because they remind us that true victory is not defeating enemies.
True victory is becoming more like Christ.
A Savior who prayed for His enemies.
A Savior who forgave His executioners.
A Savior who turns hatred into mercy and ashes into beauty.
If this message stirred your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
What part of your story are you asking Jesus to rewrite?
Your testimony may be the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
You will also gain access to deeper discipleship content while helping expand the reach of biblical truth to more lives that need the hope of the Gospel.
Because every share spreads truth.
Every testimony points people to Jesus.
And every redeemed story becomes evidence that grace still wins.
The enemy thought Saul's story ended in tragedy.
The enemy thought David's years in caves were wasted.
The enemy thought the cross was the end.
But God has always been writing a greater story.
And He is still writing yours.
The chapter you are grieving may not be the chapter God is finishing.
Because Jesus Rewrites Everything.
The grace that carried David through the valley is still reaching for you today.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Can Emotional Affairs Be Worse Than Physical Affairs?
paragraphs:
Can Emotional Affairs Be Worse Than Physical Affairs?
The Betrayal That Begins Long Before Two Hands Ever Touch—How Jesus Exposes the Hidden Affairs of the Heart and Still Offers Grace
There is a kind of betrayal that leaves no lipstick on a collar.
No hotel receipts.
No suspicious photographs.
No undeniable evidence.
Yet somehow...
it shatters a marriage just the same.
Sometimes even deeper.
Because the greatest betrayals do not begin in the bedroom.
They begin in the heart.
They begin in conversations that should never have become safe places.
In messages deleted before anyone could see them.
In laughter that belonged to someone else.
In secrets disguised as "just friendship."
In emotional dependence that quietly replaced covenant intimacy.
And by the time bodies finally meet...
the heart often crossed the line months—or even years—earlier.
That is why one of the most uncomfortable questions Christians can ask is this:
Can an emotional affair actually be worse than a physical affair?
Not because physical adultery is somehow less sinful—it is not.
But because emotional affairs often deceive people into believing they have remained faithful while their hearts have already abandoned the covenant God established.
The Bible refuses to define faithfulness merely by physical boundaries.
Jesus goes much deeper.
Far deeper than most of us are comfortable admitting.
Because heaven has always measured love from the inside out.
When Jesus preached what we now call the Sermon on the Mount, He confronted a culture that believed righteousness was mostly about outward behavior.
But Jesus exposed the heart.
He declared:

"You have heard that it was said, 'You shall not commit adultery.' But I tell you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart." (Matthew 5:27–28)
The Greek text reads:

πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν
(pas ho blepōn gunaika pros to epithymēsai autēn)
The crucial word is ἐπιθυμέω (epithymeō).
It means far more than noticing beauty.
It describes a deliberate, cultivated desire.
A longing that chooses possession.
A heart that has already begun moving toward someone who does not belong within God's design for that relationship.
Jesus was not inventing a new command.
He was revealing what God had already declared centuries earlier.
The Tenth Commandment never prohibited only actions.
It prohibited coveting.
The Hebrew says:
לֹא תַחְמֹד (Lo tachmod)
The verb חָמַד (chamad) means to crave, desire, covet, or set one's heart upon something that belongs to another.
Long before adultery became physical...
coveting had already become spiritual.
God has always been after the heart.
This is why emotional affairs are so spiritually dangerous.
Many people convince themselves:
"We never kissed."
"We never slept together."
"We're just talking."
"We understand each other."
"We're only friends."
But somewhere along the journey...
your spouse stopped being the first person you wanted to tell about your day.
Someone else became your emotional refuge.
Someone else became your source of affirmation.
Someone else became the person who understood your fears.
Someone else occupied sacred space that God intended marriage to protect.
Marriage was never designed to be merely physical exclusivity.
It is covenant.
The Hebrew word often associated with covenant relationship is בְּרִית (berith).
A covenant is not simply a legal agreement.
It is a sacred bond established before God Himself.
That covenant includes the body.
But it also includes trust.
Loyalty.
Emotional safety.
Spiritual intimacy.
Shared burdens.
Shared joys.
Shared hearts.
An emotional affair quietly transfers these treasures elsewhere.
That is why many wounded spouses say something surprising.
"The sex hurt."
"But the lies destroyed me."
"The secrecy destroyed me."
"The fact that they shared their heart with someone else—that broke me."
Because intimacy is not merely physical.
The Bible repeatedly joins body and soul together.
In Genesis we read:
"So they shall become one flesh."
The Hebrew expression is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד (basar echad)
Often translated "one flesh."
But this union extends beyond anatomy.
Scripture consistently presents marriage as whole-person union.
Body.
Mind.
Heart.
Spirit.
That is why betrayal of the heart matters.
King Solomon warned:
"Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it." (Proverbs 4:23)
The Hebrew says:
מִכָּל־מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ
(Mikkol mishmar netzor libbekha)
The word לֵב (lev) means much more than emotions.
In Hebrew thought, the heart represents the center of thought, desire, will, motives, and decision-making.
Everything flows from there.
Including adultery.
Including faithfulness.
Including repentance.
Perhaps the greatest biblical illustration is King David.
David's physical adultery with Bathsheba did not begin on the rooftop.
It began much earlier.
He allowed desire to remain.
He entertained it.
He cultivated it.
James later describes this deadly progression.
The Greek reads:
ἡ ἐπιθυμία συλλαβοῦσα τίκτει ἁμαρτίαν
(hē epithymia syllabousa tiktei hamartian)
"Desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin."
Notice the imagery.
Sin has a pregnancy.
Actions are born from desires already nurtured.
The affair begins inside.
Then eventually becomes visible.
This should terrify us.
Not because God delights in exposing sinners.
But because hidden sin grows strongest in darkness.
And emotional affairs specialize in darkness.
They survive through secrecy.
Private messages.
Private jokes.
Private emotional dependence.
Private dreams.
Private affection.
Private loyalty.
All while convincing us:
"We're doing nothing wrong."
Yet Scripture repeatedly warns that whatever captures the heart eventually directs the life.
Jesus asks:
"Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also."
Who receives your emotional treasure?
Who hears your deepest fears first?
Whose approval matters most?
Whose messages brighten your day?
Whose silence disappoints you?
Whose opinion shapes your decisions?
These questions often reveal more than we want to admit.
Yet before condemnation begins to consume anyone reading this...
the Gospel interrupts.
Because Christianity is never ultimately a story about exposed sinners.
It is a story about a pursuing Savior.
Consider the woman caught in adultery.
Everyone expected stones.
Jesus offered truth.
Then grace.
He never called sin acceptable.
He never minimized adultery.
He never lowered God's holiness.
But neither did He abandon the sinner.
He simply said:
"Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more."
Grace did not erase holiness.
Grace restored people back toward holiness.
That remains the invitation today.
Maybe you recognize yourself in this article.
Perhaps your affair never became physical.
Perhaps your marriage has already suffered because someone else occupied your heart.
Perhaps you are the wounded spouse carrying invisible scars.
Perhaps you are the one desperately trying to rebuild trust.
Perhaps you are still hiding.
The Gospel says there is still hope.
Repentance is not merely feeling guilty.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) literally describes a transformed mind leading to a transformed life.
It is a complete turning toward God.
Real repentance deletes conversations.
Ends secret relationships.
Confesses honestly.
Accepts consequences.
Rebuilds trust slowly.
Invites accountability.
Returns emotional intimacy to where God intended it to live.
Inside covenant.
With your spouse.
Before the Lord.
None of this is easy.
But Jesus never promised easy.
He promised Himself.
And Christ is enough to restore what sin has broken when hearts truly surrender.
One faithful share may become God's instrument to rescue a marriage, awaken a wandering believer, or point a broken heart back to Christ.
Return to it whenever you need to remember that the heart must be guarded long before temptation becomes visible.
Every purchase helps expand the ministry while equipping believers with Christ-centered resources that encourage daily discipleship.
Because one article may stir your heart...
but a lifetime of God's Word can transform your life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She Chose the Better Part
paragraphs:
She Chose the Better Part
The Lesson I Learned From Mary Sitting at Jesus' Feet—and Why It Changed Everything
I used to think faith was mostly about doing more.
More serving.
More volunteering.
More helping.
More fixing.
More proving.
More trying to convince God that I was serious enough, committed enough, useful enough to deserve His approval.
Then one day, I found myself exhausted.
Not because life was hard.
But because I was trying to carry a relationship that God never asked me to carry alone.
I was busy for Jesus.
Yet somehow far from Jesus.
That is why the story of Mary sitting at His feet hits differently the older I get.
