The greatest miracle was learning to trust God before the water arrived.
Because that is where many believers are today.
You're standing in a dry valley.
You are looking at a barren marriage.
A struggling family.
A prodigal child.
A failing business.
A painful diagnosis.
A silent prayer life.
A wound nobody knows about.
And because you cannot see rain, you assume God is not moving.
But Scripture repeatedly shows the opposite.
One of the most beautiful words in the New Testament is the Greek word:
"χάρις" (charis)
Meaning grace.
Not earned favor.
Not deserved blessing.
Not human achievement.
Grace.
The unearned kindness of God toward undeserving people.
That grace reaches its highest expression in Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest desert in human history was not geographical.
It was spiritual.
Humanity was separated from God.
Broken by sin.
Lost in rebellion.
Spiritually thirsty.
Unable to save itself.
The prophet Isaiah wrote:
"Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters." (Isaiah 55:1)
The invitation was never ultimately about physical water.
It pointed toward Christ.
Jesus stood and cried out in John 7:37:
"If anyone thirsts, let him come to Me and drink."
The Greek text says:
"ἐάν τις διψᾷ, ἐρχέσθω πρός με καὶ πινέτω"
Ean tis dipsa, erchestho pros me kai pineto.
"If anyone thirsts, let him come to Me and drink."
Jesus was revealing that every human heart is searching for something only He can provide.
Forgiveness.
Peace.
Purpose.
Hope.
Restoration.
Life.
The miracle in the desert points beyond itself to the greater miracle of the Gospel.
Because God did not merely provide water for thirsty soldiers.
He provided a Savior for thirsty souls.
And this is where our story becomes deeply personal.
Every one of us has a scandal.
Some carry public scandals.
Others carry hidden ones.
Regrets.
Failures.
Addictions.
Broken relationships.
Shameful decisions.
Secret sins.
Moments we wish could be erased forever.
The enemy wants us to believe those chapters define us.
That our failures are the final version of our story.
But Jesus specializes in rewriting stories.
Peter denied Him.
David committed adultery.
Rahab was a prostitute.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The woman at the well carried a painful past.
Yet grace rewrote every chapter.
That is why our mission has always been simple:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
The cross is the ultimate proof.
At Calvary, what looked like defeat became victory.
What looked like death became life.
What looked like a scandal became salvation.
Through Christ's sacrifice, sinners became sons and daughters.
The guilty became forgiven.
The condemned became redeemed.
The broken became restored.
The desert became a river.
And maybe that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear today.
Just because you don't see rain does not mean God has forgotten you.
Just because you don't see movement does not mean Heaven is inactive.
Just because your valley looks empty does not mean God is finished writing your story.
The water may already be on its way.
Perhaps even now God is working beneath circumstances you cannot see.
Preparing provision.
Preparing healing.
Preparing restoration.
Preparing redemption.
Preparing a testimony that will one day leave you speechless.
Be honest.
How many times has God already carried you through situations that looked impossible?
How many prayers did He answer in ways you never expected?
How many valleys became testimonies?
If this message touched something deep within your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
Someone who thinks God has forgotten them.
Someone who needs a reminder that God still provides water without rain.
"I still trust Him in the desert."
Or simply:
"Jesus rewrote my story."
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
Return to it whenever circumstances seem impossible.
And perhaps the most beautiful truth of all is this:

The same God who brought water into a desert without rain is still bringing hope into hopeless places, grace into scandal, life into dead situations, and redemption into stories the world has already written off.
Because your valley is not the end.
Your failure is not the end.
Your pain is not the end.
Your scandal is not the end.
Jesus always has the final word.
And when He writes the ending, grace becomes greater than everything that came before.
The desert never gets the last sentence.
Christ does.
The water was coming long before they ever saw it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She Said, “If You Really Love Me…”—The Night I Almost Traded My Soul for One Moment
paragraphs:
She Said, “If You Really Love Me…”—The Night I Almost Traded My Soul for One Moment
When Love Demands What God Forbids, It Isn't Love That Is Speaking.
"If you really loved me, you would."
Few sentences have destroyed more convictions than those seven words.
Not because they are true.
But because they sound believable when they come from someone you don't want to lose.
Maybe you've heard them.
Maybe they weren't spoken exactly that way. Maybe it sounded softer.
"Everyone else does it."
"We're getting married someday anyway."
"Don't you trust me?"
"Why are you making such a big deal about it?"
Or maybe the pressure never came through words at all.
Just silence.
Long hugs.
Late nights.
Locked doors.
Lingering kisses.
The feeling that saying "no" one more time might mean saying goodbye forever.
Many Christian men secretly wrestle with something they feel ashamed to admit.
They expected temptation to come from strangers.
They never expected it to come from the woman they prayed for.
No one talks about that enough.
Because we assume the man is always the one pushing.
Sometimes he is.
Sometimes he isn't.
Sometimes the man is the one fighting to obey Christ while the woman he deeply loves keeps asking him to compromise.
That battle is real.
And God sees it.
The world laughs at purity because the world no longer remembers what holiness costs.
But heaven does.
Scripture never teaches that love is proven through sexual surrender before marriage.
It teaches exactly the opposite.
The apostle Paul writes:
The Greek word translated "sexual immorality" is πορνεία (porneía).
It is broader than adultery.
It refers to every form of sexual intimacy outside God's covenant of marriage.
Paul isn't creating a cultural rule.
He is revealing God's heart.
The passage continues:
"...that each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor." (1 Thessalonians 4:4)
The Greek reads:
ἐν ἁγιασμῷ καὶ τιμῇ (en hagiasmō kai timē)
"Within holiness and honor."
Not guilt.
Not shame.
Honor.
Because your body was never designed to become proof that someone loves you.
Your body already belongs to Christ.
Paul later writes:
The phrase "bought with a price" comes from the Greek:
ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς (ēgorásthēte gar timēs)
Purchased at immeasurable cost.
Jesus didn't shed His blood so we could casually surrender what He redeemed.
Sometimes we think the greatest danger is lust.
But often the greater danger is emotional fear.
Fear of rejection.
Fear of loneliness.
Fear that obedience will cost us the relationship.
And maybe it will.
But losing someone because you obeyed God is never a true loss.
Losing intimacy with God to keep someone is.
Joseph understood this.
Genesis tells us that Potiphar's wife pursued him day after day.
She wasn't subtle.
She wasn't embarrassed.
She wanted him.
Joseph could have justified it.
Nobody would know.
Nobody was watching.
He was lonely.
Far from home.
Unfairly enslaved.
He deserved comfort.
Instead he asked one unforgettable question:
"How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?" (Genesis 39:9)
Notice what he didn't say.
He didn't say,
"What if I get caught?"
He didn't say,
"What will people think?"
He said,
"How could I sin against God?"
The Hebrew word for wickedness is רָעָה (ra'ah)—evil, moral corruption, that which wounds covenant faithfulness.
Joseph saw temptation through God's eyes.
Not merely through human consequences.
Real love never asks someone to disobey the One who created them.
The apostle John writes:
The Greek says:
ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ Θεοῦ (hē agapē tou Theou)
The love of God.
Biblical love is never separated from obedience.
Not because obedience earns salvation.
But because genuine love naturally desires to honor the One who first loved us.
Jesus Himself declared:
"If you love Me, you will keep My commandments." (John 14:15)
The Greek is beautifully simple:
Ἐὰν ἀγαπᾶτέ με, τὰς ἐντολάς μου τηρήσετε.
"If you love Me, My commandments you will keep."
Love.
Then obedience.
Not pressure.
Not manipulation.
Not emotional bargaining.
The culture says,
"If you love me, prove it physically."
Jesus says,
"If you love Me, trust Me completely."
Those are two entirely different gospels.
One ends in temporary pleasure.
The other leads to eternal life.
If your girlfriend becomes angry because you refuse sex, don't immediately assume she's evil.
She may be struggling.
She may have wounds.
She may have learned from culture that physical intimacy is how love is secured.
Respond with gentleness.
With honesty.
With compassion.
But don't move the boundary God has already drawn.
Grace never requires compromising truth.
Jesus was "full of grace and truth" (John 1:14), never one without the other.
Perhaps the hardest truth is this:
Someone can genuinely care about you and still influence you toward sin.
Peter loved Jesus.
Yet Jesus had to tell him,
"Get behind Me, Satan!" (Matthew 16:23)
Not because Peter belonged to Satan.
But because Peter's counsel opposed God's purpose.
Affection does not automatically make advice godly.
The heart is capable of loving someone deeply while still needing transformation.
That's why every relationship must be surrendered beneath Christ's authority.
Ask yourself honestly.
If saying "no" to sexual sin ends the relationship...
What exactly was holding the relationship together?
If holiness destroys the romance...
Was Christ ever at the center?
Marriage is meant to reflect Christ and His Church (Ephesians 5:25–32).
A marriage cannot faithfully picture Christ if its foundation is built upon continual disregard for His commands.
God's standards are not arbitrary restrictions.
They are loving protections.
Every command is rooted in His holy character and His desire for our flourishing.
When we fail—and many have—we are not beyond hope.
The Gospel is not for the morally flawless.
It is for repentant sinners.
King David committed adultery.
Peter denied Christ.
The woman caught in adultery expected stones.
Instead she encountered Jesus.
He neither excused her sin nor condemned her to hopelessness.
He said,
"Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more." (John 8:11)
Grace forgives.
Grace transforms.
Grace calls us forward.
This is why our message has always been:
Maybe your story already includes compromise.
Maybe you've crossed boundaries you promised never to cross.
Maybe guilt has whispered that purity is impossible now.
The cross says otherwise.
The empty tomb says otherwise.
Repentance is not pretending the past never happened.
It is turning toward the Savior who can redeem what sin tried to destroy.
No relationship is worth losing Christ.
No moment of pleasure is worth grieving the Holy Spirit.
No temporary acceptance is worth sacrificing eternal joy.
The greatest love story has never been about finding the perfect girlfriend.
It has always been about being found by the perfect Savior.
Bring it to Jesus today.
Your testimony may become the encouragement another believer desperately needs tonight.
Sometimes one shared message becomes the turning point in someone's walk with Christ.
There may come a day when you need to read these words again before making a decision you'll never forget.
If your desire is to glorify God through advancing His truth, your partnership becomes part of that mission.
One act of obedience today may become the testimony that rescues someone else tomorrow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Is Flirting at Work a Form of Cheating?
paragraphs:
Is Flirting at Work a Form of Cheating?
The Smile That Cost More Than a Kiss: When Innocent Conversations Become Silent Betrayals
There are affairs that begin in hotel rooms.
There are affairs that begin with a simple "Good morning."

Not every betrayal starts with touching hands. Some begin with prolonged eye contact. Some begin with private jokes that your spouse would never understand. Some begin with emotional safety that slowly replaces spiritual intimacy at home. Some begin with a coworker who simply "gets you."
And that's what makes this conversation uncomfortable.
Because most people don't think they're crossing a line while they're still standing several feet away from it.
The question isn't merely whether flirting at work is cheating.
The deeper question is this:
Why do we crave attention that doesn't belong to us?
Be honest.
Have you ever looked forward to seeing one specific coworker just a little more than everyone else?
Have you ever smiled at a notification and quickly turned your phone over?
Have you ever rehearsed a conversation before walking into work?
Have you ever shared struggles with someone at work before sharing them with your spouse?
Have you ever justified it by saying...
"We're just friends."
"It's harmless."
"They understand me."
"Nothing physical happened."
Most betrayals have those exact words written across their first chapter.
Scripture repeatedly warns us that sin rarely arrives looking like destruction.
It arrives looking harmless.
Beautiful.
Comforting.
Exciting.
Reasonable.
That is why Proverbs says,
"Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life." (Proverbs 4:23)
The Hebrew says:

נְצֹר לִבְּךָ מִכָּל־מִשְׁמָר
(Netzor libbekha mikol mishmar)
Literally,
"Guard your heart above every guard."
Notice something remarkable.
God does not first command us to guard our hands.
Or our lips.
Or even our bodies.
He commands us to guard our heart.
Because every visible sin first becomes an invisible affection.
Long before David committed adultery with Bathsheba, his heart had already drifted toward desire (2 Samuel 11).
Long before Judas betrayed Jesus with a kiss, greed had already made a home inside him (John 12:6).
Long before Peter denied Christ publicly, fear had quietly taken root.
Everything visible begins invisibly.
Jesus took this even further.
In Matthew 5:28 He said,
"But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart."
The Greek text reads,

πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
(pros to epithymēsai autēn)
The key word is ἐπιθυμέω (epithymeō).
It means much more than noticing beauty.
It means to cultivate desire.
To intentionally entertain longing.
To feed what should be starved.
Jesus completely dismantled the idea that sin only begins when physical boundaries are crossed.
According to Christ...
The battlefield is the heart.
This doesn't mean every compliment is sinful.
It doesn't mean men and women cannot work together.
Jesus Himself spoke respectfully with women.
Paul served alongside faithful women in ministry.
The Bible never condemns healthy friendship.
What Scripture condemns is cultivating emotional intimacy that belongs exclusively inside the covenant of marriage.
Flirting is rarely about words.
It is about intention.
It asks questions like...
"Do I secretly enjoy this attention?"
"Would I speak this way if my spouse were standing beside me?"
"Would I hide these conversations?"
"Would I be comfortable reading these messages out loud to my husband or wife?"
"Would Jesus feel honored sitting beside me?"
If the answer makes your stomach tighten...
That feeling may be mercy.
Not condemnation.
Mercy.
Because conviction is one of the greatest expressions of God's love.
The Holy Spirit does not expose us to shame us.
He exposes us to rescue us.
The workplace has become one of the greatest testing grounds for modern believers.
Many spend more waking hours with coworkers than with their own families.
Shared deadlines become shared frustrations.
Shared frustrations become shared vulnerability.
Shared vulnerability becomes emotional dependence.
Emotional dependence becomes attachment.
Attachment becomes secrecy.
Secrecy becomes compromise.
Compromise becomes devastation.
James explains this progression with astonishing clarity.
"But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death." (James 1:14–15)
The Greek word translated "lured" is ἐξελκόμενος (exelkomenos).
It was originally used for drawing prey out with bait.
Satan rarely drags believers into adultery.
He baits them.
The bait is attention.
Validation.
Admiration.
Feeling understood.
Feeling desired.
Feeling appreciated.
Things every human heart longs for.
Which is why marriage cannot survive on legal commitment alone.
It must be continually nourished by intentional love.
If you are married, ask yourself...
When was the last time you flirted with your spouse instead of someone else?
When was the last time you laughed together?
Prayed together?
Held hands?
Sent an encouraging message?
Pursued each other like you once did?
Many marriages don't die because someone found a better person.
They die because someone stopped pursuing the person God already gave them.
The Gospel speaks directly into this.
Because every one of us has been spiritually unfaithful.
The Old Testament repeatedly describes Israel's idolatry as adultery.
God remained faithful.
His people wandered.
Yet He pursued them.
Hosea's marriage became a living picture of God's redeeming love.
A faithful husband.
An unfaithful bride.
Sound familiar?
That is our story.
And then came Jesus.
The Bridegroom.
The One who loved an undeserving bride.
The One who gave Himself while we were still sinners.
The One who restores what sin destroys.
The One who rewrites endings that everyone else calls impossible.
Romans 5:8 reminds us,
"But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
Grace never minimizes sin.
Grace magnifies the Savior.
If flirting has become emotional infidelity...
Repent.
Not tomorrow.
Today.
Repentance is not merely feeling guilty.
The New Testament word is μετάνοια (metanoia).
It means a change of mind that produces a change of direction.
Delete the conversations.
Rebuild boundaries.
Confess where appropriate.
Invite accountability.
Pursue holiness.
Not because you fear losing your marriage.
Because you love Christ.
Every marriage is ultimately meant to reflect Him.
Ephesians 5 points us beyond romance toward redemption.
Every faithful husband reflects Christ.
Every faithful wife reflects the Church.
Every restored marriage whispers the Gospel.
Every forgiven sinner proclaims the cross.
Maybe you have already crossed the line.
Maybe your marriage feels broken beyond repair.
Maybe shame has convinced you that your story is finished.
But the cross has never met a scandal it could not redeem.
The empty tomb has never encountered a failure too great for resurrection.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
David committed adultery and murder.
The Samaritan woman had multiple broken relationships.
Yet Jesus rewrote every one of those stories.
Not because sin was small.
Because grace is greater.
That is the heartbeat of our mission.

If someone you love is standing closer to temptation than they realize, don't keep this to yourself. Every share has the potential to place the Gospel in front of someone who may never open a Bible on their own.
One guarded heart today may spare a lifetime of tears tomorrow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Lesson Hidden in a Gentle Answer
paragraphs: The Lesson Hidden in a Gentle Answer
The Quiet Power That Can Stop a War, Heal a Family, Restore a Soul, and Reveal the Heart of Christ
There are moments that change the course of a life forever, and most people expect those moments to arrive with thunder.
A dramatic confrontation.
A shocking revelation.
A powerful sermon.
A crisis that forces everything into the open.
But some of the greatest miracles God performs do not arrive with noise.
They arrive through a gentle answer.
One sentence.
One response.
One moment when someone had every reason to strike back but chose grace instead.
Most of us know what it feels like to be wounded by words.
A careless comment.
A sarcastic remark.
A betrayal from someone we trusted.
A criticism we never saw coming.
A message that ruined our day.
A conversation we replay in our minds years later.
Words have started wars, destroyed friendships, divided churches, shattered marriages, and wounded hearts so deeply that scars remained long after the voices faded.
Yet hidden inside Scripture is a lesson so powerful that many people read past it without realizing how much of life depends on it.
Proverbs 15:1 says:
“A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.”
The Hebrew text reads:
"מַעֲנֶה־רַּךְ יָשִׁיב חֵמָה וּדְבַר־עֶצֶב יַעֲלֶה־אָף"
Ma'aneh-rakh yashiv chemah, u'devar etzev ya'aleh af.
A more literal rendering would be:
“A gentle response turns back fury, but a painful word causes anger to rise.”
Notice what the verse does not say.
It does not say the gentle answer proves the other person is right.
It does not say truth should be compromised.
It does not say evil should be ignored.
It says something far more profound.
A gentle answer has the power to redirect destruction.
It can stop the spread of wrath before it consumes everything in its path.
The world teaches the opposite.
If someone insults you, insult them harder.
If someone humiliates you, make sure they regret it.
If someone attacks you, strike back with greater force.
But the Kingdom of God often moves in ways that appear weak to the world while possessing unimaginable strength.
Jesus demonstrated this repeatedly.
When falsely accused, He remained composed.
When mocked, He did not retaliate.
When reviled, He entrusted Himself to the Father.
The Apostle Peter wrote:
“When He was reviled, He did not revile in return; when He suffered, He did not threaten...” (1 Peter 2:23)
The Greek word translated “reviled” is loidoreō, meaning to insult, abuse verbally, or heap shame upon someone.
Christ endured it all.
Yet He answered differently.
Not because He was weak.
Because He was stronger than His enemies.
Anyone can lose control.
Not everyone can surrender control to God.
The lesson hidden in a gentle answer is not merely about communication.
It is about spiritual transformation.
The tongue reveals the condition of the heart.
Jesus said:
“For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” (Matthew 12:34)
The Greek phrase is:
ek gar tou perisseumatos tēs kardias to stoma lalei.
Literally:
“Out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks.”
The mouth is often a mirror.
When bitterness fills the heart, bitterness eventually escapes.
When pride fills the heart, pride eventually speaks.
When anger fills the heart, anger eventually erupts.
But when Christ transforms the heart, something remarkable begins to happen.
Gentleness appears where rage once lived.
Patience appears where hostility once ruled.
Grace appears where revenge once seemed justified.
Many people reading this can probably remember a moment when a gentle answer changed everything.
Perhaps a husband expected another argument and instead received understanding.
Perhaps a wife expected criticism and instead received compassion.
Perhaps a child expected punishment and instead received guidance.
Perhaps a sinner expected condemnation and instead encountered Jesus.
That last one is the story of the Gospel itself.
Humanity rebelled against God.
We sinned.
We wandered.
We chose darkness.
We broke what was good.
We deserved judgment.
Yet God's answer to our rebellion was not immediate destruction.
It was Jesus.
John 1:14 declares:
“And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”
The Greek reads:
Kai ho Logos sarx egeneto kai eskēnōsen en hēmin.
The eternal Logos.
The divine Word.
The Creator entered creation.
Not with a sword in His hand.
But with nails waiting for His hands.
Not to crush sinners.
But to save them.
This is why the Gospel remains the greatest story ever told.
God's response to our scandal became grace.
Our failure became an opportunity for redemption.
Our guilt became the backdrop against which His mercy shined brightest.
The woman caught in adultery expected stones.
Instead she met Jesus.
The thief on the cross expected death.
Instead he found paradise.
Peter expected rejection after denying Christ.
Instead he received restoration.
Again and again, Scripture reveals the same breathtaking truth:
Jesus rewrites everything.
The enemy writes shame.
Jesus writes redemption.
The enemy writes failure.
Jesus writes restoration.
The enemy writes endings.
Jesus writes new beginnings.
That truth reaches far beyond ancient history.
It reaches into your story.
Maybe someone has spoken harsh words over your life.
Maybe you were told you would never change.
Maybe you carry regret from mistakes nobody else knows about.
Maybe you still hear echoes from your past.
But the cross of Christ declares something greater than every accusation.
Romans 8:1 says:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
No condemnation.
Not less condemnation.
Not reduced condemnation.
No condemnation.
Because Jesus took upon Himself what we deserved.
This is why a gentle answer is not merely a communication strategy.
It is a reflection of Christ.
Every time grace interrupts hostility, the Gospel becomes visible.
Every time mercy overcomes revenge, the Gospel becomes visible.
Every time kindness triumphs over cruelty, the Gospel becomes visible.
And perhaps that is the hidden lesson many people miss.
The gentle answer is powerful because it points to the Savior who first answered us with grace.
As you read these words, think about the conversations waiting for you.
The message you have not answered.
The relationship hanging by a thread.
The argument that keeps resurfacing.
The wound that still hurts.
What would happen if Christ governed that response?
What would happen if grace spoke first?
What would happen if the cross became visible in your words?
You may never know how many battles God prevents through one Spirit-filled response.
You may never know how many hearts soften because you chose gentleness over retaliation.
You may never know how many lives are changed because someone encountered Jesus through your words.
But heaven knows.
And eternity will reveal what grace accomplished.
If this message exposed something hidden in your heart, be honest.
Your testimony may be the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
You never know whose marriage, friendship, family, or faith may be touched by a lesson hidden in a gentle answer.
Because one gentle answer may change a conversation.
One conversation may change a life.
And one encounter with Jesus can change eternity.
The same mouth that once spoke judgment over your story now speaks grace through the scars of a risen Savior.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The One Boundary That Saves Relationships
paragraphs:
The One Boundary That Saves Relationships
The Word We Fear Saying Is Often the Door God Uses to Protect Love, Restore Trust, and Rewrite Broken Stories.
There is one word that many people struggle to say.
No.
Not because it is difficult to pronounce.
Because it is difficult to live.
Some people say "yes" until they lose themselves.
Some say "yes" because they fear rejection.
Some say "yes" because they confuse sacrifice with obedience.
Some say "yes" because they believe keeping everyone happy is the same as loving them.
But years later, they wonder why they feel exhausted...resentful...empty...or even spiritually distant from God.
The painful truth is this:
Many relationships are not destroyed by hatred.
They are destroyed by the absence of godly boundaries.
The greatest acts of love are not always giving more.
Sometimes they are knowing where love must stop enabling sin.
Sometimes holiness looks like saying, "No."
That sounds harsh in a culture that celebrates unlimited tolerance.
But Scripture paints a very different picture.
God Himself is love (1 John 4:8).
Yet God is also the One who established boundaries from the very beginning.
Before sin entered the world, the Lord lovingly gave Adam one boundary.
"And the LORD God commanded the man, saying, 'You may surely eat of every tree of the garden, but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat...'" (Genesis 2:16–17, ESV)
The Hebrew word translated "commanded" is צָוָה (tsavah), meaning to command, appoint, or charge with authority. It was not an arbitrary restriction. It was a loving command meant to preserve life.
God's first boundary was not designed to steal joy.
It was designed to protect it.
The serpent's first temptation was not simply about fruit.
It was about convincing humanity that boundaries are burdens instead of blessings.
That lie has never changed.
Today we hear it differently.
"If you really loved them, you wouldn't say no."
"If you're a good Christian, you'll always keep giving."
"Don't make people uncomfortable."
"Keep the peace at all costs."
But biblical peace is never purchased by abandoning truth.
Jesus Himself embodied perfect love, yet He constantly practiced perfect boundaries.
He walked away from crowds.
He withdrew to pray.
He refused to perform miracles merely to entertain skeptics.
He confronted religious hypocrisy.
He even told people "not yet."
In John 2:4, when His mother informed Him that the wedding had run out of wine, Jesus replied:
τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοί, γύναι; οὔπω ἥκει ἡ ὥρα μου (Ti emoi kai soi, gynai? Oupō hēkei hē hōra mou.)
Literally:
"What is that to me and to you, woman? My hour has not yet come."
This was not disrespect.
It was the language of divine timing.
Jesus refused to allow even loving family expectations to dictate His Father's mission.
His identity was rooted in obedience to God, not the pressure of people.
That is one of the healthiest boundaries ever demonstrated.
The apostle Paul taught something equally powerful.
"Bear one another's burdens..." (Galatians 6:2)
Only four verses later he writes,
"For each will have to bear his own load." (Galatians 6:5)
At first glance, these verses seem contradictory.
They are not.
The Greek words are completely different.
In Galatians 6:2, Paul uses βάρος (baros), meaning an overwhelming burden that someone cannot carry alone.
In Galatians 6:5, he uses φορτίον (phortion), referring to one's personal responsibility or assigned load.
The distinction changes everything.
Christians are called to help carry crushing burdens.
We are not called to carry someone else's lifelong irresponsibility.
There is a difference between compassion and codependency.
There is a difference between grace and enabling.
There is a difference between forgiveness and allowing abuse to continue unchecked.
Jesus forgave sinners.
He never partnered with sin.
One of the greatest misunderstandings inside Christian homes, churches, friendships, and even marriages is believing that unconditional love means unconditional access.
It does not.
God's love is unconditional.
Many of His relationships are conditional.
Israel experienced blessings when walking in covenant obedience and consequences when rejecting Him.
Jesus welcomed all who came to Him.
Yet He also said,
"If you love Me, you will keep My commandments." (John 14:15)
The Greek word ἀγαπᾶτέ (agapate) expresses covenantal, self-giving love.
The word τηρήσετε (tērēsete) means to guard, preserve, carefully keep.
Love and obedience were never enemies.
They were always companions.
Healthy boundaries are not walls that imprison people.
They are fences that protect what God has entrusted to us.
Without fences, gardens become trampled.
Without banks, rivers become floods.
Without skin, the human body cannot survive.
Boundaries are not evidence of selfishness.
They are evidence of stewardship.
Even heaven itself has boundaries.
Jesus spoke repeatedly of doors that open and doors that close.
Not everyone enters.
Not because God lacks love.
Because love never abolishes holiness.
Many people reading this are carrying wounds that were never theirs to carry.
You've become everyone's rescuer.
Everyone's therapist.
Everyone's financial backup.
Everyone's emotional sponge.
Everyone's emergency contact.
Except almost no one asks how your soul is doing.
Somewhere along the way, you confused being needed with being loved.
Jesus never measured His worth by how many people depended on Him.
He measured everything by the Father's will.
Perhaps that is the boundary your heart desperately needs.
Not another apology.
Not another explanation.
Not another sleepless night trying to keep everyone happy.
Perhaps what God is asking from you today is quiet obedience.
The courage to lovingly say,
"I cannot support what dishonors Christ."
"I forgive you, but I cannot continue this unhealthy pattern."
"I love you enough to stop enabling your destruction."
Those words may sound painful.
But wounds cleaned by truth heal far better than infections hidden by false peace.
Proverbs reminds us,
"Faithful are the wounds of a friend." (Proverbs 27:6)
Love tells the truth.
Love protects.
Love corrects.
Love sometimes walks away—not from hatred—but because holiness refuses to participate in what destroys souls.
The cross itself teaches us this.
Jesus welcomed sinners with open arms.
But He never lowered God's standard to gain followers.
Instead, He fulfilled the standard we never could.
He bore our sins, not by approving them, but by paying for them.
The greatest boundary ever established was the separation created by sin.
The greatest bridge ever built was the Cross.
There, justice and mercy embraced.
Scandal met grace.
Death met Life.
Hell met Heaven's King.
And Jesus rewrote everything.
That is why our message has never been behavior modification.
It has always been transformation through Christ.
The boundary that saves every relationship is ultimately this:
God remains God.
We are not.
When we surrender our identities, our fears, our people-pleasing, our pride, and our relationships to Christ, He teaches us how to love with both compassion and courage.
Grace without truth becomes compromise.
Truth without grace becomes cruelty.
Jesus is both.
That is why He changes everything.
If someone immediately came to mind while reading this, don't keep this message to yourself. You never know who has been praying for an answer that arrives through something you shared.
Because sometimes the holiest word you'll ever speak is "no"—and God uses that one boundary to protect the "yes" that truly matters.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: What "Ask and You Shall Receive" Really Means
paragraphs:
What "Ask and You Shall Receive" Really Means
The Verse Millions Quote—But Few Truly Understand
Somewhere tonight, a tired mother is whispering a prayer through tears.
A father is staring at an unpaid bill.
A young believer is asking God why the healing never came.
A widow is wondering why heaven feels silent.
A struggling Christian is praying the same prayer for the hundredth time.
And in the middle of all that pain, one verse keeps echoing:
"Ask and it will be given to you; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened to you." (Matthew 7:7)
Many have quoted it.
Many have preached it.
Many have misunderstood it.
Because if we're honest, there are prayers we asked for that never happened.
There are doors we knocked on that never opened.
There are answers we sought that never arrived the way we expected.
So was Jesus wrong?
Or have we been hearing His words through the lens of our desires instead of through the heart of the Gospel?
The answer changes everything.
The original Greek text records Jesus saying:
"Aiteite kai dothēsetai hymin; zēteite kai heurēsete; krouete kai anoigēsetai hymin."
The verbs Jesus used are written in a form that implies ongoing action.
A more literal understanding would be:
"Keep asking."
"Keep seeking."
"Keep knocking."
This was never a promise of instant gratification.
It was an invitation into persistent relationship.
Jesus was not teaching a spiritual vending machine.
He was teaching dependence upon the Father.
Yet somewhere along the way, many people began treating prayer as a transaction.
If I ask correctly, God must give.
If I have enough faith, God must answer exactly how I want.
If I say the right words, heaven becomes obligated.
But Scripture never teaches that God serves us.
It teaches that God loves us.
And love does not always give us what we request.
Love gives us what we truly need.
That distinction is the difference between disappointment and discipleship.
When Jesus spoke these words, He was speaking within the larger context of God's fatherhood.
Just a few verses later He says:
"Which of you, if your son asks for bread, will give him a stone?" (Matthew 7:9)
Notice what Jesus is revealing.
The focus is not the request.
The focus is the Father.
The confidence of prayer is not based on getting everything we want.
It is based on knowing who God is.
The Hebrew understanding behind prayer was never primarily about changing God's mind.
It was about aligning the human heart with God's will.
In Hebrew thought, prayer was deeply relational.
The word often associated with prayer is תְּפִלָּה (tefillah), carrying the idea of self-examination, intercession, and communion with God.
Prayer was not merely presenting demands.
Prayer was surrendering the soul.
That changes everything.
Because suddenly the question becomes:
What if the greatest answer to prayer isn't receiving what you asked for?
What if the greatest answer is becoming who God created you to be?
Think about Jesus Himself.
In Gethsemane He prayed:
"Father, if You are willing, remove this cup from Me. Nevertheless, not My will, but Yours be done." (Luke 22:42)
The prayer was sincere.
The request was real.
Yet the answer was no.
Not because the Father didn't love the Son.
But because a greater redemption was unfolding.
Had God answered Jesus' immediate request, humanity would still be lost in sin.
The Cross was born from a prayer that was answered differently than requested.
Let that settle in your heart.
Some of the greatest works of God emerge from prayers that seem unanswered.
The Apostle Paul understood this too.
Three times he pleaded for his thorn in the flesh to be removed.
Three times heaven remained silent.
Then came God's answer:
"My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is made perfect in weakness." (2 Corinthians 12:9)
Paul asked for removal.
God gave grace.
Paul wanted escape.
God offered strength.
Paul sought comfort.
God produced transformation.
The request was denied.
The prayer was answered.
Because God's answers are often deeper than our expectations.
The tragedy is that many people walk away from God when they don't receive exactly what they requested.
But imagine if every prayer was answered exactly as we demanded.
How many disasters would we create?
How many wrong relationships would we force?
How many destructive desires would we pursue?
How many idols would we mistake for blessings?
The Father sees what we cannot.
He sees ten years ahead.
He sees the hidden consequences.
He sees dangers invisible to us.
His wisdom is not limited by our understanding.
That is why Scripture repeatedly links prayer to God's will.
In 1 John 5:14 we read:
"If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us."
Not according to our cravings.
Not according to our timelines.
Not according to our impatience.
According to His will.
And this is where the Gospel transforms the entire conversation.
Because ultimately, "Ask and you shall receive" finds its deepest fulfillment not in earthly blessings but in Jesus Christ Himself.
Humanity's greatest need was never wealth.
Never comfort.
Never success.
Never influence.
It was reconciliation with God.
Our deepest problem was sin.
The Greek word used throughout the New Testament is ἁμαρτία (hamartia), meaning to miss the mark.
We wandered.
We rebelled.
We fell.
We became separated from the holy God who created us.
And yet heaven responded.
Humanity asked for meaning.
God gave Christ.
Humanity asked for hope.
God gave Christ.
Humanity asked for forgiveness.
God gave Christ.
Humanity asked for life.
God gave Christ.
The greatest answer God has ever given is not a thing.
It is a Person.
Jesus Christ.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
And that is why our theme remains:
Because every believer has a scandal.
A secret.
A failure.
A regret.
A chapter they wish they could erase.
Yet Jesus specializes in rewriting stories.
Peter denied Him.
David committed adultery.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Samaritan woman carried shame.
The thief on the cross wasted his life.
Yet grace had the final word.
The Cross is the ultimate proof that God can transform the worst scandal into the greatest testimony.
Maybe you've been asking God for answers.
Maybe you've been knocking on a closed door.
Maybe you've been seeking clarity through confusion.
Do not mistake delay for abandonment.
Do not mistake silence for absence.
Do not mistake God's wisdom for rejection.
The same Savior who carried the Cross is carrying you.
The same Lord who conquered death is still writing stories.
The same grace that transformed sinners into saints is available today.
And perhaps the greatest prayer you can pray right now is not:
"Lord, give me what I want."
But:
"Lord, give me more of You."
Because when you receive Christ, you receive what your soul was actually searching for all along.
If this message stirred your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
What prayer are you still trusting God with?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
Because sometimes the answer to prayer isn't the door opening.
Sometimes it's discovering that Jesus was standing beside you while you were knocking.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Lesson I Learned From Jacob’s Unfair Employer
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From Jacob’s Unfair Employer
When the Person Who Kept Cheating You Became the Unexpected Tool God Used to Build You
Some wounds do not come from enemies.
They come from people who smile at you.
People who promise one thing and deliver another.
People who keep moving the finish line after you've already exhausted yourself trying to reach it.
If you've ever worked hard only to watch someone else take the credit...
If you've ever remained loyal while someone manipulated your trust...
If you've ever wondered why God allowed dishonest people to have power over your life...
Then the story of Jacob and his unfair employer may hit closer to home than you expect.
Because this is not merely an ancient story about sheep, wages, and family disputes.
It is a story about us.
It is a story about every believer who has cried silently, "Lord, why do You keep allowing this?"
And it is one of the clearest demonstrations that even when people rewrite the rules against you, God is still writing the ending.
The story unfolds in Genesis 29–31 when Jacob fled from his brother Esau and arrived in the land of his relatives. There he met a man named Laban, his uncle.
At first, Laban appeared generous.
Welcoming.
Helpful.
Trustworthy.
But appearances can be dangerously misleading.
Jacob fell deeply in love with Rachel and agreed to work seven years to marry her.
Scripture says:
"So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her." (Genesis 29:20)
Seven years.
Not seven weeks.
Not seven months.
Seven years.
Yet on the wedding night, Laban deceived Jacob and gave him Leah instead.
The irony is impossible to miss.
Years earlier, Jacob himself had deceived his father Isaac.
Now deception had come back to meet him.
Not as punishment alone.
But as a lesson.
A refining fire.
A mirror.
A path toward transformation.
Laban then required Jacob to work another seven years for Rachel.
Fourteen years.
Imagine the disappointment.
Imagine the betrayal.
Imagine realizing the person you trusted most had deliberately manipulated your future.
Yet Jacob stayed.
Not because Laban deserved loyalty.
But because God was still working.
Many believers misunderstand what God is doing when unfair people enter their story.
We assume God has abandoned us.
Jacob's story reveals the opposite.
Sometimes God allows difficult people because He is shaping something inside us that comfort never could.
Years later Jacob would describe his experience this way:
"These twenty years have I been with thee... and thou hast changed my wages ten times." (Genesis 31:41)
Ten times.
Laban repeatedly altered the agreement whenever it benefited him.
Every time Jacob adapted, Laban changed the rules again.
Many readers know exactly what that feels like.
The promotion that never came.
The business partner who lied.
The family member who manipulated.
The boss who exploited.
The ministry leader who used your gifts but never valued your heart.
You worked faithfully.
They moved the goalposts.
You stayed honest.
They stayed dishonest.
You prayed.
Nothing seemed to change.
But hidden beneath the frustration was a reality Jacob could not yet see.
God was prospering him anyway.
One of the most beautiful statements in the entire narrative comes from Genesis 31:42:
"God hath seen mine affliction and the labor of my hands."
Pause there for a moment.
God saw it.
Every unfair paycheck.
Every broken promise.
Every sleepless night.
Every tear.
Every disappointment.
God saw it all.
The Hebrew word translated "seen" carries the idea of attentive observation. God was not casually aware of Jacob's suffering.
He was intimately watching.
Closely involved.
Deeply concerned.
The same God who saw Jacob sees you.
The same God who watched every injustice against Jacob watches every injustice against His children today.
Nothing escapes His notice.
Nothing.
When Jacob finally confronted Laban, he was no longer the manipulative young man who had arrived decades earlier.
The deceiver had become dependent upon God.
The schemer had become a worshiper.
The self-reliant man had learned surrender.
That transformation may have been God's greatest blessing of all.
The very person who seemed to be blocking Jacob's future became one of God's instruments for shaping Jacob's character.
The lesson becomes even more powerful when viewed through the lens of the Gospel.
The New Testament reveals a truth that echoes throughout Scripture.
God specializes in turning human evil into redemptive good.
The greatest example is Jesus Christ Himself.
Humanity's worst scandal became Heaven's greatest act of grace.
Religious leaders plotted.
False witnesses lied.
Political leaders compromised.
Crowds demanded crucifixion.
The Son of God was rejected by the very people He came to save.
From a human perspective, it looked like evil had won.
But three days later everything changed.
The cross was never God's defeat.
It was God's plan.
The Greek words Jesus cried from the cross in John 19:30 were:
"Τετέλεσται" (Tetelestai).
"It is finished."
Not defeated.
Finished.
Completed.
Accomplished.
The debt of sin paid in full.
The work of redemption secured forever.
What looked like the ultimate injustice became the ultimate victory.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
This is why our theme remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Perhaps that is why Jacob's story resonates so deeply.
Many of us are waiting for God to remove the difficult person.
Meanwhile God may be using that very situation to build a deeper faith, stronger character, greater dependence, and a testimony that will one day encourage countless others.
Jacob eventually left Laban's household blessed beyond anything he could have imagined.
Not because Laban became fair.
He never truly did.
Not because circumstances became perfect.
They didn't.
But because God's faithfulness proved greater than human dishonesty.
That same promise remains true today.
If someone has mistreated you, do not let bitterness become your identity.
If someone has betrayed you, do not let resentment write your future.
If someone keeps changing the rules, remember that they do not control your destiny.
God does.
The God of Abraham.
The God of Isaac.
The God of Jacob.
The God who sees.
The God who remembers.
The God who redeems.
The God who turns scandals into testimonies.
The God who takes broken chapters and writes beautiful endings.
In Aramaic, one of the most precious names for God is "Abba" (ܐܒܐ).
Father.
Not a distant ruler.
Not a detached observer.
Father.
The Father who watched over Jacob.
The Father who sent His Son.
The Father who still walks beside His children through every disappointment, injustice, betrayal, and unanswered question.
And maybe that is exactly what someone reading this needed to hear today.
The unfair employer does not get the final word.
The manipulator does not get the final word.
The betrayer does not get the final word.
Your failures do not get the final word.
Your past does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
And when Jesus speaks, redemption always has the final chapter.
If this message strengthened your faith, don't let it stop with you.
One day you may discover that the person who wounded you was never holding back your destiny—God was quietly building it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Psalm 37:4 Is Not a Blank Check from God
paragraphs:
Psalm 37:4 Is Not a Blank Check from God
The Verse Most Christians Misunderstand—and the Beautiful Truth Hidden Inside It
What if one of the most quoted promises in the Bible is also one of the most misunderstood?
What if the reason some believers feel disappointed with God is because they have spent years expecting Psalm 37:4 to mean something David never intended it to mean?
Many have memorized it.
Many have highlighted it.
Many have claimed it.
Yet few have slowed down long enough to truly understand it.
"Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart." (Psalm 37:4)
At first glance, it almost sounds like a divine guarantee that God will give us whatever we want.
A better job.
A bigger house.
A relationship.
Financial success.
Healing.
Recognition.
The fulfillment of every dream.
But is that really what David was saying?
Or is there something much deeper hidden beneath the surface?
Something so beautiful that once you see it, you can never read this verse the same way again.
Because Psalm 37:4 is not primarily about getting what you want.
It is about becoming someone whose greatest desire is God Himself.
And that changes everything.
The Hebrew text reads:
וְהִתְעַנַּג עַל־יְהוָה וְיִתֶּן־לְךָ מִשְׁאֲלֹת לִבֶּךָ
Ve-hit'anag al-YHWH ve-yitten lekha mish'alot libbekha.
The word translated "delight" is hit'anag (הִתְעַנַּג).
It means to take exquisite pleasure in, to find deep joy in, to be softened by, to enjoy fully.
David is not talking about a casual acknowledgment of God.
He is describing a heart that treasures God above everything else.
A heart that finds satisfaction in God's presence.
A heart that loves God more than His gifts.
This is why context matters.
Psalm 37 was written during a time when David observed wicked people prospering while righteous people suffered.
Sound familiar?
Even today we watch corrupt people rise.
Dishonest people succeed.
Ungodly people gain influence.
Meanwhile faithful believers often wonder why obedience seems harder than compromise.
David addresses that frustration directly.
Before verse 4 he says:
"Fret not yourself because of evildoers."
In Hebrew, the word translated "fret" carries the idea of burning with anger, anxiety, envy, and inner agitation.
David is essentially saying:
Stop comparing.
Stop obsessing over what others have.
Stop measuring God's goodness by somebody else's success.
Instead, delight yourself in the Lord.
Find your joy in Him.
Trust Him.
Rest in Him.
Wait for Him.
And then comes the promise.
"He will give you the desires of your heart."
Notice what David does not say.
He does not say God grants every wish.
He does not promise instant prosperity.
He does not teach a biblical version of manifestation.
Rather, the promise is connected to delight.
The person who truly delights in God experiences something supernatural.
God begins transforming their desires.
The heart changes.
The priorities change.
The cravings change.
The ambitions change.
The deepest longing becomes aligned with God's will.
The more we love Christ, the more we begin wanting what Christ wants.
This truth echoes throughout Scripture.
Jesus said:
"But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you." (Matthew 6:33)
The Greek word for seek is ζητεῖτε (zēteite), meaning to pursue passionately, continually, and intentionally.
Jesus was not teaching people to chase blessings.
He was teaching them to chase God.
When God becomes the treasure, everything else finds its proper place.
That is exactly what David was teaching centuries earlier.
The greatest miracle in Psalm 37:4 is not that God gives us our desires.
The greatest miracle is that He changes our desires.
Many people come to God wanting His hand.
Few come wanting His heart.
Yet throughout Scripture, God repeatedly invites us beyond transactions and into relationship.
Think about the prodigal son.
He wanted the inheritance.
The father wanted the son.
One desired gifts.
The other desired relationship.
How many of us have approached God the same way?
Praying only when we need something.
Seeking Him only during crises.
Measuring His faithfulness by whether He fulfills our plans.
Then life falls apart.
The promotion never comes.
The relationship ends.
The diagnosis arrives.
The prayer seems unanswered.
And suddenly we wonder where God is.
But sometimes the unanswered prayer is not God's absence.
Sometimes it is God's mercy.
Because if God gave us everything we wanted before transforming our hearts, many of us would wander further away from Him.
The greatest evidence of God's love is not that He gives us everything we ask for.
It is that He refuses to let us settle for anything less than Himself.
This becomes even clearer when we look at Jesus.
In the Garden of Gethsemane, facing the cross, He prayed:
"Not my will, but yours be done."
The Greek reads:
οὐ τὸ θέλημά μου ἀλλὰ τὸ σὸν γενέσθω
Ou to thelēma mou alla to son genesthō.
This is the ultimate picture of delighting in God.
Jesus treasured the Father's will above His own comfort.
And because He surrendered, the greatest scandal in human history became the greatest story of grace ever told.
A bloody cross became a symbol of redemption.
A criminal's execution became humanity's salvation.
A sealed tomb became the doorway to eternal life.
This is the Gospel.
This is our story.
This is why we say:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He rewrites failures.
He rewrites addictions.
He rewrites betrayals.
He rewrites shame.
He rewrites broken marriages.
He rewrites prodigals.
He rewrites scars.
He rewrites sinners.
And perhaps today He wants to rewrite your understanding of Psalm 37:4.
Maybe the verse was never about getting everything you wanted.
Maybe it was always about discovering the One your soul was truly searching for.
The truth is that every human heart carries a longing nothing in this world can satisfy.
Money cannot satisfy it.
Success cannot satisfy it.
Relationships cannot satisfy it.
Achievements cannot satisfy it.
Only Christ can.
As Augustine famously wrote, "Our hearts are restless until they rest in You."
David understood that truth.
Paul understood that truth.
Jesus embodied that truth.
And the invitation remains the same today.
Delight yourself in the Lord.
Not because He is useful.
Not because He can make your life easier.
Not because He can give you what you want.
But because He is worthy.
Because He is beautiful.
Because He is holy.
Because He is Savior.
Because He is King.
Because He first loved you.
If this message stirred something inside your heart, do not keep scrolling.
Sit with it.
Pray through it.
Ask God to reveal where your desires may have drifted from Him.
It may be the encouragement their soul desperately needs.
What desire has God been transforming in your life lately?
Your testimony may encourage someone else who is fighting a battle you cannot see.
Your support helps us proclaim the Gospel, create biblical resources, and reach people who desperately need hope in Christ.
One simple way to glorify God is by helping spread His truth.
One day you may realize that the greatest prayer God ever answered was the one He lovingly said "no" to because He was leading you to something infinitely better—Himself.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why the Sons of Sceva Thought Power Could Be Borrowed
paragraphs:
Why the Sons of Sceva Thought Power Could Be Borrowed
They Used the Name of Jesus Like a Tool… Until the Demons Answered Back
Some stories in Scripture are so shocking that they feel almost uncomfortable to read.
This is one of them.
Because hidden inside a strange encounter with demons, public humiliation, and seven terrified brothers running naked through the streets is a warning that still confronts the modern Church.
A warning about borrowed faith.
Borrowed authority.
Borrowed Christianity.
And the devastating difference between knowing about Jesus and actually belonging to Him.

The story unfolds in Ephesus, a city overflowing with spiritual confusion. Magic was normal. Occult practices were common. People chased power through rituals, incantations, secret names, and mystical formulas. In a culture obsessed with supernatural control, many believed power could be accessed if you simply learned the right words.
Then Jesus entered the picture.
Through the preaching of Paul, lives were transformed. Miracles occurred. Demonic oppression was broken. The Gospel spread with undeniable force.
And people noticed.
Especially the sons of a Jewish chief priest named Sceva.
Luke records:
“Then certain of the vagabond Jews, exorcists, took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, ‘We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth.’” (Acts 19:13)
The Greek text uses the phrase:

ὁρκίζω ὑμᾶς τὸν Ἰησοῦν
(horkizō hymas ton Iēsoun)
Literally:
“I command you under oath by Jesus.”
Notice something immediately.
They were not preaching Jesus.
They were not following Jesus.
They were not surrendering to Jesus.
They were attempting to use Jesus.
To them, the name of Christ was not a Savior to worship.
It was a formula to exploit.
A spiritual tool.
A shortcut to power.
A religious technique.
And before we judge them too quickly, we should ask ourselves an uncomfortable question.
How many people today approach Jesus the same way?
Some want His blessings without repentance.
His protection without obedience.
His promises without discipleship.
His power without surrender.
His crown without His cross.
The sons of Sceva believed authority could be borrowed because they misunderstood where spiritual authority originates.
In Scripture, authority is never detached from relationship.
Never.
When Jesus sent out His disciples, authority flowed from union with Him.
When the apostles cast out demons, authority flowed from submission to Him.
When believers prayed, authority flowed from belonging to Him.
The Hebrew worldview never separated power from covenant relationship.
Throughout the Old Testament, God's people understood this deeply.
The Hebrew word for knowing someone is יָדַע (yada').
It means far more than intellectual awareness.
It speaks of intimacy.
Relationship.
Personal connection.
Covenant closeness.
The sons of Sceva knew the name.
But they did not know the Person.
And demons know the difference.
Then comes one of the most terrifying moments in the entire New Testament.
Acts 19:15 records:
“And the evil spirit answered and said, ‘Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye?’”
The Greek text is astonishing.
Τὸν Ἰησοῦν γινώσκω, καὶ τὸν Παῦλον ἐπίσταμαι· ὑμεῖς δὲ τίνες ἐστέ;
(Ton Iēsoun ginōskō, kai ton Paulon epistamai; hymeis de tines este?)
“Jesus I know.
Paul I recognize.
But who are you?”
The demon acknowledges Jesus.
The demon recognizes Paul.
But the seven men possess no spiritual identity.
No spiritual authority.
No covenant standing.
No relationship with Christ.
They attempted to wield a sword they had never been given.
The result was catastrophic.
Scripture says:
“And the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, and overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.” (Acts 19:16)
Naked.
Humiliated.
Exposed.
Broken.
Everything they thought they possessed vanished in a single moment.
And suddenly the story becomes deeply personal.
Because exposure is often God's mercy.
Many people spend years constructing religious appearances.
Church attendance.
Christian vocabulary.
Social media faith.
Religious routines.
Yet beneath the surface there is no genuine surrender.
No repentance.
No intimacy with Christ.
No transformed heart.
Then life arrives.
A diagnosis.
A betrayal.
A crisis.
A tragedy.
A temptation.
A loss.
And what was merely borrowed cannot survive the storm.
Only what is genuinely rooted in Christ remains.
The sons of Sceva wanted power.
God wanted relationship.
That is still the great divide today.
Jesus never invited people into a system of religious performance.
He invited them into Himself.
The Greek word often translated “abide” is:
μένω (menō)
Meaning:
“To remain.”
“To dwell.”
“To stay connected.”
Jesus said:
“Abide in me, and I in you.” (John 15:4)
Not visit.
Not borrow.
Not imitate.
Abide.
Remain.
Live in Him.
Everything changes when authority flows from intimacy rather than imitation.
The aftermath of the sons of Sceva's failure reveals something extraordinary.
Fear spread throughout Ephesus.
People realized Jesus was not a magical formula.
He was Lord.
Acts 19:17 says:
“And the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified.”
Then something remarkable happened.
People publicly confessed sin.
They abandoned occult practices.
They burned their expensive magic books.
Repentance swept through the city.
The scandal became a doorway to grace.
And isn't that exactly what Jesus does?
Again and again throughout Scripture.
A murderer named Moses becomes a deliverer.
An adulterer named David becomes a man after God's own heart.
A denier named Peter becomes a pillar of the Church.
A persecutor named Saul becomes the Apostle Paul.
And seven humiliated brothers become a warning that still points people toward genuine faith two thousand years later.
Because Jesus specializes in rewriting stories.
The enemy writes shame.
Jesus writes redemption.
The enemy writes failure.
Jesus writes restoration.
The enemy writes condemnation.
Jesus writes grace.
The enemy writes endings.
Jesus writes new beginnings.
That is why the Gospel remains the greatest story ever told.
Not because people are good.
But because Christ is.
Not because sinners are strong.
But because grace is stronger.
Not because failures disappear.
But because Jesus redeems them.
Maybe as you read this, you recognize something of yourself in the sons of Sceva.
Maybe you've been borrowing someone else's faith.
A spouse's faith.
A parent's faith.
A pastor's faith.
A church's faith.
Maybe you've known about Jesus for years without truly knowing Him.
Today can change that.
The Gospel is not an invitation to perform.
It is an invitation to surrender.
The Son of God entered human history, lived the sinless life we could never live, died for our sins upon the cross, and rose again victorious over death.
The power of Christ was never meant to be borrowed.
It was meant to transform.
And that transformation begins when a sinner stops reaching for power and starts reaching for Jesus.
Be honest. This may have hit harder than you expected.
Someone you know is trying to survive on borrowed faith right now.

If this ministry has encouraged you, strengthened your faith, or helped you understand Scripture more clearly, supporting it is one practical way to participate in spreading the Gospel and glorifying God through the stewardship of resources He has entrusted to us.
Because one day every borrowed thing will be stripped away, and only what was built through a real relationship with Jesus Christ will remain.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Was Eve Created From a Rib?
paragraphs:
Why Was Eve Created From a Rib?
The Forgotten Love Story Hidden in Genesis That Explains Why Jesus Came for You
Most people think the story begins with a rib.
It doesn't.
It begins with a loneliness that existed in a perfect world.
Think about that.

Before sin entered creation...
Before death...
Before sickness...
Before betrayal...
Before shame...
Something was not good.
The first "not good" in the Bible appears in Genesis 2:18.
The Hebrew text says:
"לֹא־טוֹב הֱיוֹת הָאָדָם לְבַדּוֹ"
Lo tov heyot ha'adam levado.
"It is not good that the man should be alone."
This statement is shocking because everything before this moment had been declared good by God.
The light was good.
The earth was good.
The seas were good.
The animals were good.
Creation was good.
Yet God looked at Adam standing in paradise and said something was still missing.
Not because Adam was defective.
Not because God had forgotten something.
But because God was about to reveal a mystery that would eventually point all the way to Jesus Christ.
Many people ask why Eve was created from a rib.
Why not from dust like Adam?
Why not from the ground?
Why not from another act of creation?
The answer is far more beautiful than most people realize.
Genesis 2:21 says:
"So the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon the man, and while he slept took one of his ribs and closed up its place with flesh."
The Hebrew word translated "rib" is:
"צֵלָע"
Tzela.
Interestingly, this word can mean more than a simple rib bone.
Throughout the Old Testament, tzela is often translated as "side."
Not merely a small bone.
A side.
A portion taken from beside.
This changes the entire picture.
God was not creating Eve as a lesser being.
He was not creating her beneath Adam.
He was not creating her from Adam's foot to be trampled.
Nor from his head to rule over him.
He created her from his side.
Close to his heart.
Beside him.
Equal in worth.
Equal in humanity.
Different in role.
But equal in dignity.
When Adam first sees Eve, the Bible records one of the first poems in human history.
Genesis 2:23 says:
"זֹאת הַפַּעַם עֶצֶם מֵעֲצָמַי וּבָשָׂר מִבְּשָׂרִי"
Zot hapa'am etzem me'atzamai uvasar mib'sari.
"This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh."
Adam is overwhelmed.
This is not the language of ownership.
This is the language of recognition.
For the first time, Adam sees someone who shares his nature.
Someone who understands him.
Someone who reflects God's design alongside him.
Someone who belongs not beneath him but beside him.
The creation of Eve is not merely about marriage.
It is about relationship.
And relationship is at the center of God's heart.
Because humanity was never created merely to exist.
We were created for communion.
With God.
With one another.
With love.
But then the scandal happened.
The serpent entered the garden.
Temptation whispered.
Trust shattered.
Sin arrived.
The relationship that began at Adam's side became fractured by rebellion.
And the damage spread everywhere.
Marriage suffered.
Families suffered.
Humanity suffered.
Creation suffered.
Every divorce.
Every betrayal.
Every broken promise.
Every lonely night.
Every wounded heart.
Every graveyard.
Every tear.
Can be traced back to that moment when humanity chose independence from God.
Yet even then, God was already writing a better ending.
Because hidden inside Eve's creation is a prophecy.
A shadow.
A picture of another man who would one day sleep.
Another side that would be opened.
Another bride that would emerge.
Thousands of years later Jesus Christ hung upon a cross.
After His death, John records a remarkable detail.
John 19:34 says:
"One of the soldiers pierced His side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water."
The Greek word used is:
"πλευρά"
Pleurá.
It means side.
The same imagery echoes Genesis.
Adam slept.
His side was opened.
A bride emerged.
Christ slept in death.
His side was opened.
And from His sacrifice emerged His bride—the Church.
This is why Paul writes in Ephesians 5:25:
Marriage was never merely about marriage.
It was always pointing toward Jesus.
The first wedding pointed toward the ultimate Bridegroom.
The first bride pointed toward the redeemed people of God.
The rib was never just a rib.
It was a signpost.
A glimpse of redemption.
A whisper of the Gospel before humanity even fell.
This is why the Bible is unlike any other book ever written.
Genesis begins with a bride coming from the side of a man.
Revelation ends with a bride united forever to the Lamb.
The story starts in a garden.
The story ends in a city.
The story starts with innocence.
The story ends with redemption.
And at the center stands Jesus Christ.
The One who rewrites everything.
Maybe that is why this story hits so deeply.
Because most of us know what it feels like to be broken.
We know loneliness.
We know rejection.
We know regret.
Some people carry secret sins they hope nobody discovers.
Others carry wounds inflicted by people they trusted.
Some feel like their failures define them.
Some feel too damaged for God to use.
Some have lived through scandals they never thought they would survive.
Yet the Gospel announces something astonishing.
Jesus specializes in rewriting stories.
The woman caught in adultery became a testimony of mercy.
Peter's denial became a platform for leadership.
Paul's persecution became a ministry of grace.
The thief on the cross became a citizen of paradise.
And your story can become another chapter of redemption.
The enemy wants you to believe your failure is the final sentence.
Jesus says it is only a comma.
The enemy says your scandal defines you.
Jesus says His grace is greater.
The enemy points to your past.
Jesus points to His cross.
The enemy says you are too far gone.
Jesus says, "Come to Me."
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that good people become slightly better.
But that dead people become alive.
Not that broken people hide their scars.
But that Christ transforms scars into testimonies.
Not that sinners save themselves.
But that Jesus saves sinners.
And perhaps that is the greatest lesson hidden inside Eve's creation.
God did not create humanity for isolation.
He created us for relationship.
Ultimately relationship with Him.
The deepest loneliness in the human heart is not solved by success.
Not by money.
Not by popularity.
Not by achievement.
It is solved only through reconciliation with the God who made us.
That reconciliation came through Jesus Christ.
The second Adam.
The perfect Bridegroom.
The Savior who opened His side so His bride could live.
Sit with it.
Pray about it.
Ask yourself whether you have truly surrendered your life to Christ.
Or simply share the testimony God is writing in your life.
Your story may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
Because when biblical truth changes a life, sharing it becomes ministry.
And when grace rewrites a story, that story becomes a testimony.
One opened side in Eden pointed to another opened side at Calvary—and both were telling the same love story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: What Women Secretly Need in a Relationship
paragraphs:
What Women Secretly Need in a Relationship
The Need Most People Never Talk About—And Why It Changes Everything
There is a question many men spend years trying to answer and many women spend years trying to explain:
"What do women really need in a relationship?"
Some think the answer is romance.
Others think it is security.
Some believe it is attention, communication, affection, provision, or commitment.
Those things matter.
But beneath all of them is something deeper.
Something that reaches beyond psychology, culture, personality tests, relationship advice, and social media opinions.
It is the longing to be deeply known and deeply valued.
Not used.
Not tolerated.
Not merely desired.
Not treated as an accessory to someone else's dreams.
But truly seen.
And if we are honest, this is not only what women need.
It is what every human heart has been searching for since Eden.
The story begins in Genesis when God created humanity in His image.
The Hebrew text says:

"וַיִּבְרָא אֱלֹהִים אֶת־הָאָדָם בְּצַלְמוֹ"
Vayyivra Elohim et-ha'adam b'tzalmo.
"So God created mankind in His own image." (Genesis 1:27)
Before there was romance, there was dignity.
Before there was marriage, there was identity.
Before there was attraction, there was divine value.
The first truth every relationship must understand is this:
A woman's deepest worth was never meant to come from a man.
It comes from God.
Many relationships fail because they ask a human being to carry a burden only God can bear.
No husband can become a savior.
No boyfriend can become a source of ultimate identity.
No romance can heal a soul separated from its Creator.
Only Jesus Christ can do that.
Yet Scripture reveals something beautiful.
While no person can replace God, God designed relationships to reflect His love.
This is why the Apostle Paul wrote:

"Ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας"
Agapate tas gynaikas.
"Husbands, love your wives..." (Ephesians 5:25)
The Greek word used here is ἀγαπάω (agapaō).
This is not a feeling-driven love.
It is sacrificial love.
Covenant love.
A love that gives instead of taking.
A love that serves instead of demanding.
A love that remains faithful when emotions fluctuate.
Many women spend years longing for this kind of love without being able to fully describe it.
Not perfection.
Not wealth.
Not endless compliments.
But security in knowing that someone's commitment is stronger than circumstances.
The world often teaches men to pursue power.
Jesus taught men to pursue sacrificial love.
The world says:
"Find someone who makes you happy."
Jesus says:
"Love as I have loved you."
The difference changes everything.
Many women quietly carry burdens few people ever notice.
The pressure to be enough.
Beautiful enough.
Successful enough.
Patient enough.
Strong enough.
Interesting enough.
Spiritual enough.
Behind confident smiles can exist silent fears.
"What if I disappoint everyone?"
"What if I am not enough?"
"What if I am only loved when I perform well?"
These fears are not exclusive to women, but countless women know exactly what they feel like.
This is why the Gospel is so revolutionary.
The Gospel declares that God's love was never earned.
Romans 5:8 tells us:
"But God demonstrates His own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
Notice the timing.
Not after we improved.
Not after we fixed ourselves.
Not after we became worthy.
Christ moved toward us while we were still broken.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
And it is the heartbeat of every healthy relationship.
The need to be loved not merely at our best but also in our weakness.
Not because we deserve it.
But because grace chooses to stay.
One of the greatest relationship mistakes people make is assuming that understanding comes automatically.
It does not.
People can share a home and still feel alone.
They can share a bed and still feel unseen.
They can exchange words every day and still never feel understood.
The book of James teaches believers to be "quick to listen, slow to speak."
Listening is one of the most overlooked forms of love.
Many women do not simply want solutions.
They want presence.
They want to know their voice matters.
They want to know someone cares enough to understand before responding.
That desire reflects something profoundly biblical.
Because throughout Scripture, God listens.
He hears.
He knows.
He responds.
Psalm 34:17 says:
"The righteous cry out, and the LORD hears them."
Imagine the comfort of being heard by the Creator of the universe.
Then imagine reflecting that same care within a relationship.
The truth is that every healthy relationship becomes stronger when both people feel safe enough to be honest.
Real intimacy grows where masks die.
Where pretending ends.
Where truth is welcomed.
Where grace is stronger than shame.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Because beneath relationship struggles often lies something much older.
A wound.
A disappointment.
A betrayal.
A rejection.
A moment that convinced someone they were not worthy of love.
Many women carry scars nobody can see.
Many men do too.
And no human relationship can completely heal those wounds.
But Jesus can enter them.
The prophet Isaiah foretold Him this way:
"He was pierced for our transgressions."
The Savior who carries scars understands ours.
The Savior who was rejected understands rejection.
The Savior who was betrayed understands betrayal.
The Savior who suffered abandonment understands loneliness.
This is why Christianity is not merely advice.
It is rescue.
The Gospel does not tell wounded people to heal themselves.
It introduces them to the One who heals.
And perhaps this is the greatest secret of all:
The deepest need in every relationship is not finding the perfect person.
It is knowing the perfect Savior.
Because when Christ becomes the center, love changes.
Pride weakens.
Forgiveness grows.
Patience deepens.
Grace multiplies.
Relationships become less about control and more about service.
Less about demanding and more about giving.
Less about self-glory and more about God's glory.
The most beautiful love story in human history was not between a man and a woman.
It was between a holy God and sinful humanity.
The scandal was our rebellion.
The grace was His cross.
The tragedy was our guilt.
The triumph was His resurrection.
The distance was enormous.
Yet Jesus crossed it.
That is why every Christian relationship ultimately points beyond itself.
Marriage points to Christ.
Love points to Christ.
Faithfulness points to Christ.
Grace points to Christ.
Everything points to Christ.
Maybe you came searching for relationship advice.
Maybe you hoped to finally understand women.
Maybe you hoped someone would explain what makes relationships work.
The answer is deeper than techniques and strategies.
People flourish where they are valued.
They heal where grace is present.
They grow where truth and love walk together.
And every one of those realities finds its source in Jesus Christ.
If this article stirred your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
What is one way Jesus has changed your understanding of love?
Your testimony may be exactly what someone else needs to hear.
Because someone reading your words may find hope through your testimony.
And remember this:
The love you have been searching for was searching for you first.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Before You Break Up… Read This First. The Conversation That Could Save More Than Your Relationship.
paragraphs:
Before You Break Up… Read This First. The Conversation That Could Save More Than Your Relationship.
Sometimes the relationship isn't dying because love disappeared. Sometimes it's dying because two wounded hearts forgot what love was meant to become. Before you walk away, let God speak before your emotions make a permanent decision.
There comes a moment in almost every relationship when silence becomes louder than words.
The text messages become shorter.
The laughter slowly disappears.
The little annoyances suddenly become unbearable.
You begin imagining life without them... not because you truly want it, but because you're exhausted.
