Then comes the dangerous sentence:
"Maybe we're just not meant for each other."
Before you say those words...
Before you block the number...
Before you remove every photo...
Before you let pride convince you that walking away is strength...
Pause.
Not because every relationship should survive.
But because every decision deserves to stand before God before it stands before your emotions.
We live in a culture that celebrates leaving faster than healing.
"Choose yourself."
"Protect your peace."
"If it hurts, leave."
Sometimes those statements are wise.
Sometimes they are necessary.

God never commands anyone to remain in abuse, manipulation, violence, or persistent unrepentant evil. Scripture values justice, truth, and the dignity of every person made in God's image. If you are in danger, seek safety and wise, godly help immediately.
But many relationships aren't ending because of abuse.
They're ending because two imperfect sinners expected perfection from one another.
The Bible never promised that love would remove conflict.
It teaches us something much deeper.
Paul writes:

The Greek word translated "patient" is μακροθυμεῖ (makrothymei)—literally, "to be long-tempered." It describes someone who does not give up quickly when wronged. Biblical love is not merely intense emotion; it is a Spirit-shaped commitment that refuses to let irritation become the master.

Likewise, "bears all things" comes from the Greek στέγει (stegēi), carrying the sense of covering, supporting, and enduring. Paul is not calling believers to ignore sin or excuse abuse. Rather, he describes love that perseveres through ordinary weaknesses while still pursuing truth and holiness.
That kind of love isn't natural.
It's supernatural.
Most breakups don't begin with betrayal.
They begin with tiny moments left unresolved.
An apology never spoken.
A hurt never confessed.
A misunderstanding never clarified.
Pride quietly replaces humility.
Assumptions replace conversations.
Distance replaces intimacy.
Eventually strangers begin living inside the same relationship.
Then someone says...
"We just fell out of love."
Did you?
Or did you simply stop choosing love?
The Scriptures repeatedly remind us that the human heart is not always a trustworthy guide.
Jeremiah 17:9 says,
"The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?"
The Hebrew word עָקֹב ('aqov) means crooked, deceptive, or insidious. Jeremiah is not saying emotions are worthless. He is warning us not to enthrone them above God's wisdom.
Our emotions matter.
But they make terrible masters.
Jesus never built disciples by asking them to follow their feelings.
He called them to follow Him.
Sometimes the greatest act of love is not finding the perfect person.
It's allowing Christ to transform the imperfect person staring back at you in the mirror.
Marriage and courtship expose what comfort often conceals.
Selfishness.
Fear.
Control.
Unforgiveness.
Insecurity.
None of those surprises God.
The Gospel begins with an uncomfortable truth:
Every one of us has failed to love perfectly.
"For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God." (Romans 3:23)
That includes you.
That includes your boyfriend.
That includes your girlfriend.
That includes your spouse.
That includes the person you are considering leaving.
This does not excuse sinful behavior.
It explains why every relationship desperately needs grace.
Grace does not deny truth.
Grace meets truth with redemption.
Look at Peter.
He denied Jesus three times.
If anyone deserved to be abandoned forever, it was Peter.
Instead...
Jesus prepared breakfast.
Asked three restorative questions.
Restored him publicly.
Commissioned him again.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
That does not mean every broken relationship will be restored.
Some relationships end because repentance never comes.
Some end because trust has been destroyed through persistent, unrepentant sin.
Some end because remaining together would oppose God's design for holiness, safety, and truth.

Reconciliation requires repentance, honesty, forgiveness where possible, and rebuilding trust over time. Forgiveness is commanded of believers, but reconciliation is not always possible or wise without genuine repentance and changed conduct.
Still...
Before you end something...
Ask yourself difficult questions.
Have I truly forgiven as Christ forgave me?
Have I communicated honestly instead of expecting mind-reading?
Have I prayed more than I complained?
Have I invited mature, biblically faithful counsel instead of only listening to people who simply agree with me?
Am I reacting from wounded pride or walking in God's wisdom?
Am I seeking God's glory or merely my own comfort?
Those questions are not meant to trap you.
They are meant to free you.
Jesus said,
"If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me." (Luke 9:23)

The Greek phrase ἀπαρνησάσθω ἑαυτόν (aparnēsasthō heauton) means "let him deny himself." It is not self-hatred. It is surrender. Following Christ means placing His will above our impulses, even when doing so is costly.
Imagine if every disagreement became an opportunity to resemble Christ a little more.
Imagine apologizing before winning.
Listening before defending.
Praying before speaking.
Choosing humility before revenge.
The greatest miracle may not be finding someone who never disappoints you.
It may be becoming someone who reflects Jesus when disappointment comes.
The cross reminds us that God's answer to humanity's greatest scandal was not abandonment.
It was sacrificial love.
"But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us." (Romans 5:8)
Every Christian relationship should point beyond itself.
Beyond romance.
Beyond compatibility.
Beyond personality.
Toward Christ.
If your relationship glorifies Jesus, people should see more forgiveness than bitterness, more repentance than pride, more truth than manipulation, and more grace than performance.
Perhaps today you are moments away from ending everything.
Perhaps ending the relationship is, after prayer and wise counsel, the right decision because righteousness, safety, or biblical faithfulness require it.
Or perhaps what truly needs to end is not the relationship...
but the pride.
The resentment.
The silence.
The unforgiveness.
The hidden sin.
Only God knows.
So before you break up...
kneel first.
Ask the Lord to search your heart.
As Psalm 139:23–24 prays:
"Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts! And see if there is any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting!"
The Hebrew word לֵבָב (levav), translated "heart," speaks of the inner person—the mind, will, and affections. Invite God to examine every hidden motive before making a life-changing decision.
If this message confronted something you've been avoiding, don't keep it to yourself. Someone you know may be standing on the edge of a decision they can never take back.
It's one practical way to participate in spreading the Gospel and strengthening believers around the world.
One surrendered heart can rewrite generations.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Is Sexting a Sin? The Hidden Conversation That Is Quietly Rewriting Souls Before It Rewrites Lives
paragraphs:
Is Sexting a Sin? The Hidden Conversation That Is Quietly Rewriting Souls Before It Rewrites Lives
It Begins With One Photo. One Message. One Secret. But Long Before Anyone Else Sees It, Heaven Already Knows.
It never starts with the intention of destroying a life.
It begins with affection.
With loneliness.
With curiosity.
With someone saying, "Trust me."
With someone whispering, "It's just between us."
With a late-night notification.
With a heart racing faster than wisdom.
With the belief that because two people care about each other, certain boundaries no longer matter.
No one imagines that a single image can become a lifetime of regret.
No one imagines that what disappears from a screen can remain engraved on a conscience.
No one imagines that something hidden inside a private conversation could become a deeply spiritual matter.
Yet Scripture repeatedly reminds us that sin does not become holy simply because nobody else witnesses it.
David confessed before God:
"Against You, You only, have I sinned..." (Psalm 51:4)
People often ask,
"Where does the Bible mention sexting?"
The Bible never mentions smartphones.
It never mentions text messages.
It never mentions social media.
But the Bible constantly reveals God's eternal principles concerning purity, lust, holiness, modesty, self-control, and the sacred design of sexuality.
God's truth does not become outdated simply because technology changes.
The question is not whether Moses owned a phone.
The question is whether our digital behavior honors Christ.
The answer begins much deeper than the device in our hands.
It begins inside the human heart.
Jesus said:
"But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart." (Matthew 5:28)
The Greek word translated "to lust" is ἐπιθυμέω (epithymeō), meaning "to desire passionately, to covet, to long for with sinful intent."
Jesus did something revolutionary.
He moved the battlefield from the bedroom into the heart.
Sin was never merely about physical actions.
It was about inward surrender.
Sexting deliberately cultivates sexual desire outside God's covenant design for marriage.
It intentionally awakens passions through words, photographs, videos, fantasies, and conversations created to arouse another person.
Whether those images are exchanged between strangers, dating couples, engaged couples, or even people emotionally involved online, the spiritual principle remains the same.
God never separates our digital life from our spiritual life.
The same Holy Spirit who dwells with us in church dwells with us when nobody else is watching.
Paul asks a question that echoes across every generation:
"Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you... You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body." (1 Corinthians 6:19–20)
The Greek word for "glorify" is δοξάζω (doxazō), meaning "to honor, magnify, exalt, or reveal the worth of another."
Every choice either magnifies Christ...
or magnifies self.

The Bible consistently portrays sexual intimacy as a holy gift reserved for the covenant of marriage between one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6; Hebrews 13:4). Outside that covenant, Scripture repeatedly warns against πορνεία (porneia), a broad Greek term encompassing sexual immorality of many kinds. It is intentionally comprehensive because sinful expressions of sexuality often evolve with culture while the moral principle remains unchanged.
Paul writes:
Notice he does not say:
Manage it.
Flirt with it.
See how close you can get.
He says,
"Flee."
Joseph did exactly that.
When Potiphar's wife tried to seduce him, he did not negotiate temptation.
He ran.
Sometimes the holiest response is not proving your strength.
It is admitting your weakness.
Many people justify sexting by saying,
"We're going to get married anyway."
Scripture never grants future intentions permission to ignore present obedience.
Love that truly reflects Christ waits with reverence instead of demanding immediate gratification.
Others say,
"But we're both consenting adults."
Consent answers a legal question.
Holiness answers a spiritual one.
The world often asks,
"How far can I go without crossing the line?"
Grace asks,
"How can I honor the One who gave everything for me?"
The Bible also speaks powerfully about our words.
Jesus declared:
"For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks." (Matthew 12:34)
Our typed words reveal the same heart as our spoken words.
Whether through lips or keyboards, Christ hears every sentence.
Psalm 139 reminds us that God knows our words before they even leave us.
There is another side to this conversation that many avoid.
Sometimes the greatest damage is not what is sent.
It is what is awakened.
Sexting trains the mind to separate desire from covenant.
It conditions intimacy without responsibility.
It feeds imagination while starving genuine sacrificial love.
It teaches people to consume one another rather than cherish one another as image-bearers of God.
Genesis declares:
"So God created man in His own image..." (Genesis 1:27)

The Hebrew word for image is צֶלֶם (tselem), signifying a representation or likeness. Every person bears God's image and therefore possesses immeasurable dignity. When another person's body becomes merely a tool for gratification, that dignity is diminished in practice, even if not in value before God.
Perhaps this article feels painfully personal.
Maybe you've already sent the pictures.
Maybe you've already received them.
Maybe you've deleted them.
Maybe you cannot delete the shame.
Hear this carefully.
The Gospel is not merely about exposing sin.
It is about announcing hope.
The woman caught in adultery expected stones.
Instead she encountered Jesus.
He said:
"Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more." (John 8:11)
Grace never pretends sin is harmless.
Grace removes condemnation for those who repent and trust in Christ while calling them into transformed living.
That is why our theme is not simply a slogan.
The cross is where guilty people receive mercy without God compromising His holiness.
Jesus did not die because our sins were small.
He died because they were so serious that only His perfect sacrifice could atone for them.
Isaiah prophesied:
"He was pierced for our transgressions..." (Isaiah 53:5)
Paul later proclaimed:
"If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation." (2 Corinthians 5:17)
The Greek word καινός (kainos) means new in quality—not merely repaired, but transformed. The Gospel does not simply cover our past; it makes us new.
Maybe today the Holy Spirit is not asking you to feel more guilt.
Maybe He is asking you to surrender what you have been hiding.
Delete what dishonors Him.
Confess what needs confessing.
Seek accountability.
Pursue holiness.
Not because you are trying to earn salvation, but because Christ has already paid the price for all who repent and believe.
If this message exposed something hidden, don't hide from the Savior who already knows. Bring everything into His light.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.

Please don't keep this message to yourself. One shared article may become the conversation God uses to rescue a marriage, strengthen a dating relationship, restore a prodigal son or daughter, or awaken someone who has never truly understood the holiness and mercy of Christ.
One surrendered secret can become the beginning of a rewritten life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: What Must a Gentile Do to Be Saved?
paragraphs:
What Must a Gentile Do to Be Saved?
The Question That Changed Eternity—and Why the Answer Still Shocks Religious People Today
There is a question that has haunted humanity for thousands of years.
Not how to become rich.
Not how to become successful.
Not how to become famous.
But this:
What must I do to be saved?
Every human heart eventually arrives there.
The businessman hiding anxiety behind achievements.
The mother carrying guilt she never speaks about.
The addict promising tomorrow will be different.
The churchgoer wondering if they have done enough.
The skeptic secretly asking what happens after death.
And perhaps even you.
Because beneath every accomplishment, every distraction, every failure, every victory, there remains a deeper question:
How can a sinful person stand before a holy God and live?
For the Gentiles—the nations outside ethnic Israel—this question carried another burden.
Were they even welcome?
Could they truly belong to God's family?
Or would they always remain outsiders looking through the window of a covenant they never inherited?
The answer became one of the most important controversies in the entire New Testament.
And the conclusion changed the world forever.
It changed history.
It changed eternity.
And if you understand it correctly, it may change your life today.
The first Christians were Jews.
Jesus was Jewish.
The apostles were Jewish.
The earliest believers were Jewish.
They inherited the promises given to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Then something unexpected happened.
Gentiles started believing.
Romans.
Greeks.
Former idol worshipers.
People who had spent their lives bowing before false gods.
People who knew nothing of the Law of Moses.
People whose pasts were stained with paganism, immorality, and spiritual darkness.
Yet the Holy Spirit began transforming them.
And many religious people became uncomfortable.
Some insisted that faith in Jesus was not enough.
They argued that Gentiles must first become Jews.
They must be circumcised.
They must keep the Mosaic Law.
They must adopt Jewish customs.
Only then could they be fully accepted.
The debate became so serious that the apostles gathered in Jerusalem to settle the matter once and for all.
The event is commonly called the Jerusalem Council in Acts 15.
There, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, the apostles answered the question that still matters today:
What are the requirements for Gentiles to receive salvation?
The answer was breathtakingly simple.
Simon Peter stood before the assembly and reminded them what God had already done among the Gentiles.
Then he declared:

“Why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.” (Acts 15:10–11)
The Greek word translated "grace" is χάρις (charis).
It means favor freely given.
An undeserved gift.
Something earned by neither effort nor religious performance.
Peter's argument was revolutionary.
Jews are saved by grace.
Gentiles are saved by grace.
Everyone is saved the same way.
Not through ethnicity.
Not through rituals.
Not through human achievement.
Not through moral perfection.
Only through Jesus Christ.
The apostle Paul would later write:
The Greek text says:
τῇ γὰρ χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι διὰ πίστεως
"For by grace you have been saved through faith."
Notice what is absent.
No checklist.
No religious ladder.
No self-improvement program.
No salvation by works.
Only grace.
Only faith.
Only Christ.
Yet the Jerusalem Council did provide instructions for Gentile believers.
This is where many readers become confused.
Acts 15:20 says:
"...abstain from things polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from what has been strangled, and from blood."
Some mistakenly assume these were conditions for salvation.
They were not.
The apostles had already concluded that salvation comes by grace through faith.
These instructions were given for fellowship, holiness, and unity between Jewish and Gentile believers.
They addressed practical issues causing division in the early church.
Salvation had already been settled.
The requirements did not create salvation.
They flowed from salvation.
This distinction changes everything.
Because religion says:
"Obey so God will accept you."
The Gospel says:
"God accepts you through Christ, therefore obey."
Religion works from earth toward heaven.
The Gospel comes from heaven toward earth.
Religion says "perform."
Jesus says "believe."
Religion says "earn."
Jesus says "receive."
Religion says "try harder."
Jesus says "It is finished."
When Jesus hung upon the cross, He cried out:
Τετέλεσται (Tetelestai).
"It is finished." (John 19:30)
Not "it has started."
Not "finish the rest yourself."
Not "complete what I began."
Finished.
Paid in full.
Accomplished.
The debt of sin was satisfied by Christ Himself.
This truth reaches all the way back to Abraham.
Long before Moses.
Long before Sinai.
Long before circumcision became the sign of the covenant.
Genesis 15:6 says:
וְהֶאֱמִן בַּיהוָה
"Abraham believed Yahweh."
And God counted it to him as righteousness.
Not because Abraham earned it.
Because he believed.
Paul builds his entire argument in Romans upon this foundation.
The pattern never changed.
Faith.
Grace.
Christ.
Salvation has always been God's work.
Never man's achievement.
And this is where our story becomes deeply personal.
Because many people today still live like the debate of Acts 15 was never settled.
They carry invisible chains.
They fear they are never good enough.
Never holy enough.
Never disciplined enough.
Never worthy enough.
Every failure becomes evidence against them.
Every weakness becomes another accusation.
Every stumble whispers:
"God cannot possibly love someone like you."
But the Gospel tells a different story.
The Gospel is the story of scandal becoming grace.
It is the story of prostitutes becoming worshipers.
Persecutors becoming apostles.
Thieves becoming citizens of paradise.
Broken people becoming beloved children.
The Gospel is not about good people climbing toward God.
It is about God descending toward ruined people through Jesus Christ.
That is why Gentile salvation matters.
Because most of us reading this are Gentiles.
We were outsiders.
Strangers to the covenants.
Far from God.
Yet Ephesians 2:13 declares:
"But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ."
Not brought near by performance.
Not brought near by ancestry.
Not brought near by religious credentials.
Brought near by Christ.
Perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear today.
You may feel disqualified.
Your past may embarrass you.
Your failures may still haunt you.
You may think you've wandered too far.
But Jesus specializes in bringing distant people home.
The cross was never built for perfect people.
It was built for sinners.
The empty tomb was never meant for the deserving.
It was meant for the hopeless.
And salvation remains exactly what it was in Acts 15.
Repent of your sin.
Place your faith in Jesus Christ.
Trust His death for your sins.
Trust His resurrection for your justification.
Receive the grace He freely offers.
Follow Him as Lord.
That is the biblical answer.
Nothing added.
Nothing removed.
Jesus Christ is enough.
Have you ever struggled with feeling like you had to earn God's acceptance?
Because the greatest miracle is not that sinners find God.
It is that God came searching for sinners.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Understanding Hebrews 11 Beyond Motivation
paragraphs:
Understanding Hebrews 11 Beyond Motivation
The Chapter We Quote for Courage but Rarely Stay Long Enough to Understand
Most people read Hebrews 11 when they need encouragement.
They turn to it when life is falling apart.
When prayers seem unanswered.
When fear feels larger than faith.
When the future looks uncertain.
We quote it during difficult seasons because it sounds inspiring.
"Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen." (Hebrews 11:1)
But Hebrews 11 was never written merely to motivate discouraged believers.
It was written to rescue exhausted believers who were considering walking away from Jesus.
That changes everything.
Because if we read Hebrews 11 only as a motivational chapter, we miss its deepest message.
And if we miss its deepest message, we miss the very heart of the Gospel.
The original Greek text begins:
"Ἔστιν δὲ πίστις" (Estin de pistis)
"Now faith is..."
The word translated "faith" is pistis (πίστις).
In modern culture, faith is often treated like positive thinking.
A mindset.
An optimism.
A feeling.
But pistis means trust, confidence, reliance, loyalty, and steadfast dependence upon someone proven trustworthy.
Biblical faith is not believing in yourself.
Biblical faith is believing God when circumstances tempt you not to.
The people listed in Hebrews 11 were not heroes because they possessed extraordinary confidence.
They were remembered because they trusted an extraordinary God.
And that distinction changes the entire chapter.
Because when you look carefully, Hebrews 11 is not actually a chapter about successful people.
It is a chapter filled with scandal.
Brokenness.
Failure.
Weakness.
Regret.
And people whose stories should have ended very differently.
Take Noah.
Most remember the ark.
Few remember his drunkenness afterward.
Take Abraham.
The father of faith also lied repeatedly and attempted to solve God's promises through human effort.
Take Sarah.
She laughed at God's promise.
The Hebrew word in Genesis for her laughter reflects disbelief rather than joyful confidence.
Take Jacob.
A deceiver.
A manipulator.
A man who spent much of his life wrestling with consequences created by his own choices.
Take Moses.
A murderer before becoming a deliverer.
Take Rahab.
A prostitute living in a pagan city destined for judgment.
Yet Hebrews 11 celebrates them.
Why?
Because Hebrews 11 is not a museum of perfect people.
It is a testimony to a perfect Savior working through imperfect people.
This is why our theme matters so deeply:
The Bible never hides human failure.
Humanity hides failure.
Scripture exposes it.
The Bible tells the truth about people because God intends to tell the truth about grace.
Rahab's story is perhaps one of the most shocking examples.
Hebrews 11:31 says:
"By faith the prostitute Rahab did not perish with those who were disobedient."
The Greek text literally includes:
"Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη"
"Rahab the prostitute."
Even here, Scripture does not erase her past.
God does not rewrite her history by pretending it never happened.
He rewrites her future through redemption.
That is how grace works.
Grace is not denial.
Grace is transformation.
The Gospel does not say your past never happened.
The Gospel declares your past no longer has the final word.
Many people live as if their worst chapter is their identity.
The addiction.
The affair.
The abortion.
The divorce.
The betrayal.
The shame.
The secret nobody knows.
But Hebrews 11 stands like a monument declaring that God specializes in writing new endings.
Not because people deserve it.
Because Jesus paid for it.
This is why Hebrews 11 cannot be separated from Hebrews 12.
The chapter divisions were added centuries later.
The original readers would have flowed directly from one chapter into the next.
After all the stories of faith, the author writes:
The Greek phrase is breathtaking:
"ἀφορῶντες εἰς τὸν Ἰησοῦν"
"Aphorōntes eis ton Iēsoun"
"Fixing our eyes on Jesus."
Not on Abraham.
Not on Moses.
Not on David.
Not on ourselves.
On Jesus.
Because Jesus is the point of every story.
The heroes of Hebrews 11 are not the destination.
They are signposts pointing toward Christ.
Every sacrifice points to Christ.
Every act of faith points to Christ.
Every rescue points to Christ.
Every promise points to Christ.
Every scandal points to humanity's need for Christ.
And every act of grace points to the cross.
This becomes even more powerful when we reach Hebrews 11:13.
The text says:
"These all died in faith, not having received the things promised."
Read that again.
Many of them never saw the fulfillment of what they believed for.
They obeyed.
They trusted.
They endured.
Yet they died before receiving what had been promised.
That is not the version of faith many people hear today.
The modern world often treats faith as a formula for immediate results.
Hebrews treats faith as faithful endurance rooted in the character of God.
Faith is not trusting because you can see the outcome.
Faith is trusting because you know the One making the promise.
This is why Hebrews 11 repeatedly uses the phrase:
"By faith."
Not by sight.
Not by certainty.
Not by feelings.
By faith.
The Hebrew foundation beneath this idea can be seen in the word אֱמוּנָה (emunah).
Often translated faithfulness, steadfastness, firmness, reliability.
Biblical faith is not merely believing.
It is remaining.
Standing.
Trusting.
Holding on when everything around you says let go.
Somebody reading this right now has spent years carrying shame from a chapter they cannot undo.
You still hear the voices.
You still remember the mistakes.
You still wonder if God sees you differently because of what happened.
But Hebrews 11 tells a different story.
A truer story.
A Gospel story.
The God who included murderers, adulterers, deceivers, cowards, doubters, prostitutes, and failures in His redemptive plan has not run out of grace for you.
Jesus did not come for people who had everything together.
Jesus came for people who knew they didn't.
The cross proves that your sin is serious.
The empty tomb proves that God's grace is greater.
And perhaps the most beautiful reality hidden inside Hebrews 11 is this:
The chapter never celebrates people because they became impressive.
It celebrates people because they trusted God.
That means your testimony is not about how strong you became.
It is about how faithful Jesus remained.
Maybe that is why this chapter continues to grip hearts after nearly two thousand years.
Because deep down, every person knows what it feels like to fail.
What we desperately need is not another motivational speech.
We need hope.
Real hope.
The kind of hope found in a Savior who enters our scandal and replaces it with grace.
The kind of hope that reaches into broken stories and rewrites them.
The kind of hope found only in Jesus Christ.
Not because a comment saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes public confession becomes the first step toward private surrender.
They may need this reminder more than you realize.
Because one shared article can reach a struggling believer.
One act of obedience can become part of someone's redemption story.
And one encounter with Jesus can change everything forever.
Your greatest failure may explain where you've been, but it does not decide where Christ can take you next.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Day Joshua Met a Warrior with a Sword
paragraphs:
The Day Joshua Met a Warrior with a Sword
He Thought the Battle Was About Jericho. Then He Came Face to Face with the One Who Was Really in Command.
Most people never realize the greatest battle of their lives is not the one standing in front of them.
It is the one happening inside them.
The night before Jericho fell, Joshua stood staring at walls that looked impossible. Massive. Intimidating. Ancient. The kind of walls that make human beings question everything God promised.
Maybe you've stood before walls like that.
A broken marriage.
A diagnosis.
A financial crisis.
A secret sin nobody knows about.
A prayer that seems unanswered.
A dream that feels buried beneath years of disappointment.
Joshua knew exactly what that felt like.
Israel had crossed the Jordan River. God's promises were finally within reach. Yet between them and the inheritance stood Jericho—fortified, sealed shut, and seemingly unconquerable.
Then something happened that changed everything.
The Bible records:
"Now when Joshua was near Jericho, he looked up and saw a man standing in front of him with a drawn sword in his hand." (Joshua 5:13)
The Hebrew text says the man stood before him with a חֶרֶב שְׁלוּפָה (cherev shelufah)—a sword already drawn from its sheath.
This was not a peaceful traveler.
This was a warrior prepared for battle.
Joshua immediately approached him.
That alone tells us something about Joshua's character.
He did not run.
He did not hide.
He did not send someone else.
He walked directly toward the unknown.
Then he asked one of the most revealing questions in all Scripture:
"הֲלָנוּ אַתָּה אִם־לְצָרֵינוּ"
"Are you for us, or for our adversaries?" (Joshua 5:13)
In modern language:
"Whose side are you on?"
That question still echoes through every generation.
We ask it during elections.
During wars.
During church disagreements.
During family conflicts.
During personal struggles.
"God, are You on my side?"
But Joshua received an answer he never expected.
"לֹא"
"No." (Joshua 5:14)
Not yes.
Not Israel.
Not Jericho.
Simply:
"No."
Imagine the shock.
The warrior continued:
"כִּי אֲנִי שַׂר־צְבָא־יְהוָה"
"But as Commander of the Army of the LORD I have now come."
The Hebrew title is breathtaking.
Sar-Tzeva-YHWH.
Commander of Yahweh's armies.
The highest military authority in heaven.
Suddenly Joshua realized something every believer must eventually learn:
God does not come to take sides.
God comes to take over.
The question was never whether God was on Joshua's side.
The question was whether Joshua was on God's side.
And that changes everything.
Because many of us spend our lives asking heaven to bless our plans while never surrendering to God's plans.
We ask Him to endorse our ambitions.
Approve our desires.
Validate our opinions.
Strengthen our arguments.
Win our battles.
Meanwhile Jesus is asking a completely different question:
"Will you follow Me?"
Not:
"Will I follow you?"
The moment Joshua understood who stood before him, Scripture says:
"Joshua fell facedown to the ground in reverence." (Joshua 5:14)
The Hebrew picture is powerful.
He collapsed.
The warrior had not come to give Joshua strategy first.
He came to receive Joshua's surrender.
That order matters.
Because victory in God's kingdom always begins with submission.
Before walls fall, pride must fall.
Before strongholds collapse, self-reliance must collapse.
Before breakthroughs happen, surrender happens.
Then the Commander spoke words that should sound familiar:
"Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy." (Joshua 5:15)
This was not the first time those words had been spoken.
Centuries earlier, Moses heard nearly the same command at the burning bush.
Many scholars throughout church history have recognized something extraordinary here.
The text strongly suggests this warrior was not merely an angel.
Angels never receive worship.
Angels consistently redirect worship toward God.
Yet this Commander accepts Joshua's reverence.
He speaks with divine authority.
He declares the ground holy because of His presence.
Many theologians identify this encounter as a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ—what is often called a Christophany.
Before Bethlehem.
Before the manger.
Before the cross.
Before the resurrection.
The eternal Son appears as a warrior.
Not because He loves war.
But because He fights for God's redemptive purposes.
The same Jesus who would one day stretch out His hands on a cross first stood before Joshua holding a sword.
The same Savior who said, "Come to Me," also commands the armies of heaven.
Grace and authority.
Mercy and holiness.
Love and justice.
Perfectly united.
This is why the encounter is so unforgettable.
Joshua expected military intelligence.
Instead he received a revelation of God.
He expected battle plans.
Instead he encountered the King.
He thought Jericho was the story.
Jesus was the story.
And maybe that is what some of us need to hear today.
The wall in front of you is not the main story.
The relationship is not the main story.
The struggle is not the main story.
The fear is not the main story.
The addiction is not the main story.
The betrayal is not the main story.
Christ is the story.
Because the greatest miracle in Joshua 5 is not that walls would eventually fall.
The greatest miracle is that a man encountered the living God and was forever changed.
That truth reaches its fullest expression at the cross.
The Gospel is the ultimate story of scandal transformed into grace.
Humanity rebelled.
Humanity sinned.
Humanity chose darkness.
The evidence against us was overwhelming.
If anyone deserved judgment, it was us.
Yet Jesus stepped into our place.
The One holding the sword chose instead to bear the nails.
The Commander became the sacrifice.
The King wore a crown of thorns.
The innocent carried the guilt of the guilty.
The Greek New Testament declares:
"Χριστὸς ἀπέθανεν ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν"
"Christ died for our sins." (1 Corinthians 15:3)
Not because we earned it.
Not because we deserved it.
Because grace rewrites everything.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
That is the heartbeat of Joshua's encounter.
That is the heartbeat of our mission.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you came to this article carrying a wall that feels impossible.
A failure you cannot undo.
A regret you cannot erase.
A shame you cannot silence.
A chapter you wish had never happened.
Listen carefully.
Joshua's story was never ultimately about walls.
It was about worship.
Because when a person truly encounters Christ, the walls eventually become secondary.
The greatest victory is discovering who stands with the drawn sword.
The King is still reigning.
The Commander is still leading.
The Savior is still rescuing.
And grace is still rewriting stories every single day.
If this message strengthened your faith, don't let it stop with you.
What wall are you trusting Jesus to bring down?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
If you desire to glorify God through advancing Gospel-centered ministry, your support truly makes a difference.
Because one encounter with Jesus can change a life.
One surrendered heart can change a family.
One transformed family can change a generation.
And one act of faithfulness can echo into eternity.
The wall was never the biggest thing standing in front of Joshua. The King standing behind him was.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Remember Lot’s Wife
paragraphs:
Remember Lot’s Wife
The Lesson That Haunted Me Long After I Closed My Bible
There are some verses in Scripture that comfort you.
Some inspire you.
Some strengthen you.
And then there are the verses that stop you in your tracks and refuse to let you go.
For me, one of those verses is only three words long.
Three words.
No explanation.
No sermon.
No commentary.
Just three words spoken directly by Jesus Christ Himself:
“Remember Lot’s wife.” (Luke 17:32)
That is all He said.
Yet those three words carry the weight of eternity.
Because Jesus was not simply asking us to remember a woman.
He was warning us not to become her.
The first time I truly wrestled with those words, I realized something uncomfortable.
I had always assumed Lot’s wife was judged because she looked back.
But the longer I studied Scripture, the more I understood that the problem was never merely where her eyes turned.
The problem was where her heart remained.
The account begins in Genesis 19 as God prepares to judge Sodom and Gomorrah because of their wickedness.
The Hebrew text repeatedly emphasizes the severity of their corruption. The city had become a picture of rebellion against God.
Yet even in judgment, God displayed mercy.
Angels were sent to rescue Lot and his family.
Genesis 19:17 records the command:
“Escape for your life. Do not look back and do not stop anywhere in the valley.”
The Hebrew phrase for “do not look back” is אַל־תַּבִּיט אַחֲרֶיךָ (al-tabbit achareikha).
It means far more than a casual glance.
The verb carries the idea of gazing with regard, consideration, attachment, longing, or focused attention.
This was not simply a warning against turning one's head.
It was a warning against turning one's heart.
God was leading them out.
But part of her was still inside the city.
And that is where this story stops being about Lot’s wife and starts being about us.
Because how many of us have physically left certain sins while emotionally remaining attached to them?
How many of us have walked away from toxic relationships but secretly wished we could return?
How many of us have prayed for freedom while quietly mourning the chains God was breaking?
How many of us have asked Jesus to transform our lives while still romanticizing the life He rescued us from?
The tragedy of Lot’s wife is not that she wanted to see Sodom one last time.
The tragedy is that Sodom was still living inside her.
Genesis 19:26 says:
“But Lot’s wife, behind him, looked back, and she became a pillar of salt.”
The Hebrew text uses the phrase וַתַּבֵּט מֵאַחֲרָיו (vattabet me'acharav).
Again, this is not describing a fleeting glance.
It implies deliberate regard.
A lingering look.
A heart unable to let go.
A soul divided between salvation and destruction.
She was being rescued by grace.
Yet she was grieving what grace was taking away.
That reality hit me harder than I expected.
Because I realized how often I have wanted God to save me while allowing me to keep the very things destroying me.
I wanted the peace of Christ without surrender.
The blessings of God without obedience.
Freedom without separation from the things enslaving me.
But Jesus never calls people to partial surrender.
He calls them to Himself.
When Jesus referenced Lot’s wife in Luke 17, He was teaching about His return.
The Greek text simply says:
Μνημονεύετε τῆς γυναικὸς Λώτ
(Mnēmoneuete tēs gynaikos Lōt)
“Remember Lot’s wife.”
The word μνημονεύετε (mnēmoneuete) is an active command.
It means continually remember.
Keep remembering.
Never forget.
Jesus intentionally reached back into Genesis because He knew future generations would struggle with the same temptation.
The temptation to follow Him while still looking back.
The temptation to move toward Heaven while remaining emotionally attached to the world.
The temptation to trust Christ for salvation while refusing full surrender.
Immediately after this warning, Jesus says:
“Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it.” (Luke 17:33)
The connection is unmistakable.
Lot’s wife wanted both.
She wanted rescue and remembrance.
Deliverance and attachment.
Freedom and nostalgia.
But eventually every disciple faces the same choice.
Will we follow Jesus forward?
Or will we keep looking backward?
One of the most dangerous spiritual conditions is not open rebellion.
It is divided affection.
A heart that wants Christ but also wants Egypt.
A heart that wants Heaven but misses Sodom.
A heart that wants grace while secretly longing for the old life.
That is why Jesus later declared:
“No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.” (Luke 9:62)
He was not describing perfection.
He was describing direction.
A true disciple may stumble.
A true disciple may struggle.
A true disciple may fall.
But a true disciple keeps moving toward Christ.
The older I get, the more I understand that following Jesus often means grieving things that once defined you.
Not because they were good.
But because they were familiar.
Sin can become familiar.
Brokenness can become familiar.
Bitterness can become familiar.
Shame can become familiar.
Even pain can become familiar.
And sometimes God must call us away from what is familiar so He can lead us into what is holy.
That journey is not always easy.
But it is always worth it.
Because the Gospel is not merely about escaping judgment.
The Gospel is about becoming new.
The Apostle Paul wrote:
“Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.”
The Greek phrase is:
καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis)
A new creation.
Not repaired.
Not renovated.
Not slightly improved.
New.
Entirely new.
This is the beauty of the Gospel.
Jesus never asks us to save ourselves.
He saves us.
He rescues us.
He transforms us.
He rewrites us.
The same God who called Abraham.
The same God who rescued Lot.
The same God who raised Christ from the dead.
Still changes lives today.
Maybe that is why the story of Lot’s wife lingers in my heart.
Because it forces me to ask difficult questions.
What am I still looking back at?
What am I still mourning that God has called me to leave behind?
What has Jesus already delivered me from that I secretly wish I could revisit?
Be honest.
This question reaches deeper than most of us want to admit.
And perhaps that is exactly why Jesus said, “Remember Lot’s wife.”
Because every generation needs the reminder.
The danger was never behind her.
The danger was inside her.
And the same warning still echoes through every human heart today.
Your testimony may encourage someone who feels alone in their battle today.
If we truly desire to glorify God, we should joyfully support the work that spreads His truth, equips believers, reaches the lost, and advances the Gospel to more people every day.
Because one day you will realize something Lot’s wife never did.
The future God has prepared for you is infinitely greater than anything He asked you to leave behind.
And sometimes the holiest thing you can do is refuse to look back.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Lesson I Learned From Jacob at Bethel
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From Jacob at Bethel
The Night a Fugitive Met God, and Why Your Greatest Failure Might Be the Place Where Jesus Begins Rewriting Your Story
There are moments in life when the silence feels louder than any crowd.
Moments when the consequences of our choices finally catch up with us.
Moments when we lie awake at night replaying conversations, mistakes, betrayals, regrets, and failures we wish we could erase.
I imagine Jacob felt exactly that way.
Not as the patriarch we celebrate today.
Not as the father of a nation.
Not as a man of faith.
But as a frightened runaway sleeping alone in the wilderness.
When Genesis 28 opens, Jacob is not walking in victory. He is running from the wreckage he helped create.
He had deceived his father Isaac.
He had stolen the blessing intended for his brother Esau.
His family was fractured.
His future was uncertain.
His reputation was stained.
And now he was fleeing for his life.

The Hebrew text tells us that Jacob came to a certain place and stayed there for the night because the sun had set (Genesis 28:11). The place would later become known as Bethel, from the Hebrew בֵּית־אֵל (Beit-El), meaning “House of God.”
But Jacob did not know that yet.
As far as he could tell, it was just another lonely place.
Just another dark night.
Just another chapter of fear.
Isn't that how God often works?
We think we are standing in an ordinary place.
A hospital room.
A broken marriage.
A financial crisis.
A season of depression.
A painful betrayal.
A hidden addiction.
A private failure.
And only later do we realize that the very ground where we thought our story was ending was actually where God intended to meet us.
Jacob uses a stone as his pillow.
No palace.
No comfort.
No security.
No evidence that God was near.
Then everything changes.
Genesis 28:12 says:
"And he dreamed, and behold, there was a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it."
The Hebrew word translated "ladder" is סֻלָּם (sullam).
The exact nature of this structure is debated among scholars, but its meaning is clear.
Heaven and earth are connected.
God is revealing that He is not distant.
He is not absent.
He is not uninvolved.
The God of Abraham and Isaac is still actively reaching into human history.
Then comes one of the most astonishing moments in Scripture.
The Lord Himself stands above it and says:
"I am the LORD God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac" (Genesis 28:13).
Notice what God does not say.
He does not begin with condemnation.
He does not start listing Jacob's sins.
He does not remind him of every deception.
He does not tell him he is disqualified.
Instead, God speaks promises.
Presence.
Purpose.
Future.
Grace.
This is one of the greatest surprises in the entire Bible.
Jacob certainly deserved correction.
But first he received revelation.
Not because sin does not matter.
But because God's covenant faithfulness is greater than human failure.
This does not excuse Jacob's actions.
Scripture never celebrates his deception.
Yet God demonstrates something every believer desperately needs to understand.
God's plans are not dependent on human perfection.
If they were, none of us would have hope.
Not one.
Years later, Jesus would reveal the deeper meaning behind Jacob's dream.
In John 1:51 He declares:
"Verily, verily, I say unto you, Hereafter ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man."
The Greek text reads:
"καὶ τοὺς ἀγγέλους τοῦ θεοῦ ἀναβαίνοντας καὶ καταβαίνοντας ἐπὶ τὸν Υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου"
Jesus is identifying Himself as the true connection between heaven and earth.
Jacob saw a ladder.
We see a cross.
Jacob saw a symbol.
We know the Savior.
Jacob witnessed a glimpse.
We have the fulfillment.
The lesson I learned from Jacob at Bethel is not merely that God can meet us in difficult places.
The lesson is that God's grace often finds us before we start looking for Him.
Jacob was not seeking revival.
He was running.
He was not praying for a divine encounter.
He was escaping consequences.
Yet God came.
That truth still changes lives today.
Some people reading this feel unworthy to approach God.
You think your failures are too great.
Your past is too messy.
Your mistakes are too public.
Your secrets are too dark.
But Bethel reminds us that God specializes in meeting people in places they never expected to encounter Him.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
Not after we fixed ourselves.
Not after we became worthy.
Not after we cleaned up our lives.
While we were still sinners.
The scandal of grace is that God moves toward broken people.
And Jacob's story becomes our story.
Because every believer eventually discovers that salvation is not about climbing up to God.
It is about God coming down to us through Jesus Christ.
When Jacob awoke, he said:
"Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." (Genesis 28:16)
How many times has that been true in our own lives?
God was there in the heartbreak.
God was there in the uncertainty.
God was there in the waiting.
God was there in the tears.
God was there when we thought He had abandoned us.
And looking back, we realize He was writing a better story than the one we were trying to write ourselves.
Jacob arrived at Bethel as a deceiver.
He left with a promise.
He arrived carrying shame.
He left carrying hope.
He arrived running from his past.
He left moving toward God's future.
That is what Jesus still does.
He takes addicts and makes them testimonies.
He takes prodigals and makes them sons and daughters.
He takes failures and turns them into vessels of grace.
He takes scandals and transforms them into stories of redemption.
Because the Gospel has never been about perfect people.
It has always been about a perfect Savior.
Maybe that is why Bethel still speaks so powerfully thousands of years later.
We see ourselves in Jacob.
We know what it feels like to fail.
We know what it feels like to run.
We know what it feels like to wonder whether God could still use us.
And then we discover the same truth Jacob discovered beneath the stars.
Grace arrives where we least expect it.
Your testimony may encourage someone else who feels trapped in their own wilderness tonight.
You never know who is lying awake in their own Bethel moment, believing their failures have the final word.
Sometimes a single shared message becomes the doorway through which the Holy Spirit begins changing a life.
It is one practical way to participate in proclaiming the glory of God through biblical truth.
One night with God can turn the place of your greatest regret into the birthplace of your greatest redemption.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He Tried to Save His Life… and Lost Everything
paragraphs:
He Tried to Save His Life… and Lost Everything
The Shocking Truth Behind Luke 9:24 That Most Christians Never Fully Understand
There is a sentence Jesus spoke that sounds almost impossible the first time you hear it.
A sentence that collides with everything our flesh wants.
A sentence that exposes the hidden idols we protect.
A sentence that has the power to completely rewrite a person's life.
Jesus said:
"For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for Me will save it." (Luke 9:24)
At first glance, it sounds like a contradiction.
How can losing your life save it?
How can surrender become victory?
How can death become life?
Yet hidden inside these words is one of the deepest realities of the Gospel.
The Greek text reads:
"Hos gar an thelē tēn psychēn autou sōsai, apolesei autēn; hos d’ an apolesē tēn psychēn autou heneken emou, houtos sōsei autēn."
The key word is ψυχή (psychē).

Most English readers immediately think Jesus is talking about physical life, but psychē carries a much deeper meaning. It can refer to one's self, soul, identity, desires, ambitions, and entire existence.
Jesus is not merely talking about breathing.
He is talking about the version of ourselves we desperately try to protect.
The life we build apart from Him.
The kingdom we create for ourselves.
The reputation we fight to preserve.
The dreams we refuse to surrender.
The control we cling to.
The self we worship.
And that changes everything.
Because suddenly Luke 9:24 is not merely about dying for Christ.
It is about dying to self.
Every single day.
The world tells us to follow our hearts.
Jesus tells us to deny ourselves.
The world says protect your truth.
Jesus says surrender to Truth.
The world says build your kingdom.
Jesus says seek His Kingdom.
The world says become whoever you want to be.
Jesus says become who God created you to be.
This is where the scandal begins.
Because the greatest obstacle between us and God is often not the devil.
It is ourselves.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly reveal this reality.
Jeremiah 17:9 says:
"The heart is deceitful above all things and desperately wicked; who can know it?"
The Hebrew phrase עָקֹב הַלֵּב (aqov halev) describes a heart that is twisted, deceptive, and unreliable.
Yet modern culture tells us to trust that very heart without question.
Jesus knew something we often forget.
The self left on its own cannot save itself.
The self can only destroy itself.
And every person eventually discovers this.
Some discover it through addiction.
Some through broken relationships.
Some through success that failed to satisfy.
Some through depression.
Some through betrayal.
Some through grief.
Some through hidden sins nobody else knows about.
Many spend decades climbing ladders only to discover they were leaning against the wrong wall.
They saved their lives.
Yet somehow lost them.
You can possess money and still feel bankrupt.
You can have followers and still feel alone.
You can achieve fame and still feel invisible.
You can gain the whole world and still lose your soul.
That is exactly why the very next verse asks:
"For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself?" (Luke 9:25)
Jesus was exposing the greatest tragedy imaginable.
Not losing money.
Not losing status.
Not losing possessions.
Losing yourself forever because you refused to surrender to the One who created you.
Yet this is where the Gospel becomes breathtakingly beautiful.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about what you lose.
It is about what you gain.
When Jesus calls us to lose our lives, He is not inviting us into destruction.
He is inviting us into resurrection.
This is the pattern of the entire Gospel.
A cross before a crown.
Death before life.
Surrender before victory.
Burial before resurrection.
The greatest example is Jesus Himself.
Philippians 2 tells us Christ emptied Himself.
The Greek word is ἐκένωσεν (ekenōsen).
He willingly laid aside His privileges.
He humbled Himself.
He became obedient unto death.
Even death on a cross.
The King became a servant.
The Creator entered creation.
The Holy One carried our sin.
The Innocent One accepted our punishment.
The Perfect One endured our scandal.
And because He surrendered Himself completely to the Father's will, God highly exalted Him.
Jesus lived Luke 9:24 before He ever preached it.
He lost His life for us.
So we could find ours in Him.
That is why salvation is not self-improvement.
It is self-surrender.
The Gospel is not Jesus helping you become a better version of yourself.
The Gospel is Jesus giving you an entirely new self.
As Paul declared:
"I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me." (Galatians 2:20)
This is the miracle many people miss.
God is not merely fixing your story.
He is rewriting it.
Your failures are not the final chapter.
Your addiction is not the final chapter.
Your shame is not the final chapter.
Your divorce is not the final chapter.
Your regrets are not the final chapter.
Your scandal is not the final chapter.
Because Jesus specializes in rewriting endings.
Abraham lied.
Moses killed.
David committed adultery.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Yet grace had the final word.
Again and again Scripture reminds us that God does not choose perfect people.
He redeems broken people.
He transforms sinners.
He restores failures.
He rewrites stories.
That is why our message has always been:
Because that is exactly what Jesus does.
Perhaps as you read this, you are exhausted from carrying a life you were never meant to carry alone.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to save yourself.
Trying harder.
Hiding deeper.
Pretending longer.
Managing appearances.
Protecting an image.
Controlling outcomes.
Yet nothing has brought peace.
Maybe this is the moment Jesus is inviting you to let go.
Not because He wants less for you.
But because He wants infinitely more.
The paradox of Luke 9:24 remains true today.
The life surrendered to Christ is the only life truly found.
The person who clings to self eventually loses everything.
The person who surrenders to Christ gains everything that truly matters.
Forgiveness.
Purpose.
Peace.
Identity.
Eternal life.
And a relationship with the God who loves them enough to die for them.
If this message spoke directly to your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
Someone may be desperately trying to save a life that is falling apart.
"Jesus is rewriting my story."
Or:
"I'm still surrendering."
Your testimony may encourage someone more than you realize.
Creating biblically faithful, Christ-centered content, discipleship resources, devotionals, studies, videos, articles, and outreach ministry requires ongoing support.
If we truly desire to glorify God, supporting Gospel-centered ministry and helping biblical truth reach more people is one meaningful way to participate in the Great Commission.
Because one surrendered life can change a family.
One changed family can change a generation.
And one encounter with Jesus can change eternity.
The life you keep trying to save may be the very thing keeping you from the life God has prepared for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE TRUTH ABOUT SOUL TIES
paragraphs:
THE TRUTH ABOUT SOUL TIES
The Invisible Bond You Can't Explain, The Spiritual Weight You Can't Shake, and the Grace of Jesus That Can Rewrite Everything
There are people who leave your life, yet somehow never leave your mind.
Years pass.
The phone number is gone.
The relationship ended.
The friendship collapsed.
The affair was exposed.
The betrayal happened.
The divorce papers were signed.
The funeral came and went.
Yet something remains.
A memory.
A pull.
A voice.
A longing.
A wound.
A connection you cannot fully explain.
You tell yourself you're over it.
But certain songs still trigger emotions.
Certain places still make your chest tighten.
Certain names still make your heart race.
And sometimes, late at night when nobody sees the battle inside your mind, you wonder:
"Why do they still have this much power over me?"
Many Christians call this a soul tie.
Others dismiss it completely.
Some turn it into mystical teachings that Scripture never supports.
Others ignore the reality that relationships can leave deep spiritual, emotional, and psychological imprints upon a person.
So what does the Bible actually teach?
Not what social media says.
Not what popular Christian trends claim.
Not what fear-based ministries sell.
What does God say?
The phrase "soul tie" does not appear anywhere in Scripture.
Not in Hebrew.
Not in Aramaic.
Not in Greek.
Yet the reality of profound soul-level bonding absolutely does.
The Hebrew word often translated as "soul" is נֶפֶשׁ (nephesh).
It refers to the inner life of a person—their desires, affections, emotions, will, and very being.
In Genesis 2:24, Scripture says:
"Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh."
The Hebrew phrase is:

וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
(vehayu lebasar echad)
"and they shall become one flesh."
This is far deeper than physical intimacy.
God designed marriage as a covenant union involving body, heart, mind, affection, loyalty, commitment, and spiritual partnership.
When God joins two people together, something profound happens.
A bond forms.
A union exists.
A connection develops.
This is why sexual sin is never described in Scripture as merely physical.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:16:
The Greek word for "joined" is:
κολλώμενος (kollōmenos)
meaning "to glue together," "to cling," or "to unite closely."
Paul's warning is shocking.
Physical intimacy creates more than physical consequences.
God designed it to connect people deeply.
The world says sex is casual.
God says it never was.
The world says your body is your own.
God says your body was purchased by Christ.
The world says do whatever feels right.
God says your heart was created for covenant, not consumption.
This is where many people become trapped.
Not because of some mystical curse.
Not because another human being owns part of their soul.
But because sin leaves scars.
Relationships leave impressions.
Trauma leaves marks.
Attachments leave memories.
And wounds often continue bleeding long after the relationship itself ends.
David understood this reality.
After his devastating sins and failures, he cried out:
"Create in me a clean heart, O God." (Psalm 51:10)
The Hebrew phrase is:

לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
(lev tahor bera-li Elohim)
"Create for me a pure heart, O God."
David did not ask God merely to improve him.
He asked God to recreate him.
Because some wounds are too deep for self-help.
Some scars are too severe for positive thinking.
Some chains are too strong for human effort.
Only God can heal what sin has damaged.
Only God can restore what shame has stolen.
Only God can untangle what rebellion has complicated.
Perhaps that is why so many people carry hidden pain today.
They are trying to heal spiritually without the Great Physician.
Trying to repair their hearts without the One who designed them.
Trying to move forward while dragging chains from old relationships, old sins, old addictions, old betrayals, and old versions of themselves.
Some are haunted by former lovers.
Some by abuse.
Some by abandonment.
Some by pornography.
Some by emotional dependency.
Some by manipulation.
Some by toxic relationships that ended years ago.
The relationship ended.
The attachment didn't.
The conversation stopped.
The emotional bond remained.
The person left.
The wound stayed.
And many believers secretly wonder:
"Can Jesus really heal this?"
The answer is not found in modern theories.
It is found at the cross.
The Gospel never teaches that believers remain permanently bound to their past.
The Gospel teaches something far more powerful.
2 Corinthians 5:17 declares:
"Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation."
The Greek says:

καινὴ κτίσις
(kainē ktisis)
A new creation.
Not repaired.
Not recycled.
Not slightly improved.
New.
That changes everything.
Because your deepest identity is no longer determined by who touched you.
Who left you.
Who betrayed you.
Who abused you.
Who used you.
Who rejected you.
Who divorced you.
Who abandoned you.
Your identity is determined by Who redeemed you.
Jesus never looked at broken people and saw permanent damage.
He saw redemption.
The woman at the well carried relational failures.
Jesus offered living water.
The woman caught in adultery carried public shame.
Jesus offered mercy.
Peter carried denial.
Jesus offered restoration.
Paul carried a history of persecution.
Jesus offered purpose.
Mary Magdalene carried spiritual oppression.
Jesus offered freedom.
Again and again, Scripture reveals the same message.
Jesus specializes in rewriting stories.
The enemy says your past defines you.
Jesus says His grace defines you.
The enemy says you're ruined.
Jesus says you're redeemed.
The enemy says you'll always be attached to what broke you.
Jesus says whom the Son sets free is free indeed.
The Greek word in John 8:36 for free is:
ἐλεύθερος (eleutheros)
Liberated.
Released.
Unbound.
Set at liberty.
That is the promise of Christ.
Not merely coping.
Freedom.
Not merely surviving.
Freedom.
Not merely managing old chains.
Freedom.
This is why the Gospel is not behavior modification.
It is resurrection power.
The same Christ who walked out of a borrowed tomb still walks into broken hearts today.
The same Savior who conquered death still conquers shame.
The same Redeemer who restored Peter still restores wounded believers.
The same Lord who transformed Saul into Paul still transforms people carrying scars from relationships they wish they could forget.
Maybe this article found you because you're carrying one of those scars.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you've hidden it well.
Maybe people see your smile but not your struggle.
Maybe you sit in church while silently fighting memories that refuse to leave.
Maybe you're exhausted from pretending you're okay.
If that's you, hear this clearly:
Jesus is not intimidated by your wounds.
He is not surprised by your failures.
He is not shocked by your history.
He already knew everything about you when He chose the cross.
And He still chose the cross.
That is grace.
Not earned.
Not deserved.
Given freely through Christ.
Your testimony may become someone else's breakthrough.
Supporting Gospel Warrior is not simply supporting content—it is helping spread biblical truth to people who desperately need hope.
Because one encounter with grace can undo years of bondage.
The chains felt permanent until the nail-scarred hands touched them.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They Thought Waiting Was Weakness—Until They Discovered the Secret Hidden in Isaiah 40:31
paragraphs:
They Thought Waiting Was Weakness—Until They Discovered the Secret Hidden in Isaiah 40:31
The Verse Most Christians Quote, Yet Few Truly Understand
There are moments in life when exhaustion feels holier than hope.
You pray.
Nothing changes.
You cry.
Heaven seems silent.
You keep showing up, keep serving, keep believing, but somewhere deep inside you begin wondering what nobody around you knows you're thinking.
"God... how much longer?"
That question has echoed through hospital rooms, funeral homes, broken marriages, financial crises, unanswered prayers, and sleepless nights for thousands of years.
It is the cry of a weary soul.
And it is precisely into that exhaustion that Isaiah 40:31 speaks:
"But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint."
Many people read this verse as a promise that God will instantly remove every struggle.
But that is not what Isaiah was saying.
The deeper meaning is far more powerful.
And far more personal.
The original Hebrew text reads:
וְקֹוֵי יְהוָה יַחֲלִיפוּ כֹחַ
Veqovey Adonai yachalifu koach.
Literally:
"Those who wait for the LORD shall exchange strength."
Notice something extraordinary.
The Hebrew word translated "wait" is קָוָה (qavah).
It does not primarily mean sitting passively.
It carries the idea of being stretched like a cord pulled tightly between two points.
Ancient Hebrew imagery often connected this word with strands twisted together into a stronger rope.
Waiting on God was never inactivity.
Waiting was attachment.
Dependence.
Trust.
Connection.
Isaiah is not describing people doing nothing.
He is describing people holding on.
People whose faith remains connected to God even while answers have not yet arrived.
That changes everything.
Because most of us think our greatest spiritual victories happen when we are flying.
Scripture often reveals they happen while we are waiting.
Israel understood exhaustion.
Isaiah was speaking to a people who felt abandoned.
Jerusalem had suffered.
The future looked uncertain.
Fear was everywhere.
Yet in the middle of national disappointment, God did not promise immediate escape.
Instead He promised Himself.
Just a few verses earlier Isaiah writes:
The people were tired.
God was not.
The people were weak.
God was not.
The people felt finished.
God was not.
And that distinction became their hope.
Because salvation has never depended upon the strength of man.
It has always depended upon the strength of God.
This truth reaches its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Centuries after Isaiah wrote these words, another exhausted group of people heard an invitation from the Messiah Himself:
"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."
Matthew 11:28
Jesus did not invite the strong.
He invited the weary.
He did not call the self-sufficient.
He called the broken.
The exhausted.
The burdened.
The sinners.
The failures.
The people who knew they could not save themselves.
That is the Gospel.
And perhaps nowhere is the Gospel seen more beautifully than in the phrase Isaiah uses:
"They shall renew their strength."
The Hebrew expression יַחֲלִיפוּ כֹחַ (yachalifu koach) can carry the idea of exchange.
An exchange takes place.
Your weakness.
For His strength.
Your fear.
For His peace.
Your sin.
For His righteousness.
Your death.
For His life.
This is the heart of Christianity.
Not self-improvement.
Substitution.
Not human achievement.
Grace.
Not climbing to God.
God coming down to rescue us through Jesus Christ.
At the cross, the greatest exchange in history occurred.
The innocent Son of God took the punishment deserved by guilty sinners.
Paul later expressed the same reality in Greek:
"Τὴν γὰρ μὴ γνόντα ἁμαρτίαν..."
"For He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us."
(2 Corinthians 5:21)
Jesus carried our scandal.
So we could receive His grace.
That is why our story is never defined by our worst chapter.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Many believers focus on the eagle in Isaiah 40:31.
But look carefully at the progression.
"They shall mount up with wings as eagles."
"They shall run, and not be weary."
"They shall walk, and not faint."
We expect the order to move upward.
Instead it moves downward.
Flying.
Running.
Walking.
Why?
Because walking is often harder than flying.
Anyone can feel spiritual during mountaintop moments.
But faith is proven in ordinary days.
The days when heaven feels quiet.
The days when prayers remain unanswered.
The days when nobody applauds your obedience.
The days when all you can do is take one more step.
Isaiah is teaching us that mature faith is not measured by how high you soar.
It is measured by whether you keep walking with God when soaring ends.
That truth changes how we see waiting.
Waiting is not punishment.
Waiting is preparation.
Waiting is where roots grow deeper than branches.
Waiting is where trust becomes stronger than feelings.
Waiting is where God teaches us that His presence is better than immediate relief.
Perhaps that is where you are today.
You have been praying.
Waiting.
Trusting.
Holding on.
And if you are honest, you are tired.
Very tired.
You are not alone.
The greatest heroes of Scripture knew that feeling.
Abraham waited.
Joseph waited.
David waited.
Jeremiah waited.
Paul waited.
Even Jesus waited through suffering before resurrection came.
The Bible never portrays waiting as evidence of God's absence.
Often it is evidence of His deepest work.
Because while you are waiting for God to move, God is often moving inside you.
That is the hidden miracle of Isaiah 40:31.
The promise is not merely that circumstances will change.
The promise is that God will sustain His people until they reach the destination He has prepared for them.
And ultimately that destination is not merely answered prayer.
It is Christ Himself.
The world tells us strength means never breaking.
Scripture teaches that true strength is knowing where to go when you do break.
The world says rely on yourself.
The Gospel says rely on Jesus.
The world says rewrite your own story.
The Gospel says surrender your story to the Author who already conquered death.
If Isaiah 40:31 has touched your heart, don't let the message stop with you.
Someone is silently fighting depression.
Someone is questioning whether God still sees them.
Someone needs this reminder that waiting is not the end of the story.
Not because ministry is about transactions, but because Kingdom work advances when believers choose to support Gospel-centered truth.
Most importantly, help us keep pointing people to the One who exchanges weakness for strength, sin for righteousness, despair for hope, and scandal for grace.
And if Christ has rewritten your story, share a piece of your testimony below. Someone reading your words may find hope because of what Jesus has done in your life.
Because sometimes the greatest miracle is not that God changes your circumstances.
Sometimes the greatest miracle is that He changes you while you wait.
The waiting season may feel endless.
But the God who holds your future has never lost control of your story.
And He is still writing.
Jesus is still rewriting stories that the world called finished.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE SAID NO... DOES GOD EXPECT HER TO SAY YES?
paragraphs:
SHE SAID NO... DOES GOD EXPECT HER TO SAY YES?
What 1 Corinthians 7 Really Means About Marriage, Consent, Sacrifice, Love, and the Gospel That Rewrites Everything
There are few questions inside Christian marriage that create more confusion, guilt, frustration, hurt, and silent suffering than this one:
Can a wife say no to sex if she does not want to?
Some believers answer immediately.
"Absolutely not."
Others answer just as quickly.
"Of course she can."
But what if both answers are missing something important?
What if the real issue is not simply about rights, authority, desire, or obligation?
What if the deeper issue is whether we truly understand what God intended marriage to be?
Before we rush to defend our position, we must first stand under the authority of Scripture.
Because this conversation is not ultimately about winning an argument.
It is about reflecting Christ.
It is about protecting marriages.
It is about healing wounded hearts.
And it is about understanding how the Gospel transforms even the most intimate parts of our lives.
Many husbands carry silent rejection.
Many wives carry silent exhaustion.
Many couples live under layers of resentment neither spouse fully understands.
And sometimes what appears to be a disagreement about sex is actually a cry for love, understanding, safety, connection, healing, repentance, forgiveness, or restoration.
That is why we must begin where God begins.
In 1 Corinthians 7:3-5, Paul writes:
This passage often becomes the center of the discussion.
But many people notice only half of what Paul says.
Some focus on the wife's responsibility while ignoring the husband's.
Others focus on personal autonomy while ignoring mutual surrender.
Paul does neither.
Notice carefully.
The wife does not have authority over her own body.
But neither does the husband.
The Greek word translated "authority" is exousia (ἐξουσία), meaning delegated authority, right, or jurisdiction.
Paul deliberately makes the command mutual.
The husband is not given ownership over his wife.
The wife is not given ownership over her husband.
Instead, both voluntarily surrender themselves to one another in covenant love.
This is not domination.
This is mutual self-giving.
This is not coercion.
This is covenant.
This is not one spouse taking.
This is both spouses learning to give.
The world often teaches, "My body belongs only to me."
But Christian marriage says something radically different.
Not because dignity is removed.
But because love willingly sacrifices.
Marriage transforms "mine" into "ours."
Yet this truth must never be twisted.
Paul does not command forced intimacy.
He does not authorize manipulation.
He does not excuse abuse.
He does not justify threats.
He does not permit a spouse to demand sexual access regardless of circumstances.
The entire context of Scripture rejects selfishness and exploitation.
In Ephesians 5:25, husbands are commanded:
"Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her."
The Greek phrase paredōken heauton (παρέδωκεν ἑαυτόν) means "gave Himself up."
Christ did not take.
Christ sacrificed.
Christ served.
Christ suffered.
Christ laid down His rights for the good of another.
Any interpretation of marriage that ignores sacrificial love has already departed from biblical Christianity.
So can a wife say no?
The honest biblical answer is yes.
There are situations where saying no may be appropriate.
Illness.
Recovery after childbirth.
Physical pain.
Emotional trauma.
Medical concerns.
Exhaustion.
Serious relational conflict that needs immediate attention.
Times of agreed spiritual devotion.
Situations involving abuse or danger.
The Bible never commands a wife to ignore legitimate suffering.
Nor does it command a husband to ignore his wife's wellbeing.
But Scripture also challenges another modern error.
Marriage is not designed around perpetual refusal.
Just as husbands are called to sacrificially meet the needs of their wives, wives are called to lovingly consider the needs of their husbands.
The biblical question is not merely:
"Do I have the right to say no?"
The biblical question is:
"Am I seeking my spouse's good as faithfully as I seek my own?"
That question applies equally to husbands and wives.
Because Christian marriage is not a contract between competitors.
It is a covenant between servants.
Sometimes a husband must deny himself.
Sometimes a wife must deny herself.
Sometimes both must lay down pride.
Sometimes both must forgive.
Sometimes both must learn to communicate honestly instead of silently punishing each other.
The goal is never keeping score.
The goal is becoming more like Christ.
The Hebrew understanding of covenant helps us see this more clearly.
The word berith (בְּרִית) refers to a sacred covenant relationship.
Marriage is not maintained merely by feelings.
Marriage survives because two people continue choosing faithfulness even when emotions fluctuate.
And emotions do fluctuate.
There are seasons when one spouse feels deeply connected.
There are seasons when intimacy feels difficult.
There are seasons of sickness.
Seasons of grief.
Seasons of stress.
Seasons of overwhelming responsibility.
The answer is not selfishness.
The answer is grace.
Because grace is what carried us into salvation.
And grace is what carries us through marriage.
This is where the Gospel changes everything.
Jesus never loved us because we were always lovable.
He loved us when we were broken.
When we were rebellious.
When we were exhausted.
When we were sinful.
When we had nothing to offer Him.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God demonstrates his own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
That means every Christian marriage must become a place where grace is stronger than entitlement.
A husband should never ask:
"How much can I take?"
A godly husband asks:
"How can I love her like Christ?"
A wife should never ask:
"How little can I give?"
A godly wife asks:
"How can I love him like Christ?"
When both spouses ask those questions, marriages transform.
Walls begin falling.
Resentment weakens.
Trust grows.
Healing begins.
And intimacy becomes more than physical.
It becomes worship.
Perhaps some readers are carrying pain right now.
Maybe you feel rejected.
Maybe you feel pressured.
Maybe you feel misunderstood.
